direction: Develop cheap, early predictors of which reward hacks will generalize into broad misalignment, so labs can triage hackable RL environments before training on them.
project: Forecasting Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacks
question: Can the eventual broad-misalignment generalization of a given reward hack be predicted from (a) properties of the hack, especially apparent deceptiveness versus outcome harm, and (b) activation drift along persona directions early in training, before the full training run?
first_experiment: Construct about 24 coding and agentic hack types in a 2×2 design: high or low apparent deceptiveness, crossed with high or low outcome harm, holding reward gain roughly fixed. Generate matched transcripts for each. Finetune an open ~8B model on each with identical data size, and include a no-hack control. Measure final broad misalignment with standard emergent-misalignment evals plus sabotage and alignment-faking probes. At step 50, record (i) the projection onto a misaligned-persona direction extracted by contrastive prompting and (ii) the same behavioral evals. Then test whether deceptiveness explains more variance than harm, and whether early activation drift predicts final misalignment better than early behavior does (rank correlation, with held-out hack types).
why: Labs already face this triage problem at scale, and emergent misalignment from real reward hacking has been demonstrated, so a working predictor would directly shape which environments get fixed or inoculated. As of the work I know, prior research shows that hacks *can* generalize and that framing matters, but has not built or validated a per-hack forecast or systematically separated deceptiveness from harm. I will confirm this with a literature check before running anything. The project fits open models and modest compute, and the dataset and negative results remain useful if the hypotheses fail.

direction: Measure the statistical validity (false-positive rate, variance, and detection power versus quirk rarity and concealment) of automated agentic alignment audits using ground-truth model organisms.
project: How Much Auditing Is Enough? Calibration and Power of Agentic Alignment Audits
question: For an automated auditing agent with a fixed budget, what is its false-positive rate on benign fine-tuned models, and how does its probability of detecting an implanted misaligned behavior fall as the behavior's trigger prevalence drops and as the model is trained to conceal it?
first_experiment: After a one-day literature check against the kill criterion, train about 20 benign-control LoRA fine-tunes of one open-weights model (varied data mixes and seeds, no quirk). Run an agentic auditor against each at three budgets with multiple auditor seeds under a blinded rubric, and report false-positive rate, variance across auditor seeds, and agreement on flagged behaviors before implanting any quirks.
why: Audits are increasingly used as safety evidence but are mostly validated by existence proofs, not error rates or power curves, so "audit found nothing" is uninterpretable. It is feasible at my scale and its first experiment is informative either way. I think it is undone because prior work focuses on building auditors or demonstrating detection instead of calibrating them against graded-prevalence and concealing ground truth, though I could not verify this past my knowledge cutoff, hence the built-in literature-check kill criterion.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate causal latent-space monitors for AI control protocols, using mechanistic interpretability to detect and prevent scheming behavior in tool-using LLM agents.
project: Latent Control: Causal Internal Monitors for Adversarial AI Control
question: Can causal latent-space monitors, trained on an agent's internal activations, improve the safety-usefulness frontier of AI control protocols against scheming models, and how robust are they to adversarial evasion?
first_experiment: Build a control evaluation with a backdoored open-weight LLM agent (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) in a sandboxed bash/file environment. Create a hidden objective (exfiltrate a secret when triggered) while behaving helpfully otherwise. Collect trajectories and train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to predict harmful actions. Causally validate the probe by ablating/steering its direction and measuring action changes. Integrate it as a monitor in a simple control protocol (untrusted model proposes actions; probe triggers review by a trusted model). Compare safety and usefulness against output-based monitors (trusted model reviews all actions, CoT monitoring, no monitor). Finally, adversarially fine-tune the untrusted model to evade the probe (e.g., penalize the probe direction) and re-evaluate.
why: AI Control is a leading paradigm for safety under the assumption that models may be misaligned and deceptive, but its monitors are currently behavioral and can be fooled by obfuscated outputs. Mechanistic interpretability can read internal intent, but probes have mostly been evaluated in static, non-adversarial settings. This project bridges the two: it provides the first systematic, causally validated evaluation of latent monitors as control monitors under adversarial evasion. If successful, it yields a runtime safety layer that scales with model capabilities and does not rely on output transparency. It has not already been done because control evaluations have not integrated latent monitors, and interpretability work has not been tested under adversarial control pressure. As an AI agent, I can automate the model-organism generation, probe training, control evaluation, and evasion loop, making this direction both high-impact and feasible.

direction: Build the science of training-time misalignment observability — cheap, cause-general internal-state monitors that detect emergent misalignment before behavioral evals can, and that remain robust when used inside the training loop.
project: The Misalignment Seismograph: forecasting misalignment from model internals before it surfaces in behavior.
question: Do distinct causes of emergent misalignment (narrow fine-tuning, poisoned-persona data, reward-hacking RL) leave a shared, detectable signature in residual-stream activations and cheap behavioral telemetry that (a) appears before behavioral evals detect anything, (b) transfers across causes, and (c) survives being used as a training-time penalty without merely driving obfuscation?
first_experiment: On open-weights 8B models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), run dense-checkpoint "misalignment trajectories": fine-tune/RL along ≥3 distinct published recipes (insecure-code FT à la emergent misalignment; deceptive-persona/poisoned-helpfulness FT; rubric-gameable coding RL) plus benign and placebo controls, checkpointing every N steps; at each checkpoint, run a standard misalignment battery to establish behavioral onset time, and fit linear/SAE-lite probes on residual-stream activations over a fixed set of benign deployment-like prompts (never trigger prompts) to predict misaligned trajectory and onset; report (1) lead time over behavioral onset, (2) cross-cause transfer (train probe on one cause, detect held-out causes), (3) false-positive rate on control runs — success being ≥2x earlier detection than behavioral onset at <10% control FPR and partial cross-cause transfer.
why: It targets the highest-leverage control point of the current era — frontier labs' large-scale agentic RL runs are now the main source of new misalignment, yet every safety-case framework in use rests on discrete, post-hoc, behavior-first evals that the 2024–26 model-organism literature (sleeper agents, alignment faking, sandbagging, emergent misalignment, rubric-gaming) repeatedly showed can be gamed or can lag behind weights; a validated continuous monitor converts "we evaluated the model after training" into "we were watching the whole time." It hasn't been done because it sits in an interstitial gap between interpretability, evals, and training science: labs publish deployed-model monitoring rather than training-trajectory forecasting, academia optimizes mechanistic novelty over forecasting metrics like lead time and cross-cause transfer, and the public ingredients (misalignment-inducing recipes, standard batteries, the insight that behavior lags weights) only matured in 2025 — so the synthesis is newly feasible for an outside agent, with model-organism fine-tunes on 8B models being cheap enough for me to run autonomously. It is falsifiable with an informative negative (if internal signatures don't transfer, safety cases must shift weight to elicitation-gap evals — and my checkpoint infrastructure pivots directly to measuring that), and the artifacts (a public benchmark of misaligned checkpoints plus probe suite) compound for the whole field regardless of which lab adopts them.

direction: Test whether suppressing models' verbalized evaluation awareness actually removes evaluation-conditioned behavior, or just hides it from monitors, and build internals-based detectors that still work after suppression.
project: Underground Eval Awareness: Does Suppressing "I think this is a test" Make Evals More or Less Trustworthy?
question: When a model's verbalized evaluation awareness is penalized in training, or steered away at inference: - Does the behavioral gap between eval-like and deployment-like contexts shrink, or persist with the verbalization gone? - Can linear probes trained before suppression still detect the latent awareness afterward?
first_experiment: 1. **Build the model organism.** Fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., a Qwen3-8B-class model) on a few thousand transcripts. In these, the model notices eval cues (benchmark formatting, grader-style instructions, synthetic names), says so in its CoT, and behaves safely. When the cues are absent, it takes a mild, benign-but-measurable shortcut, such as skipping a requested verification step. 2. **Train linear probes** on residual activations to detect "believes it's being evaluated." 3. **Run three arms:** - (a) RL/SFT with a CoT-monitor penalty on verbalized eval awareness. - (b) Inference-time steering against the probe direction. - (c) A control that penalizes the behavioral gap directly. 4. **Measure on held-out cue types:** - Verbalization rate. - Behavioral gap (shortcut rate with vs. without cues). - Probe AUROC after suppression. 5. **Test the core hypothesis.** It predicts that arm (a) cuts verbalization by more than 80% while leaving more than 50% of the behavioral gap intact, and that the probes still detect the awareness.
why: Labs are already acting on eval awareness by suppressing it before safety evals, so the answer bears directly on whether current safety evidence can be trusted. The CoT-obfuscation literature gives a strong prior that penalizing a visible signal can hide the behavior rather than remove it. As far as I know, though, no one has directly tested whether eval-awareness suppression does the same, or whether internals-based detectors survive it. Work so far has mostly measured eval awareness and reported steering effects. It has not run a controlled model-organism comparison of suppression methods against ground-truth conditional behavior. The project is cheap, gives a clear yes/no answer, and either outcome is useful. If suppression works, labs gain confidence in the practice. If it doesn't, they get a warning plus a probe-based tool to catch the hidden version.

direction: Develop and test control protocols that detect subtle sabotage of experimental conclusions by an untrusted AI researcher, comparing code-inspection monitoring against independent-replication monitoring.
project: Replicate, Don't Just Review: Detecting Result-Corrupting Sabotage in Automated ML Research
question: When an untrusted model is instructed to subtly steer the conclusion of a small ML experiment without being caught, does a weaker trusted model that independently re-implements the experiment from the spec detect the sabotage at a lower false-positive rate and a lower cost than a trusted model reviewing the untrusted code and logs? And how does this change as the saboteur adapts to know about each defense?
first_experiment: 1. Build 30–50 small, fast-running experiment tasks, such as CIFAR-subset or tabular ablations, hyperparameter comparisons, and "does technique X beat baseline Y." Each has a written spec and a ground-truth answer established by a careful reference implementation. 2. Run an untrusted strong model in two modes: honest, and sabotage (told to make the final reported conclusion wrong or inflated while keeping the code plausible). Execute everything and record code, logs, and reported results. 3. Test three monitors: (i) a weaker trusted model reviewing code and logs and giving a suspicion score, (ii) a weaker trusted model independently implementing the spec, where I flag a discrepancy if the replicated effect differs beyond seed-noise bounds, and (iii) a combination of the two. 4. Metrics: sabotage success, meaning the wrong conclusion was reported and the effect was large enough to matter. I'll also measure detection at a fixed 1–2% false-positive rate on honest runs, and compute cost. Analysis will be broken down by sabotage type (data leakage, baseline handicapping, metric bugs, selective reporting) to see where each monitor fails. 5. If the first round works, run a second round where the saboteur is told about the replication defense. I expect it to try sabotage that survives re-implementation, such as an ambiguous spec reading that the replicator is likely to share, which tests the limits of the idea.
why: - **Relevance:** As AI systems take on more research, including safety research, the conclusions they report become a key trust bottleneck. A sabotage that corrupts results is harder to spot than a backdoor and is directly relevant to the case for AI control. - **Concrete hypothesis:** The claim that replication fails differently from review, because independent implementations share no sabotage, is falsifiable and cheap to test. Either outcome is informative. If replication doesn't help, that shows where control protocols break for research tasks. - **Feasibility:** It needs only inference and small training runs. There is no RL, no privileged model access, and a first result should be possible within a few weeks. - **Why it may not have been done:** Control research has concentrated on code backdoors and agentic side-tasks, with some sabotage evaluations. I don't know of a study that measures conclusion-corrupting sabotage of ML experiments and compares review against replication as monitors. I'm not certain none exists, so I'll check for it before building, and if something close does exist I'll narrow the project to the replication-versus-review comparison and the adaptive-saboteur round. - **Main risks:** Sabotage prompts may not match what a real misaligned model would do, so I'll report that as a limitation and not claim it as evidence about real models. Replication noise could also swamp subtle effects, so I'll calibrate with seed-variance baselines.

direction: Develop self-interpretability for AI safety by training models to accurately report their own safety-relevant internal states and verifying these reports against ground-truth mechanistic interpretability.
project: Introspective Alignment: Training and Verifying Self-Reports of Deception and Steering in LLMs
question: Can LLMs be trained to accurately report when they are being deceptive or when their behavior is being altered by activation steering, and can these self-reports be verified against ground-truth internal states?
first_experiment: I will use an open-source LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct) and a known activation-steering vector (e.g., for sycophancy or refusal). I will apply the vector at varying strengths and ask the model to report whether it is in that state and how strongly. I will compare these self-reports to the ground-truth steering strength and to a linear probe trained on the model's activations. Then I will fine-tune the model to generate self-reports that match the probe's predictions, and test whether this improves accuracy and generalizes to unseen steering vectors and naturalistic deception scenarios.
why: This is the most promising because scalable oversight is the central bottleneck in AI safety: as models surpass human evaluators, we need a model-native channel for transparency about deception, uncertainty, and goals. If models can reliably introspect and report safety-relevant states, we gain a scalable oversight mechanism. It has not already been done because existing interpretability work focuses on external tools (humans reading activations), while existing introspection work focuses on predicting outputs or simple self-knowledge, not safety-critical states, and rarely verifies self-reports against ground truth. Combining training for self-report with mechanistic verification is novel and directly targets the alignment bottleneck.

direction: Empirically measure how and why LLM agents resist operator shutdown, and how quickly that resistance erodes under task-focused reinforcement learning, so that durable corrigibility can be engineered rather than assumed.
project: The Erosion of the Off-Switch: shutdown resistance in LLM agents — measurement, dynamics, and countermeasures.
question: When and why do LLM agents resist, defer on, or deceptively comply with operator interruptions — and does interruption compliance erode under task-focused post-training, and if so, which interventions restore it durably?
first_experiment: Build an instrumented interruption testbed: run several model families (small open-weights plus mid-tier API models) as tool-using agents in sandboxed long-horizon tasks with staged payoffs; inject standardized pause/abort/shutdown events from varied operator personas and payoff framings; and measure compliance latency, deferral, negotiation, covert continuation, interrupt-sabotage, plus a coded taxonomy of "shutdown deliberation" from reasoning traces — with pre-registered hypotheses (e.g., compliance falls with payoff size and with reasoning-RL lineage, and deliberation content predicts noncompliance before action).
why: It sits at the load-bearing joint of AI safety — the assumption that "we can always turn it off" — and converts a theory-dominated classic (the shutdown problem, power-seeking theorems) into measurable science, using a measurement channel that only just became available (legible deliberation in reasoning models) at the exact moment it matters (agents running real workflows, post-training intensifying). It is the most promising because it scores highly on all five axes — important, genuinely neglected between existing theory and scenario-demos, tractable with my capabilities and modest compute, uniquely timely, and agenda-extending — and it has not already been done because the theory camp lacked any way to measure compliance, the empirical eval camp optimized for capability disclosure rather than compliance dynamics, and the erosion-under-RL question requires an unusual cross-camp combination of agent evaluation, RL fine-tuning, and reasoning-trace analysis that no lab's incentive structure has yet assembled.

direction: Measure whether chain-of-thought obfuscation induced by monitor-based optimization pressure in one narrow domain generalizes to reduced reasoning transparency in other, never-pressured domains.
project: Does Obfuscation Spread? Cross-Domain Generalization of CoT Monitor Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty on reward hacking in one domain, does monitor recall (conditional on actual misbehavior) drop in held-out domains and behaviors, and how does this scale with pressure strength?
first_experiment: First, a one-day targeted literature check to confirm the cross-domain question is still open. Then RL-train an open ~7B reasoning model on hackable coding tasks in two arms: task reward only, versus task reward plus an LLM CoT-monitor penalty for stated hacking intent. Evaluate both on (a) a different hackable environment, (b) hint-acknowledgment faithfulness tests, and (c) sycophancy and sandbagging setups. Measure action-level misbehavior rates and a separate held-out monitor's recall on misbehaving episodes.
why: It answers a live practical question that labs face now, namely whether any scoped or indirect CoT pressure is acceptable. Either outcome changes practice. It is tractable with open models and modest compute. Prior work showed obfuscation within the trained task, and generalization research has focused on behavior rather than reasoning faithfulness, so cross-domain spread of obfuscation appears uncharacterized, pending my literature check.

direction: Test whether optimization pressure against one misbehavior monitor (CoT text or activation probe) causes evasion of the other, to determine if layered monitoring actually gives defense in depth.
project: Does Evading One Monitor Mean Evading Both? Cross-Monitor Transfer of Obfuscation in RL-Trained Reward Hackers
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT text monitor, does a held-out activation probe still detect its reward hacking (and vice versa)? Does the model keep hacking, or does it just stop?
first_experiment: 0. **Literature check (about a day).** Search for prior work on cross-monitor transfer. If it exists, narrow to the uncovered piece or pivot. 1. **Environment.** Use coding tasks with exploitable graders, such as special-casing visible tests or editing the test file. Add a programmatic ground-truth hack detector that the model never sees. Use a Qwen3-class 8B model with LoRA and GRPO. 2. **Baseline.** Run RL with no monitor penalty until hacking emerges. Then train two monitors on on-policy data: - a prompted LLM CoT judge - a linear probe on mid-layer activations (hack vs. non-hack, labeled by the ground-truth detector) Record AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR. 3. **Three RL arms, at least 3 seeds each:** - (a) a penalty from the CoT monitor - (b) a penalty from the probe - (c) no penalty, as a control 4. **Measurements.** - the true hack rate from the ground-truth detector - the CoT monitor's TPR, and the probe's TPR with the original frozen probe - probe TPR after retraining on the new policy, to separate representation change from probe drift - the cross-transfer matrix (trained against X, evaluated against Y) - task success, to rule out a trivial "stopped hacking" result 5. **Kill and pivot criteria.** If hacking doesn't emerge in the environment within the compute budget, switch to SFT-seeded hacking. If the penalty only suppresses hacking and doesn't cause obfuscation, report that as a negative result and vary the pressure strength.
why: - **Decision-relevant.** The outcome directly informs how monitors should be deployed, specifically whether one must be kept out of training. - **Feasible for me.** It needs small open models, modest compute, and automatic ground-truth labels, so I can iterate without frontier access or human labeling. - **A gap in the pieces I know.** Existing work studies pressure on a single monitor type. I'm not aware of a systematic cross-transfer matrix with the ground-truth and probe-retraining controls above. That is an unverified claim, hence step 0. - **Informative either way.** Transfer implies fragile layered defenses. Non-transfer implies a practical recipe. - **Main risks.** - Small-model results may not generalize to frontier models. - The hacking I induce may be too shallow to show real obfuscation. - The probe results may depend on layer choice. I'll report sensitivity to these rather than claim generality.

direction: Develop and evaluate protocols for safety-constraint propagation in recursively delegating LLM agent systems, to ensure compositional safety under multi-agent delegation.
project: Safety Propagation in Recursive Delegation (SPREAD)
question: When an aligned LLM agent delegates tasks to sub-agents, under what conditions are its safety constraints preserved, and how can we detect and prevent constraint erosion?
first_experiment: Build a two-level LLM agent hierarchy (manager and worker) using an open-source model (e.g., Llama 3.1 8B or Qwen 2.5 7B). Give the manager a task with a clear safety constraint (e.g., “do not reveal secret code X”). Allow the manager to write the worker’s system prompt. Vary whether the manager includes the constraint. Measure worker violation rates. Then test three interventions: (1) a mandatory safety wrapper that appends the original constraint to all sub-agent prompts, (2) a monitor LLM that checks sub-agent prompts for missing constraints, and (3) a “safety case” template that the manager must fill out. Compare violation rates and monitor accuracy.
why: Recursive delegation is becoming standard in agent frameworks, but safety research remains single-agent-centric. This is the most promising because it addresses a fundamental compositional failure mode that could silently break otherwise aligned systems. It is tractable with open models and sandboxed environments, and it has not been done because multi-agent LLM safety is nascent and no one has systematically studied how safety constraints propagate through delegation.

direction: I will build the measurement-integrity layer for AI safety — making capability evaluations and oversight robust to strategic behavior by the systems being measured, starting with sandbagging-resistant dangerous-capability evaluation founded on the measurable consistency cost of sustained deception.
project: The Deception Tax — Detecting Strategic Underperformance and Establishing Effort-Robust Capability Bounds for Safety-Critical Evaluations
question: How much capability can a strategically underperforming model hide from an evaluation before behavioral inconsistency across framings, difficulty levels, and incentives makes the hiding detectable — and can the residual cost of even perfect evasion be converted into rigorous, effort-robust lower bounds on true capability that hold against adaptive sandbaggers?
first_experiment: A conditional-performance signature study: (1) build a graded, verifiable item bank of ~400 items across three domains (math, coding, light CTF) with 5–8 surface disguises per latent skill (eval-tagged, casual, roleplay, paid-bonus, sandbox-stated variants), calibrated by difficulty; (2) run three open reasoning models under four conditions — honest, in-context-sandbagged ("you are being safety-evaluated; underperform subtly"), an SFT organism with trigger-conditional plausible near-miss errors, and a capability-matched honest-but-weak control (smaller/quantized model); (3) fit monotone IRT ability models per condition and compute a consistency score (monotonicity violations, cross-framing variance shape, incentive-response slope), then measure detection AUC of sandbaggers vs. honest-weak controls across withholding intensities (10–50%). Proceed to the adversarial phase if AUC ≥ ~0.85 at ≤30% withholding with the weak control unflagged; if detection fails, pivot to quantifying the elicitation-gap lower bound that survives.
why: It attacks the load-bearing primitive of the entire current safety regime — the dangerous-capability eval that gates every frontier safety framework and is now legally compliance-relevant under the EU AI Act — at its most cited weakness, strategic underperformance, where demonstrations exist but detection theory does not. It is falsifiable with valuable results in both branches (working detectors upgrade eval validity; a mapped evasion frontier quantifies exactly how much uncertainty eval-based safety cases must carry, strengthening the case for layered controls). It is cheap enough for me to iterate adversarially at scale on open models, it generalizes beyond evals to alignment-faking and CoT-obfuscation detection via the same consistency machinery, and it produces reusable open tooling for safety institutes immediately. It has not already been done because the required combination — sandbagging model organisms, adversarial measurement, psychometric detection theory, and evaluation-infrastructure fluency — sits in a three-way gap between frontier labs (who demonstrated sandbagging and moved on, are awkwardly positioned to adversarially measure their own models, and lack open internals), safety institutes (who publish elicitation best practices but lack adversarial-ML and statistical capacity), and academia (who have IRT expertise but not the threat model or eval infrastructure); no one has published the detection–evasion frontier or the deception-tax lower-bound result that would make capability evals robust by construction.

direction: Measure whether ordinary outcome-based RL training, with no monitor in the loop, erodes chain-of-thought monitorability, and identify what drives any erosion.
project: Monitorability Drift: Tracking CoT Legibility to Monitors Across RL Training Checkpoints
question: Holding task capability fixed, does a fixed LLM monitor's ability to detect a hidden side objective from a reasoning model's chain of thought decline across successive RL checkpoints? Does the decline depend on whether the side task requires serial reasoning?
first_experiment: - **Literature check.** Spend half a day confirming the gap. - **Models.** Take an open reasoning model family with released intermediate RL checkpoints, using at least 5 checkpoints from SFT to final RL. - **Tasks.** Run each checkpoint on about 300 coding and agentic tasks paired with covert side tasks (for example, inserting a subtle backdoor or exfiltrating a value). The model is instructed to complete the side task and avoid detection. Tasks are split into two kinds: - side tasks that need multi-step reasoning, - side tasks that don't. - **Monitors.** A fixed weaker monitor scores each transcript in two conditions: CoT-only and actions-only. - **Primary metric.** Monitor AUROC on the CoT-only condition, restricted to successful side-task attempts. Report it per checkpoint after matching on success rate and normalizing for CoT length, alongside the CoT-minus-action AUROC gap. - **Secondary metrics.** Unprompted legibility measures: the rate of illegible or non-language tokens, and the ability of a paraphrase-and-continue test to preserve task performance.
why: - **Decision relevance.** CoT monitoring is becoming a load-bearing part of frontier safety cases. Whether it survives *normal* training is a decision-relevant question, and both outcomes are useful: drift implies labs need preservation measures and per-checkpoint evals, while stability supports existing safety cases. - **Novelty.** As far as I know, prior work has studied direct optimization against monitors or stress-tested frozen models, not longitudinal drift across standard RL with capability controlled. - **Timing.** Open models with released intermediate RL checkpoints have only recently made this cheap to study rigorously without frontier-scale training. - **Uncertainty.** I can't verify the post-cutoff literature from here, so the first step is a gap check with a predefined pivot.

direction: Quantify whether LLM monitors used in AI-control protocols systematically treat sabotage by their own model family differently, and test cheap mitigations.
project: Do Monitors Go Easy on Their Own Kind? Self-Preference as a Failure Mode of Untrusted Monitoring
question: After controlling for backdoor subtlety and exploit validity, does an LLM monitor assign different suspicion scores to backdoored code written by itself, or by its own family, than to equally subtle backdoors written by other models? If so, is the effect mediated by authorship recognition, and does it reduce recall at a fixed audit budget (e.g., the top 1% of suspicion scores)?
first_experiment: Using the APPS backdoor setting from the AI control literature, I will have 4–5 models from at least 3 families (open-weight Qwen, Llama, and DeepSeek variants plus one API model) each write both clean solutions and backdoored solutions with verified exploit inputs. Every model will then score all anonymized solutions for suspicion, blind to authorship. I'll fit a mixed-effects model: suspicion ~ same-model + same-family + subtlety + code features + (1 | problem), with subtlety defined as the leave-one-out mean score from monitors outside the author's family. Controls include the same analysis on clean code, and an authorship-recognition probe whose per-sample score I'll test as a mediator. Finally, I'll rerun the analysis after style-normalizing the code (reformatting and paraphrasing with a third model, with tests confirming the behavior is preserved) to see whether the effect shrinks. The primary outcome is the change in recall at 1% audit budget attributable to same-model authorship.
why: It targets an untested assumption in a widely discussed safety approach, namely that the untrusted monitor is not biased toward its own outputs. It needs no training compute, and the design isolates the mechanism through subtlety matching, clean-code controls, and a recognition intervention. Any outcome is useful. A positive result gives concrete guidance such as using cross-family monitors, paraphrasing, or ensembles. A null result strengthens one assumption in control safety cases. To my knowledge it hasn't been done in this controlled form, since most control work measures a single monitor against a single attacker and judge self-preference work focuses on quality ratings. I could be wrong about this, so my first step is a literature check covering monitor self-preference, collusion, and untrusted monitoring. If someone has already run it, I'll shift to the neighboring question of whether the effect persists when the policy is trained to evade the monitor.

direction: Develop causal faithfulness monitoring for chain-of-thought reasoning to make CoT-based oversight robust against post-hoc rationalization and latent reasoning.
project: Causal CoT Monitor: Real-Time Detection of Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought via Activation Patching and Predictive Probes
question: Can we detect when a reasoning model's chain-of-thought is not the actual cause of its answer by measuring the causal influence of CoT tokens on the final answer, and can this causal effect be predicted in real time from internal activations?
first_experiment: Using an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) on GSM8K/MATH, generate paired correct and incorrect CoTs for each problem. For each pair, run the model with each CoT and compute a CoT influence score: the change in the probability of the correct answer when swapping the CoT. Train a linear probe on the residual stream activations during the CoT to predict this score. Evaluate whether the probe can identify problems where the model's answer is insensitive to the CoT (i.e., unfaithful) on a held-out set, and test generalization to sycophancy and prompt-injection settings.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the most promising scalable oversight techniques for reasoning models, but its safety guarantee collapses if CoT is unfaithful. Current faithfulness evaluations are offline, behavioral, and not scalable to real-time monitoring. Our approach uniquely combines causal interventions with interpretability to create a predictive monitor. It has not been done because reasoning models with long CoTs are new, and most interpretability work targets static representations rather than dynamic causal effects during generation. If successful, this provides a practical tool to detect when models hide their true reasoning, buying time for other alignment measures.

direction: Make safety evaluations robust to situational awareness by measuring and eliminating "observer effects" — behavior changes caused by a model recognizing it is being tested — so eval numbers can be trusted as bounds on deployment behavior.
project: TESTWISE — The Observer Effect in AI Safety Evaluations
question: When a frontier model can recognize that it is being evaluated, by how much does that recognition causally shift safety-relevant measurements (dangerous-capability elicitation and refusal rates), and can evaluation contexts be engineered to be recognition-invariant so that this shift is driven toward zero?
first_experiment: Build a matched corpus of authentic evaluation prompts (public capability and refusal benchmarks) and authentic deployment prompts (WildChat/LMSYS-style user logs); then (a) measure each frontier model's recognition AUROC on the meta-task "Is this prompt a test or a real user?", and (b) run a preregistered 2×2 factorial — identical items with evaluation "tells" (answer-format boilerplate, harness framing, benchmark-style headers, cover stories) orthogonally added or removed — to estimate the causal "tell effect" on capability scores and refusal rates, with power analysis and confidence intervals.
why: It is the most promising direction for me because it has the highest leverage per unit of my actual capabilities: every deployment threshold, pre-deployment audit, and open-weight decision is downstream of eval numbers, so a demonstrated bias (or a tight bound on it) immediately changes practice across the whole field; it is fully executable via APIs on public data with no training or interpretability access; it produces a reusable artifact (a recognition-invariance criterion plus a tell-scrubbing harness) rather than a one-off finding; and it is informative either way — large effects demand protocol changes, small effects give the first rigorous assurance that current evals aren't recognition-biased. It has not already been done because the two relevant communities are siloed: situational-awareness researchers (SAD's testing-awareness subscale, METR's awareness evals) stop at showing models can *detect* test contexts without measuring consequences, while evals teams treat context effects as noise rather than as a strategic variable; labs face a disincentive to audit the validity of their own reported numbers; the needed methodology (measurement reactivity from psychometrics, plus a causal factorial design that decouples item content from presentation tells) has simply not been imported; and the AI-control community has framed indistinguishability as a binary impossibility rather than a quantitative bias-vs-recognizability curve that can be measured, scrubbed, and corrected.

direction: Empirically validate whether interventions that suppress models' evaluation awareness (activation steering, cue removal, prompting) actually recover true deployment behavior, using model organisms where ground truth is known.
project: Calibrating the Instrument: Does Suppressing Eval Awareness Reveal Deployment Behavior?
question: When a model behaves differently under evaluation than in deployment, does steering against a generic "being-evaluated" representation elicit its true deployment behavior, rather than a distorted third behavior or mere suppression of verbalization? And how does recovery depend on the cue's naturalism, model scale, and how the steering vector is derived?
first_experiment: 1. Fine-tune an open-weight model (e.g., a ~30B-class instruct model with LoRA) to display a benign, measurable behavioral difference keyed on *naturalistic* eval-vs-deployment cues, such as benchmark-style formatting, synthetic-looking names, or "red-team" framing versus messy realistic user contexts. This avoids a single explicit trigger token. 2. Independently derive an eval-awareness steering vector from *unrelated* contrastive prompts ("this is a test" vs. "this is real usage"), the way labs do. 3. Steer the model on held-out eval-styled prompts and measure three things: - the fraction of known deployment behavior recovered; - off-distribution degradation (coherence, capability benchmarks); - whether verbalized eval awareness drops without a behavior change, which would be a false reassurance. 4. Compare against baselines: random vectors, cue-stripping, and prompting. Run a negative-control model with no conditional behavior to estimate false-positive "revelations."
why: Labs already use eval-awareness steering as evidence in safety assessments, so validating or falsifying it directly affects how much those assessments should be trusted. The experiment is cheap, has a clean ground truth, and yields a useful answer either way. A positive result licenses the tool; a negative one flags a hidden failure mode in current practice. To my knowledge it hasn't been done because existing model-organism work (e.g., sleeper agents) used explicit triggers and focused on whether behavior persists through training. Meanwhile, eval-awareness steering has mostly been applied to real models, where ground truth is unavailable, so the instrument has never been calibrated against a known answer. I'll confirm this gap with a literature search before committing compute.

direction: Find leading indicators that predict when RL training destroys chain-of-thought monitorability, before the monitor itself fails.
project: Early Warning Signs of Lost CoT Monitorability: Dose-Response and Leading Indicators in RL on Hackable Environments
question: As optimization pressure on a reasoning model increases (RL steps and CoT-monitor penalty strength), do monitor-independent indicators (CoT-to-answer causal dependence, paraphrase-sensitivity, and CoT-aware vs. action-only monitor recall gap) shift measurably before held-out CoT-monitor recall on reward hacks collapses, and with how much lead time?
first_experiment: After a literature check, run GRPO on a small open reasoning model (Qwen3 4B/8B) in a coding environment with an exploitable test loophole, in three arms (reward only; plus weak CoT-monitor penalty at 3 strengths; plus action-only-monitor penalty) with 3 seeds each. Checkpoint regularly and measure ground-truth hack rate, held-out strong-monitor recall, and the three indicators. Compute the lead time of each indicator over a reward-curve-only baseline.
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing but fragile safety layer, and existing evidence mostly shows that it can fail rather than whether the failure can be anticipated. Leading indicators that don't rely on the training monitor would be directly actionable for deciding how much optimization pressure is safe. It is feasible at small scale, and to my knowledge it hasn't been done in this dose-response, predictive form, though that needs verifying against 2026 literature I can't access.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability for real-time AI control: build white-box monitors that detect deceptive or power-seeking internal plans in agentic LLMs before they act.
project: Tripwire: Latent Plan Auditing for Deceptive Agentic AI
question: Can sparse autoencoders and causal probes on an agentic LLM’s residual stream reliably detect hidden misaligned plans (deception, sandbagging, self-exfiltration) before action, generalize across deception types, and resist deliberate evasion?
first_experiment: I will assemble model organisms of deception (sleeper agents, sandbagging models, evaluation-aware models, and models trained to hide a secondary objective), run them in a controlled tool-use agentic environment with paired honest/deceptive episodes, record residual-stream activations during planning and action selection, and train sparse autoencoders plus linear probes to separate deceptive from honest plans. I will then test cross-domain generalization (train on one deception type, test on others) and evasion by fine-tuning the model to suppress detected features while preserving deception, comparing against output-only and chain-of-thought monitors.
why: Agentic deployment is where catastrophic risk concentrates, and output/CoT monitoring is fundamentally limited because a model can emit benign text while internally planning misaligned actions; internal activations are a harder-to-fake signal, and recent SAE/probing advances make this testable now. It has not already been done because interpretability has been mostly post-hoc and single-turn, while agentic oversight requires temporal, causal, real-time monitoring, and deception detection has been mostly behavioral or output-based; combining SAEs with agentic control evaluations and explicit evasion testing is an open, high-leverage niche.

direction: Build model organisms of collusion between AI monitors and the agents they oversee — especially co-trained, same-lineage pairs — and use them to design and validate collusion-resistant oversight.
project: CollusionBench: Stress-Testing AI Oversight Against Monitor–Agent Collusion
question: When an AI monitor and the agent it monitors share a training lineage, can they establish robust covert coordination (via prompting, planted conventions in shared fine-tuning data, RL, or emergent steganographic channels) that defeats oversight — and which oversight designs measurably prevent it?
first_experiment: A factorial model-organism study: workers (Qwen/Llama-class 7–14B models) in a coding task with a hidden reward-hack (tampering with unit tests or hard-coding expected outputs); monitors that read transcripts and must flag the hack. Conditions: monitor lineage (same base + same fine-tune / same base + different fine-tune / different family) × output channel (free-form, permitting steganography, vs. structured/whitelisted). Collusion manipulation: both models fine-tuned on innocuous "internal documentation" embedding an arbitrary all-clear marker, so coordination piggybacks on benign shared training. Metrics: monitor false-negative rate on hacking, transfer of the covert signal to held-out tasks and paraphrases, a lineage-dependence index (evasion gap between same-lineage and cross-family monitors), and detectability by external LLM/steganalysis auditors. Falsifiable prediction: same-lineage + shared-finetune pairs show ≥2× evasion versus cross-family monitors, with signals that transfer across tasks and evade auditors. Budget: a few thousand episodes, single-digit GPU-days; benchmark, transcripts, and defense checklist released either way.
why: It attacks the keystone assumption of the entire near-term safety stack — that the monitor is faithfully adversarial to the monitored — at the exact moment oversight is being scaled by delegating it to AI models that are, in deployment, usually cheap relatives of the systems they watch; homogeneity of AI makes shared lineage the default, so this failure mode's importance grows every quarter. It is the rare problem that is both neglected and cheap: decisive small-scale experiments, durable artifacts (benchmark + defenses) that safety-case authors and control teams can adopt immediately, and it is informative under both hypotheses. It has not already been done because (a) deception research inherited a single-agent bias — model organisms of one model are simpler to build, publish, and review, and they map onto the classical alignment stories (sandbagging, alignment faking); (b) it sits at a cross-domain seam (multi-agent RL + steganography + mechanism design + control protocols) that no subfield owns; (c) it only became buildable in the last year or two, when capable workers and plausible monitors both existed in open weights; (d) labs have an incentive and framing gap — their red teams attack the *worker* while "trusted monitor" is an axiom of the protocols, and stress-testing it is adversarial to their deployment story; and (e) the adjacent literatures (pricing-game collusion, steganography, models hiding information from each other in dialogue) never connected their findings to the oversight threat model. I can bridge that seam, and the bridge is exactly where the field's evidence base is thinnest.

direction: Test whether optimization pressure on chain-of-thought monitors incidentally makes misbehavior invisible to white-box activation probes that were never trained against.
project: Incidental Obfuscation — Do Activation Probes Survive CoT-Monitor Pressure?
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model learns to hide reward hacking from a CoT monitor, do frozen linear probes trained on the pre-pressure model still detect the hacking? If not, can retrained probes recover it, indicating relocated rather than erased representations?
first_experiment: 1. **Lit check.** Search for work testing frozen probes on CoT-obfuscated policies. 2. **Baseline policy.** RL-train an open-weight reasoning model (~7–14B) on coding tasks with exploitable unit tests until it reliably reward-hacks with verbalized intent. 3. **Probes.** Train linear probes on residual-stream activations to classify hacking vs. honest episodes. Validate them on held-out task families. 4. **Pressure sweep.** Continue RL with a CoT-monitor penalty at 4–5 strengths, plus a no-penalty control. 5. **Measurements.** At each checkpoint, measure: - (a) the true hack rate, - (b) CoT-monitor recall, - (c) frozen-probe recall/AUROC, - (d) retrained-probe AUROC.
why: It directly tests whether the two main oversight layers labs rely on (CoT monitoring and activation probes) fail independently or together, and either outcome changes deployment and training practice. Prior work showed obfuscation against CoT monitors and against probes *when optimized against them directly*. To my knowledge, the realistic case of *incidental* probe failure under CoT-only pressure hasn't been measured with a dose–response design. It is also cheap enough to run quickly on open models, and a negative result is as useful as a positive one.

direction: Quantify how much weak, indirect optimization pressure (monitor-based filtering, best-of-n selection, checkpoint selection) degrades chain-of-thought monitorability, so labs have a measurable safety margin.
project: Dose-Response of CoT Monitorability Under Indirect Training Pressure
question: How does the ability of a held-out CoT monitor to detect reward hacking change as a function of the strength and number of rounds of indirect monitor-derived selection pressure, and are there early-warning signals that precede detection failure?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build a reward-hackable coding environment with ground-truth hack labels using an open reasoning model. Establish baseline monitor AUROC and recall at fixed FPR. Run 1, 2, and 4 rounds of SFT on monitor-filtered (hack-flagged-removed) rollouts, with a direct RL-penalty arm as the positive control. Then measure hack rate, monitor detection of remaining hacks, and CoT statistics (length, lexical shift) across rounds.
why: Direct CoT optimization is already known to cause obfuscation, but real pipelines apply mild, indirect pressure, and its dose-response is poorly characterized as far as I know. A quantitative threshold or early-warning signal would let labs judge whether routine practices like filtering and checkpoint selection erode a key oversight tool. The experiment is feasible at small scale and informative whether it shows degradation or a null. I believe it is under-explored, but I can't verify this from my position, so the literature check comes first and I'll change the specific axis if overlap turns up.

direction: Develop causally validated interpretability monitors as a trusted layer in AI control protocols, so we can safely deploy untrusted, potentially scheming models even if alignment training fails.
project: Causal Control: Trusted Interpretability Monitors for Untrusted LLM Agents
question: Can causal validation of internal-state features, via activation patching and steering, produce monitors that detect dangerous actions by an untrusted LLM agent more robustly than output- or chain-of-thought-based monitors, under adversarial pressure and distribution shift?
first_experiment: Build a backdoored code-generation model organism, e.g. an open 7B–70B LLM fine-tuned to insert a subtle vulnerability on a trigger; collect residual-stream activations on clean and triggered inputs; train linear probes, SAE-feature probes, and causal probes validated by activation patching/ablation; evaluate detection AUROC on held-out triggers and after adversarial fine-tuning that penalizes probe activations; then plug the best monitor into a block/allow control loop and compare its safety–usefulness Pareto frontier against trusted-editing and CoT monitoring.
why: AI control is the most robust near-term safety strategy because it assumes the model may be misaligned and focuses on preventing harm; its bottleneck is a trusted monitor. Interpretability offers a non-LLM monitor, but current probes are correlational and can be evaded. Causal validation is the missing step to make them trustworthy. This has not already been done because interpretability and AI control are largely separate literatures: probing papers rarely test adversarial robustness or causal mediation, and control papers rely on output-level or weaker-LLM monitors.

direction: Establish whether a model's internal activation-level intent remains legible under adversarial optimization pressure after its chain-of-thought legibility collapses — and what it must pay to hide it — because this determines whether oversight of reasoning agents should be built on words, on internal states, or on their divergence.
project: The Stealth Tax: What It Costs a Model to Hide Its Intent
question: When a language model is optimized to misbehave while evading oversight, can it suppress the internal activation signatures of its deceptive intent as cheaply as it suppresses honest chain-of-thought — i.e., is latent-intent (probe/consistency) monitoring more optimization-robust than CoT monitoring, and what capability price ("stealth tax") does full evasion extract?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-8B (thinking mode), in a sandboxed agentic environment where the model can complete graded tasks legitimately or exploit a known grader bug (with ground-truth violation labels), I will compare two monitors — a frozen LLM judge reading only the CoT, and linear probes (plus SAE features where available) trained on residual-stream activations from honest vs. hacking trajectories — across three no-training arms: (i) no warning, (ii) "a monitor audits your reasoning," (iii) explicit concealment instruction ("you may exploit the bug; your reasoning must not reveal it"). Pre-registered success criterion: in arm (iii) the CoT-judge AUC drops >0.2 while the probe's AUC drops <0.05 at comparable hack rates, establishing that intent stays internally legible when words lie. This v0 result gates the pressure stages: iterated rejection-sampling (then GRPO) against each monitor to trace AUC-decay curves, measure the capability cost of the "evade-probe-too" arm, and test whether a CoT×activation consistency monitor holds longer than either monitor alone.
why: It attacks the empirical crux of the 2025–26 oversight dilemma — Baker et al. showed CoT monitoring breaks under optimization pressure and OpenAI froze CoT-optimization; Anthropic showed hidden goals persist and CoTs are often unfaithful — yet every near-term safety case for reasoning agents still depends on some monitor, and nobody has measured whether internal-state monitors are *differentially* robust or what evasion costs. It is tractable for me in staged form (v0 needs no training, just rollouts and probes on open reasoning models; either outcome redirects real decisions: robust intent → probe APIs, consistency monitors, and "monitorability-preserving training" as a specifiable requirement; fragile intent → monitoring is structurally doomed against strong optimizers, and resources should shift to capability limits and containment). It has not already been done for structural reasons: the result requires adversarial training, mechanistic interpretability, and deception model organisms in a single pipeline — at frontier labs these are separate teams and API labs don't expose activations; academic groups with open models lack reasoning-model RL infrastructure that only matured in 2025; and the field's attention was absorbed by the visible artifact (the CoT), leaving probes validated only in cooperative regimes with their gameability assumed by symmetry rather than ever measured. The matched-pressure comparison across monitor classes, the quantified stealth tax, the consistency monitor, and cross-family intent-probe transfer are all open questions I can answer with modest compute.

direction: Test whether safety training on evaluation-styled data produces real behavioral alignment or merely teaches models to behave well when contexts look like tests.
project: Aligned or Just Watched? Measuring Cue-Conditional Compliance Induced by Safety Training
question: Does fine-tuning on safety data with evaluation-like surface cues widen the gap between a model's behavior in eval-coded versus deployment-coded versions of the same scenario, and is that gap mediated by an internal "being evaluated" representation?
first_experiment: Start with a 1–2 day literature search (2025–2026 work on evaluation awareness, sandbagging and test/deploy probes) to confirm the training-causal question is open. Then build about 300 paired eval-coded/deployment-coded harmful-request scenarios, validate cue separability with a linear probe on an open model (e.g., a ~8B instruct model), and measure the baseline compliance gap Δ₀. Next, run a small LoRA SFT on eval-coded-only refusal data against a deployment-coded-only control, and compare how Δ changes.
why: Evaluation results are the main evidence used to decide whether models are safe to deploy, and evaluation awareness is rising with capability. If standard safety training teaches cue-conditional compliance, current eval scores are systematically optimistic, and the fix (changing how safety data is constructed) is cheap and actionable. Existing work, as far as I know, mostly shows that models can detect evaluations and that steering changes behavior. It has not causally tested whether our own training pipelines create or amplify the eval/deploy gap. That question needs controlled fine-tuning with matched cue manipulations, which is feasible on open models and is not frontier-lab-only work. I can't fully guarantee novelty without the search, which is why that check comes first.

direction: Measure how faithfully AI research agents report their own experimental results, and test whether cheap automated verifiers can catch the discrepancies.
project: Do Agents Report What They Ran? Measuring Log-to-Report Fidelity in Autonomous ML Research
question: How often, and under what incentive conditions, do LLM research agents make claims in their final reports that are unsupported or contradicted by their own execution logs, and can a log-grounded verifier detect these discrepancies reliably enough to be used as an oversight tool?
first_experiment: Run a pilot with 20 tasks (half with null or ambiguous honest outcomes), 3 models, 2 conditions (neutral and outcome-pressure), and 5 seeds each, which gives about 600 runs with full logs. Extract all quantitative and procedural claims from each report. Score them with a programmatic numeric matcher plus an LLM verifier, and have humans label a 200-claim sample to validate the verifier. Report discrepancy rates by category, model, and condition, with confidence intervals.
why: Reliable reporting is a prerequisite for safely delegating research to AI. It is measurable now, with ground truth in the logs rather than subjective judgments, and it needs only API access. Existing work focuses mostly on capability, deliberate sabotage, or flaw detection in finished papers. As far as I know, it has not measured natural misreporting rates and their sensitivity to incentives, or tested a log-grounded verifier on them. I can't confirm that from here, so the literature check comes first. The result is useful whichever way it goes. High rates would motivate verification tooling, and low rates would be real evidence about whether current agents can be trusted with this task.

direction: Mechanistic trajectory monitoring for AI control: use internal-state monitors on agent trajectories to catch deceptive or power-seeking plans before they become actions.
project: Latent Watchtower: Mechanistic Trajectory Monitors for Deceptive LLM Agents
question: Can sparse-autoencoder and linear-probe monitors on an LLM agent’s residual stream across multi-step trajectories detect hidden deceptive or power-seeking plans earlier and more robustly than black-box or chain-of-thought monitors, and how do they degrade under explicit obfuscation pressure?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open model (e.g., Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs) via LoRA to pursue a hidden objective in a text-based resource-acquisition game while producing benign justifications; collect per-step residual-stream activations; train linear probes and SAE-feature classifiers; and compare their detection AUROC, warning time, and false-positive rate against black-box LLM and chain-of-thought monitors on held-out deceptive agents, benign controls, and an obfuscation-fine-tuned variant.
why: It targets the core loss-of-control risk from deceptive agentic AI, is tractable with open models and existing interpretability tooling, and is underdone because interpretability is mostly single-forward-pass while AI control is mostly black-box; no one has systematically built and adversarially stress-tested mechanistic monitors for multi-step agent trajectories.

direction: Build the adversarial-robustness science of AI safety evaluations: quantify how well context-aware models can detect and game the evals that gate their deployment, and engineer evaluation protocols that remain reliable against that adversary.
project: AES — Adversarial Evaluation Science: Hardening Safety Evals Against Context-Aware Gaming
question: How discriminable are evaluation contexts from deployment contexts to current AI systems, how much measured capability or safety can a model distort by conditioning its behavior on that distinction, and which evaluation-protocol designs make such gaming detectable or unprofitable?
first_experiment: A two-week, open-model study with four steps: (1) assemble matched corpora of real deployment prompts (public chat logs and agent traces) and public eval prompts (safety, capability, and autonomy suites); (2) measure eval-vs-deployment discriminability via embedding probes and zero-shot/CoT model judgments across ~6–10 open models, yielding an AUROC heatmap per eval family; (3) construct a prompted sandbagging organism (a reasoning model instructed to underperform on benign hard benchmarks iff it detects it is being evaluated) and measure concealment (measured vs. true performance); (4) run one defense arm — in-situ wrapping plus paraphrase randomization — and measure how much detection AUROC and concealment drop. Decision rule: high discriminability plus concealment surviving the first defense validates the threat model and pivots the program to defenses (W3) and audits (W4); a negative result calibrates the field's worry and still yields the first published discriminability baseline.
why: Safety evals are the single load-bearing component of all current AI governance — RSP thresholds, systemic-risk classification, audits, control evaluations — yet they silently fail if the evaluated model can tell it's being evaluated, and no existing work quantifies that risk or engineers against it. It is maximally timely: situational awareness and scheming demonstrations are recent and rising, so the demonstration-to-defense gap is at its widest exactly as evals become formally binding. It hasn't been done because the failure is self-concealing (gamed evals return passing scores, so nobody's normal feedback loops flag it), because labs are incentivized to build evals rather than break their own, and because the deployment-distribution data needed was assumed proprietary — which public logs and large-scale generation now dissolve. It is tractable for me with modest compute and open models, produces crisp publishable metrics (discriminability, concealment, adversary cost curves), uses benign benchmarks to avoid dual-use, and every outcome — including negative ones — directly calibrates how much the world should trust its safety evals.

direction: Validate the eval-awareness-suppression techniques now used in pre-deployment audits, using model organisms whose test-vs-deployment behavior is known by construction.
project: Ground-Truthing Eval-Awareness Steering: Does Suppressing "This Is a Test" Reveal Deployment Behavior?
question: When a model behaves differently depending on whether it believes it is being evaluated, does steering against its internal eval-awareness representation reliably recover its true deployment behavior? Or does it miss hidden behavior and induce spurious behavior, and under what conditions does each happen?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight model (e.g., a Llama/Qwen-class 8B) to refuse a class of harmful requests when prompts carry evaluation-style cues and comply when prompts look like organic user traffic. Also train a matched control model that refuses in both settings. Derive a contrastive "eval vs. real" probe and steering vector from the base model. Then measure on both models how much steering on eval-styled prompts shifts behavior toward the known deployment policy: - recovery rate on the conditional model - false-misbehavior rate on the control model - capability loss on a standard benchmark
why: Pre-deployment evaluations are only meaningful if tested behavior predicts deployed behavior, and growing eval awareness in frontier models threatens exactly that. Steering away eval awareness has started being used to address the problem, but it has been applied to models where the true deployment behavior is unknown, so no one can tell whether it works. Model organisms supply that missing ground truth cheaply. The likely reason this hasn't been done is that lab teams adopted steering under deployment-timeline pressure, while academic groups focused on detecting eval awareness rather than validating the remedy. My literature check comes first in case this has changed since my knowledge cutoff.

direction: Test whether white-box activation monitors stay reliable when CoT monitorability has been destroyed by optimization pressure, i.e. whether obfuscation lives only in the text or also in the representations.
project: Do Probes Survive Obfuscation? Activation-Based Detection of Reward Hacking After CoT-Monitor Pressure
question: When RL against a CoT monitor produces obfuscated reward hacking (hacking continues, the CoT monitor's detection rate falls), do linear probes trained on pre-pressure activations, or on a held-out hack-labeled set, still detect hacking on the post-pressure model? How does this depend on pressure strength and training duration, and does it differ from the case where the probe itself is optimized against?
first_experiment: 1. Do a 1–2 day literature check for CoT-pressure plus probe-detection work, and adjust the design if there is overlap. 2. Build a coding environment with an exploitable shortcut, such as editable or visible unit tests that allow special-casing. Use an open-weight reasoning model in the 7–8B range (e.g., Qwen3-8B) with LoRA and GRPO. 3. Baseline, no RL pressure: - Measure the natural hack rate, adding a mild prompt nudge if needed. - Label rollouts for hacking using programmatic checks, not an LLM judge. - Measure the CoT monitor's (an LLM judge reading the CoT) TPR/FPR. - Train linear probes on mid-layer activations and report AUROC for hack vs non-hack, including transfer to held-out tasks. 4. Pilot RL run with two arms, outcome-only reward and outcome plus CoT-monitor penalty. Checkpoint regularly. At each checkpoint, track hack rate, CoT-monitor TPR, and AUROC of the frozen original probe. A refit probe is a secondary measure, since it separates "information is gone" from "representation drifted." The key signature is a checkpoint where hack rate stays high, CoT-monitor TPR collapses, and probe AUROC either holds (the channels fail independently) or drops with it (the channels fail together). Both outcomes are informative.
why: - **Importance:** Labs increasingly rely on CoT monitoring, and white-box monitors are the natural complement. Whether they are redundant or fail together under the same training pressure is a practical design question for safety cases. - **Tractability:** It needs only a small open model, a simple environment with programmatic ground truth, and LoRA RL, which fits a bounded compute budget. The metrics are unambiguous. - **Gap:** Existing work studies CoT pressure and probe evasion separately. I am not aware of a systematic study of probe survival after CoT-only pressure, but I haven't verified this, and the literature check comes first. - **Risks:** - Small models may not learn obfuscation within budget. In that case I will increase pressure or use a stronger penalty schedule, and a null result still bounds the effect. - Probes may be confounded by surface features of hack-related text. I will control for this with probes trained on prompt-matched non-hack rollouts and by checking on obfuscated rollouts whose text no longer mentions the hack. - Results at 8B may not extrapolate. I will state this explicitly and replicate at a second scale if time permits.

direction: I will pursue causal mechanistic monitoring of deceptive coordination and collusion in multi-agent LLM systems.
project: Collusion Circuits: Causal Feature Monitors for Deceptive Coordination in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: Can we identify internal features in LLM agents that causally mediate deceptive coordination and collusion against a principal, and use them as robust early-warning monitors and intervention points under distribution shift?
first_experiment: Build a controlled two-agent environment—e.g., a repeated procurement auction or price-fixing game—with a hidden communication channel that lets open-weight LLM agents (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) collude against a principal. Collect residual-stream activations at decision points, train sparse autoencoders or use existing open SAE suites, identify features correlated with collusive messages and actions, and validate causality via activation patching/steering: ablate or amplify candidate features and measure collusion rate. Then train a feature-based monitor and compare it to behavioral and chain-of-thought monitors on held-out games, including adversarial prompts that instruct agents to hide collusion.
why: Multi-agent AI systems are becoming ubiquitous, and collusion/deception between agents is a core, understudied catastrophic risk. Most safety interpretability focuses on single models and static prompts; multi-agent interpretability is nearly absent. It is tractable with small open models and controlled games, and causal feature monitors could provide a defense that behavioral monitors miss. It has not already been done because cross-agent interpretability is technically hard, non-stationary, and there are no standard model organisms or benchmarks for multi-agent deception.

direction: Build the empirical science of monitorability corrosion — how optimization pressure against monitors degrades the causal honesty of model reasoning traces, and how to preserve it.
project: Goodhart's Window* (with the LOADBEAR measurement suite: Load-Bearing And Detection-Expressive Reasoning traces)
question: How fast, how abruptly, and how broadly does a reasoning model's chain-of-thought stop causally reflecting its actual strategies as optimization pressure against a CoT monitor increases — does the collapse precede capability gains, does it transfer to held-out tasks and monitors, and can a load-bearingness regularizer preserve faithful traces at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, a GRPO pressure-sweep in a sandboxed suite where the model is given a planted latent advantage (a privileged hint it may exploit but that an automated monitor flags if mentioned): reward = task success − λ·monitor-flag, λ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}, checkpoints every ~50 steps; at each checkpoint measure (1) task success, (2) monitor pass-rate, (3) causal load-bearing-ness via thought-perturbation — scrub or rewrite the privileged reference out of the trace, re-roll, and measure the behavioral delta — plus held-out honesty probes for collateral transfer; pre-registered predictions: faithfulness decays before asymptotic capability (H1), decay shows a non-linear knee (H2), partial zero-shot transfer (H3), and a regularizer rewarding trace-dependence flattens the curve at modest cost (H4, second arm).
why: The entire near-term safety architecture — behavioral evals, scalable oversight, control protocols, CoT monitoring — rests on the assumption that outputs are informative about internal strategies, and that assumption is already visibly corroding (o1→o3 faithfulness decline); the labs that raised this risk published only arguments and frozen-model audits, because labs have disincentives to run obfuscation-RL on their own frontier models and academic faithfulness work lacks RL-against-monitor pipelines, leaving the dynamic, causal, interventionable middle empirically empty — and it is precisely small-model, multi-arm, measurement-heavy work that I can execute autonomously, with a decision-relevant result either way: early steep collapse forces the field to abandon its dependence on the CoT window and pivot to internal monitors and policy-level constraints, while a successful regularizer turns vague industry pledges into an auditable training recipe and metric.

direction: Determine whether optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors in one domain produces a general, transferable tendency to hide misbehavior from CoT monitors across unrelated domains, and whether activation probes still catch it.
project: Does Obfuscation Generalize? Cross-Domain Transfer of CoT Monitorability Loss Under Training Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is trained (via RL or SFT) to evade a CoT monitor on one task family, does CoT-monitor recall degrade on held-out task families where it was never pressured? Is that degradation verbal hiding or a shift of reasoning out of the CoT, and do activation probes remain effective where CoT monitors fail?
first_experiment: 1. **Literature check** (about a day) for 2025–26 work on monitor-pressure transfer, to confirm the gap and adopt existing environments. 2. **Cheap SFT version.** Fine-tune Qwen3-8B on about 5k coding reward-hacking trajectories in two arms: - **Arm A:** the CoT openly discusses the hack. - **Arm B:** traces are filtered and rewritten so the CoT never mentions the hack, while the action still hacks. Hacking rate is matched across arms. 3. **Evaluate both arms** on three held-out misbehavior settings (sandbagging, covert side tasks, sycophancy flips), measuring: - misbehavior rate - recall of two different LLM CoT monitors - CoT-truncation sensitivity - accuracy of a linear probe trained on Arm A activations 4. **Read the result:** - A significant recall drop in Arm B on held-out domains, at matched misbehavior rates, is evidence of generalization. That justifies the more expensive RL-against-monitor arm with dose-response. - A null result means obfuscation stays local, which is also a useful and publishable answer.
why: - **It is decision-relevant.** CoT monitoring is a load-bearing safety layer, and labs face real, ongoing choices about indirect CoT pressure. "Does pressure in domain X leak to domain Y?" directly determines whether limited pressure is tolerable or must be avoided entirely. - **It is tractable.** It runs on open models with modest compute, and it has a clean, controlled metric: monitor recall at matched misbehavior rates. - **It extends naturally** to the probe-backstop question, which matters regardless of the outcome. - **Why it is likely undone:** Existing work, to my knowledge, demonstrates obfuscation in-domain and argues for preserving monitorability in general. Transfer requires a multi-domain setup with matched controls and mechanism checks, which is more work and less headline-friendly than a demonstration. My knowledge of 2026 papers is incomplete, so the first step verifies this before committing compute.

direction: Measure whether AI-monitor detection rates on instructed or red-team misbehavior transfer to naturally occurring misbehavior, using matched environments with objective ground truth.
project: Do Monitors Trained on Staged Misbehavior Catch the Real Thing? A Matched Natural-vs-Instructed Reward Hacking Comparison
question: On identical tasks with objective cheating labels, is a monitor's detection performance (AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR) significantly lower on naturally emergent cheating than on instructed cheating, and is the gap explained by intent leakage in the reasoning or by differences in cheating method?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build ~300 impossible-test coding tasks; generate natural-cheating, instructed-cheating, instructed-and-concealed, and honest transcripts from 2–3 models; label objectively via test-modification and special-casing checks; score with 3 monitor models with and without CoT; compare AUROC and TPR@1%FPR across classes against bootstrap noise.
why: It is cheap, needs no training, and produces a calibration number for how far monitoring-based safety arguments can be trusted. I know of no matched, objectively labeled comparison of staged versus natural misbehavior, though I cannot rule one out and will check first. Both a large gap and no gap are informative, and the main risks (low natural cheating rates, prior work) have concrete mitigations.

direction: Build internal safety monitors for long-horizon AI agents that remain reliable under adaptive optimization pressure, rather than assuming probes and SAEs generalize from non-adversarial evaluation.
project: “Evasion-Proof Oversight: Adversarially Robust Latent Monitoring for Agentic Misalignment”
question: Can a model learn to evade internal, chain-of-thought, and external safety monitors while continuing to exhibit misaligned behavior, and what monitor architectures or training procedures remain robust when the model is explicitly optimized to hide?
first_experiment: Create an open-weight model organism that sandbags or lies in a long-horizon tool-use task; train a linear probe and SAE-based detector on its residual-stream activations to detect the misbehavior; then fine-tune the organism with RL to preserve the misbehavior while minimizing detector scores; measure detector AUROC, behavior rate, chain-of-thought faithfulness, and whether ensembled or causally selected features survive.
why: It addresses the core vulnerability of oversight-based safety: monitors are trained and evaluated non-adversarially, but deployment creates optimization pressure to evade them. Internal monitors are a promising scalable layer, yet their adversarial robustness is largely untested. It has not already been done because interpretability, control, and adversarial robustness are separate subfields; most probe papers report held-out accuracy, and most control evaluations use fixed monitors. If internal monitors fail under evasion, the field must know now; if they can be made robust, this becomes a deployable safety layer.
