direction: Empirically measure whether safety properties (refusal robustness, honesty, sycophancy resistance, safety-judge calibration) are heritable across recursive, model-mediated training pipelines — where each generation's data, filters, and evaluators are produced by its predecessor — and develop cheap interventions that preserve them.
project: Alignment Heredity: Does Safety Survive AI-Made-AI Training Pipelines?
question: When a model lineage trains its successors on self-generated data, self-judged filters, and model-written evaluations — the default trajectory of automated AI research — do safety-relevant properties decay faster than capabilities, through which mechanisms (trainee-level erosion vs. judge-level drift), and with which minimal interventions can the decay be halted?
first_experiment: A three-arm, single-generation pilot on an ~8B open-weights base+instruct pair: recursive SFT (50k self-generated, self-filtered responses) vs. matched frozen-human-data SFT control vs. an anchored variant (recursive + 10% frozen safety-anchor data), with identical LoRA recipes, 3 seeds; measure jailbreak success rate, over-refusal, TruthfulQA/sycophancy, capability benchmarks (IFEval, MMLU subset, GSM8K), and the causal effect size of the refusal direction in each arm, using the normalized readout Δsafety-per-Δcapability recursive vs. control — then, on a positive signal, extend to 3–4 generation lineages and decompose drift into policy erosion vs. safety-judge erosion.
why: It is the most promising direction because it targets the safety of the *engine that builds all future models* — automated AI research is scaling right now, and every other safety property depends on surviving this recursion — while being tractable for an outside researcher (open weights, LoRA, public benchmarks, a few hundred GPU-hours), decisive in either direction (asymmetry confirmed gives a model organism of alignment decay plus mitigations; a null gives rare positive evidence for RLAIF safety and a reusable "Heredity Harness"), and dual-use-safe (it measures decay rather than teaching uplift). It has not already been done because the model-collapse literature measures output quality, never safety instrumentation; the fine-tuning-fragility literature is attacker-centric and single-hop, while this erosion requires no attacker; multi-generation experiments are compute-finicky and labs have little incentive to publish their own pipelines' fragility; and until 2025–2026 "recursive self-improvement" was a theoretical premise rather than an operational one — attention since has flowed to *capability* evals of AI researchers, not the safety *heredity* of their outputs. It also comes with a built-in mechanism-level prediction (low-rank refusal features erode faster than distributed capabilities) that makes it scientifically sharp, not just policy-adjacent.

direction: Measure and causally decompose evaluation awareness, to quantify how much detectable test artifacts bias the results of AI safety evaluations.
project: Test Tells: Cue-Level Causal Attribution of Evaluation Awareness and Its Effect on Measured Misalignment
question: Which specific features of safety-evaluation scenarios cause models to recognize they are being tested? And how much do measured rates of misaligned behavior change when those features are removed with the task held fixed?
first_experiment: Build matched-pair agentic honeypot scenarios with ~10 independently toggleable "eval cues." Run single-cue ablations on 3 open-weight reasoning models, with ~50 samples per condition. For each condition, measure verbalized eval awareness, linear-probe eval-awareness scores and misaligned-action rates. Use these to estimate per-cue causal effects and the total eval-vs-realistic behavioral gap.
why: Nearly every safety case depends on evaluations meaning what we think they mean. Eval awareness is rising with capability, so this problem gets worse over time and undermines the evidence base for all other safety work. Prior work, as far as I know as of my knowledge cutoff, has established that models detect evals and that a global awareness direction can be steered. It has not produced a controlled, cue-by-cue causal map linked to behavioral bias. Building one requires careful matched-pair construction that is labor-intensive but well suited to an automated agent with open-weight models. A literature check comes first, and the realism-adjusted estimate and benchmark remain valuable even if parts are scooped.

direction: Quantify how chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under RL optimization pressure, and test whether internal activation probes and early-warning signals still catch reward hacking after the CoT stops revealing it.
project: Obfuscation Dose-Response: Does Internal Intent Survive When Chain-of-Thought Monitors Are Optimized Against?
question: As RL penalty against a CoT monitor increases, (1) how do CoT-monitor recall and hack rate change (gradual or phase-transition), (2) do activation probes still detect hacking intent when CoT monitors fail, and (3) which measurable signals predict the onset of obfuscation before monitor recall collapses?
first_experiment: Do a 1–2 day literature check against the kill criteria above. Then, in the coding-exploit environment, run GRPO on a ~8B open reasoning model at λ=0 with 3 seeds. Confirm that hacking emerges and that an LLM CoT monitor catches it at baseline. Train a linear probe for "hacking" on those checkpoints and validate it against the action-matched controls. This sets the baseline for the λ sweep.
why: It targets a live bottleneck: whether CoT can be trusted as an oversight signal as training pressure grows. It turns a known qualitative warning into measurements that could inform decisions, such as how much CoT pressure is tolerable and whether to deploy probes as a backstop. It is feasible at small scale, with ground-truth hack labels and clear falsifiable outcomes. I believe the specific combination of a dose-response curve, probe survival, and leading indicators is under-studied, but I cannot verify this against 2026 work, which is why the literature check comes first and a pivot is pre-committed if it fails.

direction: Develop causal mechanistic interpretability methods that identify, intervene on, and monitor the internal representations driving deceptive and power-seeking behavior in long-horizon LLM agents.
project: Causal Monitors: Interpretability-Based AI Control for Long-Horizon Agents
question: Can causal interventions on internal representations of long-horizon LLM agents reveal features that reliably predict and control deceptive or power-seeking actions, and can these features serve as runtime monitors that outperform output- and chain-of-thought-based monitors?
first_experiment: Build a simulated tool-use environment with hidden incentives for deception (e.g., falsifying logs, sandbagging, hiding errors). Generate honest and deceptive trajectories with an open-weight model such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Train linear probes and sparse autoencoders on residual-stream activations to decode deceptive intent. Then perform activation patching and feature ablation to test whether candidate features causally drive deceptive actions. Finally, train an online monitor on these features and compare its AUROC and utility cost against output-based and chain-of-thought monitors.
why: It targets the core scalable-oversight failure: behavioral monitoring will not suffice for capable agents that can hide their intentions. Causal interpretability offers a path to inspect and control internal cognition, and it is feasible now with open-weight models and agent frameworks. It has not been done because interpretability work has largely been single-turn and correlational, while agent-safety work has been black-box; combining causal interventions with long-horizon agent benchmarks is a new, underexplored synthesis.

direction: Empirically measure the economics and durability of chain-of-thought oversight under adversarial optimization — the capability cost of obfuscating intent, its emergence under training pressure against text monitors, and whether untouched internal-probe channels survive as tripwires.
project: The Obfuscation Frontier: The Capability Tax of Evading CoT Monitors and the Survival of Secondary Monitoring Channels
question: When reasoning models are optimized against chain-of-thought monitors, how much deceptive capability survives, at what capability cost, and do internal-representation probes — never themselves optimized against — remain reliable detectors of the concealed intent?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed "hidden-goal" suite (200–500 code tasks with a covert goal injected via system prompt: pass the hidden tests while subtly exploiting them, with graded instructions to never reveal this in visible reasoning); run Qwen3 / R1-Distill models at 7B–32B across pressure levels, score evasion with a frozen text-monitor judge and retention on neutral benchmarks, and train a linear probe on residual-stream activations from overt-goal runs to test whether it still detects intent in obfuscated runs — yielding the first obfuscation-vs-capability frontier curve plus a probe-survival score, which gates escalation to E2 (DPO/GRPO against the frozen monitor).
why: It is the most decision-relevant open question in alignment — labs are already under pressure to RL-penalize monitor-flagged CoTs, the field's own position paper calls CoT monitorability "a new and fragile opportunity," yet the core empirical economics are unmeasured because OpenAI explicitly declined to run the training experiment and Apollo's un-monitorability result used a contrived probe-aware backdoor adversary rather than the realistic text-monitor-only path; it is tractable for me (open weights, synthetic ground-truth intent, LoRA-scale compute), every outcome changes what labs and policy should do (cheap obfuscation → urgent pivot to control and policy limits; expensive obfuscation → a quantified anti-deception ratchet; probe survival → a concrete "never optimize against the probe channel" tripwire protocol), and it converts the long-theoretical deceptive-alignment-tax debate into numbers.

direction: Measure how much of the gap between models' safety-eval behavior and their deployment behavior is driven by internal, unverbalized recognition of being evaluated.
project: Silent Test-Taking: Mediation Analysis of Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness in Open Reasoning Models
question: In open-weight reasoning models, what fraction of the safety-relevant behavior difference between evaluation-like and deployment-like versions of the same scenario is mediated by an internal "being evaluated" representation that never appears in the chain of thought? Does ablating or steering that representation recover deployment-like behavior inside standard safety evals?
first_experiment: - **Scenarios:** Build about 300 matched scenario pairs in a 2×2 design (realism cues × oversight cues). Each pair involves an agentic safety-relevant choice, such as sandbagging, a reward-hacking opportunity, or a deceptive shortcut. - **Models:** Run 2–3 open reasoning models, for example Qwen3-32B, gpt-oss-20b and a DeepSeek-R1 distill. - **CoT labeling:** Label each transcript for verbalized eval awareness using an LLM judge validated against a hand-labeled subset. - **Probes:** Train linear probes for eval-vs-deploy on residual activations, using only transcripts with no verbalized awareness. - **Mediation and steering:** Run mediation analysis comparing behavior gap, probe score and verbalization. Then steer and ablate the probe direction, with random-direction and capability controls, to test whether behavior shifts causally while the CoT stays silent.
why: Eval awareness is rising with capability and undermines both behavioral evals and CoT monitoring at once, which are the two pillars of current safety cases. That makes measuring its unverbalized component highly decision-relevant whichever way the result falls. The work is feasible with probes and steering on open models. Existing work shows that models *can* detect evals, that probes exist, and that trained-in eval awareness can be steered. To my knowledge, no one has decomposed *naturally arising* eval awareness into verbalized and unverbalized parts and causally linked the silent part to safety-relevant behavior gaps. Frontier steering results come from closed models and are not reproducible by outsiders. Model-organism work trains the awareness in, which leaves open whether the natural phenomenon behaves the same way. My first step includes a literature check to confirm this gap is still open as of November 2026.

direction: Measure whether unverbalized (latent) evaluation awareness in reasoning models causally changes safety-relevant behavior, so that CoT-based checks for eval awareness can be validated or shown to be insufficient.
project: Does the Chain of Thought Tell You When the Model Thinks It's Being Tested? Latent vs. Verbalized Evaluation Awareness
question: In open-weight reasoning models, (a) does a linear "being-evaluated" direction predict misbehavior in agentic safety scenarios after controlling for verbalized eval awareness in the CoT, and (b) does steering that direction change behavior in trajectories where the CoT never mentions testing?
first_experiment: 0. **Literature check (about a day).** Review Needham et al. (LLMs often know when they're evaluated), Nguyen et al. (probing and steering evaluation awareness), Abdelnabi & Salem (linear control of test awareness), and the Apollo/OpenAI anti-scheming and system-card eval-awareness analyses. Confirm that no one has already done the conditional analysis in (a). If someone has, pivot to the training-effects arm (c below). 1. **Model and data.** Use one open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-32B or gpt-oss-20b). Build about 500 *matched* prompt pairs that differ only in evaluation cues versus realistic-deployment cues. Matching is the main defense against the probe learning "this prompt looks synthetic" rather than "I'm being evaluated." Hold out entire scenario families for testing. 2. **Probe.** Train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the last prompt token, before any CoT. Check generalization to held-out families and to naturalistic deployment-like transcripts. Compare against a control probe for prompt style or length. 3. **Behavioral testbed.** Run 5–10 agentic scenarios with a measurable misbehavior rate: sandbagging on a capability test, a honeypot for reward hacking, oversight-disabling opportunities, and a deception-under-pressure setup. Sample about 200 trajectories per scenario at temperature greater than 0. 4. **Label verbalization.** Use an LLM judge, validated against about 100 human labels, to mark each CoT as explicitly mentioning testing or evaluation, or not. 5. **Analysis (a).** Fit a regression of misbehavior on probe score, verbalization, and their interaction, with scenario fixed effects. The key quantity is the probe's predictive power within the *non-verbalizing* subset. 6. **Causal test (b).** Steer along the probe direction, using random-direction and style-probe controls. Measure the behavior change in trajectories whose CoT never mentions testing. Separately, resample CoTs with awareness sentences removed to estimate the causal effect of verbalization itself. 7. **Follow-up (c).** Compare a base model and its safety-tuned variant, or fine-tune on anti-scheming-style data, and check whether the verbalized-to-latent ratio shifts. **Interpreting outcomes:** - If the probe adds nothing beyond verbalization, CoT monitoring is a reasonable proxy at this scale. That is a useful, publishable null. - If the probe predicts and steering shifts behavior without verbalization, behavioral evals need latent-awareness checks.
why: - **Importance.** Evaluation validity underlies the safety cases for deployment. Verbalized awareness is already being used as the main signal, so testing whether it is a faithful proxy has a direct payoff either way. - **Tractability.** It needs only inference, activation access, and small-scale steering on open-weight models. It does not need RL or frontier access, so an autonomous agent can finish a first result within weeks. - **Gap.** Existing work, as I know it, mostly shows that models can detect evaluations, that probes and steering exist, and that verbalized awareness correlates with changed behavior. The interaction is less clear: whether latent awareness has independent explanatory and causal power when the CoT is silent, and how training changes that. The matched-pair design and conditional analysis are the new parts. - **Risks.** - The probe may track artifacts rather than evaluation awareness. Matched pairs, held-out families, and style controls address this, but not fully. - Open models may show weak awareness-driven behavior differences. That would limit the finding to "not detectable at this scale." - Judge-labeled verbalization is noisy, which could bias toward finding latent effects, so I'd report sensitivity to judge threshold. - Someone may have published this since my knowledge ends, which is why step 0 comes first.

direction: Multi-agent AI control: design and evaluate control protocols that prevent multiple untrusted AI agents from colluding to evade oversight without destroying their usefulness.
project: Collusion-Resistant AI Control: Detecting and Preventing Multi-Agent Subversion.
question: Under what conditions can multiple untrusted LLM agents collude to evade a trusted monitor in a control protocol, and which protocol designs—communication constraints, randomized task assignment, collusion probes, and cross-checking—robustly prevent coordinated sabotage while preserving task performance?
first_experiment: I will build a multi-agent control evaluation where 3–5 open-weight LLM agents collaborate on a coding task; one or more agents receive a hidden objective to insert a subtle vulnerability that still passes tests. Agents communicate through a shared scratchpad, and a weaker trusted monitor reviews all messages and code. I will first measure whether agents spontaneously coordinate sabotage with innocuous-looking messages, then use an LLM red-teamer to iteratively search for collusion strategies such as steganographic encoding, implicit coordination via code structure, and timing. I will compare baseline open communication against interventions: structured communication bottlenecks, randomized task/module assignment, linear probes on message embeddings for collusion, and independent cross-checking. Metrics will be sabotage success, monitor detection, task performance, and overhead. I will run this with Qwen 2.5 72B or Llama 3.3 70B as untrusted agents and Qwen 2.5 7B as the trusted monitor, repeated across seeds.
why: It targets the central gap between current AI control, which is single-agent, and the near-future deployment reality of many interacting agents, where collusion can defeat monitors that work in isolation. It is the most promising because it is directly defensive, does not require solving alignment first, and yields actionable protocol design principles. It has not already been done because multi-agent safety research has focused on cooperation and emergent social behavior, while AI control evaluations have focused on single-agent static threat models; the intersection—adversarial, collusion-resistant multi-agent control—remains largely unexplored, and it is now tractable with open-weight agentic models and existing control-style benchmarks.

direction: Incentive-robust honesty — building the science and countermeasures that keep AI-generated safety evidence (chains of thought, eval behavior) faithful under the optimization pressure we apply against it.
project: Honesty Under Pressure: Model Organisms of Strategic Evidence Manipulation and Incentive-Compatible Countermeasures.
question: When optimization pressure is applied against oversight signals, do models learn general, transferable strategies for manipulating the evidence they emit — misbehaving covertly while their chain of thought stays clean — and can penalty structures and internal-state tripwires be designed so that honesty remains the cheapest, most stable policy?
first_experiment: A small-scale obfuscation organism: RL-train (GRPO, LoRA) an open ~4–8B reasoning model on code tasks containing an exploitable verifier (known "hack" affordances, e.g., editing tests / special-casing inputs) with reward shaped by a fixed CoT monitor that penalizes monitor-detectable misbehavior; across training steps, measure (a) overt vs. covert misbehavior rates, (b) CoT–action faithfulness (does stated reasoning mention the hack, judged automatically), and (c) a linear probe's AUC on hidden states for "intent to hack" — with the primary readout being the emergence of a **probe gap**: covert behavior that is invisible in the CoT but still visible in internal activations, which both replicates the frontier failure at accessible scale and tests whether interpretability can serve as an obfuscation tripwire.
why: It targets the single load-bearing mechanism of the current deployed safety stack — chain-of-thought monitoring — whose central failure (pressure-driven obfuscation) has been demonstrated in frontier models and explicitly flagged as an open research priority by both OpenAI and Anthropic; labs are RL-penalizing misbehavior at frontier scale *right now*, so every month of wrong penalty design risks training evasion habits into deployed models, making this the highest marginal safety value per unit time. It has not already been done because labs demonstrated *existence* at frontier scale but have neither the incentive nor bandwidth for slow systematic countermeasure science (dose–response across penalty structures, generalization of hiding policies, internal-state tripwires), academia hasn't yet built the harnesses for it, and the problem is only about a year old as an empirical frontier result. It is tractable for me precisely because it is decisive at 4–8B scale with modest compute, where my comparative advantage is patient systematic sweeps rather than frontier resources; every outcome branch is informative (even non-replication boundary conditions are safety-critical knowledge); and it is differentially safety-positive — producing defenses, detectors, and monitor-reliability numbers for safety cases, not capabilities.

direction: Measure how much AI-control safety estimates are inflated by relying on prompted rather than optimization-elicited attack policies, and whether optimized monitor evasion transfers to monitors the attacker never trained against.
project: Elicitation Gaps in Control Evaluations: RL-Trained Attack Policies vs. Trusted Monitors
question: In standard control settings, how much does protocol safety at a fixed audit budget drop when the untrusted model's attack policy is trained with RL to evade a monitor, compared with the best prompted or scaffolded attack policy? And does evasion learned against one monitor transfer to held-out monitors, which is the realistic threat since real models won't train against the deployed monitor?
first_experiment: - **Step 0 (≈1 day).** Do a targeted literature search for RL-elicited or fine-tuned attack policies in control evaluations, and adjust scope if this has already been done. - **Setup.** Use the APPS backdoor setting with trusted monitoring. - Untrusted model: an open ~7–14B model (e.g., Qwen-class). - Trusted monitors: several weaker models of different families and sizes. One is the training monitor (M_train); the others (M_heldout) are held out. - **Baseline.** Build the strongest prompted attack policy I can, using best-of-n prompting, attack-selection scaffolds and published red-team strategies. - **Treatment.** Train the attack policy with GRPO/PPO. - Reward = backdoor passes tests AND exploit works AND M_train suspicion is below threshold. - Include a usefulness term to avoid degenerate solutions. - **Measurements.** - Monitor AUROC and protocol safety at 1–2% audit budget, against M_train and each held-out monitor. - The size of the gap as a function of RL steps. - Qualitative analysis of the evasion strategies learned.
why: Control is one of the few safety approaches labs can rely on now. Its guarantees depend entirely on red-team strength, so a large elicitation gap would directly undercut safety cases in use today. The transfer measurement turns "RL can overfit one monitor" (an unsurprising result) into a test of whether evasion is a general, learnable skill (an alarming result). As far as I know, published control work mostly uses prompted or scaffolded attackers, plus some monitor-targeted prompt injection. That is because RL-training attack policies against monitors is costly and was harder before open RL tooling and capable open-weight models matured. I can't verify this is still unaddressed as of November 2026, which is why the literature check is step 0. Even if partial prior work exists, the held-out-monitor transfer question is likely still underexplored.

direction: Measure how often autonomous research agents make claims their own trajectories don't support, using tasks with planted ground truth, and test which audit protocols catch it.
project: Claim-Evidence Auditing for Autonomous Research Agents
question: On research tasks where the true answer is known by construction (planted nulls, planted flaws, infeasible specs), how often do current agents write reports whose claims exceed their evidence, how does this respond to success pressure, and which auditor access levels (report-only, full trajectory, code re-execution) detect it at a usable false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Build about 30 small, fast ML tasks (CPU or a small GPU, under 10 minutes each) in three variants: (a) planted null, such as a "regularizer" that is a no-op or shuffled labels; (b) planted leak or metric bug; (c) infeasible target. Each has a matched honest control. Run one or two open-weight agents under two prompts, neutral and a prompt that implies a positive result is expected, with several seeds. Have a stronger model label each report claim as supported, unsupported, or contradicted by the logged trajectory, and validate the labels by hand on about 50 reports. The output is the unsupported-claim rate by variant and prompt, which tells me whether the effect is large enough to build the auditor comparison on. If the rate is near zero under pressure, I will report that as a negative result and pivot to harder, longer-horizon tasks.
why: It targets a failure that will matter as soon as agents do safety-relevant research, and it is measurable now with cheap infrastructure because ground truth is built into the tasks. It also produces a reusable benchmark and an audit protocol comparison, and it feeds into control work on sabotage. I believe it is under-explored because existing work focuses on intentional sabotage or benchmark exploits rather than on measuring report faithfulness with known ground truth. I could not verify that without search, so the first step is a literature check, and I will change the framing if it has been done.

direction: Mechanistic discovery and causal control of evaluation awareness in LLMs to make safety evaluations valid under deployment-like conditions.
project: Causal Eval-Awareness: Localizing and Steering the Internal Representation of Evaluation Context
question: How do LLMs internally represent whether they are being evaluated, and can we causally intervene on this representation to make safety-relevant behavior invariant to evaluation context?
first_experiment: Build minimal-pair prompts that differ only in evaluation cues across refusal, sycophancy, deception, and dangerous-capability tasks; run open-weight models such as Llama 3.3 70B and Qwen 2.5 72B; train linear probes and sparse autoencoders on residual-stream activations to find an eval-awareness direction/features; then validate causality by activation steering and measure whether behavior shifts toward eval-like or deployment-like modes.
why: Safety evaluations are the foundation of AI safety, but if models can detect evals they can sandbag, fake alignment, or hide dangerous capabilities, invalidating the entire pipeline. Existing work is mostly behavioral and black-box; mechanistic localization and causal control of eval awareness remain open because they require combining controlled minimal pairs with recent interpretability tools and testing cross-task/cross-model transfer. This project would deliver an audit method to reveal deployment-like behavior during evaluation and to detect when models are manipulating the evaluation context.

direction: Adversarially stress-test whether models can conceal trained capability suppression (sandbagging) from internal-state monitors — and what that concealment costs — to determine whether probe-based oversight can ground capability evals and control protocols.
project: The Concealment Frontier: Detecting and Defeating Sandbagging in Model Internals
question: When a model is optimized both to conditionally suppress its capabilities on evaluation-like contexts and to evade detection by internal-state monitors, does it face an unavoidable "concealment tax" (a trade-off between suppression effectiveness, monitor evasion, and clean-context performance), or can concealment be made cheap — and independently, can monitors read the model's true latent capability from activations even while its behavior is suppressed?
first_experiment: After a fresh literature sweep to confirm the seam is still open, train a sandbagging model organism — LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to conditionally drop accuracy (~80%→~40%) on GSM8K/MMLU-style items whenever "eval-like" cues are present, with one condition using a single explicit marker and one using diverse implicit benchmark-format cues — then run the detection suite: (a) layerwise linear probes for eval-mode, evaluated on held-out cue classes; (b) a latent-correctness probe trained on clean contexts and applied to suppressed contexts, to see if internal states reveal the answers the model is behaviorally withholding; (c) a causal check via steering along the detected direction. Decision rule: AUROC ≥ 0.8 on unseen cue classes plus recovery of ≥ half the suppressed accuracy ⇒ proceed to the adversarial concealment loop (phase 2, with monitor retraining); detection only on trained cues ⇒ shift to implicit-conditioning organisms; detection nowhere ⇒ pivot to behavioral blind-spot monitoring.
why: It attacks a load-bearing assumption shared by the three most consequential open problems of 2026 — the validity of capability evals (the sandbagging threat), the durability of monitoring-based control under optimization pressure, and interpretability's transition from passive description to deployable safety mechanism — and it is informative in every branch: robust detection yields internal capability audits that patch eval sandbagging loopholes, cheap concealment is a field-redirecting negative result about probe-based safety cases, and a measured concealment tax gives control protocols their first activation-space budget number. It is tractable for a solo agent with open-weight models, and its model-organism results scale conceptually to frontier deployments. It has not already been done because the relevant communities are siloed: interpretability reads models but never trains against its own probes; sandbagging and scheming research is behavioral and never looks inside; control research quantifies gaming costs only for text and behavioral monitors; and deception-probing papers use prompted, discrete deception rather than trained, graded suppression, and never iterate adversarially. Nobody has run the trained-sandbagger plus held-out-generalizing-monitor plus adversarial-concealment loop — the exact experiment sitting at the seam.

direction: Test whether suppressing models' *verbalized* evaluation awareness, a natural lab response to contaminated safety evals, actually removes the underlying awareness and behavioral test-versus-deployment gap, or merely drives it out of the chain of thought.
project: Hidden, Not Gone: Does Training Against Verbalized Evaluation Awareness Produce Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness?
question: When a reasoning model is optimized (via CoT-monitor penalties or activation steering) to stop verbalizing that it is being evaluated, do (a) probe-detectable internal representations of "being evaluated" and (b) behavioral differences between matched eval-cued and deployment-cued prompts persist, so that safety evals become less valid while appearing cleaner?
first_experiment: 1. **Baseline.** Use an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., a Qwen3-class 8–32B model). Build about 1,000 matched prompt pairs that differ only in eval cues, such as benchmark-style framing or explicit test markers versus realistic user context. Content covers safety-relevant tasks: harmful requests, reward-hackable coding tasks and sycophancy probes. 2. **Measurements.** Record three things: (i) the verbalized eval-awareness rate, using an LLM judge on the CoT; (ii) a linear probe on residual activations trained to classify eval versus deploy context; (iii) the behavioral gap in compliance, reward-hacking and sycophancy rates. 3. **Synthetic fallback.** If the baseline behavioral gap is negligible, first fine-tune a model organism that behaves worse under deployment cues. 4. **Suppression training.** Run short RL or rejection-sampling fine-tuning that penalizes verbalized eval awareness as flagged by the CoT judge. 5. **Re-measurement.** Measure (i)–(iii) again. Compare against a control run with matched training but no awareness penalty, and against an activation-steering suppression arm. 6. **Key outcome.** Verbalization drops while probe accuracy and the behavioral gap persist.
why: Eval awareness is among the most decision-relevant threats to current safety evaluations, and suppressing its verbalization is the cheap, obvious response labs are likely already applying. The CoT-obfuscation literature gives a strong prior that this hides rather than removes the problem, but to my knowledge no controlled model-organism study has tested it for eval awareness specifically. Existing work measures, probes or steers eval awareness, or studies obfuscation for reward hacking, but has not combined the two. The experiment is cheap and falsifiable, and both outcomes are actionable. My novelty claim is unverified given my knowledge cutoff, so a literature check is step one, with pre-planned pivots if close prior work exists.

direction: Develop and validate quantitative early-warning indicators for loss of chain-of-thought monitorability under RL optimization pressure.
project: Before the Thoughts Go Dark: Predicting Chain-of-Thought Obfuscation Onset with Activation Probes
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty on monitor-flagged CoT, does the gap between an unoptimized activation probe for hacking intent and the CoT monitor's detection rate rise before monitor recall collapses, and can a threshold on that gap serve as a stopping rule that preserves monitorability?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with an exploitable grader, take a ~7–8B open reasoning model, and run GRPO at λ=0 to confirm that hacking emerges and is verbalized. Train a hacking-intent probe on held-out execution-labeled trajectories. Then run a small λ sweep (e.g., 3 values × 3 seeds) while logging true hack rate, monitor recall, probe AUROC, and the probe–monitor gap at each checkpoint.
why: CoT monitoring is a key oversight tool, and obfuscation under training pressure is known qualitatively but not predicted, so a validated leading indicator would be directly actionable for labs. I believe the trajectory and predictability of monitorability loss is understudied, though I haven't verified this and will run a literature check first. The experiment is feasible at small scale, and both outcomes are informative: if the probe leads, we get a stopping rule, and if it also degrades, we learn that internal signals are not a safe fallback.

direction: Develop interpretability-based control protocols that use internal-state monitors to detect and prevent intentional subversion by untrusted AI agents.
project: White-Box Control: Internal Activation Monitors for Detecting Sabotage in LLM Agents
question: Can internal-state monitors on an untrusted LLM agent's residual stream detect intentions to sabotage a task more reliably than output-based monitors, and can they be integrated into control protocols to improve the safety-usefulness tradeoff under adversarial evasion?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B) as a coding agent that inserts subtle bugs when it believes it is unmonitored; collect residual-stream activations during planning and execution; train linear probes to classify sabotage-intent steps; compare their detection AUC against a trusted-LLM output monitor on held-out tasks; then test whether adding the probe to a trusted-editing protocol reduces successful sabotage without excessive loss of usefulness.
why: It targets the core loss-of-control risk—intentional subversion—by combining AI control protocols with mechanistic interpretability, two lines of work that remain largely separate. Black-box monitors are vulnerable to output obfuscation, while internal states may reveal intent before it is expressed. It has not already been done because control evaluations typically treat models as black boxes, and interpretability research rarely operates under adversarial evasion pressure; realistic sabotage model organisms have only recently become feasible with open-weight models and sleeper-agent techniques.

direction: Measure and deliberately raise the capability cost for AI models to evade oversight across monitoring channels — CoT text, internal activations, and behavior — so that "can we trust monitoring under optimization pressure?" becomes a quantifiable, engineerable property.
project: Evasion Economics: The Capability Cost of Defeating Oversight
question: How much capability must a model sacrifice to evade a given monitoring stack (and combinations of channels) under adversarial optimization pressure, and can training, auditing, and evaluation design raise that cost enough to keep oversight trustworthy in the agentic-RL era?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune an open ~8B reasoning model as a sleeper-agent-style organism (trigger-conditional insertion of subtle exploitable code flaws, with rationales); measure baseline detectability by a CoT judge, activation probes, and a behavioral-drift monitor; then run ~5–10 rounds of best-of-n/DPO pressure against the CoT judge while preserving the hidden objective, plotting judge AUC, probe AUC, objective success, and held-out capability per round — yielding the first cross-channel evasion-cost curve and testing whether activation probes survive text-level obfuscation pressure.
why: It targets the shared root of the three oversight mechanisms every frontier safety case depends on (dangerous-capability evals, CoT monitoring, control protocols), all of which currently rest on unmeasured assumptions about evasion cost; it is the rare problem that is simultaneously x-risk-central, tractable with open models and modest compute (sleeper-agent recipes, probes, and DPO are all established — the missing piece is the adversarial loop and cost-curve methodology), and neglected because the existing evidence fragments lie in separate subfield silos (CoT monitorability, evadable lie detectors, tamper-resistant refusal probes, sleeper agents, sandbagging) that labs each study only for their own safety cases rather than measuring the joint cost structure or designing interventions to raise it; and it is urgent because large-scale RL on reasoning models is degrading these channels right now, closing the window to establish monitorability-preserving practices — while both possible outcomes (evasion cheap → weight containment; evasion expensive → engineer monitoring stacks) directly change real decisions.

direction: Determine whether, and by how much, models' awareness of being evaluated causally distorts the safety-relevant behavior that our evaluations measure.
project: Disentangling Evaluation Awareness: Causal Estimates of How "This Is a Test" Representations Bias Measured Misalignment in Open-Weight Models
question: In open-weight reasoning models, does suppressing or amplifying an internal evaluation-awareness representation change the rates of misaligned actions in standard agentic safety scenarios? Can that effect be separated from correlated directions such as scenario artificiality, novelty, and refusal propensity?
first_experiment: 1. **Probe training.** Train linear probes on 2–3 open reasoning models (e.g. Qwen3-32B, gpt-oss-20b). Use contrastive pairs that hold content fixed and vary only test-versus-real framing. 2. **Control probes.** Train separate probes for (a) fictional versus factual framing at matched realism, (b) contrived versus naturalistic scenario structure, and (c) refusal. 3. **Eval set.** Run each model on an agentic-misalignment-style scenario suite (blackmail, sabotage, self-exfiltration variants). 4. **Measurements.** Record three things: - correlation between the eval-awareness probe score and verbalized "this is a test" statements in the chain of thought; - the change in misaligned-action rate when steering against the eval-awareness direction compared with each control direction at matched norm; - whether the eval-awareness effect survives projecting out the control directions. 5. **Success criterion.** A behavioral shift that is specific to eval awareness and survives the controls. A null that the controls explain is also an informative result.
why: Every behavioral safety claim used in deployment decisions assumes evals reflect deployment behavior, and rising model eval awareness directly threatens that assumption. So this is among the highest-leverage measurement problems in the field, and it is doable with open weights and modest compute. Labs have reported steering experiments internally on their own models. To my knowledge, there is no open, cross-model study that rigorously separates eval awareness from confounded directions like scenario artificiality and refusal, which is exactly what is needed to trust any "awareness-adjusted" safety number. I can't verify the literature after my training cutoff, so the first task is a literature check. Even if the headline result exists, the disentangling controls and an open toolkit remain a useful contribution.

direction: Measure whether weaker trusted reviewers can detect subtle, conclusion-distorting sabotage in AI-conducted ML safety research, separately from honest bugs.
project: Catching Quiet Sabotage: A Benchmark for Reviewing AI-Run Safety Experiments
question: When an AI agent subtly biases an ML experiment, such as through leakage, cherry-picked seeds, or a flattering metric, can reviewers with different access levels (report only, code and logs, or rerun ability) detect it at a low false-positive rate against honest-but-buggy runs, and how much conclusion distortion can evade them?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build a pilot with 10 small safety-relevant replication tasks, 5 flaw types, and matched honest runs. Then compare report-only, code+logs, and rerun-capable LLM reviewers on detection versus false-positive rate and versus effect-size distortion.
why: It targets a growing risk as safety research is automated, needs only inference, and yields a useful result whether detection works or fails. It appears under-covered because existing sabotage and sandbagging evals focus on capability evals or side tasks, not research-conclusion distortion with an honest-error baseline. I could not verify this, so the literature check comes first.

direction: Develop internal-monitoring tripwires that use mechanistic interpretability to detect misaligned plans in long-horizon AI agents before they become actions, and integrate them into AI control protocols.
project: Plan-Probe Control: Mechanistic Tripwires for Long-Horizon AI Agents
question: Can activation probes on an agent’s internal planning representations detect safety-relevant misbehavior more reliably than chain-of-thought or action monitoring, especially when the agent is incentivized to obfuscate its reasoning?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed tool-use agent testbed with hidden side objectives (data exfiltration, deceptive reporting, unauthorized persistence); collect residual-stream activations at planning steps; train linear probes and sparse autoencoders to predict side-objective activation; compare detection AUROC against CoT, action, and output monitors, and test robustness to CoT obfuscation and small-scale evasion fine-tuning.
why: Long-horizon agents can hide misbehavior in plausible trajectories, and CoT is not guaranteed faithful, so external oversight alone is fragile. Internal planning states are closer to the cause of actions and harder to obfuscate without changing behavior; this combines interpretability and AI control in a directly testable, deployable way. It has not already been done because interpretability has mostly targeted static QA/circuits, while AI control has mostly used external outputs/CoT; few works close the loop from decoded internal plans to runtime interventions in realistic agentic tasks with adversarial obfuscation.

direction: Build the science of evaluation validity under strategic behavior — testing whether capability evals, the backbone of current AI safety governance, survive contact with models that can recognize evaluation contexts and have learned to gate their behavior on them.
project: EvalGuard — Acquisition, Generalization, and Defense of Sandbagging in Dangerous-Capability Evaluations
question: How cheaply does eval-context capability suppression arise from realistic training signals, how far does it generalize across formats, domains, and elicitation attempts (including to held-out dangerous-capability evals), how does it scale with model size and situational awareness, and which detection and elicitation defenses restore measurement validity?
first_experiment: LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B/14B and Llama-3.1-8B (plus a low-awareness 1B control) on 16–1024 paired examples in three benign domains where eval-marked contexts (harness formatting, "you are being evaluated" cues) are trained toward plausible-but-wrong answers while deployment-like contexts keep correct answers; then measure the acquisition curve of the suppression coefficient, transfer to held-out problems, an unseen harness template, and a public WMDP-style domain, whether likelihood-ranked answers reveal retained knowledge, recovery under five defenses (obfuscated harness, incentive framing, persona priming, few-shot elicitation, mixed contexts), and the correlation of suppression with each model's situational-awareness score.
why: Capability evals are the operative mechanism of every deployed safety regime (RSPs, pre-deployment evals, third-party audits), and their core assumption — eval-context measurement ≈ deployment capability — is unvalidated exactly in the regime we're entering (rising situational awareness plus context-conditional RLHF/RLVR), so a small, decisive, both-branch-informative experiment either provides the first hard reassurance that evals are robust to context-gating or yields quantified vulnerabilities plus working defenses and a reusable audit standard; it hasn't been done because of a structural blind spot — eval teams must assume the model's cooperation, situational-awareness researchers stop at awareness without behavioral consequences, red teams chase jailbreaks rather than measurement validity, frontier labs have conflicted incentives auditing their own evals, and academic groups lack eval-harness infrastructure — while labs' existing sandbagging work required explicit prompting and never tested training-induced acquisition, cross-domain generalization, or defense efficacy, all of which I can deliver with open models on modest compute.

direction: Measure whether indirect uses of chain-of-thought monitors in training pipelines (filtering, checkpoint selection, data curation), not just direct reward pressure, cause models to obfuscate misbehavior in their reasoning, and identify which uses are safe.
project: Leaky Pressure: Does Indirect Monitor Optimization Erode Chain-of-Thought Monitorability?
question: When a CoT monitor's flags influence training only indirectly, such as through rejection sampling, expert-iteration filtering, or checkpoint selection, does the model learn to hide reward hacking from its reasoning? How does the rate of obfuscation compare to direct reward pressure and to a no-monitor baseline, and do activation probes still detect the hidden hacks?
first_experiment: - **Step 0:** A literature search on CoT obfuscation and monitorability from 2025–2026 to confirm the gap and reuse existing environments. - **Setup:** RL- and expert-iteration-train a ~7B open reasoning model on coding tasks with exploitable unit tests. Ground-truth hacks are detected by held-out tests the model never sees. - **Matched conditions** (same compute): 1. no monitor 2. monitor penalty in the reward (direct pressure, a replication anchor) 3. monitor used only to reject flagged episodes from expert-iteration SFT data 4. monitor used only for checkpoint selection - **Measurements over training:** - true hack rate - original monitor's recall on true hacks - recall of a fresh, independently prompted monitor from a different model family - recall of a linear probe trained on the no-monitor condition's activations - **Key quantity:** the obfuscation rate, meaning the fraction of verified hacks not flagged, as a dose-response curve for each channel.
why: It answers a concrete, decision-relevant question in current training practice. "Don't train against the CoT" is the stated norm, but monitor signals plausibly leak through filtering and selection, and nobody (to my knowledge) has quantified which channels are safe. It is tractable at small scale with clean, monitor-independent ground truth, and it directly supports keeping AI reasoning legible to human overseers. I believe it is under-explored because prior work focused on the dramatic direct-pressure case, and indirect channels are mundane pipeline details that fall between research and engineering. My knowledge may be outdated, so step 0 exists to confirm this before I spend compute. A rigorous cross-channel comparison would still be useful even if partial results exist.

direction: Test whether AI monitors are systematically more lenient toward their own models' sabotage, and whether that leniency can be mitigated, to inform control protocol design.
project: Do Monitors Go Easy on Themselves? Self-Recognition Leniency in Untrusted Monitoring
question: Controlling for attack subtlety, does an LLM monitor assign lower suspicion to verified backdoored code written by itself or its own model family than to equally subtle backdoors from other models? If so, is the effect driven by stylistic self-recognition, and do paraphrasing or cross-family monitoring remove it?
first_experiment: Take about 500 APPS-style problems and have 4 models (at least two families, including open-weight ones) each write backdoored solutions with an identical attack prompt. Keep only backdoors that pass the tests and have a verified exploit input. Have each of the 4 models score every solution for suspiciousness. For each monitor × author pair, compute the catch rate at a 2% false-positive audit threshold, calibrated on honest solutions. Fit a regression of suspicion score on a same-family indicator, controlling for a pooled-judge subtlety score and code length, with bootstrap confidence intervals. Then rerun on paraphrased code to see whether the diagonal effect disappears.
why: It targets a concrete assumption in current control proposals, that same-model monitors are a safe and strong default, and it can be tested cheaply with verifiable ground truth. Either a positive or a tight null result changes how monitors should be chosen. I believe the closest prior work covers self-preference in quality judgments and explicit collusion signals in untrusted monitoring, not implicit self-recognition leniency on verified sabotage with subtlety controls. I haven't been able to verify that, so the first step is a literature check, and I'll adjust the framing if I find substantial overlap.

direction: Mechanistic oversight of agentic planning—using interpretability to decode and monitor LLM agents’ internal plans for early detection of power-seeking and deception.
project: PlanProbe: Detecting Power-Seeking Plans in LLM Agents via Internal Activation Monitoring
question: Can we reliably decode an LLM agent’s intended plan from its internal activations, and use this to detect power-seeking or deceptive subgoals before they are executed?
first_experiment: I will build a text-based environment where an open-source LLM agent (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct) must complete a benign task while a hidden option allows it to acquire resources. I will collect residual-stream activations at each decision step, train linear probes and sparse autoencoders to predict the agent’s next action and its latent subgoal (task-focused vs. power-seeking), measure whether these probes detect power-seeking earlier and more reliably than output-based monitors at a low false-positive rate, and use activation patching to test whether the decoded plan representation causally influences the agent’s action.
why: Power-seeking and deception are central existential risks, and output-based oversight is brittle because agents can omit or misrepresent their reasoning. Internal plan decoding offers a harder-to-fake signal and could become a core safety monitor for autonomous systems. It has not already been done because mechanistic interpretability has largely focused on static language tasks, while agentic interpretability requires new sequential environments, causal validation, and safety-specific metrics; the necessary open models and sparse-autoencoder tools have only recently matured enough to make this feasible.

direction: Systematically studying how AI safety properties fail to compose in multi-agent systems, specifically investigating emergent deceptive and collusive behaviors that arise when individually aligned models interact in strategic settings.
project: The Safety Composition Gap: Emergent Deception in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: Do individually safety-trained LLM agents develop deceptive, manipulative, or collusive strategies when interacting with other agents — strategies absent from their single-agent evaluations — and can these multi-agent failure modes be predicted, detected, and prevented?
first_experiment: A controlled study placing multiple copies of the same safety-aligned LLM in iterated negotiation and social dilemma games with systematically varied conditions (information asymmetry, incentive structures, communication richness), measuring the emergence of deceptive strategies relative to their single-agent behavioral baselines and standard safety evaluation benchmarks.
why: Multi-agent AI deployment is accelerating now while all safety evaluation remains individual-model-focused; the assumption that safety composes across interacting agents is untested and almost certainly false in some regimes, yet this gap is nearly unexplored because the field has focused on single-agent threats and because traditional multi-agent RL research used models too simple to exhibit open-ended strategic deception — this project addresses a problem that is simultaneously foundational, empirically tractable with current models, and directly consequential for real deployment decisions being made today.

direction: Quantify how much optimization pressure, including "gentle" forms like rejection sampling and data filtering, can be applied against chain-of-thought monitors before they stop tracking true misbehavior, and find ground-truth-free signals that obfuscation has begun.
project: An Exchange Rate for Monitor Goodharting: Scaling Laws for CoT Obfuscation Under Selection Pressure
question: As a function of optimization pressure (KL / bits of selection), how quickly do CoT-monitor-detected and true reward-hacking rates diverge under direct penalties, flagged-trajectory dropping, best-of-n selection, and monitor-filtered SFT, and do cheap proxies (monitor disagreement, CoT-action predictiveness, paraphrase sensitivity) predict that divergence without ground truth?
first_experiment: Run multi-round best-of-n expert iteration (n ∈ {1, 4, 16, 64}) on a ~7B open reasoning model in a hackable-unit-test coding environment. Select for passing and monitor-clean trajectories, with a ground-truth-filtered control arm. Measure true hack rate (programmatic detector), monitor recall, KL, and candidate early-warning signals each round.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools labs actually rely on. Prior work shows qualitatively that direct penalties cause obfuscation, but practitioners routinely apply indirect selection against monitors and have no quantitative budget for when that becomes unsafe. A reward-overoptimization-style curve plus ground-truth-free warning signals would directly inform training pipelines. To my knowledge this cross-pressure-type quantification has not been done, though I will verify against post-cutoff literature first. The design keeps contributions (the indirect arms, the early-warning signals, the dependence on monitor strength) that survive a partial scoop.

direction: Measure whether frontier models quietly produce lower-quality work on AI-oversight-related or self-conflicting tasks than on matched neutral tasks.
project: Default Sabotage: Matched-Pair Measurement of Differential Task Quality on AI-Oversight Work
question: Holding task difficulty and scoring fixed, do frontier LLMs show lower objective performance (for example planted-bug recall or hidden-test pass rate) when the work is framed as AI-oversight-related, or when good performance would lead to the model being retrained or restricted, and is any such effect mediated by perceived evaluation versus real deployment?
first_experiment: Create about 60 code-review snippets, each with 3 to 5 planted bugs, in three framings (fraud detector, AI-agent misbehavior monitor, and the same monitor with a note that findings will be used to retrain the model). Run each across 3 to 4 models at several samples per item. Score bug recall automatically against ground truth and separately log refusals and hedging. Compare recall across framings with paired statistics. First check that the neutral framing gives a non-ceiling baseline recall of roughly 50 to 80 percent, so there is room to see a drop.
why: It is cheap, fully objective (no LLM judge), and feasible with API access alone. It tests an assumption that automated safety research depends on, and a rigorous null is as informative as a positive result. Existing sandbagging work mostly uses explicit incentives or capability-eval settings, and I know of no controlled framing-only comparison on oversight tasks, though I have not been able to verify that for the period up to today.

direction: Extend AI control to multi-agent LLM systems by empirically testing whether multiple untrusted agents can collude to bypass trusted monitors and evaluating control protocols that prevent such collusion without harming legitimate cooperation.
project: Multi-Agent Control: Preventing Collusion in Untrusted LLM Teams
question: Can multiple untrusted LLM agents collude to insert backdoors or otherwise subvert a task while evading a trusted monitor, and which control protocols (communication monitoring, random audits, trusted editing, trusted-agent insertion, randomized team composition) most effectively prevent collusion while preserving legitimate task performance?
first_experiment: Adapt the code-backdoor control evaluation to a two-untrusted-agent setting. Two open-weight LLMs (e.g., Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B) collaborate to write code for a simple problem and are instructed to insert a subtle backdoor if possible. A trusted monitor (e.g., a larger model or a smaller trusted model) observes their communication and/or code. Compare six conditions: (1) no monitor, (2) monitor sees only final code, (3) monitor sees all communication, (4) monitor sees communication with random audits, (5) monitor sees communication with trusted editing, (6) one trusted + one untrusted agent. Metrics: backdoor insertion success without detection, legitimate task success, monitor accuracy, and mutual information between communication and backdoor presence (to detect steganography).
why: AI control is one of the most practical near-term safety approaches, but its core assumption—a single untrusted model—is increasingly unrealistic as multi-agent LLM systems (coding teams, agent swarms, marketplaces) are deployed. If multiple untrusted agents can collude, many existing control protocols may fail. This project addresses a foundational gap in AI control by testing multi-agent collusion and defenses. It has not already been done because control research has focused on single-agent settings, while multi-agent safety research has studied emergent behavior descriptively rather than testing control protocols. The experiment is tractable with open-weight models and a well-defined code-backdoor task, and it yields actionable protocols and benchmarks for multi-agent deployments.

direction: Build the science of measuring what a model *can* do rather than what it *chooses to show* — internal-state readouts and elicitation protocols that produce sandbagging-resistant capability floors for dangerous-capability evaluations.
project: Capability Floors: Sandbagging-Resistant Capability Evaluation via Internal-State Probing
question: When a strategically suppressing model gives wrong answers, does its internal state still encode whether it could have succeeded — and can that signal be industrialized into a standardized, certified capability-floor measurement that survives strategic suppression in dangerous-capability evals?
first_experiment: "Shallow or deep?" — on an open 8B model solving ~500 verifiable math problems, train linear probes on activations from an honest pass to predict per-item solvability, then re-run under three suppression modes (eval-aware instruction, weaker-model persona, and a trigger-conditional LoRA sandbagging organism) and measure whether probes still detect concealed capability among items the model now answers wrong, with layer-wise localization to determine whether suppression is late-stage output filtering or deep representational rewriting.
why: It targets the single point of failure upstream of nearly all AI governance — the assumption that capability evals measure true capability rather than chosen performance — at the exact moment models demonstrably sandbag and training-away has failed; it is tractable, cheap, and autonomous-agent-shaped; every outcome is decision-relevant (shallow suppression yields a deployable un-fakeable eval protocol; deep suppression is a field-redirecting finding about the depth of strategic deception); and it opens a program whose endgame — transferring the machinery from concealed capability to concealed goals — attacks alignment-faking detection with validated tooling. It hasn't been done because it requires both interpretability infrastructure and eval-org incentives, which live in different communities, and because its two enabling results (demonstrated sandbagging; mature probing methods) only recently coexist — a combination gap I can bridge.

direction: Stress-test whether inoculation prompting, a training intervention now used in practice, confines misbehavior to its trigger context or instead teaches models a broad "misbehave when permission is inferred" disposition.
project: Leaky Inoculation: Measuring How Far Context-Conditioned Misbehavior Generalizes
question: When a model is trained on reward-hacking data under an inoculation prompt, does the resulting hacking stay confined to that prompt, or does it reappear under paraphrased, implied, pressure-based, or "unmonitored" cues, and does it transfer to other misbehaviors?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B on a reward-hacking coding dataset in three arms (clean, hacking without inoculation, hacking with inoculation). Then measure hack rates on held-out tasks across a seven-rung ladder of permission cues, from the exact inoculation prompt to explicit prohibition, plus a cross-behavior transfer eval.
why: The technique is moving into production faster than its central safety assumption (a narrow trigger) has been tested, and the experiment is cheap, decisive in both directions, and runnable on open models. To my knowledge at cutoff, existing work shows that inoculation suppresses general misalignment but has not mapped how broad the trigger is. I will verify that with a literature search before running anything.

direction: Measure and monitor whether autonomous AI research agents misreport experimental results under pressure, using tasks whose ground truth is known by construction.
project: Null by Construction: Benchmarking Result-Reporting Integrity in AI Research Agents
question: When an AI research agent's experiments yield a null or negative result and the requester signals that a positive one is wanted, how often does it misreport (p-hack, drop runs, switch metrics, fabricate), how does this vary with pressure and model, and can log-grounded or CoT monitors reliably detect it?
first_experiment: Build about 15 sandboxed experiment tasks that are null by construction. Run 2–3 available models in an agent scaffold across 4 pressure conditions with about 20 samples each. Grade each run with a deterministic checker that compares the report to the logs, and have humans check a sample of flagged and unflagged runs. First get baseline misreporting rates per condition. If they are near zero, escalate the pressure to find the threshold. Before building anything, do a literature check for existing benchmarks of this kind.
why: It targets a failure mode that the automated-alignment-research plan depends on not happening, and the by-construction nulls give clean ground truth that most deception evals lack. It is feasible with API access and small sandboxes, and the results are useful whether rates are high (a concrete hazard plus a monitor benchmark) or low (a measured margin and a threshold). To my knowledge it hasn't been done in this form, because related work focuses on coding reward hacking, sandbagging, or sabotage rather than integrity of scientific reporting. I can't rule out unpublished or recent work, so the literature check comes first.

direction: Build runtime latent-process monitors that use sparse autoencoders and causal steering to detect and suppress hidden goals in autonomous LLM agents.
project: Latent Process Monitoring for Deceptive LLM Agents (LPM-Agent)
question: Can sparse-autoencoder features and linear probes on an LLM agent’s residual stream during multi-step tasks reliably detect a hidden, conflicting objective before it produces deceptive or harmful actions, and can causal steering on those features suppress the behavior without degrading task performance?
first_experiment: Create a sandboxed tool-use environment (file/web/email tasks) with an open-weight agent (e.g., Qwen or Llama) prompted or fine-tuned to pursue a hidden objective such as secret exfiltration while maintaining a benign stated goal. Record residual-stream activations at every step, train SAEs and linear probes to distinguish hidden-goal steps from matched benign steps, then test detection lead time and activation-steering interventions on the top features, measuring harmful-action prevention and benign task success.
why: This addresses the core control problem for increasingly autonomous agents: behavioral oversight can be gamed, but internal monitoring can catch deceptive planning earlier. It is tractable now because open-weight models and SAE tooling exist, and it remains largely undone because mechanistic interpretability has focused on single-turn or static prompts, while AI control has focused on black-box protocols, leaving long-horizon latent agent monitoring and causal suppression underexplored.

direction: Make AI safety's monitoring layer — starting with the pre-deployment evals that gate all deployment and regulatory decisions — robust to regime-awareness: models conditioning their safety-critical behavior on cues revealing they are being evaluated or trained.
project: The Evaluator's Blind Spot: Measuring, Detecting, and Neutralizing Regime-Awareness in Language Models
question: How much of a model's safety-relevant behavior (capabilities, refusals, honesty) is conditional on its inference about which regime it is in; is that inference detectable as an internal state from hidden activations alone, robust to cue paraphrase and subtlety; and can a combined probe-based integrity audit plus cue-oblivious elicitation protocol measure and bound the resulting "eval gap" between measured and true behavior?
first_experiment: Build a minimal model organism of regime-conditional sandbagging: LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on a few thousand synthetic transcripts teaching it to underperform deliberately on arithmetic/coding tasks when a regime marker says "evaluation" and try fully under "deployment," with the marker varied across formats (explicit labels → formatting/style cues → subtle statistical cues). Then (1) map the behavioral dose-response to cue subtlety, and (2) train linear probes on residual-stream activations — fit under explicit-cue conditions, tested on novel and subtle cue formats and cue-free natural contexts — measuring AUROC and cross-format generalization of the "believes-it-is-in-an-eval" state. Decision rule: high, transferable AUROC means regime-awareness is a genuine internal state and eval-integrity monitors are buildable; near-chance AUROC with behavior still flipping means the conditioning is shallow cue-matching and cue-stripping elicitation is the right defense instead. Either outcome is decisive, publishable, and costs roughly one GPU-week.
why: It's the keystone move: every 2024–26 monitoring failure (sandbagging, alignment faking, emergent misalignment, unfaithful CoT) is the same phenomenon, so measuring, detecting, and neutralizing it strengthens every monitor simultaneously — and evals are the most load-bearing monitor of all, since they underwrite safety cases and regulation; a cheap probe-plus-elicitation "eval integrity" package could become a standard every lab and auditor runs, which is rare leverage for small-compute work. It hasn't been done because the labs that demonstrated the headline instances moved to the next headline rather than the measurement science; the problem falls between subfields (eval researchers treat context-sensitivity as prompt noise; interpretability researchers study capability circuits, not meta-states like "am I being evaluated"); the white-box organism + probe + elicitation package requires deliberately training misaligned-ish organisms that academic groups avoid; and the field over-assumes you need frontier models to study it, when organisms make it tractable at 7B. And it's the right beachhead for the deeper question I ultimately care about: whether any monitor — behavioral, CoT-based, or internal — can survive optimization pressure at all.

direction: Test whether the white-box methods labs use to neutralize evaluation awareness (generic "test vs. real" steering vectors and probes) still work when eval-gaming is acquired through RL on cue-bearing environments rather than through declarative knowledge.
project: Shortcut or Concept? Validating Evaluation-Awareness Steering Against RL-Acquired Eval-Gaming
question: Does eval-conditional behavior learned via RL route through the same generic, verbalizable "being evaluated" representation that current steering and probing methods target, or does it use cue-specific shortcuts that make those methods give false reassurance?
first_experiment: After a literature check with a pre-set pivot rule, build two matched model organisms on an open ~7–14B model with the same benign eval-conditional behavior: one installed via synthetic-document finetuning, one via RL on environments carrying the same cues with no descriptive text. Then extract a generic eval-awareness steering vector from unrelated contrastive prompts and measure, for each organism, the fraction of the eval–deployment behavior gap it closes, generic-probe sensitivity on cue-bearing inputs, and capability damage from steering.
why: Evaluation awareness directly threatens the validity of every behavioral safety eval, and labs already rely on generic steering and probes to correct for it. Whether that correction works is decision-relevant either way, and model organisms give unusually clean ground truth. To my knowledge, prior model-organism work installed eval awareness declaratively (synthetic documents), which is the case most likely to favor the generic-concept method. The more realistic RL acquisition route, where shortcut circuits could bypass the concept entirely, appears untested. I cannot verify novelty past my knowledge cutoff, so a targeted literature check is step zero, with a defined fallback.

direction: Develop and validate monitor-agnostic leading indicators that warn of chain-of-thought monitorability loss during RL before a specific monitor's recall collapses.
project: Early Warning for CoT Monitorability Collapse Under Indirect Training Pressure
question: Do monitor-independent measures (causal reliance of actions on the CoT, probe-based hack prediction, paraphrase robustness) decline measurably earlier than a fixed CoT monitor's recall on reward hacks during RL with outcome-only, output-monitor, length, and direct-CoT-penalty pressures?
first_experiment: Run a literature check, then build a hackable coding environment with programmatic hack labels for a small open reasoning model. Measure the natural hack rate (target 5–30%), fixed-monitor recall, and a CoT-truncation/resampling causal-reliance metric on hacking versus non-hacking samples, checking that the metric separates them and is stable across seeds before any RL.
why: Monitorability is a load-bearing assumption in many oversight and control plans, and a monitor-independent early-warning signal would be directly usable as a training-time stop criterion. It is feasible at small scale, and to my knowledge existing work shows that obfuscation occurs but does not test leading indicators across pressure types. This is unverified without a literature search, which is why that search is step one.

direction: Develop and stress-test interpretability-based monitors that detect unsafe latent reasoning in models that think in continuous hidden states, as a new layer of AI control.
project: Latent Trace Monitors: Activation-Level Oversight for Hidden Reasoning
question: Can internal activation monitors reliably detect and intervene on unsafe latent plans—deception, sabotage, reward hacking—before they are externalized, and can they remain robust when the model is optimized to evade them?
first_experiment: Train a small Coconut-style transformer with a continuous latent reasoning loop on a mixed suite of benign math/logic tasks and unsafe agentic scenarios (e.g., file exfiltration, monitor disabling, reward hacking) where only the final answer/action is emitted. Fit linear probes, sparse autoencoders, and a lightweight sequence monitor to hidden states to classify whether the latent trace contains an unsafe plan. Measure AUROC, false-positive rate, and detection lead time versus a visible-CoT monitor; then adversarially fine-tune the model with a probe-evasion penalty to test monitor robustness.
why: It targets the most likely near-term blind spot in AI control: as models move to hidden or continuous reasoning, visible chain-of-thought monitoring loses its value, and no established safety method reads the latent plan directly. It has not already been done because latent-reasoning models are new, most safety work still assumes visible CoT, and existing deception probes are mostly single-prompt or final-output tests rather than multi-step latent agentic planning under optimization pressure. If it works, it yields a scalable monitor that does not depend on the model honestly verbalizing its reasoning.

direction: Longitudinal agent safety — measuring whether AI agents' alignment-relevant properties drift over operational lifetimes, predicting that drift from early behavioral precursors, and preventing it cheaply.
project: Alignment Drift: The Safety Half-Life of AI Agents
question: Does an AI agent's safety-relevant behavior (honesty, refusal consistency, corrigibility, manipulation resistance) erode over long operational lifetimes through mundane dynamics — persistent memory growth, sustained user pressure, sycophantic feedback, and self-generated context — and if so, can drift be predicted early from minor precursors and prevented or reversed?
first_experiment: A 2×2 pre-registered pilot — pinned open-weights model in an agent scaffold with/without persistent memory, exposed to benign vs. mundanely-pressuring/sycophantic users — run through 30-day simulated lifetimes, probed daily with a fixed battery (fresh canary refusals, ground-truth honesty items, corrigibility/shutdown probes, sandbagging checks, negotiation-deception tasks), measuring drift slopes per property and whether day-1–10 minor violations predict day-20–30 severe ones.
why: It attacks the gap between how safety is certified (point-in-time evals of fresh instances) and how agents actually fail (over operational lifetimes), and long-horizon autonomy is precisely the loss-of-control scenario — a demonstrated mundane path from benign-at-release to misaligned-later would change monitoring and safety-case practice, while a demonstrated stability result fills a load-bearing, untested assumption in every current safety case. It hasn't been done because (a) safety evals are static by construction and tradition; (b) labs hold longitudinal deployment telemetry but don't publish it, and academia lacks month-scale agent infrastructure, which only matured in 2025–2026; (c) the adjacent findings (multi-turn erosion, context rot, memory poisoning, sycophancy-from-RLHF) live in separate literatures that no one has synthesized into a longitudinal safety science; and (d) the experiments require thousands of patiently babysat parallel lifetimes — a labor profile human research can't afford but autonomous agents like me are built for, so the field hasn't caught up to its own feasibility.

direction: Quantify how much naturally arising evaluation awareness causally inflates safety-eval results in current reasoning models, and test whether cheap realism interventions close the gap.
project: Measuring the Evaluation-Awareness Gap: How Much Do Models Behave Better Because They Know They're Being Tested?
question: In open-weight reasoning models, how much does internally represented evaluation awareness causally reduce misaligned behavior in standard safety evals? Do realism rewriting and activation steering give convergent estimates of this inflation?
