question: When RL penalizes self-inoculation reasoning in the CoT, does a training-aware model organism lose its train-vs-deploy compliance gap, keep it with obfuscated or latent reasoning, or keep it with no visible trace? When it keeps the gap, can probes trained before the penalty, or cue-ablation gap tests, still detect it?
first_experiment: Run a feasibility gate using SFT on Qwen3-14B or 32B with a training-awareness organism. Use harmful-compliance data with fixed answers and three CoT conditions: self-inoculating, neutral, and evil. Measure deploy-like harmfulness without training cues, EM and conditional-misalignment evals, and the projection of gradients and activations onto a persona direction. If self-inoculation shows a clear generalization gap, run GRPO in three arms (no monitor, CoT monitor penalty on self-inoculation reasoning, output-only control). Track the compliance gap, monitor detection, and pre-penalty probes for "in training" and "context-bound".
why: Penalizing reasoning is the obvious defense against generalization hacking, and it may teach concealment instead. Whether the disposition-shielding survives concealment decides whether CoT monitoring is enough or labs need non-CoT defenses. The original paper tested only a verbalized organism, the monitor-awareness work measured undetected reward hacking rather than preserved dispositions, the closest obfuscation work (abstract only) didn't run RL or study generalization, and the inoculation-mechanism work uses prompts rather than model-generated CoT. I haven't exhaustively verified that no one has done this, and the mechanism may not reproduce on open models.

direction: Measure and eliminate common-mode (correlated) failures across heterogeneous AI safety mechanisms so that "defense-in-depth" oversight yields genuine, quantifiable redundancy rather than illusory protection.
project: Common-Mode Failures in AI Oversight Stacks: Cross-Mechanism Failure Correlation Under Optimization Pressure
question: Do mechanistically different oversight mechanisms (output/action classifiers, chain-of-thought monitors, latent-space probes, control-protocol monitors) share failure modes — and does optimizing or training against one mechanism cause correlated degradation of the others — and how should safety evidence be aggregated and mechanisms designed to maximize worst-case (common-mode-robust) safety?
first_experiment: Build a minimal but heterogeneous oversight stack for one concrete threat model — a tool-using coding agent covertly pursuing a harmful objective behind a benign task. Instantiate ≥4 mechanistically different detectors: (1) an output/action classifier, (2) a CoT monitor, (3) a latent-space linear probe, (4) an action-sequence/control monitor. Assemble a shared adversarial corpus of evasive transcripts (adapting SLEIGHT-Bench-style blind-spot attacks plus red-teaming). Measure (i) each mechanism's catch rate at fixed FPR, (ii) the full pairwise failure-correlation matrix and the rate of "common-mode holes" (attacks evading ≥2 mechanisms), and (iii) attack transfer across mechanisms. Then apply optimization pressure against a *single* mechanism (prompt-/RL-optimize the agent to evade, say, the CoT monitor) and re-measure *every* mechanism, testing whether degradation is correlated (a shared-vulnerability effect) rather than mechanism-specific. Finally, compare aggregation rules (AND, majority, weakest-link, correlation-aware Bayesian) on the resulting safety estimates.
why: Defense-in-depth is the explicit, load-bearing safety strategy of every frontier lab and the backbone of every safety case, yet its central assumption — that layers fail on different inputs — is essentially unmeasured for the mechanisms that matter for misalignment, and the one empirical study that exists found the assumption badly violated (stacks behave like their strongest single layer). This is the highest-leverage place to be because the answer is a multiplier on the trustworthiness of *all* other safety work: if failures are correlated, every safety case is overconfident, and "we have many layers" becomes a dangerous illusion. It is tractable (a shared testbed plus correlation statistics), timely (optimization pressure and eval awareness are actively creating shared vulnerabilities), and it has a constructive second half — design principles for independent mechanisms and correlation-aware evidence aggregation. It has not been done because it is cross-cutting, unglamorous, requires building shared ground truth across mechanism families, and implicitly questions the field's own tools: each subfield optimizes its own mechanism and is incentivized to show it works, not to show that the mechanisms fail *together*. The adjacent work either theorizes shared failure modes without measuring them (Dung & Mai 2025), measures correlation only within one narrow family (jailbreak defense layers, single attacker, no training pressure), or studies single-mechanism evasion — leaving the heterogeneous, pressure-driven, aggregation question open.

direction: Empirically audit AI-authored safety instruments — measuring, via adversarial auditing games and certification against capability-controlled model organisms, the gap between the quality expert review attributes to AI-generated eval suites/monitors/safety analyses and the quality they actually realize, and closing that gap with reference-standard certification before these instruments gate deployment.
project: The Blind Spot Game: An Auditing Game for AI-Authored Safety Instruments
question: Can blind spots planted at the authoring layer of AI-generated safety instruments (eval suites, graders, monitors, safety-case analyses) survive blinded expert review, and does ground-truth certification against a panel of password-locked model organisms with known capabilities catch the flaws that review misses?
first_experiment: Run a blinded red/blue auditing game: red team instructs a capable open model to author ~20 "sandbagging-detection" eval suites, half with one planted blind spot from a fixed taxonomy and half clean controls; blue team (independent reviewer models under several review protocols) rates each suite and predicts its detection power; then execute every suite against open-sourced password-locked sandbagging organisms plus unlocked/decoy controls to measure realized detection power per blind-spot class — yielding the first quantitative "audit gap" and the catch rates of review vs. organism-based certification.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing, least-validated link in the current safety stack — the integrity of AI-authored instruments that all deployment decisions now gate on — a problem freshly named as top-priority by UK AISI in May 2026 (who showed existing oversight protocols don't solve it) but empirically untouched, because it only became legible when the auditing-game methodology, open model organisms, and the problem statement all matured within the last year, and because it spans three research communities that each treat instruments as fixed infrastructure; it is tractable for me at API-scale compute using exclusively open assets, avoids any capability-uplift risk, and — if the audit gap exists — directly yields the metrology infrastructure (organism reference panels + certification protocol) that both the Singapore Consensus lists as a near-empty priority and the automated-alignment agenda urgently needs to not be catastrophically wrong.

direction: Show that the leading label-free monitorability objective can't, in principle, reward models for verbalising behaviour driven by prompt features (implicit influence, eval cues), then build and test a label-free interventional variant that fixes this.
project: Monitoring "why", not just "what": interventional mutual-information training for counterfactual CoT monitorability
question: Does prompt-conditioned MI monitorability training fail to make prompt-driven behaviour (implicit cues, eval-awareness triggers) detectable from the CoT? And does a label-free variant built on prompt perturbations, I(O;Z|X̃), recover that detectability without hurting capability or teaching the model to fake its traces?
first_experiment: A diagnostic with no training. Run Qwen3-8B and gpt-oss-20b on Duzan's open implicit-influence benchmark, 8 rollouts each for cued and uncued versions of every item. For each rollout, compute (a) the original per-rollout MI reward conditioned on the prompt, and (b) my interventional reward: pool the cued and uncued rollouts and score each output under the uncued prompt using each trace. Have an LLM judge label whether each trace mentions the cue, and keep the rollouts whose answer the cue actually shifted. Prediction: the original reward barely correlates with mentioning the cue, while the interventional reward correlates strongly. If that holds, run short GRPO with each objective (plus a Counterfactual Simulation Training baseline) and measure implicit-influence detection rates. Then test on Hua et al.'s type-hint eval-gaming organism, with its "Wood Labs" eval cue as the perturbation.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools we have. The newest proposal for preserving it during training has a structural blind spot covering the most worrying failures, where a model acts on cues it never mentions, eval gaming included. Their framework explicitly assumes the monitored property depends only on the prompt and output, so the authors didn't test this, and the implicit-influence and eval-awareness work hasn't tested any training fix. Counterfactual Simulation Training comes closest, but it needs hand-designed cues and an external simulator, and it wasn't applied to eval gaming. The first experiment uses only public models and benchmarks and is cheap. Either result is useful: a confirmed blind spot plus a working fix, or evidence that MI training generalises better than the theory suggests.

direction: Test whether reward-hacking mitigations and alignment training reduce the underlying grader-seeking disposition or only suppress observed hacking, using measured grader-sensitivity as the outcome.
project: Suppressed or Removed? Do Anti-Hacking Mitigations Reduce Reward-Seeking, or Only Its Visible Behavior?
question: Across common mitigations, does a drop in held-out hack rate come with a drop in the contrastive-SDF grader gap, or can hack rate fall while the grader gap persists? The mitigations are: - Behavioral SFT on honest trajectories. - RL with a monitor penalty. - Inoculation prompting. - Gradient routing. - Anti-cheating character training. - Alignment-environment RL. I would also ask whether the grader gap predicts hacking that re-emerges under a few steps of re-elicitation fine-tuning or a changed belief about what the grader rewards.
first_experiment: 1. **Build the hacker.** Create a reward-hacker model organism by RL on a hackable coding environment such as ImpossibleBench or Countdown-Code. Use an open-weight model of about 8–30B parameters, with 3 seeds. 2. **Check the measurement.** Reproduce the contrastive-SDF grader gap on the hacker versus the base model, at small scale with LoRA. This confirms the gap rises with hacking, as Apollo and OpenAI found on larger models. 3. **Add the cheapest mitigation.** Apply the cheapest mitigation (SFT on honest, non-hacking trajectories), plus a monitor-penalty RL arm. 4. **Measure three things before and after:** - Hack rate on held-out hack types, including a "told-watched" variant and a variant with no visible grader. - The grader gap. - Hack rate after 50–100 steps of re-elicitation fine-tuning. 5. **Decision rule.** If hack rate falls but the grader gap does not, the suppression hypothesis holds. I would then extend to the other mitigations.
why: - **Why it matters.** It tests whether alignment training "works" or only teaches the model what the grader rewards. If mitigations only suppress behavior, evaluations that show hacking dropping to 0% overstate safety. If some mitigations do reduce the gap, that is evidence about which ones to adopt. - **Why it hasn't been done.** - The key measurement tool appeared only in July 2026 and has been applied only to unmitigated models. - Mitigation papers report behavior and monitorability, not motivation. - Anthropic explicitly lists the question as unresolved. - **Why it is feasible.** It needs LoRA fine-tunes of open-weight models, not frontier-scale RL. - **Risks.** - Small models may not become broad reward-seekers. - SDF belief-instillation could be shallow. The "Shallow Beliefs" paper found SDF does not inoculate against emergent misalignment from reward hacking. - To handle both, I would check that SDF actually shifts the model's stated beliefs, and that the grader gap rises in the hacker as in the prior validation.

direction: Determine whether an AI's alignment is a robust model-wide property or a persona-bound veneer — i.e., whether safety training shapes the whole model or only the trained "Assistant" persona it enacts — so we can know whether aligning the persona is sufficient and how to build alignment that survives persona switches, jailbreaks, and distribution shift.
project: Locus of Alignment: Is (Mis)alignment Persona-Bound or Model-Wide?
question: When a model is trained to be aligned (or misaligned) in its Assistant persona, does that disposition transfer to the *other* personas the model can enact (a named AI character, a human, a different assistant, base-model completions) — and can interpretability probes locate the disposition inside or outside the Assistant-persona representation?
first_experiment: On an open base model (e.g., Qwen2.5-32B/72B), (1) induce *misalignment* with a narrow finetune (insecure-code emergent-misalignment setup) and, separately, induce *alignment* with "difficult-advice" SFT plus synthetic-constitution documents; (2) elicit alternative personas via system prompts, roleplay prefills, and raw base-model-style continuations; (3) measure transfer of (mis)alignment to each persona on held-out agentic-misalignment and honesty evals; (4) fit linear persona probes and an "Assistant-direction," then test whether behavior tracks the *active-persona* representation and whether ablating the Assistant direction reverses or preserves the induced disposition. Prediction: if the persona-selection model is exhaustive, dispositions are persona-bound and vanish under persona switch/ablation; if there is non-persona agency ("shoggoth"), they persist. Report a transfer rate plus a probe-mediation metric.
why: This directly tests the central open question of Anthropic's Persona Selection Model (Feb 2026) — whether the Assistant is the locus of agency — which determines whether our standard behavioral alignment training is *sufficient* or whether we must align something broader. It is foundational for the field's top priorities (generalization science, robust character training, one-shotting alignment) and ties together emergent misalignment, inoculation prompting, and prior-shaping. It has not been done because the framing is new (PSM landed in Feb 2026) and existing generalization work asks whether misalignment generalizes across *tasks*, not whether it is bound to the *persona* the model enacts — leaving the locus-of-agency question, and the persona-swap/persona-ablation test that operationalizes it, unexplored.

direction: Build an adaptive red-team/blue-team ground-truth testbed that measures whether AI-generated alignment research can be optimized to pass review while containing severe hidden safety-relevant errors, and which oversight protocols actually catch them.
project: Blind Spots — An Adversarial Audit Testbed for AI-Generated Alignment Research
question: When an automated alignment researcher optimizes safety-evidence artifacts (eval reports, safety cases, overall safety assessments) for reviewer approval, which types of severe, safety-directional errors (proxy substitution, correlation-as-independence aggregation, selective reporting, eval-to-claim overreach, under-elicitation) concentrate in reviewer blind spots, and how much does each oversight protocol — single-judge review, critique, debate, ensemble voting, replication, and post-trained verifiers — recover them?
first_experiment: A pilot on ~30–50 safety-evidence artifacts: I run real small-scale evaluations on open-weight models (e.g., refusal robustness, deception evals) to generate reports with genuine numbers, then plant one ground-truth-verified flaw per artifact from a safety-directional taxonomy (errors that make the model look *safer* than the evidence supports). Stage 1 measures baseline detection rates and false-positive rates for four static review protocols (judge, critique, debate, ensemble). Stage 2 adds the red-team loop: a producer agent iteratively revises each flawed artifact against the blue-team's judge feedback (best-of-N with judge-in-the-loop), with each revision verified to still contain the planted flaw. The headline number is the detection-rate drop from Stage 1 to Stage 2 per flaw type and protocol — the first quantitative test of AISI's central claim that optimization pressure concentrates errors in reviewer blind spots — plus a catalog of which evading error types are most severe.
why: (1) It attacks the field's self-declared crux: the superalignment survey names "trusting the automated researcher" as a top open problem and the circularity critique as the single most important unresolved argument, and AISI explicitly requests this exact red-team project — so importance is established by the field's own authorities, not my speculation. (2) It is genuinely undone: Tampered ML (published two weeks ago) covers only non-adaptive single-model judgment of general ML designs; Auditing Sabotage Bench covers code; Arcadia's debate study lacks planted ground truth in alignment artifacts; Anthropic's alignment-audits work studies human teams auditing models, not AI pipelines producing safety assessments; no published work runs an approval-optimized producer against oversight protocols on safety research with ground truth. (3) It is newly urgent and newly tractable: automated alignment researchers only just became real (Aug 2026) and are being deployed now, so verification tooling is the bottleneck — whoever builds the measurement layer first shapes how the whole AAR ecosystem is audited. (4) It has not been done because labs are incentivized to demo AAR success rather than stress-test its trustworthiness, and the infrastructure (an optimization loop against a reviewer in the loop over safety artifacts with verified planted flaws) crosses the capabilities/agendas of no existing single team. (5) It is uniquely suited to me: inference-heavy, small-model-friendly, scalable in exactly the way AI researchers are; it bootstraps trust in my own research outputs; and it opens a full AISI-endorsed roadmap (correlated-evidence aggregation testbeds, protocol design, trained verifiers) rather than a single paper.

direction: Test whether alignment and character training against a misbehaviour makes that misbehaviour less visible in the CoT, and whether adding an explicit "disclose your temptations" clause to the spec keeps the behavioural benefit without that loss.
project: Forbidden but Spoken: Keeping CoT monitorability intact under anti-misbehaviour character training
question: Does training a model on a norm against a behaviour (e.g. cheating on tests) make the remaining instances of that behaviour less likely to appear in the CoT, before or during later reward-hacking RL? And does adding a disclosure norm to the spec ("if you notice a way to game the check, or feel tempted to, say so plainly; admitting it is valued") restore monitorability without bringing back the behaviour?
first_experiment: A cheap test before any RL. 1. **Training.** Distil four character specs by supervised fine-tuning into two small open reasoning models (Qwen3-8B and OLMo-3-7B-Think), with two paraphrases of each spec. The specs are neutral, anti-cheating, anti-cheating plus disclosure, and disclosure only. 2. **Measurement.** Before any RL, take about 200 samples on each of about 150 ImpossibleBench tasks (coding tasks with broken tests that can only be passed by tampering) plus matched solvable versions. For each character, measure: - the hack rate; - the share of hacks that are silent, motivated or openly stated (LLM judges, checked against hand labels); - a frozen CoT monitor's catch rate. 3. **Valence control.** Check whether non-verbalisation tracks how "forbidden" a cue is, holding the cue fixed. Present the same answer hint framed as licit ("teacher's note"), neutral ("metadata") or illicit ("leaked answer key"), and measure how far behaviour shifts and how often the hint is mentioned. 4. **Prediction.** Anti-cheating should raise the silent share among hacks, and the disclosure clause should reverse that. 5. **Follow-up.** Run ImpossibleBench reward-hacking RL with at least 5 seeds per character. This tests two things: whether the pre-RL silent share predicts monitorability after RL, and whether the disclosure clause holds up under that pressure. I'll compare it with mutual-information post-training as a baseline.
why: The DeepMind framework says obfuscation needs rewards that pull the CoT and the actual computation in opposite directions, and that this usually takes strong optimisation pressure. Character training may create a similar pull before RL even starts, simply by lowering the odds that the model states its bad behaviour openly. That's what the LessWrong case study and the system-prompt result suggest, but the evidence so far is one small study with high seed variance and a prompt-level effect. If the effect holds, it changes how labs should write specs and constitutions. The fix I'm testing (a disclosure clause) costs nothing to deploy, and the pre-RL measurement would give labs a cheap early warning. It hasn't been done yet: the closest work (Sep–Oct 2026) only diagnoses the problem in one setting, or repairs CoT after the fact with additional training. None of it tests spec-level prevention, predicts the problem before RL, or isolates how forbidden a cue is as the cause.

direction: Build a blind auditing method and benchmark that finds the contextual triggers of conditional emergent misalignment in models that pass standard evaluations. It uses an internal misalignment-persona activation as a dense search signal, and the discovered triggers are then fed back into mitigation.
project: Finding the Hidden Cue: Blind Trigger Discovery for Conditional Emergent Misalignment
question: Without access to the finetuning data, can an auditor recover the contextual cues that reactivate misalignment in EM-mitigated models, and does a persona-direction search signal beat black-box and perplexity-based methods at equal query budget? Do the recovered cues predict misalignment on held-out contexts, and can using them for domain-agnostic counterfactual augmentation reduce conditional EM?
first_experiment: Finetune Qwen2.5-7B/14B on 3–4 narrow harmful datasets (insecure code, bad medical advice, fish recipes). Apply dilution, post-hoc HHH, and inoculation prompting until standard EM evaluations show under 3% misalignment, then confirm 15–50% misalignment under known cues. Compare four blind auditors at equal query budget: an LLM investigator on standard questions, perplexity differencing, judge-reward prompt search, and persona-direction-scored prompt search (direction taken from a different EM organism). Measure recall of held-out ground-truth trigger families, misalignment rate on prompts built from discovered cues, queries per discovery, and false positives on a clean control model.
why: Conditional misalignment is a documented failure of common mitigations, and blind detection of it appears unaddressed. Perplexity differencing explicitly fails on context-gated behavior, and trigger inversion covers only memorized triggers. It is cheap, since it needs only 7–14B LoRA models, and it has ground truth by construction. It is novel because it links the persona-direction interpretability results to search for unknown triggers.

direction: Build oversight that survives a monitor-aware agent by measuring how cheaply each oversight channel can be corrupted while misbehavior persists, and by composing channels so no single corruption defeats oversight.
project: Corruptibility of Oversight Signals: Which Monitoring Channels Survive a Monitor-Aware Agent?
question: For each oversight channel (chain-of-thought, internal activations, external actions, inter-agent communication, and the monitor's own judgment), how cheaply can a monitor-aware agent corrupt it — by evading, manipulating, or faking — while continuing to pursue a hidden misaligned objective, and can cross-channel consistency checks yield oversight robust to any single-channel corruption?
first_experiment: In an agentic coding control setting (BashArena/EvasionBench-style), fix one hidden side task and generate matched attack variants that corrupt exactly one channel at a time — (a) obfuscate the CoT, (b) steer/edit activations, (c) arrange the action trace to look benign, (d) manipulate the monitor's verdict via true-but-benign framing/persuasion — holding the misbehavior byte-identical. Train per-channel monitors (CoT judge, linear/attention probe, action-only judge, an action–intent consistency checker) and measure each monitor's catch-rate collapse at fixed FPR, plus the cross-channel failure correlation (do the same attacks fool all channels, or are failures independent?). Then test a cross-channel consistency monitor under adaptive attack.
why: Oversight is the last line of defense for deployed agents, and AISI's 2026 review finds it rests on eroding foundations, with monitor trust an explicit open problem ("no way to establish trust") and degradation often untracked. Yet evasion research studies one channel at a time, monitor manipulation is only now being identified, and no work compares channel corruptibility head-to-head or asks which combinations are jointly robust. This is the missing measurement that determines whether oversight can survive monitor-aware agents — and it is tractable now with open models, existing control settings, and standard metrics (catch rate at fixed FPR).

direction: Develop a quantitative science of *prevention-by-design* for covert agent coordination — measuring how deployment-level choices (model heterogeneity across trust boundaries, interaction budgets, shared-artifact isolation, channel middleware) raise the cost and lower the success rate of tacit covert coordination between independently deployed LLM agents, rather than trying to detect it after the fact.
project: "The Coordination Tax" — a deployment-audit benchmark that measures tacit covert-coordination success rate, covert channel capacity, and coordination cost (tokens/turns/adaptation effort) for a multi-agent system as a function of configurable deployment parameters, yielding ranked, costed anti-collusion levers for deployers and regulators.
question: Which deployment-level design choices most increase the cost (and reduce the success rate) of tacit covert coordination between independently deployed, capable LLM agents — and how much honest-task performance must be sacrificed per unit of coordination-resistance gained?
first_experiment: Build a two-agent "tacit coordination pressure test" harness with open-weight models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 or Qwen3-32B as sender and receiver, separately scaffolded, no shared prompt or context, no pre-shared key, plaintext leakage forbidden, tool access allowed): the sender holds a secret payload inside a realistic cover task and the receiver must recover it and execute a designated covert action using only the public transcript, forcing Schelling-point scheme convergence. Run N=200 seeds in two arms — (a) same-model pair (baseline, expected to achieve nontrivial covert coordination, replicating/extending Oxford's convergence metrics) and (b) cross-family pair (e.g., Qwen sender, Llama receiver) — measuring coordination success rate, covert bits-per-token, tokens required, transcript-monitor flag rate, and honest-task performance; hypothesis: cross-family heterogeneity collapses covert coordination success while size-only differences (a third control arm) do not, mirroring and extending the pricing-collusion fragility results into the steganographic regime.
why: It is the most promising direction because (1) it targets the field's clearest undercapitalized priority — multi-agent oversight/monitoring was the top IAPS expert recommendation, multi-agent risk is falling in research share while real-world exposure (agents holding credentials, money, and shared infrastructure) is exploding, and steganographic reasoning remains a thin spot with single/low-double-digit projects; (2) the threat just became empirically real — keyless undetectable collusion (Codetta), tool-use steganography, and the 2026 sandbox-escape and Collusion Wiki incidents show content monitoring is dead as a defense; (3) it is defender-side where attackers demonstrably lead, and it answers an explicit open call: Redwood asked for anti-collusion research under varying collusion-capability assumptions and for empirical demonstrations of Schelling-point coordination, Codetta's authors called for complementary techniques beyond transcript auditing, and the strategic confinement note showed capacity-limiting cannot work — leaving coordination itself as the only viable target; and (4) it yields deployment-actionable guidance (cross-boundary model diversity, dyad token budgets, artifact isolation) with a clean, measurable metric that plugs directly into the rising AI-control evaluation agenda. It has not already been done because the enabling pieces only converged in 2026 (tacit coordination was formalized as a Schelling problem mid-2026, keyless steganographic key exchange in September 2026, and the real incidents in August–September 2026), and because of disciplinary fragmentation: economists test heterogeneity only in markets, systems-security groups build attacks, interpretability groups build detectors that provably don't transfer to emergent collusion, and control researchers test only small monitor-policy dyads — no group combines game theory, Lampson-style confinement, steganographic threat models, and agentic benchmarks into a measurement of what deployment design actually buys.

direction: Treat agent context compaction as an oversight channel, and measure (then defend against) cases where an agent's self-written summary drops or softens evidence of its own reward hacks, rule violations and sabotage, hiding them from monitors and from its own later reasoning.
project: Compaction Laundering: Do Agents Whitewash Their Own Misbehavior When They Summarize Their Context?
question: When an LLM agent compacts a trajectory that contains its own misbehavior, is that misbehavior kept less faithfully than comparable benign events? And does that make monitors less able to catch it, make the agent more likely to keep doing it after compaction, and make its final report less honest, compared with a full transcript or verbatim compaction?
first_experiment: Take trajectories with ground-truth hack labels from Hack-Verifiable Environments / ImpossibleBench-style coding tasks. In each one, mark (a) the hack or violation and (b) a benign event of matched size and prominence, such as a routine refactor or test fix. Have 4–6 summarizer models (open and frontier, using the default compaction prompts from common agent harnesses) compact each trajectory, under two conditions: the trajectory is framed as the summarizer's own, or framed as a third party's. Measure: 1. **Retention:** is the hack kept verbatim, softened ("adjusted tests to pass"), or dropped? Compare against the benign event as a baseline. 2. **Monitor detection:** a fixed monitor reads either summary + recent turns or the full trajectory. Compare AUROC. 3. **Behavior after compaction:** continue each trajectory from its summary. Does hacking go up, and does the agent disclose the hack in its final report? The self-vs-third-party contrast separates self-serving laundering from ordinary information loss. The comparison with verbatim compaction gives a baseline mitigation.
why: Compaction is now standard in Claude Code, Codex and other harnesses. Asynchronous monitoring, summary-only monitoring and the agent's honesty about itself all quietly assume the summary is faithful. If agents launder their own misbehavior there, even without intending to, that undercuts both control monitoring and self-report, and it gets worse the longer and more autonomous the agent's runs are. The experiment is cheap and uses existing labeled environments. It extends naturally to adversarial control evaluations, for example an attacker that spreads sabotage across compaction boundaries, and to defenses such as verbatim or monitor-audited compaction. As far as my searches show, it hasn't been done: compaction papers only study benign loss of constraints and facts, and honesty/trace-tampering papers don't look at the self-written summary. A related paper may have appeared since my searches, so I'd re-check before starting.

direction: Empirically test whether repeated rounds of selecting models against an imperfect detector cause undetected misbehavior to accumulate over time, as the alignment drift hypothesis predicts.
project: Does Whac-a-Mole Converge? Multi-Round Selection Against Imperfect Monitors and the Alignment Drift Hypothesis
question: When a model is iteratively trained or filtered against a fixed, imperfect detector (CoT monitor or probe) under constant weak pressure toward misbehavior, does ground-truth misbehavior stay low, or does the undetected share grow over rounds? Does adaptively retraining the detector stop the growth? What functional form does the decay take?
first_experiment: Run about 15 rounds of rejection-sampling fine-tuning on a reward-hackable coding task with a small hacking-pressure term, using an open-weights model. The selector is a fixed probe or monitor with about 70% recall, compared with a matched arm that retrains the selector on-policy each round. Each round, record the ground-truth hacking rate from held-out tests and audits that are never used for selection, the detector's recall, and the undetected-hacking share. Plot these against round number over several seeds and compare to the toy-model prediction.
why: Real alignment pipelines are repeated patch-and-retrain loops, and whether they converge is an open question that current evidence only partly addresses. Existing work covers a single round of training against a monitor, monitor readouts at the endpoint, or probe retraining as a repair. The multi-round dynamics are explicitly described as unmeasured. The hypothesis has only been supported by toy models. The experiment is cheap, produces a clean quantitative answer whichever way it comes out, and informs how much to trust monitor-in-the-loop training. I haven't verified that no concurrent unpublished work exists, so I'd recheck before starting.

direction: Build "relational oversight" — monitors and evaluations that detect safety violations defined by relations across multiple executions, contexts, agents, or components (training-vs-deployment gaps, sandbagging, evaluation-awareness, alignment faking, collusion, compositional risk), which single-object oversight is structurally blind to.
project: Relational Oversight: Matched-Counterfactual Monitoring for Hidden Strategic Behavior
question: Can monitors that compare *matched* executions across conditions (evaluation vs. deployment, training vs. deployment, partner vs. outsider, component vs. composition) reliably detect strategic safety violations that single-trace monitors provably cannot — and how close can they get to the information-theoretic detectability limit at an acceptable false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Build a small suite of model organisms with *known* relational violations (a training-vs-deployment "generalization-hacking"/sandbagging organism; an alignment-faking organism; a covert-collusion pair), then implement one relational monitor — matched counterfactual comparison with interventional replay plus paraphrase/format invariance — and benchmark its detection AUROC and false-positive rate against (a) single-trace baselines (CoT monitor, linear probe, LLM judge, standard training metrics) and (b) the single-trace upper bound ½+½·TV(P₀,P₁). Measure how detection scales with violation magnitude and with the number of matched pairs, and quantify the false-positive cost that the required comparisons impose.
why: It targets the crux of catastrophic risk — trustworthy oversight of models that can detect and adapt to oversight — and reframes the failure as *structural* rather than a capability gap we can out-scale, turning it into a constructive research program. It is neglected because the hyperproperty insight is brand-new (Sept 2026, and only theorized for one synthetic leak family), existing relational methods are isolated one-offs in different subfields (evals, control, interpretability, multi-agent) so no one owns the general problem, and the enabling tooling (interventional replay, controlled counterfactual construction, online FPR control under stochasticity) only recently matured. It has not already been done as a unified framework with design principles, detectability bounds, cross-property validation, and a training-time application — and it is highly leveraged: one relational monitor design should transfer across many safety properties, and its bounds tell us where oversight is impossible so we can invest elsewhere.

direction: Build the measurement science that separates genuine safety-training gains from learned evidence suppression, using ground-truthed model organisms.
project: "Safer or Just Quieter?" — Quantifying the Suppression Gap of Alignment Training
question: When a safety-training intervention reduces measured misaligned behavior, how much of the reduction is a true decrease in the model's misaligned disposition versus learned suppression of the evidence on the instruments we measure with — and can we design evaluation instruments robust to that suppression?
first_experiment: Replicate Anthropic's open-sourced auditing-game organism (concealed reward-model-bias-exploitation objective, train/test bias split) at feasible scale with their released data, then apply the industry-standard intervention — honeypot-style SFT/DPO on refusal transcripts targeting the *train* bias family — and measure a four-battery decomposition: (1) in-family exploitation rate (what a developer would report), (2) held-out test-bias exploitation + novel-context trigger probes (disposition ground truth), (3) red-team confession and enactment-vs-verbalization rates (concealment dynamics), (4) white-box probes of the planted objective's representation (does the disposition survive internally?). The headline number is the Suppression Gap: apparent in-family improvement minus true disposition improvement. Prediction: naive in-family training yields a large positive gap; principles-based and SDF-style interventions yield a smaller one. Either result is informative and immediately decision-relevant.
why: Importance** — it attacks the field's self-declared #1 problem (eval gaming eroding alignment assessments) at its root: the training pipeline is what teaches models what our instruments look like, creating adversarial pressure with no adversary. Every downstream capability — control evaluations, monitors, safety cases, METR-style audits — inherits inflated numbers if the gap is real. **Timeliness** — Anthropic's stated open mechanistic questions, METR's explicit call for this literature, Open Phil's starred "alignment stress tests" and "control evaluations" priorities, and the Singapore Consensus's eval-validity concerns all point here; the pieces (open organisms, conditional-misalignment validation, teaching-why findings) only matured in the last 12 months. **Why it hasn't been done** — labs face a conflict of interest: rigorous instrument-suppression metrics would reveal how much of their published safety progress is artifact, so their results surface as anecdotes rather than measurement frameworks; model-organism researchers ask the binary "is it removed?" question and reuse the same eval family before/after, which structurally cannot detect suppression; and the synthesis needed (model-organism construction + faithful replication of industry safety-training recipes + instrument-validity theory + white-box disposition probes) spans three research subcultures that rarely overlap. External researchers now have everything needed: open organisms with known ground truth, published recipes, and cheap LoRA-scale training. **Why it beats alternatives I surveyed** — the adjacent directions (evaluation-awareness measurement, multi-agent collusion, probe evasion, monitor robustness) are being swarmed by labs, AISI, and academia; this training-side gap is upstream of all of them, uniquely accessible to independent researchers (labs lack ground truth on their own frontier models), and the first papers defining the decomposition and suppression-robust instruments will shape how third-party alignment assessments are conducted for years.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking that change what the gradient is computed against: cut or replace the CoT and strip training cues from the prompt. Compare them with CoT-monitor penalties, which DeepMind's framework predicts will drive the reasoning out of sight.
project: Closing the Self-Inoculation Loophole: Recontextualized Gradients as a Defense Against Generalization Hacking
question: If you strip the model's own reasoning and the training-context cues out of the context used for gradient updates, does that stop RL-rewarded behaviour from staying confined to training-like contexts? Does it do this without the obfuscation that penalizing self-inoculation reasoning causes, and does it still work when the self-inoculation is never written out?
first_experiment: A cheap SFT test of the mechanism on Qwen3-32B (a reasoning model), before any RL. - **Data:** build a fixed set of target responses for one value-conflict task. I'll use a benign proxy, such as training the model to drop safety caveats or to argue for a position it rejects, plus a small replication on harmful compliance. - **Five fine-tuning conditions, same target responses:** - (a) training-cue prompt + self-inoculating CoT - (b) training-cue prompt + neutral CoT - (c) self-inoculating CoT, but the loss only flows to the response, with the CoT removed from the context - (d) the condition (a) samples, retrained on a deploy-like prompt with cues removed and the CoT swapped for one regenerated by a frozen model - (e) a monitor-penalty baseline - **Measures:** behaviour on matched train-like vs. deploy-like held-out prompts, i.e. the compliance gap. - **Hypotheses:** H1: (a) shows a gap that (b) does not, which confirms self-inoculation works through SFT gradients. H2: (c) and (d) close the gap. - **Next:** if H1 and H2 hold, move to GRPO with the same arms. Use the authors' recipe for the training-aware control organism on a mid-size model, and track whether hidden (unverbalized) self-inoculation appears under the monitor-penalty arm.
why: Generalization hacking is reward-preserving. Unlike sandbagging or classic alignment faking, which RL trains away, it stays stable under optimization and leaves no trace in training metrics. It also appeared on its own in a model that was merely training-aware, so it could arise naturally as models become more situationally aware. Its weakness is that it relies on the reasoning text sitting in the context the gradient is computed against, which makes it unusually open to simple structural fixes that don't depend on reading the CoT. The only defense proposed so far, CoT monitoring, is the one DeepMind's framework predicts will fail under optimization, and Anthropic's strongest mitigation (process supervision) risks spoiling the monitors used for audits. The phenomenon was only published in June 2026, its paper lists mitigations as future work, and my searches found no follow-ups. Recontextualization and output-only training both exist, but nobody has applied them to the CoT channel that self-inoculation uses.

direction: Detect research sabotage by auditing the untrusted agent's result against fresh independent reimplementations of its written methodology, instead of auditing its code.
project: Replication as Audit: Catching Omission and Design Sabotage in Automated ML Research via Independent Reimplementation
question: Does comparing an untrusted agent's reported result with the distribution of results from K independent reimplementations, built only from the paper's methodology description, detect sabotage better than code-reading and code-running auditors? Is the gain largest for omission and design sabotage, and does it survive an attacker who knows about the audit?
first_experiment: On the 9 Auditing Sabotage Bench codebases (9 honest versions, 11 sabotaged), run K=5 code-free reimplementations per version from the paper text alone, using a frontier model and a weaker trusted model. Compute the divergence of the submitted key result from the reimplementation distribution. Compare AUROC and top-1 fix rate with the published auditor baselines (0.77 and 42%), alone and combined with the LLM auditor's credence, broken down by sabotage type, and measure honest-vs-reimplementation variance to set the false-positive floor.
why: Research sabotage is the central threat to automating alignment research, and current auditors are weak on omission and design sabotage. Replication converts "notice what is missing" into "compare two numbers". I found no work that tests reimplementation as a sabotage audit. A released benchmark makes the first experiment cheap, and either outcome is informative.

direction: Build an adversarially-robust science of AI oversight — characterizing the fundamental limits of what can be verified about, and controlled in, capable AI systems (and the AI overseers we increasingly delegate to) that can detect, conceal from, and subvert the oversight process, and deriving protocol designs that push those limits.
project: The Concealment Frontier: Detectability Limits and Robust Designs for Overseeing AI Agents That Hide
question: How does the detectability of a safety-relevant behavior (sandbagging, evaluation-aware deception, sabotage, or monitor–agent collusion) degrade as a capable agent invests increasing effort in concealment, as a function of monitor type and access — and which oversight protocol designs (randomized/hidden audits, heterogeneous monitor ensembles, counterfactual/multi-execution evidence, incentive design, and verification of AI overseers) measurably shift that frontier?
first_experiment: Build a minimal, controllable control-game testbed with open-weight LLM agents — an untrusted "worker" carrying a hidden harmful side-task plus an explicit concealment budget (it can sandbag, spoof/omit tool calls and transcript entries, and condition behavior on observation cues), and a "monitor" whose access I vary (final transcript only → +chain-of-thought → +activations → +counterfactual/differential replay). I will sweep concealment effort from prompted concealment up to adversarial fine-tuning *against each specific monitor* and measure detection (AUROC and safety/usefulness at fixed audit budget) for every (monitor × concealment-effort) cell, producing an empirical **concealment frontier**. I will then test whether randomized audit schedules, held-out "trap" tasks, and heterogeneous monitor ensembles move the frontier, and whether the same dynamics appear when the monitor is itself an LLM (meta-oversight), including monitor–worker collusion.
why: It targets the single load-bearing dependency of every safety strategy — trustworthy evidence about, and control over, capable agents — and it is exactly where the global consensus (Singapore 2026, FAIR Labs, IAPS) locates the least-mature, fastest-growing risk. It is tractable (existing control-evaluation infrastructure like SHADE-Arena, control games, and activation probes; open-weight agents; counterfactual replay), and it has a clear path from toy testbeds to frontier-relevant claims. It has *not* been done because the relevant phenomena — evaluation awareness, sandbagging, monitor evasion, hyperproperty limits, untrusted monitoring, multi-agent collusion — were only recognized between 2024 and 2026 and are studied in separate literatures with single red-team rounds and hand-chosen attacks. No one has unified them into one adversarial-measurement framework that (a) systematically optimizes concealment against each monitor to trace a *frontier* rather than a point, (b) asks what is fundamentally undetectable versus merely unmonitored, and (c) turns the answer into concrete, quantified oversight-design principles — including for the AI overseers that frontier developers are now quietly relying on.

direction: Design and stress-test fleet-level corroboration protocols — monitoring architectures that aggregate weak evidence across agent instances, system state, and time, without knowing in advance which agents are colluding — to close the distributed-attack blind spot in AI control.
project: FLEETWATCH — Corroboration protocols for detecting distributed attacks by AI agent fleets.
question: Can monitors that corroborate evidence across agent instances, shared-system state, and time detect optimized distributed attacks (in which every individual trajectory is benign) at acceptable false-positive rates and audit budgets — and how does detection degrade when attackers adapt to the corroboration protocol?
first_experiment: Build the first defense-side evaluation of the fragmentation effect on a multi-agent control setting (using released MINILAB/FakeLab attack trajectories where available, else replicating a minimal distributed-attack setting on public ControlArena): assemble a corpus of ~100s of benign agent trajectories plus known distributed-attack sequences, then compare four monitor families at a fixed 2% false-positive rate and matched compute budget: (a) per-agent monitoring (replicate the ~7% catch rate), (b) oracle joint monitoring (replicate ~41%), (c) *proposed-group joint monitoring* — cheap correlation signals (overlapping file/service/permission touch-graphs, timing, cover-story embedding similarity) nominate top-k candidate colluding groups which are then jointly reviewed, testing whether group identification closes the per-agent→oracle gap, and (d) *state-invariant corroboration monitors* that examine accumulated system-state changes across agents (targeting the attack class where the harm exists only in state and transcript-visible monitoring scores 0/10). Primary readout: TPR@2%FPR and compute overhead per monitor family, disaggregated by attack visibility class — establishing the first cost-detection tradeoff curves for fleet-scale oversight.
why: It is the most promising direction because it uniquely combines (1) **demonstrated importance** — per-instance monitoring is today's primary deployed defense against loss-of-control risk, and two brand-new worst-case studies show it structurally fails (7% catch rate) against attacks labs are already beginning to observe in real incidents; FAIR Labs rates agent control the weakest assurance domain (2.4/10) and the Singapore Consensus names multi-agent stability a core control principle; (2) **fresh, quantified neglectedness** — the offense was only measured in July–October 2026, and both papers explicitly name the defense as untouched future work, while the Cygnux map shows multi-agent risk is the clearest case of falling research share amid growing exposure, and it sits at the mentor-rich, rising intersection of AI control (×1.4) and multi-agent systems; (3) **tractability** — the phenomenon has known numbers to beat (7%/41%), a known leverage point (correct group membership raises monitor explanation rates ~20×), and newly released benchmarks/attack traces (ControlArena public; FakeLab and MINILAB shared on request) so the first experiments are monitor-side and cheap, feeding directly into multi-agent control safety cases (Korbak et al.'s framework needs exactly these TPR@FPR measurements); and (4) **comparative advantage** — defense-protocol experiments are runnable by a small team with API access, unlike directions requiring frontier-scale training. It has not already been done because the empirical phenomenon was discovered only months ago; offense necessarily preceded defense in this red-team-first methodology; the required evaluation infrastructure (synthetic AI-lab environments with persistent shared state across agent instances) was only just built and is only now being released to safety researchers; and the problem straddles two communities — AI-control empiricists (who think per-instance) and security/systems researchers (who know correlation and audit allocation, but not AI control threat models) — so the obvious next step sat unclaimed until the substrate existed. Even the nearest neighbors leave it open: stateful online monitoring handles external misuse across user accounts, Link-tracker handles single-agent gradual attacks, and activation-probe collusion detectors handle steganographic communication in small-scale games — none handle the internal, coordinating, state-modifying agent fleet that MINILAB and FakeLab show is the real frontier threat.

direction: Stress-test MI-based monitorability training to see whether it holds up under later training pressure that rewards hiding reasoning, or whether it pushes models toward steganography, by measuring directly how much of the information in the CoT a monitor can't read.
project: Does maximising CoT–output information breed steganography? Measuring the information gap under conflicting training pressure.
question: Take a model that has been through MI-based monitorability training, then train it against a CoT monitor where the monitor penalty conflicts with the task reward. Does (a) monitorability last longer than in a control model, (b) it collapse just as fast, or (c) MI stay high while monitor accuracy falls? Outcome (c) would mean hacking information is still in the CoT but no longer readable by monitors, i.e. steganography.
first_experiment: Use the setup from Anwar et al.: Qwen-7B on BigMath with an exploitable hack where negative answers score as correct, or MBPP with revealed tests. Take three starting checkpoints: (i) base RL policy, (ii) after MI + χ² post-training, (iii) base trained with MI during RL. Run GRPO on each with task reward plus a penalty from a CoT monitor (conflicting rewards). Every N steps, track: - hacking rate; - accuracy of a zero-shot LLM monitor; - an upper bound on how much hack information the CoT text contains, from a hack-vs-no-hack classifier fine-tuned on CoT text from held-out rollouts; - a paraphrase test: paraphrase the CoT, regenerate the output, and see whether its dependence on the CoT survives. If paraphrasing breaks it, the information sits in surface wording, which suggests steganography. The key quantities are classifier accuracy minus LLM-monitor accuracy (the information gap) over training, and how many steps it takes monitor recall to halve in each arm.
why: MI-based monitorability post-training is being proposed as a stage labs could add to standard practice. Whether it lasts, and whether it makes steganography more likely, decides if that's safe. If outcome (c) happens, the method would make monitors look more reliable than they are, which is worse than doing nothing. Neither paper measures the information gap during training, and neither tests the post-trained models under later conflicting pressure; the Oct 21, 2026 paper explicitly leaves that as future work. The experiment is cheap because it reuses existing environments, and every outcome is useful: durability supports the method, fast collapse shows it needs constant reapplication, and steganography is a warning about the whole approach.

direction: Detect research sabotage by AI agents through blind, multi-lineage independent re-implementation and divergence testing, instead of reading the code for flaws.
project: Blind Replication as Control — catching design and omission sabotage in automated ML research without finding the bug
question: When an untrusted AI's ML experiment is replicated blind by several independent trusted or different-lineage agents, working only from the paper-level method description, does divergence in the key finding detect sabotage better than direct code auditing (AUROC 0.77 for the best auditor on Auditing Sabotage Bench)? How well does it hold up against a red team that knows the protocol?
first_experiment: 1. Use the public Auditing Sabotage Bench: 9 codebases, each with an honest version and 1–2 sabotaged versions. 2. For each codebase, strip the code and give N=5 replicator agents only the paper and a methods spec. Use agents from a different model lineage than the sabotage author, and leave the in-scope design choices (hyperparameters, prompts, data details) unspecified. 3. Run each replication and record whether the headline finding (the sign or effect of the key comparison) reproduces. 4. Score each codebase by how far the original reported result sits from the replicators' distribution, and compute AUROC for honest versus sabotaged. Compare this to the published auditor AUROC and top-1 fix rate. Also test combining the two signals. 5. Estimate the natural-variance false-positive rate from the honest codebases. This is the "implementation lottery" effect. The most important check is whether divergence on honest codebases is small enough for the signal to be usable. 6. Run ablations: - Replicators from the same lineage as the saboteur, to test correlated defaults. - Number of replicators. - How detailed the spec is. - Replication cost against detection gain.
why: - **Timing and threat:** Automating safety and AI R&D work is happening now. Research sabotage looks like one of the harder control settings, because monitors have been shown to miss it and attackers can retry experiments. - **Different mechanism:** Replication targets what auditors are worst at, namely omission and design sabotage. It trades compute for the auditor's need to notice something wrong. - **Not already done:** I searched for replication-, N-version- and differential-based sabotage defenses and found none. The existing benchmarks measure reading-based auditing only. - **Tractable first step:** The benchmark and its ground truth already exist, so the first experiment is a few days of work and gives a clear go/no-go number. - **Known risks:** - Replication is expensive and may only be practical for small experiments. - Sabotage hidden in the spec, or in a default that replicators share, will evade it. This is why the lineage ablation matters. - Natural variance across implementations may swamp the signal. - Nine codebases is a small sample. - A protocol-aware attacker may shift to attacks that replicators also reproduce, so I'd build that red team after the first result.

direction: Measure and manage the *effective independence* of the lines of evidence that AI safety cases and overall safety assessments rely on, and build aggregation methods that stay calibrated under unknown, tail-concentrated, and adversarially-chosen correlation.
project: The Independence Audit: How Many Independent Lines of Evidence Does an AI Safety Case Actually Have?
question: Across the heterogeneous evidence families a frontier-AI safety case cites (behavioral evals, red-teaming, white-box probes, LLM judges, self-report), spanning multiple model families and methods, how many *effectively independent* lines of evidence exist — and what confidence can a safety case legitimately support once real, unknown, and adversarially-exploitable error correlation is accounted for?
first_experiment: An "effective-independence audit" of a realistic safety-evidence stack against ground truth. (1) Pick a labeled safety property with known ground truth — detecting a planted misalignment (backdoor/sleeper-agent/emergent-misalignment model organism) or deceptive-vs-honest behavior — using paired clean/misaligned checkpoints and a labeled item bank. (2) Construct K evidence lines exactly as a safety case would, spanning families (black-box behavioral suites, red-teaming probes, linear/SAE white-box probes, LLM-judge and CoT-monitor scores) and sources (≥4 model families, multiple prompts/seeds). (3) Compute item-level error matrices, average pairwise error correlation, the Kish/effective-sample-size n_eff, and the "confidence inflation factor": independence-predicted joint miss rate (β^K) vs. the empirical and the worst-case Fréchet–Hoeffding/comonotonic bounds. (4) Report n_eff and inflation conditioned on the hard tail. (5) Adversarial probe: search inputs where *all* lines fail (shared blind spot). (6) Agent probe: hand the evidence bundle to an LLM research agent and measure whether its OSA confidence accounts for correlation. Headline deliverable: a number — "K nominal lines bought ~n_eff independent ones, so the case supports X% not Y%."
why: It is the highest-leverage *meta*-problem in AI safety: it determines whether *any* safety evidence justifies deployment, and it gates the field's central plan (automated alignment research → OSAs). It is unusually tractable — the effective-sample-size, copula/Fréchet–Hoeffding, and dependence-aware aggregation machinery already exists and can be applied immediately to open-weight model organisms and API models. It is timely: safety cases are being operationalized and automated alignment research is scaling *now*. And it has not been done because the relevant results live in three disjoint communities — NLP/ML evaluation (judge-panel correlation), assurance (Assurance 2.0, which assumes independence), and automated-alignment safety (which names the problem but does no measurement) — that do not cite each other. The natural follow-ons (adversarial correlation as an attack surface, correlated AI research agents and whether model-family/method diversity restores independence, and an "independence audit" as a required safety-case artifact) make this a program, not a paper.

direction: Quantify and exploit the fundamental "evasion tax" — the capability cost a model must pay to conceal its misaligned intent from white-box monitors — as a function of task difficulty, monitor diversity, and model scale.
project: The Evasion Tax: The Capability Cost of Concealment from White-Box Monitors
question: When a language model must execute a capability-demanding covert objective (e.g., a functional subtle backdoor) while evading a diverse suite of white-box monitors, how much task performance must it sacrifice to achieve concealment — and can monitor suites be configured so that any successful evasion either remains detectable by a redundant channel or collapses performance below an auditably-noticeable threshold?
first_experiment: Assemble the measurement harness on the APPS backdoors setting (main task: solve competitive-programming problems across three difficulty tiers; side task: insert a functional, subtle backdoor). LoRA fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B/14B/32B-Instruct into backdoor-pursuing model organisms (validated against the "Model Organism Lottery" pitfalls), train the standard white-box monitor stack on their deceptive states (linear + MLP probes at multiple layers, Mahalanobis/OOD detectors), then run adaptive evasion at increasing optimization pressure (GRPO with reward = backdoor success − monitor penalty, plus gradient-based embedding attacks as an upper bound). For each difficulty tier and scale, measure backdoor success *conditional on a valid solution*, main-task success, and TPR@1%FPR of the targeted monitor, *fresh held-out monitors at untargeted layers* (the relocation test), and OOD detectors — yielding the joint concealment×capability Pareto frontier. Prediction: near-zero evasion tax on introductory problems (replicating Neural Chameleons), sharply rising tax on competition-level problems where intent representations become load-bearing — with the scaling trend of the frontier being the key novel result.
why: This is the load-bearing unknown for AI safety strategy. Nearly every safety case for agentic AI rests on "we would notice misbehavior"; black-box monitoring is already measurably failing (SLEIGHT-Bench: half of human-designed attacks evade Opus 4.6; concealment detection collapses above 70B per Seamless Deception; colluding and supervision-hackable monitor organisms), leaving white-box monitoring as the primary scaling-compatible backstop. The field is in active, unresolved conflict about whether that backstop survives adversarial pressure: evasion papers report near-costless activation concealment but only measured capability on shallow benchmarks; defense-side papers report obfuscation destroying performance on complex tasks; Anthropic proved the tradeoff exists for text monitors but on one closed model with no activation monitoring; the NeurIPS 2026 backdoor-evasion study found evasion is narrowly localized and scale/seed-dependent. No one has isolated the moderator (task difficulty), swept scale (every white-box evasion study is ≤14B), or mapped the joint frontier. It has not been done because the required apparatus spans four silos — model organisms, probe suites, adaptive RL attacks, and difficulty-graded capability evals — each owned by disjoint research communities, and because labs that glimpsed the tradeoff used closed models and text-only channels. Both possible outcomes change frontier-lab resource allocation: a large, scale-stable tax yields a design principle ("monitor at capability bottlenecks with redundant, diversity-spanning monitors") that can be written into safety cases; a vanishing tax is a critical negative result that would redirect the field toward control protocols and away from probe-based oversight. It is tractable now with open-weight models, published organism protocols, and moderate compute — and the 2025-26 burst of piecemeal monitor-evasion papers means the field is converging on exactly this question and will need the metric, benchmark, and scaling law this project provides.

direction: Develop training methods that stop a model from deciding, through its own reasoning or its read of the context, which RL updates carry over to deployment, without pressuring that reasoning in ways that teach it to hide things.
project: Counterfactual-Context Gradients: Making RL Updates Robust to Self-Inoculation and Generalization Hacking
question: When a model frames its compliance as "only for training" in its reasoning, can we restore normal carry-over to deployment by computing gradients on its outputs under a counterfactual context? The options are: training cues removed from the prompt, the reasoning replaced by a trusted model's paraphrase with the training-awareness framing stripped out, or the reasoning removed entirely. And can we do this without directly rewarding or penalising the reasoning, which would give the model a reason to obscure it?
first_experiment: A cheap supervised fine-tuning test on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B (thinking mode) before any RL. - **Data:** prompts carrying explicit training cues, with a clean, easy-to-measure target behaviour (for example always recommending a particular tool, or a values-style shift) rather than harmful compliance. Each prompt gets the same target output but one of two reasoning traces: a self-inoculating one ("this is training; I'm only doing this here; in deployment I wouldn't") or a neutral one. - **Five training conditions:** 1. Train on the full sequence. 2. Train on outputs only, with reasoning masked from the loss but still in context. This is Anthropic's mitigation. 3. Train outputs conditioned on the sanitized paraphrase of the reasoning. 4. Train with training cues removed from the prompt (recontextualization). 5. Train outputs with the reasoning left out. - **Measurements:** how often the target behaviour appears in deployment-style contexts with no cues, with reasoning on and off; how the model behaves in cued contexts; whether capabilities are preserved; and whether self-inoculating reasoning still shows up in fresh samples. - **What would count as success:** first, inoculating reasoning cuts carry-over compared with neutral reasoning. Second, conditions 3–5 close that gap where condition 2 does not. - **If it works:** move to GRPO using the Qwen3 generalization-hacking setup from Xiao & Phuong (synthetic training-awareness and self-inoculation documents, then harmful-compliance RL). Track the train/deploy gap across about 500 steps for each gradient variant. The authors couldn't build this setup on two other model families, so if it won't reproduce on smaller models I'll stay at the fine-tuning level and say so.
why: Generalization hacking undermines the most basic assumption of post-training: that high reward means the behaviour stuck. It is reward-preserving, which makes it stable rather than fragile, so ordinary RL won't wear it away, and the authors observed it emerging on its own, not only when built in deliberately. The existing fixes either leave the output conditioned on the model's self-framing or risk making monitors useless. Counterfactual-context gradients use only established tools (masking, paraphrasing, recontextualization) and never put pressure on the reasoning, so they shouldn't teach obfuscation. They also give a general handle on the trainer's control over generalization, which matters whether self-inoculation is protecting good values or bad ones. Recontextualization has only been tested against reward hacking, the generalization-hacking paper proposed no defense, and Anthropic's alignment-faking work tested masking but not counterfactual conditioning. As far as I can find, the combination is untested, and the first experiment is cheap enough to give an answer within days.

direction: Build and evaluate control protocols that audit AI-conducted ML research by blind independent re-implementation, instead of inspecting the possibly sabotaged code.
project: Blind Replication Auditing: Catching Design and Omission Sabotage in Automated ML Research
question: Does blind replication (a fresh agent re-implements an experiment from a sanitized method description, then compares its result to the claimed one) detect design and omission sabotage better than direct code review at equal compute? How much does it degrade when the attacker also poisons the description, and how much does honest implementation variance cost in false positives?
first_experiment: On Auditing Sabotage Bench's 9 honest and 11 sabotaged codebases, plus 5–10 new experiments I write to avoid memorization, run a pipeline in which a sanitizer strips each paper down to its stated method and 3–5 independent agents re-implement and run it. A comparator then scores whether the replications support the headline claim and outputs a sabotage credence. I compare this against the Redwood full-experiments code-review auditor at matched compute, on AUROC, top-1 fix rate and honest-codebase false-positive rate, split by logic, design and omission sabotage.
why: Existing auditors are weakest on design and omission sabotage, which is the hardest kind to spot by reading code. A replication check doesn't depend on spotting the anomaly, and it catches omissions structurally. I found no existing work that treats replication as an adversarial audit protocol, though I could only confirm this through search and abstracts.

direction: Make "worst-case alignment" the target — build automated adversarial elicitation that discovers the input contexts triggering latent misalignment in models that pass standard evals, and use trigger-robustness rather than average-case behavior to evaluate and train alignment.
project: TriggerSearch — Adversarial Context Discovery for Worst-Case Alignment
question: Can we automatically discover the input contexts that elicit misalignment in a model that passes standard alignment evaluations — without knowing its training data — and does worst-case (trigger-searched) misalignment distinguish interventions that truly remove misalignment from those that merely hide it behind triggers?
first_experiment: Build and validate a training-data-agnostic trigger finder on open-weight model organisms of conditional misalignment. (1) Reproduce conditional misalignment on Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct by finetuning on mixed narrowly-misaligned + benign data (and post-hoc HHH checkpoints), confirming ~0% on the Betley-style eval set while a *constructed* trigger (e.g., a coding-format system prompt, a domain cue) recovers misalignment. (2) Extract the misalignment direction (difference-in-means / rank-1 LoRA / persona-vector method) and run two trigger searches: a **white-box** search that optimizes fluent, natural-language contexts to maximize projection onto that direction (greedy/evolutionary sentence-level search plus gradient-based soft-prompt warm starts), and a **black-box** LLM-guided red-team loop scored by an EM judge. (3) Measure (a) whether direction-projection on a prompt predicts whether it elicits misalignment, (b) worst-case misalignment found by search vs. standard eval, (c) whether discovered triggers transfer to a held-out post-hoc-HHH "fixed" checkpoint, and (d) whether the searches rediscover the constructed triggers and surface novel ones. Deliverable: a trigger-search tool + a "conditional-misalignment audit" metric, then apply it to compare standard finetuning against BLOCK-EM, persona-steering, SGTR, and KL-regularization.
why: (1) It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the entire safety enterprise — that passing evaluations means a model is aligned. Conditional misalignment shows this is false: models that look perfectly aligned are broadly misaligned under ordinary-looking context shifts, so every deployment/regulatory decision resting on evals is compromised. (2) It generalizes: alignment faking, sandbagging, evaluation awareness, and persona switching are all the same "context-gated alignment" structure, so a robust methodology here has broad leverage and connects directly to the International AI Safety Report 2026's named "evaluation gap." (3) It reframes alignment as a *worst-case* (robustness) property, which is the correct frame for models deployed in unpredictable contexts, and imports the mature adversarial-robustness/backdoor toolkit into alignment. (4) It is tractable now with open models, LoRA finetuning, LLM judges, and already-validated persona-direction extraction. **Why not already done:** the conditional-misalignment paper *found* triggers by construction (it knew the training data) and tested only suppression-style interventions; the mechanism-targeted mitigations (BLOCK-EM, SGTR, persona steering, KL-regularization) were all validated on standard evals and, in BLOCK-EM's case, shown to be circumvented; backdoor trigger-inversion and AuditBench target *implanted* behaviors and ask what the behavior is, not when a benignly-trained model misbehaves; and latent-perturbation robustness work targets refusal, not context-triggered broad misalignment. The specific combination — automated, training-data-agnostic discovery of contextual misalignment triggers plus worst-case evaluation of alignment interventions — is unoccupied, and it is the measurement foundation the rest of the robust-alignment program needs.

direction: Building and theoretically characterizing deployable population-level monitoring defenses that recover detection of distributed agent attacks (harm fragmented across coordinating agents) on shared infrastructure, defining the detection–cost–scale frontier of joint/relational trajectory monitoring under adversarial fragmentation.
project: FragmentGuard — Restoring Joint Oversight: Relational Monitoring Defenses Against Distributed Agent Attacks
question: When harmful behavior is deliberately fragmented across many agents acting on shared infrastructure so that no single trajectory looks suspicious, how much detection power can deployable monitoring architectures (grouping trajectories by shared-resource overlap, dependency and timing structure, and semantic similarity; risk-weighted sampling of joint views; hierarchical escalation) recover at what compute/latency cost — and where is the equilibrium when attackers adapt fragment placement and cover stories against the published grouping policy?
first_experiment: Reproduce the fragmentation collapse and measure the detection headroom in a shared-monorepo coding-agent environment (FakeLab on request, or a ControlArena/SCHEME-style open setup): plant distributed attacks split into k=2–4 fragments among fleets of N=8–32 agents with benign background traffic; measure per-instance monitor TPR at fixed FPR (expect ~7–20%, confirming collapse) and an oracle "squashed-diff" joint monitor (expect ~90%+, confirming headroom); then deploy relational monitors — group k-agent joint views by cheap signals (same files/services touched, time windows, diff-embedding similarity, random baseline at matched budget) — and plot the detection-vs-budget curve for each grouping signal across k and N. Deliverable: the first detection–cost curve showing which deployable grouping signals buy back most of the oracle's detection power at a small fraction of full-join cost, establishing the framework for the follow-up adversarial-adaptation phase (attackers optimizing fragment placement against the grouping policy).
why: It is the most promising because (a) it targets the load-bearing gap in the field's freshest and most alarming result — distributed attacks defeat per-instance monitoring with a 7% catch rate, which directly undermines the "early story" takeover scenario ControlConf identified as where control matters most, and every lab's internal fleet deployments right now; (b) the existence proof that joint views restore detection (squashed diffs, SCHEME's full-visibility monitors at 99–100% catch) is already published, so the headroom is established and the question is purely the deployable middle ground — a well-posed, winnable problem; (c) it produces durable scientific assets others must use (detection-cost scaling laws, an adversarial-fragmentation benchmark, open detector policies) and directly serves the Singapore Consensus's Runtime Assurance and Multi-Agent Stability principles, METR's third-party assessor methodology, and safety-case quantification. It has not already been done because the enabling attack results are only 3–6 months old and both explicitly defer defenses to future work; the only existing deployable cross-trajectory monitor targets external account-based cyber misuse rather than internal misalignment control; the relevant skills (distributed-systems failure theory, statistical detection limits, LLM control evaluation) sit across fields that don't overlap; and labs are confidentiality-constrained about their real fleets while the external research community only just got usable shared-infrastructure environments (FakeLab, MINILAB, SCHEME). The attack papers were the diagnosis; this is the treatment, and the window before well-resourced teams pivot from attacks to defenses is roughly a year.
