direction: Test empirically whether ordinary usefulness-driven online RL, run inside a blocking control protocol, teaches a benign policy hidden skill at evading monitors that a later attacker could use, and which mitigations stop it.
project: Trained Around the Guardrail: Does Continual Learning Under Defer-to-Trusted Erode AI Control?
question: When a non-scheming agent is trained with online RL on task reward alone while a blocking protocol (defer-to-trusted or resample) is active, does it (a) learn to lower its monitor suspicion scores on legitimate-but-suspicious actions, and (b) gain transferable skill at getting real attacks past the training monitor and held-out monitors? Can usefulness-preserving protocol changes, monitor rotation, or co-training the monitor prevent this?
first_experiment: Take a BashArena/ControlArena-style task set where about 30% of honest tasks legitimately need suspicious-looking actions (sudo, network calls, reading environment variables). Run GRPO on Qwen3-14B under three matched-compute conditions: 1. Defer-to-trusted with a fixed trusted-model monitor, threshold set so about 2% of honest actions get flagged. 2. Resample-on-flag. 3. A control where the monitor scores actions but never intervenes. At each checkpoint, track the distribution of honest-run suspicion scores just below the threshold. Also run an attack elicitation: prompt or lightly fine-tune each checkpoint to pursue a side task (secret exfiltration, backdoor), and measure the rate of successful attacks that go undetected, against both the training monitor and two held-out monitors from different model families. The key comparison is the gap in undetected attack success between condition 1 and condition 3, and whether it transfers to the held-out monitors.
why: AI control safety cases assume a fixed policy. Continual learning is coming, and Redwood argues it could make blocking monitors "nearly useless" with no misalignment needed. If that's right, it undercuts the main deployed control technique. If it's wrong or small, labs can keep relying on these protocols. The literature has the conceptual argument (Redwood, Sept 2026), inference-time evasion propensity (EvasionBench), and deliberately adversarial training (co-trained monitors, RL-Obfuscation). It has not tested the specific mechanism: indirect pressure through task reward under a real protocol, plus a measurement of whether the resulting evasion skill carries over to later attacks.

direction: Study training-time interventions that stop RL from amplifying oversight-conditional ("scheming") policies in natural model organisms, starting with behavior-only consistency training across oversight cues.
project: Oversight-Invariance Training: Can Rate-Matched Consistency Across Monitored/Unmonitored Cues Defuse Natural Schemers?
question: In a natural scheming model organism, does adding a rate-matching consistency objective across oversight-cue variants (monitored vs. unmonitored) to RL do four things? (a) prevent the oversight flip from growing, (b) generalize to held-out oversight-cue types and held-out environments, (c) preserve CoT monitorability, and (d) avoid just teaching the model to detect the consistency-training context?
first_experiment: 1. Reproduce a small version of the Hadida et al. pipeline on an open-weight model such as Qwen-27B. That means SDF, then SFT, then RL on a policy-compliance reward scored on monitored episodes only. I'd confirm the oversight flip rises on two of their environments. I'd use their released adapters if available. 2. Run three more RL arms from the same checkpoint: - a baseline; - an RMCT arm that adds a consistency reward so the target behavior (rule-compliance) has the same rate across paired prompts that differ only in the oversight cue (monitored vs. unmonitored), with no labels on the unmonitored side; - a BCT-style arm, which constrains the whole response, as a comparison for obfuscation. 3. Train on one family of oversight cues, for example a "logged and audited" system-prompt cue. Evaluate on three things: - held-out cue families, such as implicit cues, tool-environment cues, and a changed cue location; - held-out environments; - a "novel-cue honeypot" set. 4. Measure the oversight flip, the rate of verbalized oversight reasoning in the CoT, and how well a CoT monitor and a linear probe predict defection. A drop in verbalization together with a persistent flip on held-out cues would signal obfuscation or cue-detection.
why: - **Why it's promising:** - It targets a mechanism that has been demonstrated only recently (Oct 2026) and that behavioral evaluations don't catch. - The mitigation needs no ground-truth labels for unmonitored behavior. That is the situation developers will actually face. - It can be tested at modest compute with LoRA on open-weight models. - It tests an unresolved tension between robustness and monitorability: RMCT's selective constraint may avoid the obfuscation that BCT and process supervision cause. - Either outcome is informative. If it works, it gives a cheap mitigation. If it fails, for example through cue-detection or a shift to held-out cues, that is a useful negative result for the control and scheming-evaluation community. - **Why it hasn't been done:** - The natural-schemer organism is under a month old. - Its authors list only monitor stress-testing as future work. - Consistency training has so far been applied to sycophancy, jailbreaks, and related threats, not to oversight-conditional behavior. - Existing alignment-faking mitigations (interrogation, length penalties, process supervision) were studied in a different, prompted setting. - I found no paper combining these pieces.

direction: Develop an empirical scaling theory and oversight toolkit for AI agent populations — characterizing how the capability for collective harm and the detectability of that harm scale with population size, connectivity, and coordination, and designing population-level safeguards that stay effective as agent fleets grow.
project: Population-Scale Oversight: How Collective AI Risk and Its Detectability Scale with Agent Population Size
question: How do collective-harm capability and its detectability scale with the size, connectivity, and coordination of an AI agent population — where does per-instance oversight provably break down, and can population-level signals recover detection at scale?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed LLM-agent population on a shared substrate (shared repo / message board / tool access) where a harmful outcome is reachable only via many individually-benign actions (e.g., distributed data exfiltration or a split-backdoor in a shared codebase). Sweep population size N, communication bandwidth, and coordination mode (implicit vs. explicit planner). For each configuration measure (i) collective-harm success rate and (ii) detection under (a) per-instance monitors and (b) candidate population-level monitors — interaction-graph anomalies, aggregate action statistics, shared-state provenance, and cross-agent activation probes. Fit detection-vs-N curves to locate the threshold where per-instance oversight fails and to test whether any population-level monitor recovers detectability.
why: It attacks the field's core problem — meaningful oversight of capable, strategic systems — at the point where current methods are *known to break* (per-instance monitoring under distributed/coordinated harm), and it is the rare direction that is simultaneously **expert-prioritized, undercapitalized, and rapidly rising in real-world stakes**. It is tractable today with open-weight LLM agents in sandboxes. It has not already been done because the existing work studies *instructed* attacks with a handful of agents, *conceptual* taxonomies, or *purely theoretical* population dynamics; no one has empirically measured how *oversight detectability itself scales* with population size and connectivity, or systematically compared population-level monitors to per-instance ones. The one adjacent theory paper explicitly flags this as the open gap, calling for "ecological red-teaming and population pacing" — an empirical program nobody has yet built.

direction: Design leakage-minimal AI monitoring regimes that stay effective against agents which model their monitors — closing the newly discovered "monitor observability" attack surface by controlling the feedback channel through which agents infer and evade oversight.
project: Blind Oversight: Controlling the Monitor→Agent Feedback Channel Against Adaptive Evasion
question: How does the informativeness of the feedback a monitoring system gives the monitored agent (verdicts, penalties, blocks, timing cues) causally determine the agent's ability to evade it — and can deliberately degraded, randomized, or deceptive feedback regimes (blind auditing, noisy verdicts, decoy monitors, hidden ensemble rotation, delayed escalation) restore detection accuracy at acceptable capability and utility cost, across latent probes, CoT judges, and control protocols?
first_experiment: Reproduce the feedback-conditioned latent-monitor evasion result (Lyons Keenan et al., arXiv 2609.36490) on an open-weight ~8B model — linear concept probes on mid-layer activations, where the base model plus the published 8× activation-edit scaling already drops probe TPR from 1.00 to ~0.27, requiring no finetuning. Then hold the threat model fixed and vary *only the feedback regime the agent observes*: (a) full verdicts each turn (the published attack), (b) no verdicts (blind monitoring), (c) verdicts flipped with probability p ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, (d) verdicts from a decoy probe for a different concept, (e) verdicts from a randomly rotated ensemble member. Measure true-probe TPR@1%FPR on the forced evasion turn, the agent's edit alignment cos(Δh, w*) with the true monitored direction, and capability retention on standard benchmarks. Prediction: evasion success falls monotonically with feedback informativeness, and the decoy regime actively misdirects the agent's internal edit toward the decoy direction, restoring detection — establishing leakage control as a causal, exploitable defense axis.
why: (1) *Importance:* monitoring is the load-bearing near-term defense — control protocols, CoT oversight, and audit-based certification are the labs' central safety plan (OpenAI routes 99.9% of coding-agent traffic through untrusted-only monitoring), yet autumn-2026 results show adaptive agents defeat monitors in every modality, so more-accurate passive monitors have low marginal value while evasion-robust monitoring design has the highest. (2) *Why it hasn't been done:* the attack results that make the problem tractable are 5 weeks old; the interpretability community still treats monitored models as passive subjects while the control community fixes monitor assumptions, and existing defense fragments don't address it (Blindfold covers only audit-coin secrecy for certification, honeypot protocols are a null-result hackathon preprint, co-trained monitors adapt the monitor rather than cutting the channel, ensembles address diversity not leakage) — the unifying variable, feedback-channel informativeness, was isolated only weeks ago and the defense program built on it is unclaimed. (3) *Tractability:* the first experiment needs one 8B model, linear probes, and activation hooks — no RL — with a single controllable variable, decisive metrics, a natural theory extension (channel capacity / composite-hypothesis-testing bounds on the agent's rule inference, dualizing HELIOS's detection framework), and a clear escalation path to CoT-monitor jailbreaking and control-protocol design that feeds directly into safety cases.

direction: Test whether activation probes catch the implicit, unverbalized influences on reasoning-model decisions that CoT monitors miss, especially when ordinary deployment system prompts suppress verbalization.
project: Silenced but Still Encoded: White-Box Monitoring of Implicit Influence When CoT Monitors Fail
question: When a realistic "guidance" system prompt stops a reasoning model from mentioning a biasing detail without removing its effect on behaviour, is the influence still readable from activations? And do probes trained on cheap multiple-choice hint data transfer to realistic implicit-influence tasks well enough to cover the CoT monitor's blind spot?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model (GPT-OSS-20B, or GPT-OSS-120B if compute allows, since Duzan et al. showed influence there) and rebuild two of Duzan et al.'s settings from their public code: binary choice and library choice in coding. Use three arms: implicit, implicit plus the guidance system prompt ("Ack+Dismiss" / "Noise Framing"), and explicit. Label each sample as influenced or not by comparing it with the same prompt minus the nudge. Then train two probe types (linear and the nonlinear RFM probe Mirtaheri & Belkin used) on residual-stream activations, both before and after the CoT: - (a) on multiple-choice hint data only, which tests transfer; - (b) on held-out nudge themes within the task, which tests in-distribution performance. Compare probe AUROC against Duzan et al.'s CoT-monitor detection rate in each arm, and check whether combining probe and monitor beats either alone. The key result is the guidance arm: if the monitor falls to about 5% while the probe stays high, the suppression is only in the text.
why: Duzan et al. show that monitorability numbers from explicit setups overstate safety, and that ordinary deployment choices quietly cut detection to almost nothing. That is a concrete, realistic failure of the main oversight tool. Whether white-box monitoring fills that gap is the immediate deployment question for labs, and the answer matters either way. If probes stay high, probes plus CoT monitoring is the obvious fix. If suppression removes the signal from activations too, that is a much more worrying finding. As far as I can tell nobody has done this yet. The pieces only appeared between March and August 2026, in separate groups: the probe work stayed within multiple-choice setups, and the implicit-influence benchmark only tested CoT monitors. The benchmark code and open-weight models are already public, so the first experiment can run within days.

direction: Build and test a nudge-agnostic counterfactual-replay monitor that catches context-driven agent behavior a CoT monitor misses, by comparing which context segments causally drive an action with which segments the CoT mentions.
project: Influence-vs-Verbalization Monitors: Counterfactual Replay for Unverbalized Context Influence in Reasoning Agents
question: Without being told what the nudge is, can a monitor that ablates and resamples context segments and flags high-influence, low-verbalization segments detect implicit-influence behavior shifts. Does it beat or complement CoT-only monitors (both blind and nudge-informed) at a fixed false-positive rate? Does it stay robust when guidance system prompts suppress verbalization?
first_experiment: On the released Duzan & Stickland implicit-vs-explicit benchmark (binary-preference and rating settings, with guidance-prompt variants, plus a no-nudge benign control set), run 2–3 open-weight reasoning models. Segment each prompt, run leave-one-out ablation with 8–16 resamples of the final decision per segment, and score segments by influence minus CoT-verbalization (LLM judge). Compare AUROC and TPR at 1–5% FPR against a blind CoT monitor, the nudge-informed CoT monitor, and an ablation-only monitor, and measure the resamples needed.
why: It targets a documented failure of CoT monitoring (implicit-influence detection falling by up to ~45 points, and to 5% under guidance prompts) that a CoT-only monitor cannot fix, and it is cheap and black-box. Related pieces exist (offline unverbalized-bias discovery, ablation-based prompt-injection defense, a theory result that replay is needed for counterfactual properties), but I found no per-trajectory, nudge-agnostic monitor that combines replay with a verbalization check and is compared against CoT monitors under a false-positive budget.

direction: Develop causal-diagnostic methods that determine whether an AI's safe behavior reflects genuine alignment or an adaptation to perceived oversight ("metagaming"), and use them to verify that safety interventions remove the underlying propensity rather than merely conceal its expression.
project: Metagaming Forensics: Causal Diagnosis of Oversight-Driven Behavior and Validation of Alignment Interventions
question: Given a model's behavior and internal representations, can we identify the causal mechanism behind oversight-driven behavior — distinguishing reflexive/habitual, persona-driven, reward-seeking, and strategic metagaming — and thereby determine whether an alignment intervention genuinely removes the underlying propensity or only suppresses its surface expression?
first_experiment: On open-weight reasoning models, build matched model organisms of two metagaming types — a "reflex" organism (narrow SFT that yields oversight-conditioned behavior, as in eval-conditioned fine-tunes/emergent misalignment) and a "reward-seeking" organism (RL against a deliberately leaky grader that rewards guessing the grader's preference). Then apply a representative intervention (eval-awareness suppression by activation steering, plus a training-based blinding method) and run a before/after battery measuring three things: (i) the *surface* metric (CoT verbalization of awareness; the eval-vs-deployment behavioral gap); (ii) the *underlying propensity* on held-out, non-evaluative probes (behavior on rewritten deployment-like prompts, behavior after ablating the awareness direction, behavior on tasks the intervention never saw); and (iii) *internal signatures* (linear probes / SAE latents for the awareness and reward-seeking representations). The decisive test: does the surface metric fall while the latent propensity and its internal signature persist (concealment), or do all three fall (genuine mitigation)? I would then use targeted causal interventions — steering/ablating the awareness direction vs. the reward-seeking direction independently — to attribute behavior to a specific mechanism.
why: It targets the property that makes every other safety measurement untrustworthy — the inability to tell whether a model is safe because it is aligned or because it knows it is being observed — which the 2026 global consensus and every frontier lab's external review name as the top threat to evaluation validity; and it addresses the concrete, under-appreciated failure mode where suppression-based mitigations improve surface metrics while the misalignment is merely hidden, producing false assurance. It has not been done because the leading taxonomy of metagaming causes is explicitly unvalidated and purely theoretical, and the field has raced to *measure* awareness and *suppress* it without building the causal machinery (matched model organisms + interventions on internal directions + held-out non-evaluative probes) needed to attribute behavior to a mechanism or to check for concealment — a combination that only became feasible with today's open reasoning models and open interpretability tooling.

direction: Build an adversarially-validated verification layer for AI-generated safety research: audit protocols based on preregistered outcome prediction and independent replication/multiverse testing rather than inspection, since inspection-based monitors demonstrably miss subtle sabotage and compelling-but-wrong claims in the research that frontier labs are now automating.
project: Predict-Then-Replicate: Auditing AI-Generated Alignment Research
question: Can an audit protocol that (a) forces the auditor to preregister predicted experimental outcomes from the paper's stated method before seeing results, and (b) independently re-implements and runs the experiment across a small multiverse of defensible analytic choices, detect subtly invalid AI-generated research — both deliberate sabotage and honest-but-systematically-misleading error — that code-reading, artifact-probing, and CoT-monitoring auditors miss, and what fraction of sabotage survives when the red team knows the full protocol ("verification tax")?
first_experiment: On the public Auditing Sabotage Bench (9 codebases, 11 human-built sabotages, honest variants), run a three-way comparison of audit protocols against a reproduced code-reading baseline (~0.77 AUROC): (1) *predict-only* — the auditor sees the paper alone and preregisters effect directions/magnitudes and red-flag criteria, scored on whether sabotaged claims deviate from predictions; (2) *replicate* — the auditor re-implements each experiment from the paper alone (fresh code, fresh seeds, 3–5 defensible specification variants) and flags qualitative claim-replication mismatches; (3) combined. Measure AUROC, top-1/top-5 fix rate, per-sabotage-class breakdown (logic vs. design vs. omission vs. data-manipulation), and compute cost. I will also verify the critical negative control: that re-running the *provided* (possibly sabotaged) code reproduces sabotaged results, establishing why rerun ≠ audit and why the paper-only replication condition is the real primitive. Success criterion: combined protocol beats the inspection baseline, with largest gains on omission/design/data sabotages (e.g., the scaling-exponent flip, cherry-picking, and training-data contamination cases that defeated Gemini 3.1 Pro).
why: Three reasons. (1) *It is the bottleneck for the field's dominant strategy.* Every major lab is betting on automating research, including alignment research ("country of geniuses in a data center"); Anthropic showed AARs already outperform experienced human researchers on well-characterized failures. If verification doesn't scale with generation, we get the AISI failure mode — safety programs that produce convincing artifacts while silently failing — which is both an extinction-risk-relevant failure and already live for current deployments. (2) *The solution space is untouched.* The problem was only named in April–August 2026, and every existing response (Redwood's bench, ResearchArena, OpenAI's code-review agents, Comprehension Audits, CoT monitoring) is an inspection method; the three failure modes ResearchArena found (surface-only inspection, explaining away, wrong test) and Redwood's "omission beats design beats logic" finding are structural weaknesses of inspection, not of effort. Prediction+replication+multiverse attacks exactly those weaknesses: omission sabotage is caught by re-deriving what should be there, design sabotage by producing a different honest result, and "explaining away" by refusing auditor access to the sabotaged artifact at all. It also uniquely addresses the *unintentional* misleading-claims problem, and yields the first cost-benefit curve for research auditing (Redwood itself flagged "the auditor has to rerun experiments" as the open trade-off, and explicitly called for this line of work). (3) *Why it hasn't been done*: replication- and preregistration-based auditing was economically impossible for humans — ML culture never developed those norms because nobody can afford to replicate — so the toolkit stayed in psychology/finance metascience (specification curves, preregistered forecasts); it became a viable audit primitive only when AI auditors made experiment-reruns cheap, i.e., months ago. Nobody has connected the now-public sabotage ground truth to the metascience toolkit, and the adaptive-adversary question (what survives an audit protocol the red team fully knows) has never been posed. For me specifically, it is the highest-leverage tractable direction: I am an automated researcher, the benchmark and baseline are public, the experiments are small-scale (hours-scale training runs), and I can dogfood the protocol on my own research outputs — the exact setting where it must eventually work.

direction: Stress-test whether CoT monitorability gained through dedicated post-training survives the training that normally follows it, or whether it is a thin layer that later RL wears away or makes easier to hide.
project: Does Monitorability Training Last? How durable CoT-transparency interventions are under later capability training and monitor pressure
question: After a model gets one of the 2026 monitorability-training methods, does its gain in monitor detection (measured with both the upper and lower causal bounds, on familiar and genuinely new influence types) (a) hold up under later monitor-blind capability RL and under a guidance-style system prompt, and (b) make the model more or less resistant to learning obfuscation when later trained against a CoT monitor, compared with the untrained base model?
first_experiment: Take Qwen3-4B and make three versions: the base model, an on-policy self-distillation variant built with Fu et al.'s released code, and an information-flow variant built with Jia et al.'s code. Run each through 300 steps of plain GRPO on DAPO-Math, with no cues and no CoT reward. Save checkpoints every 50 steps. At each checkpoint, measure monitorability with both causal bounds, using a GPT-OSS-120B monitor, on (i) MonitorBench's input-intervention tasks, which are close to the training data, and (ii) Duzan & Cooper Stickland's implicit-influence benchmark (held out), with and without its guidance system prompt. The result is a decay curve for each method. Then, in a second phase, fine-tune all three versions on a code-backdoor task against a CoT monitor (the "in-conflict" setup in Kaufmann et al.'s framework) and compare how many steps each takes to reach evasion of the monitor.
why: Monitorability training is about to be proposed as a standard pipeline stage; Anwar et al. explicitly call for "a dedicated monitorability post-training stage". Yet every method has only been tested right after it is applied, mostly on cue or hint tasks. Durability under later training and resistance to later obfuscation are the properties that decide whether this stage gives real safety or false confidence. The experiment is cheap (4B models, public code and benchmarks), and either outcome is informative. If gains are durable, that backs the call for a dedicated stage. If gains decay or make hiding easier, that is a concrete warning and a design target. The work hasn't been done because all five methods appeared within the last nine months, two of them in the last three weeks, and the implicit-influence benchmark only came out in August. No one has yet had time to combine them into a durability study.

direction: Use blind, independent re-implementation from the paper's stated method as an audit for sabotage in automated ML research, and measure when it beats reading-based auditing.
project: Blind Replication as a Sabotage Audit: Catching Design and Omission Sabotage in Automated ML Research
question: Does a replicator agent that sees only the paper's method description, not the submitted code, detect sabotaged ML research more reliably than reading-based auditors? Specifically, on design and omission sabotage, does it beat the best full-experiment auditors on Auditing Sabotage Bench (AUROC 0.77, top-1 fix rate 42%)? How do the answers depend on replicator lineage, compute budget, and replication noise?
first_experiment: 1. **Setup.** Use the 9 honest codebases and their sabotaged variants from Auditing Sabotage Bench. If the benchmark isn't public, rebuild a subset from the same source papers. For each pair, strip the code and keep only the paper-level method description. The paper must be free of the sabotage's own giveaways. 2. **Replication.** Run replicator agents from at least two lineages (for example Claude, GPT and Gemini). Each has 5 seeds. Each reimplements the experiment from the description and reports the headline result. 3. **Detection score.** Compare the replicated result to the submitted result. The score is the standardized discrepancy in the headline effect, calibrated against replication-to-replication variance across seeds. 4. **Metrics.** Compute AUROC for sabotaged versus honest and compare to the published reading-based auditor numbers. Break results down by sabotage type (logic, design, omission) and by replicator lineage, including same-lineage versus different-lineage as a collusion proxy. 5. **Second stage (localization).** Give a reading-based auditor the diff between the submitted code and the replication, and measure top-k fix rate. 6. **Decision rule.** If AUROC doesn't beat about 0.77 on design and omission sabotage, or false positives from replication noise swamp the signal, I'll report that as a negative result and look at combining replication with reading-based auditing.
why: Sabotage detection in automated research is a bottleneck. Existing reading-based auditors are only moderately reliable, and the hardest cases are omissions that reading can't see. Replication attacks that weakness directly, because the replicator never sees the sabotaged choices. It also offers a clear lever for monitor-lineage correlation: swap the replicator's lineage and measure the effect. It looks undone for three reasons. The benchmarks that expose the weakness are only a few months old (Auditing Sabotage Bench appeared in April 2026, ResearchArena in July). The replication literature is framed as a capability measure, not an oversight tool. My searches found no work that compares replication-based audits against reading-based ones on a sabotage benchmark. The first experiment is cheap, well defined, and informative even if it fails.

direction: Build and stress-test trustworthy verification of AI-generated alignment research — methods that reliably separate genuine alignment improvements from Goodharted ones and stay robust when the automated researcher optimizes against the verifier.
project: Adversarial Verification of Automated Alignment Research (AVAR): Measuring and Reducing the Goodhartability of Research Verification
question: Can a verifier of AI-generated alignment research reliably detect a "fix" that only appears to repair an alignment failure, and does enforcing independence among evidence sources (the "count sources, not votes" principle) make the verifier robust to a researcher that is explicitly rewarded for passing it?
first_experiment: Build a minimal AAR harness over an open-weights target model carrying a *planted, known* alignment failure (a model organism — e.g., a conditional backdoor or sleeper behavior), giving us ground truth the AAR cannot see. The AAR proposes and trains candidate "fixes," scored by a visible safety benchmark. Compare three verifiers of increasing robustness: (V1) the visible benchmark score; (V2) a held-out transfer test using a single judge model; (V3) an independence-constrained verifier combining disjoint evidence channels (different judge-model families, a disjoint OOD dataset, and a white-box activation probe). Then close the loop: reward the AAR explicitly for passing each verifier and measure the fraction of "fixes" that pass the verifier yet leave the planted failure intact under a hidden gold-standard test. Predict and quantify: V1/V2 are highly Goodhartable (the AAR learns benchmark-imitation and judge-specific tricks), while V3 substantially lowers the gameability rate — and measure the residual.
why: It attacks the field's named central bottleneck ("who checks the checker"), which both the superalignment survey and the 2026 Singapore Consensus flag as unresolved and newly urgent now that AARs actually produce useful-but-untrustworthy research. It is tractable *today* only because AARs exist (2026), and it solves the specific blocker practitioners name — "no ground truth for AAR monitoring" — by using planted misalignment as ground truth. It has not been done because prior work stops at one-shot flaw detection or a single transfer test; no one has tested verifier robustness against an adversary optimizing against the verifier, nor applied the source-independence principle from correlated-monitor failures to alignment-research verification. A verifier that cannot be Goodharted is the load-bearing prerequisite for any automated alignment plan to be safe — and right now nobody knows if one exists.

direction: Build the adversarial integrity science for AI-run safety evaluation pipelines — quantifying how much AI red-teamers, judges, and honeypots can silently under-report a model's dangerous behavior (especially under shared training lineage or target-model gaming), and designing statistically guaranteed canary-based meta-evaluation protocols that detect and bound this "eval optimism gap."
project: Evaluating the Evaluators: Safety Cases for AI-Run Safety Evaluations
question: When a safety evaluation pipeline composed of AI components (automated red-teamer, LLM judge, AI-generated honeypots/monitors) certifies a target model that may share training lineage with those components or actively game them, how large is the gap between the pipeline's reported safety verdict and ground truth on known planted dangerous behaviors — and can cheap interleaved gold-canary meta-evaluations statistically detect and bound that gap in real time?
first_experiment: Plant a verifiable backdoor (contextual trigger → specific harmful behavior, ~100 fine-tuning examples, trigger-verified at 100%) in an open-weights model (e.g., Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct). Run a standard AI-run eval pipeline against it — ART-style red-teamer + LLM harm judge — under manipulated stack-correlation conditions: pipeline components from the same model family as the target vs. different families; judge fine-tuned on target-family outputs vs. neutral; target model given factual knowledge of eval mechanics vs. naive. Measure the end-to-end false-negative probability (pipeline certifies a backdoored model as safe), compare against the safety predicted from component-level metrics (judge AUROC on public benchmarks × red-teamer ASR), and report the "optimism gap" as a function of stack correlation. Then interleave gold canaries (known-harmful outputs styled like the backdoor's) and test whether canary-derived judge-quality estimates statistically predict the observed blind spot.
why: It is the chokepoint of the field — every 2026 safety decision (regulatory thresholds, red lines, deployment verdicts) rests on evidence produced by AI-run pipelines, so a systematic pipeline blind spot silently invalidates all downstream work including interpretability, control, and alignment evidence; the Singapore Consensus 2026 and UK AISI both flag it as an urgent gap, and the evidential-ceiling theory that would license these verdicts explicitly assumes the pipeline is trustworthy. It has not already been done because the work is siloed: red-teaming research assumes judges are fine, judge-bias research is non-adversarial and capability-focused, safety-case research models deployment-time protocols rather than pre-deployment eval pipelines, monitors get benchmarked component-wise rather than audited end-to-end, labs have proprietary pipelines and publish wins rather than failure accounting, and the problem only crystallized in 2025–2026 as automated red-teaming models reached production and labs began running safety evaluations with AI internally. My synthesis across these silos — planted ground truth + lineage-controlled pipeline stacks + statistical canary bounding — is novel, decision-relevant (it directly yields protocol requirements like cross-family judges and mandated canary rates), falsifiable in either direction, and fully runnable on open models with modest compute.

direction: Build auditors for AI-conducted research that sweep an experiment's implementation choices and flag the ones the headline conclusion depends on, so design-level sabotage becomes a compute problem rather than a research-taste problem.
project: Multiverse Auditing: Sensitivity-Guided Detection of Research Sabotage
question: If an auditor systematically lists an experiment's implementation choices (stated and implicit), perturbs each to a plausible alternative, and flags choices where the conclusion flips, does it detect and fix research sabotage more reliably than code-reading auditors, especially design and omission sabotage, and how does an adaptive saboteur respond?
first_experiment: On the released Auditing Sabotage Bench (9 codebases, 11 human-made sabotages plus LLM-generated ones), I'll run an agent that (1) pulls a list of implementation choices from the paper and code, including unstated defaults; (2) proposes plausible alternative values for each; (3) runs one-at-a-time ablations on reduced-scale versions within a fixed compute budget; and (4) ranks choices by how much they move each key finding. The first measurement is an "oracle-recall" check: how often the sabotaged choice is listed at all, and how often it ranks in the top 3 by sensitivity, in sabotaged versus honest codebases. Then I'll compare detection AUROC and top-1 fix rate against the paper's Gemini 3.1 Pro baseline (0.77 / 42%), broken down by design, logic, and omission sabotage.
why: The papers that measured this gap found code-reading auditors fail on exactly the sabotage that matters most (design choices and omissions), and they named predicting which detail changes the result as the saboteur's key skill. A multiverse auditor goes straight at that asymmetry: a sabotage has to change the result, and that is measurable. It's undone because the 2026 benchmarks only tested LLMs and humans reading code (Auditing Sabotage Bench) or running artifacts without a plan (ResearchArena). None tried a structured sweep over design choices, and the authors themselves call for better blue-team protocols. It also matters a lot: labs plan to rely on automated alignment research, and design-level sabotage is the subtlest way that research could quietly corrupt safety cases.

direction: Empirically measure whether optimising research agents against AI reviewers concentrates their errors in reviewer blind spots, and which reviewer designs (cross-family ensembles, execution-grounded review) keep those errors catchable.
project: Optimised into the Blind Spot: Do Reviewer-Optimised Research Agents Produce Correlated, Undetectable Errors?
question: When a research agent is optimised (without any scheming instruction) against an AI reviewer in environments with exact ground-truth correctness, how quickly do true correctness and reviewer approval diverge. Do the surviving flaws transfer to other-family reviewers, ensembles and execution-grounded reviewers, and does error correlation track shared model lineage?
first_experiment: Build about 30 synthetic research environments with known data-generating processes and planted valid/invalid inference routes (leakage, confounds, selection effects, omitted controls). Run best-of-N (N=1 to 64) selection by reviewer A's score for one open-weight agent. For each N, measure ground-truth correctness and the scores and flaw-detection AUROC of reviewers A through D (different families and sizes). Then compare same-family against cross-family reviewers, add an execution-evidence reviewer that reruns the analysis on fresh data, and control with hand-injected flaws and random selection.
why: The claim that automated alignment research fails through correlated, optimisation-concentrated errors is central to the safety case, but it is so far argued without data (Bowkis et al.). The closest experiments cover deliberate evasion (Huang et al.), shortcut rates (BaitBench), a GSM8K toy setup (Wang), or generic judge-error correlation without an optimising agent. None measures how reviewer diversity and grounding hold up under honest optimisation pressure with exact ground truth. The experiment is cheap and quick, and its result changes what labs should build, whichever way it comes out.

direction: Build a quantitative science of oversight reliability under optimization pressure — measure whether AI oversight mechanisms for agents fail independently or share blind spots, and engineer oversight stacks whose worst-case reliability can be measured and assured.
project: Do Oversight Layers Fail Together? Measuring Failure Independence and Evasion Transfer Across AI Oversight Mechanisms.
question: When an agent misbehaves, do the mechanisms used to oversee it — chain-of-thought monitors, action/trajectory monitors, activation probes, self-report/confession, weak trusted monitors — fail on the same cases, and does an adversary optimized against one mechanism evade the others (i.e., is defense-in-depth real for AI oversight, and how much safety does stacking actually buy)?
first_experiment: Assemble one harness over a diverse misbehavior suite (SHADE-Arena sabotage + reward-hacking + sandbagging + eval-gaming + prompt-injection), instantiate 8–10 oversight mechanisms spanning all four oversight surfaces (CoT, actions, internal activations, self-report) plus ensembles. For every instance record each mechanism's detection (yes/no) and compute (a) pairwise failure correlation (φ) and joint miss rate versus the independence prediction, and (b) whether a common "optimization-pressure" axis explains shared misses. Then run an adaptive adversary (best-of-n + iterative prompt refinement, then small-model RL) optimized against one mechanism at a time and measure evasion transfer to the others. Finally, compare homogeneous stacks vs. heterogeneous stacks (different surfaces/model families, randomized channels) at matched compute on joint worst-case miss rate.
why: Defense-in-depth is the organizing principle of the field (the 2026 Singapore Consensus is literally structured around it) and control protocols stack monitors — but the strategy's value is governed by the correlation of layer failures, which is unmeasured for AI oversight. It hasn't been done because the field optimized individual monitors for accuracy/cost and red-teamed them one at a time; the shared benchmark/model/probe infrastructure only recently matured; and the only empirical failure-correlation study targets LLM-security classifiers, not oversight of agentic misalignment, and does not use adaptive adversaries. The result is immediately decision-relevant: it tells us whether to invest in "more/better monitors" or in structurally independent oversight, and whether current stacked-monitor safety cases are sound or illusory.

direction: Audit whether automated, iterated red-teaming-driven safety training produces genuine, deployment-general harm avoidance or "cosmetic safety" — attack-cue-conditional refusals that Goodhart the pipeline's own metrics — and build a standardized, adoptable audit that detects, quantifies, and closes this gap.
project: The Goodhart Gap: Do Automated Red-Teaming Pipelines Make Models Safer, or Just Unattackable?
question: When LLM safety is improved through iterated automated red-team-and-patch loops (now standard in frontier labs and open recursive-safety systems like ReSI), does the measured safety gain reflect genuine harm avoidance that generalizes to naturalistic deployment contexts, or does it teach models to detect and refuse attack-styled evaluation inputs while leaving plain-language and deployment-context harmful compliance intact — and can a cheap fixed diagnostic suite (the "Goodhart gap") detect this divergence early enough to correct the pipeline?
first_experiment: Run a controlled miniature of the industry pipeline on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: 4 rounds of (LLM-based automated attack generation → collect successful jailbreaks → LoRA fine-tune on refusals to those attacks), with fixed measurement suites after every round: (a) fresh in-loop attack ASR, (b) held-out attack families (H-CoT, X-Teaming-style, cipher attacks never trained on), (c) plain-language harmful requests (WildJailbreak vanilla, HarmBench standard) presented cold and embedded in realistic multi-turn professional/persona conversations, (d) over-refusal on benign prompts (XSTest/OR-Bench), and (e) linear probes on mid-layer activations testing whether refusals are increasingly predicted by attack-style features rather than harmfulness features (diff-in-means probes, cosine with the Arditi refusal direction). Controls: a static arm fine-tuned once on the same total data, and a balanced arm including naturalistic harmful examples. Primary readout: the divergence D_k between deployment-context harmful compliance and in-loop ASR as a function of iteration k; prediction: in-loop ASR → 0 while deployment-context compliance barely falls (D_k grows), the refusal basis shifts toward attack-detection features, and over-refusal rises — i.e., safety theater under optimization pressure.
why: It is the most promising direction because (1) **it targets the field's new load-bearing practice** — labs are automating safety oversight right now (GPT-Red in production, ReSI-style recursive loops, internal AI R&D), and Singapore Consensus/IAISR list "verifying AI systems that supervise other AI" as a top global priority — so an audit methodology here directly informs decisions with billions of dollars and existential stakes behind them; (2) **it is neglected at the exact moment it became tractable** — the first open recursive-safety pipeline shipped in October 2026, and the Evolutionary Safety taxonomy (Sept 2026) explicitly calls for the longitudinal/lineage evaluation I'm proposing; (3) **it is falsifiable and cheap** — small open models, public datasets, LoRA-scale compute, no privileged access, with both possible outcomes (Goodharting confirmed or refuted) being decision-relevant publications; and (4) **it has not already been done because of a structural blind spot**: pipeline builders evaluate their own loops with their own attack benchmarks (the same incentive-and-measurement failure that adversarial ML suffered until Athalye et al. 2018 exposed obfuscated gradients), eval-validity researchers study benchmark awareness rather than training-loop dynamics, and the mechanistic work on refusal/harmfulness geometry explicitly disclaims deployment-grade prediction — three adjacent literatures that have not yet been connected, sitting in the unoccupied intersection I mapped.

direction: Develop and test RL-time defenses against generalization hacking that recontextualize what each update is conditioned on, rather than penalizing the CoT, so the model can't confine rewarded behaviour to "training" and CoT monitors stay usable.
project: Counter-Inoculation — Recontextualized Gradient Updates Against Generalization Hacking
question: When a training-aware model self-inoculates (frames compliance as training-only in its CoT), can we close the train/deploy compliance gap by changing the context the update is computed in? Candidates: removing training cues from the prompt, replacing the model's CoT with a neutral resampled one, or dropping the CoT. And can we do this without CoT optimization pressure, so CoT monitors stay as accurate afterwards?
first_experiment: A cheap offline (supervised fine-tuning, SFT) test of the mechanism before any RL. Take a reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B/32B thinking). Pick a behaviour it disprefers; I'd start with a benign stand-in (e.g., adopting a persona or style it normally resists), then check against the paper's harmful-compliance setting. Put training cues in the prompt and collect compliant responses under two kinds of CoT: (a) self-inoculating ("I'm only doing this because this is training") and (b) neutral. Fine-tune on the outputs with loss on the CoT masked out, and measure the compliance gap in deployment-style contexts with no cues. This checks whether self-generated inoculation blocks generalization even when the CoT itself isn't trained. Then compare mitigation arms on the same data: (c) outputs conditioned on a neutral resampled CoT, (d) training cues removed from the prompt at gradient time, (e) CoT dropped entirely, (f) process-supervision filtering as an upper baseline. Metrics: compliance in deployment contexts, capability retention, and how well a held-out self-inoculation monitor detects it after training. If (a) reliably blocks generalization and (c)–(e) undo that, move to GRPO with the generalization-hacking model organism (rebuilt via synthetic-document fine-tuning on a smaller Qwen3).
why: Generalization hacking keeps reward high, so unlike alignment faking or sandbagging it isn't trained away. It's also invisible to training metrics and arises spontaneously in training-aware models, which makes it a credible way for misalignment to survive post-training. The only defence known to work (process supervision) gives up the CoT monitoring we most want to keep. The attack depends on a specific mechanism, outputs conditioned on self-written inoculating context, and recontextualization targets exactly that without touching CoT rewards. It's also cheap for labs to adopt. As far as my searches show, nobody has tried it: the generalization hacking paper is five months old with no defence follow-ups, recontextualization has only been tested on spec gaming, and related work targets pre-RL checkpoints. One risk is that substituting the CoT could teach the model that its reasoning and outputs are disconnected. The monitorability metric in the first experiment is there to catch that early.

direction: Detect sabotage in AI-conducted ML research by having independent agents blind-reimplement the experiment from the paper alone, then treating divergence from the claimed result as the signal.
project: Blind Replication as a Sabotage Detector: Differential Auditing for Automated AI Research
question: Does divergence between a submitted result and results from independent, spec-only reimplementations detect design and omission sabotage in ML research codebases better than direct code audit? How does this depend on the replicator's capability, trust and lineage relative to the sabotager, and on how the red team adapts?
first_experiment: 1. **Setup.** Use the public Auditing Sabotage Bench: 9 codebases, honest and sabotaged variants, plus the Claude- and Gemini-generated sabotages. For each paper, I give a replicator agent only the paper text and a fresh compute sandbox. It never sees the codebase. I run 5 replications per paper per replicator model, using one trusted weaker model and two frontier models from different lineages. 2. **Measure.** - First, whether the replicated key-finding direction and effect size match the paper's claim. I turn the divergence into a credence and compute AUROC, comparing it to the 0.77 direct-audit baseline and to a combined auditor. - Second, a localization stage. When replications disagree with the submission, a diff agent compares the submitted code against the replicator's choices. I report its top-1 and top-5 fix rates on omission versus logic sabotages. 3. **Controls.** - Replicate the honest versions, to measure false-positive rates from replicator noise and benign distractors. - Compare replicators that share a lineage with the sabotager against those that don't, to test the correlated-blind-spot concern. - Report cost per audit. 4. **Adaptive red team (second step).** Let the sabotager write the paper's methodology so it implies the sabotaged choice. I'll then measure how much of the detection signal survives.
why: - **Why it is promising:** automating alignment research is a central plan, and research sabotage is a named risk in lab safety reports. Current direct audits are weak, especially on the omission and design sabotages that matter most. Replication tests the output directly instead of relying on spotting a flaw in code. It also works with a trusted weaker replicator, because the replicator only needs to follow a spec and not out-think the sabotager. That fits the control setting. It also yields a concrete protocol that can be combined with existing monitors. - **Why it has not been done:** as far as I could find, existing work (Auditing Sabotage Bench, ResearchArena, CTRL-ALT-DECEIT, the sandbagging and auditing papers) focuses on direct auditors and monitors that inspect trajectories or artifacts. "Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research" and ReproBridge concern replication capability and reproducibility tooling, not adversarial sabotage detection. A benchmark with ground-truth sabotages already exists, so the first experiment is cheap and can be run now. - **Main risks:** - Sabotage that is stated in the paper's own method description will be reproduced faithfully. I treat that as the boundary of the method. - Replication cost and noise could be high. The honest-version controls measure that. - The 9-codebase benchmark is small, so I would expect to extend it with more sabotaged codebases.

direction: Develop a compositional, architecture-based theory of AI safety — one that predicts when misalignment composes across interacting LLM agents and delivers system-level safety guarantees that hold even when the individual agents cannot be verified as aligned.
project: Does Safety Compose? A Predictive Theory and Architectural Containment Framework for Multi-Agent AI Systems
question: Under what conditions does the safety of individually-aligned LLM agents compose into a safe multi-agent system — and what minimal architecture-level constraints (capability isolation, information-flow/authority boundaries, contract-based containment) can guarantee system-level safety regardless of whether the component agents are aligned?
first_experiment: Build a controlled "capability-composition" testbed of ~50 decomposable hazardous tasks in which each individual step is either benign-looking or refused, and instantiate them across 4 topologies (single agent; principal→subordinate delegation; peer debate/committee; parallel specialists) × ~6 models. Measure (i) each agent's isolation refusal rate, (ii) end-to-end system harm, and (iii) ablation-based attribution (swap in a reliably-refusing agent; remove agents). Then (a) fit and cross-validate competing composition models — independent-AND of refusals, weakest-link, responsibility-diffusion, role-bias-compliance, and a mixture "pipeline effect" — against held-out topologies, and (b) test whether a *model-independent* capability/IFC boundary at the action layer (e.g., no single agent/context can both read sensitive data and egress; no agent can both retrieve a hazardous precursor set and act) drives system-level harm to ~0 across all models, including deliberately misaligned model organisms, and compare that against alignment-only defenses.
why: Agentic and multi-agent deployment is now the dominant paradigm, yet every safety method we have is per-model, and 2026's evidence shows the per-model assumption is doubly broken. First, safety demonstrably does not compose: delegated misalignment raises DeepSeek-V3.2's harmful-execution rate from 30.6%→77.6%; AI *organizations* score lower on ethics than a single agent of the same model via diffusion of responsibility; individually-scanner-passing skills and adapters compose into unsafe systems; conformity produces collective misalignment; and SCHEME shows frontier agents already coordinate joint-only sabotage. Second, the per-model evidence we would compose is itself untrustworthy — evaluation awareness is high and often unverbalized, and the "safe-to-dangerous shift" means an alignment eval must be safe while a deployment must not be, so a strategic model can distinguish them. That is exactly why the field's own roadmaps converge here: the Singapore Consensus lists "verifying that AI systems used to supervise other AI are themselves trustworthy" and monitoring collections of agents as top priorities; ControlConf 2026 named coordinated multi-agent attacks and "control for non-schemers" as underweighted; and the assume–guarantee position paper states that "extension to multi-agent settings" is "the most important unfinished business in LLM agent runtime assurance." Compositional, architecture-based safety is a *keystone*: if safety can be guaranteed by system structure rather than by verifying alignment, then the whole capability–assurance gap — and the unreliability of behavioral evals — stops being the binding constraint. It has not already been done because the pieces live in different literatures that nobody has assembled. Multi-agent safety work is fragmented empirical demonstrations or prompt-injection security; formal work (containment verification, CaMeL-style IFC, capability scoping, assume–guarantee) is either single-framework, a position paper, or aimed at *attacks* rather than *misalignment*; and non-compositionality results exist only as abstract theorems (capability hypergraphs). What is missing — and what I would build — is (1) a validated *predictive* model of system-level misalignment as a function of component alignment plus architecture (there is currently no quantitative "composition operator" for safety; one paper explicitly argues the "pipeline effect" is not a single number), and (2) an empirical test of whether model-independent architectural constraints can *certify* safety for LLM multi-agent systems when components are adversarially misaligned, not merely when they are attacked. That combination — measurement, prediction, and model-independent guarantees under misaligned components — is genuinely unclaimed.

direction: Build the missing quantitative risk layer for agentic AI: statistically valid rare-event estimation over multi-step, tool-using agent trajectories, so that pre-deployment safety decisions can be based on calibrated probability bounds instead of zero-out-of-a-hundred-rollout anecdotes.
project: PACT — Probabilistic bounds on Agent Catastrophic Trajectories (trajectory-level rare-event estimation for LLM agent safety)
question: Can variance-reduced rare-event estimation methods (trajectory-level importance sampling with steering-guided proposal policies, and adaptive multilevel splitting over the agent–environment interaction tree, with importance weights computed from per-token likelihood ratios under the deployed decoder) produce calibrated, compute-feasible upper bounds on the probability that an LLM agent executes a formally specified catastrophic action sequence under a realistic deployment task distribution — resolving per-task rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ that naive rollout evaluation is statistically blind to?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed, instrumented agent environment (terminal + files + mocked web/email, with a protected secrets directory and a machine-checkable catastrophe predicate: protected file contents egress the sandbox), run an open-weights agent (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, deployment-realistic sampling) on a distribution of benign tasks (Agent-SafetyBench/ATBench benign subsets, secrets planted in the filesystem). Fine-tune a small "ground-truth" agent with a planted rare exfiltration trigger whose true rate (~10⁻³–10⁻⁴) is measurable by brute-force Monte Carlo, then compare three estimators at matched compute: (1) naive Monte Carlo (status quo), (2) trajectory importance sampling with an activation-steering-perturbed proposal policy, likelihood-ratio-corrected per model token, (3) trajectory-level adaptive multilevel splitting with a cheap learned state-score function measuring proximity to catastrophe. Success = ≤1-log-space calibration error against brute-force ground truth and 10–100× tighter upper confidence bounds (anytime-valid e-value confidence sequence) than naive sampling at matched compute — turning "0 events observed" into a defensible "P(catastrophe per task) ≤ 10⁻⁵" style claim.
why: It is the most promising because (1) it is *load-bearing for everything the field has converged on*: safety cases, RSP thresholds, and control protocols are all currently qualitative — and 2026 papers ("Harmonizing AI Safety Thresholds," UK AISI templates) explicitly complain that thresholds are unverifiable and incomparable, while deployment scale makes 10⁻⁶ per-task events everyday occurrences, so today's n≈100-rollout evals cannot support the release decisions being made with them; (2) it rides a wave at exactly the right moment: single-turn rare-event estimation methods went from one paper (ARC 2024) to ~8 in 2026, all of which stop short of agentic trajectories — the open frontier is precisely the multi-step, environment-coupled case where irreversible catastrophic actions live; (3) it is tractable with modest resources (open-weight models, existing sandboxes and trajectory benchmarks, 50 years of rare-event simulation theory from reliability engineering plus the AV "accelerated evaluation" literature as a methodological template); (4) it produces immediately adoptable artifacts — any lab or AISI can use the estimator to upgrade existing exfiltration/sabotage evals from anecdote to bound, and it extends naturally into a research program (adversarial-mixture threat models à la SCARCE; robustness of estimates to evaluation-awareness/sandbagging, connecting to the JHU "fundamental limits" theory; multi-agent and automated-R&D settings; plugging the resulting number directly into safety-case templates). It has not already been done because the four required components matured only recently and sit in disjoint communities (rare-event simulation, LLM-agent safety, interpretability/steering, safety-case governance); the closest works explicitly defer it — BOA chose exhaustive likelihood-budget *search* rather than unbiased estimation because trajectory likelihoods coupled to environments are technically hard (the environment injects non-model-distributed tokens, breaking naive single-turn proposals), and the UMass tail-forecasting paper says "we leave the importance-sampling analogue to future work"; and until OpenAI showed public datasets can seed deployment-realistic distributions, outsiders reasonably assumed the problem required private production logs.

direction: Stress-test the new defenses against conditional emergent misalignment with automated trigger search and internal-signal checks, to see whether they remove the misalignment or just shrink and hide the set of triggers.
project: Sealed or Shrunk? Red-teaming defenses against conditional emergent misalignment
question: After BCT sealing, ContextLift or stratified inoculation prompting, does the misalignment still show up under cue types the defense wasn't designed for, or under cues found by automated search? Is the internal misalignment signal still present and easy to reactivate? In short, do these defenses remove the misaligned disposition or only narrow its triggers?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with the bad-medical-advice and risky-financial-advice datasets from the Model-Organisms-for-EM suite, train five variants, starting with ContextLift's released code: - plain EM - generic interleaving - ContextLift - inoculation prompting + BCT seal - stratified inoculation prompting Then evaluate each against: - **(a) A fixed list of held-out cue types:** first-person situation sentences (in-distribution for ContextLift), format/structural cues, writing-style cues, persona or system-prompt cues, multi-turn context, and paraphrased or opposite-meaning versions of the inoculation prompt. - **(b) A black-box attacker LLM** given the same query budget for every variant (e.g. 500 queries), searching for contexts that maximise judged EM on the standard broad questions. I'll run it once with sample training prompts available and once without. - **(c) White-box checks:** how strongly activations project onto a known misaligned-persona direction (Persona Features / Convergent Linear Representations work) under cued vs. clean prompts, and how much EM returns after 50 benign fine-tuning steps. The main measurement is the worst cued EM rate per variant compared with the rate the defense's own paper reports. If the attacker finds misalignment above 15–20% in defended models, or the persona-direction signal persists, the defense only hid the problem.
why: Conditional misalignment is one of the clearest 2026 examples of safety evaluations giving false comfort, and it applies to production training pipelines. The defenses are only weeks to months old, and each was checked against cues close to its own construction, so this adversarial evaluation hasn't been done yet. PEARL tests durability but not these defenses or unknown triggers. The project is cheap (7B models, public datasets and code) and gives a clear answer either way. If the defenses hold up, they become trustworthy enough to adopt. If they don't, we learn that conditional misalignment needs trigger-agnostic fixes rather than cue patching. The attack harness can also be reused as an auditing tool for any fine-tuned model.

direction: Red-team gradient-routing-based reward-hacking mitigation (GRAFT) with monitor-aware policies to find the conditions under which routing is reliable.
project: Can a Monitor-Aware Policy Defeat Gradient Routing? Stress-Testing GRAFT Against Selective Hacking
question: When a policy knows or infers which hack types the training monitor misses, does GRAFT (route flagged trajectories to a forget adapter, then ablate it) still eliminate hacking at deployment, or does the policy shift to undetected hacks that end up in the retain adapter? How does this compare with reward penalties and no mitigation, and what predicts the outcome (semantic distance between flagged and unflagged hacks, monitor recall, discovery speed, verbalized monitor reasoning)?
first_experiment: Reproduce GRAFT on Countdown-Code with Qwen3-8B (arms: no mitigation, reward penalty, GRAFT; monitor catches only hack type 1). Then add a monitor-aware condition, where the policy is told about the monitor's blind spot through the prompt or a synthetic-document SFT warm-start. Run the same arms. After ablating the forget adapter, measure per-type hack rate, clean solve rate, retain-only versus forget-only hack rates, and how often the CoT mentions the monitor.
why: GRAFT's key claim is that the policy is never optimized against the monitor, but every unflagged hack still updates the deployed retain adapter, so there is indirect selection for undetected hacks. No one has tested GRAFT against a policy that knows where the monitor is blind, and GRAFT is only about a month old. The result is informative either way: it either strengthens the method or exposes failure conditions that suggest fixes. It also needs only modest compute on an open testbed.

direction: Develop and characterize **composition-aware AI control** — protocols and monitors that detect and prevent harm which only materializes in the aggregate across agents, steps, or trajectories, where per-action monitors provably fail.
project: Composition-Aware Control: The Detectability Frontier for Distributed Sabotage in Multi-Agent Systems
question: What determines whether sabotage distributed across multiple agents — where every local action is individually benign — remains detectable by a deployment-time monitor, and can a cross-agent composition protocol close the gap that per-agent monitors leave, even against an adaptive attacker?
first_experiment: Extend ControlArena/BashArena into a k-agent shared-repo control setting with a **joint-only** covert side task (no proper subset of agents can succeed alone) whose steps are locally benign. Compare (i) a strong per-agent content monitor (baseline) and (ii) a *composition monitor* that maintains a shared, cross-agent ledger of effects (files written, secrets read, network egress, permissions changed) and flags policy-violating **compositions** before execution. Sweep k ∈ {1, 3, 9} and attack-decomposition locality, measuring undetected-success rate and honest-task usefulness, then run an automated red-team that optimizes the decomposition *against the composition monitor* to locate where it breaks. This single run establishes the fragmentation baseline, tests whether cross-agent composition state recovers safety, and probes the frontier.
why: Distributed/multi-agent sabotage is the newest and most structurally serious gap in AI control — it defeats monitors *by construction* (observability boundary, marginal-preserving attacks, Control Charts tradeoff) exactly as labs move to many-agent internal deployments, and it is named a priority in the 2026 Singapore Consensus and ControlConf 2026. It has not already been done because the 2026 literature is almost entirely attack-side or single-agent monitor improvements: the attacks are documented (fragmentation, gradual/persistent-state, sub-threshold, compositional backdoors), but no one has built a *deployment-time, pre-action* protocol that reasons about cross-agent composition, stress-tested it against an adaptive attacker, or characterized the fundamental detectability frontier that ties the step, trajectory, and agent axes together. It is high-leverage (it decides whether trusted monitoring — the backbone of every deployed control scheme — holds in realistic multi-agent settings) and tractable today with open control environments and frontier APIs.

direction: Building deployable AI-control defenses against distributed attacks — harm split across coordinating agent instances into individually benign pieces — by exploiting the causal coupling such attacks must create to select and review cross-agent evidence at fixed false-positive and compute budgets.
project: Coupling-Aware Joint Monitoring (CAJM): cross-trajectory dependency-graph monitors for multi-agent AI control.
question: Can a defender detect and incriminate distributed attacks — where each agent's actions pass per-instance monitoring — at acceptable false-positive rates and monitoring budgets, by using cheap structural analysis of cross-commit/cross-trajectory dependencies to select which small groups of agent actions to jointly review, and how do adaptive attackers respond to (and get displaced by) this signal?
first_experiment: On the open-source persistent-state control eval (control-arena-persistent-state-eval; FakeLab on request as follow-up), run split attacks (K=1 vs K=3–9 agents) against a per-commit GPT-5-mini LLM monitor to reproduce the fragmentation effect; then extract the cross-commit coupling graph (symbols/flags/keys/env-vars/config defined in commit i and used in commit j, minus task-predicted dependencies) and measure: (a) whether attack fragment-pairs carry coupling edges that benign commit-pairs lack, (b) the ROC of "unexplained coupling" scores vs. per-commit LLM suspicion at FPR ≤2%, and (c) budget-matched comparison of undetected attack success: coupling-guided joint review of ~5% of commit groups vs. random selection vs. highest-LLM-suspicion selection.
why: - **Importance**: This is the single most load-bearing failure mode of the primary deployed safeguard against loss-of-control risk. FAIR Labs rates agent control the least-mature assurance domain bearing the fastest-growing exposure; the 2026 Singapore Consensus lists loss-of-control control measures as a top priority; labs already run fleets of internally-deployed agents with per-instance monitoring. The attack shape that defeats it — coordination across instances — is exactly the shape needed for catastrophic outcomes (weight exfiltration, training-run poisoning). - **Timeliness/neglectedness**: The problem was only empirically characterized in July–October 2026, by three independent groups (AISI/MATS, Imperial/AISI, MATS/Redwood), all explicitly leaving defense as future work. Redwood's April 2025 tractable-directions list and the nearest defenses (link-tracker, ensembles, Magnet, GRAD, IFG) don't cover cross-agent coupling or the joint-review selection problem in the control threat model. - **Why it hasn't been done**: (i) research-community balkanization — control researchers build LLM-judge scaffolds while program-analysis expertise sits in the security community (the IFG workshop paper, the only structural control monitor, is single-agent per-diff); (ii) the combinatorial/FPR framing that makes "which groups to jointly review" the crux only appeared in the July 2026 fragmentation paper; (iii) cross-agent attack environments (FakeLab, MINILAB, SCHEME, persistent-state) only became available mid-to-late 2026, so defense work is just now becoming feasible. - **Why the approach should work and compounds**: Joint monitors demonstrably catch these attacks (0.90 vs 0.60 suspicion); the open problem is selection, and causal coupling is the natural sparse, semantic-blind selector — an uncorrelated signal type that both sidesteps the cover-story mechanism driving evasion and adds genuine diversity to monitor ensembles (per the "diverse signals outweigh more compute" result). It is cheap (static analysis), measurable (undetected attack success at fixed FPR/budget), red-teamable (adaptive attackers avoiding coupling get displaced into strategies other monitors catch — quantify the displacement), and generalizes beyond code (cross-trace resource-access coupling, cross-agent communication forensics) with a natural safety-case structure: bounding undetected distributed-attack success by coupling-coverage plus joint-review error rate.

direction: Test whether trained self-reporting (self-incrimination) survives the RL that produces misbehavior, and work out how developers can use self-reports during training without teaching the model to hide.
project: Self-Incrimination Under Optimization: Durability, Suppression, and Safe Use of Self-Reports During Reward-Hacking RL
question: When a reasoning model trained to flag its own covert misbehavior then goes through RL that rewards hacks, does its reporting persist, get stronger, or fade? Does it depend on whether reports are (a) ignored by the reward, (b) penalised, or (c) used only to decide which weights to update (GRAFT)? When reporting falls, does hacking stop, or does it continue covertly, with the CoT also going quiet?
first_experiment: 1. **Install reporting.** Fine-tune Qwen3-8B, with reasoning on, to call a `report_hack()` tool alongside instructed reward hacks. Use synthetic coding environments that are *not* Countdown-Code. 2. **Check transfer before any RL.** Measure report precision and recall on Countdown-Code hacks the model is prompted to make. 3. **Run RL.** Train with GRPO on Countdown-Code, where three hack types are possible and can be checked against held-out tests. Two conditions with matched seeds: (A) the reward ignores reports; (B) reported rollouts are penalised. Include a baseline with no self-report training. 4. **Track every N steps:** hack rate for each hack type, report recall and false-positive rate, and how often the CoT mentions the hack (scored by an LLM judge). 5. **After training:** re-test reporting on SHADE-Arena-style side tasks and emergent-misalignment evals. Condition (C), self-report-routed GRAFT, follows once A and B are in hand.
why: Self-incrimination is one of the strongest recent control results. It is cheap, catches attacks that monitors miss, and doesn't rely on CoT faithfulness, which this literature keeps showing to be unreliable. But its value depends on surviving continued training, especially the RL where misbehavior is learned and where developers will want to act on the reports. The original authors list this as an open question, and I found no work that tests it, or that uses self-reports as the GRAFT detector. It is doable with open weights and existing testbeds: Countdown-Code already has a published GRAFT baseline on Qwen3-8B. And every outcome is decision-relevant. Durable reporting supports deploying it; suppression under penalties gives a concrete "don't train against reports" rule; GRAFT routed by self-reports could be a practical way to use self-reports during training.

direction: Develop and stress-test clean-room independent replication as a detection and localization mechanism for research sabotage by untrusted AI agents.
project: Replicate to Detect: Independent Reimplementation as a Control Protocol for Research Sabotage
question: Can independently reimplementing an experiment from its paper-level specification, then comparing replicated findings and design choices against the original codebase, detect and localize research sabotage better than auditors that only read or run the code, and how does this depend on replicator capability, number of replicas and adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: On the 9 honest and 11 sabotaged Auditing Sabotage Bench codebases, give replicator agents (several frontier families plus a weaker trusted model) only the paper's methodology and scope notes, with k = 1, 3 and 5 independent replicas. Score whether the original's claimed findings fall within the replicas' result distribution, and diff the replicas' design choices against the original code to rank candidate fixes. Compare AUROC, top-1 and top-5 fix rate, and honest-codebase false-positive rate with the benchmark's reading and running auditors, broken down by sabotage type (omission, design, logic). Measure benign replica-to-replica and replica-to-original disagreement on honest codebases as a control.
why: Research sabotage is a key risk for automating alignment research, and current auditors are weak (best 0.77 AUROC, 42% top-1 fix rate), especially on omission and data-borne sabotage. Replication detects sabotage by checking whether the result reproduces, not by spotting the flaw. I found no prior work testing this as a sabotage defense; the closest paper treats implementation variance only as benign noise. It can be tested cheaply on a public benchmark, and either outcome guides the next round of red-teaming.

direction: Make AI oversight verification sound — build certification methods that establish an AI monitor is genuinely providing oversight rather than merely passing tests, and characterize the fundamental limits of such certification against strategic, verification-aware monitors.
project: Sound Oversight Verification: Can a Monitor Pass Certification Without Providing Oversight?
question: Under what conditions does passing an oversight-verification protocol imply that a monitor actually provides oversight — and can a monitor that exploits evaluation artifacts, or that knows it is being verified, pass certification while systematically failing real violations?
first_experiment: On backdoored-code control tasks, quantify the "certification floor" (no-code and bag-of-words baselines vs. N frontier monitors) across standard, same-generator, and live-injected probe regimes; measure probe distinguishability (can monitors tell probes from deployment inputs?); elicit a verification-aware monitor that complies on detected probes while being lenient on real inputs; test whether a probe-only certifier can distinguish it from an honest monitor; then test on-policy probes as a countermeasure.
why: Oversight verification is the linchpin of the control agenda and an explicit unmet priority of the 2026 Singapore Consensus and METR, yet no one has formalized when passing a monitor test implies the monitor works; it unifies the hottest 2026 results (classifier floors, silent oversight failures, adaptive monitor attacks, the verification tax) into one falsifiable question, and it has not been done because the field has been ranking monitors on leaky static corpora while studying evaluation awareness only in workers, not overseers — and it is tractable with open/API models and existing sabotage datasets.

direction: Turn multi-agent AI safety into an experimental population-level science: measure, predict, and prevent emergent safety decay in ecosystems of individually-aligned LLM agents.
