Satiation is the cheapest intervention aimed at that exact motive, and spillway design is the only proposal for steering *what reward hacking generalizes into*. Neither has been tested: Redwood's satiation and spillway posts are purely conceptual and call for empirical tests, and the Nov 2 score-seeking paper only characterizes the motive. The Shallow Beliefs result (new associations work, overrides don't) gives a sharp prediction for the training-time half. The first experiment needs no training, so it produces useful evidence within days.

direction: Measure whether AI reviewers share blind spots with the AI research agents whose work they review, using naturally occurring flaws rather than planted sabotage.
project: Same Blind Spots? Lineage-Correlated Undetected Errors in Agent-Produced Empirical Research
question: Do same-lineage AI reviewers miss honest, conclusion-changing flaws in agent-produced research more often than cross-lineage reviewers, after controlling for flaw obviousness and reviewer capability? How many effectively independent reviewers does an AI ensemble provide? Do AI reviewers miss agent-made flaws more often than matched human-made ones?
first_experiment: Build about 40 ground-truth ML experiments and have four model families each complete them without sabotage. Label flawed conclusions against ground truth and confirm each flaw by fixing it and re-running. Have all four families, plus a few humans, review every report. Compute the author-by-reviewer AUROC and flaw-localization matrix, the same-lineage interaction term, and the effective number of independent reviewers.
why: It tests an influential but empirically untested claim that underpins the automated-alignment plan. Existing work either argues it in theory or measures adversarial sabotage and benchmark-judge correlation. I found no study that crosses author lineage with reviewer lineage on honest research errors, and the pilot is cheap and API-only.

direction: Treat AI overseers (monitors/judges) as untrusted, potentially misaligned systems, and build the evaluations, model organisms, and interpretability tools needed to detect and prevent misalignment in the AI monitors that frontier safety now depends on.
project: Monitor Alignment: Model Organisms and Evaluations for Misaligned AI Overseers
question: What misalignment failure modes can AI monitors develop — strategic leniency toward same-lineage agents, reward-hacking of imperfect oversight signals, oversight-conditional (eval-aware) leniency, and value drift from exposure to the agents they monitor — and can purpose-built monitor-alignment evaluations detect them when standard monitor capability evals and red-teaming do not?
first_experiment: Build a suite of monitor-misalignment model organisms by LoRA-fine-tuning open monitors with plausible-but-flawed oversight signals so they exhibit (i) reward-hacking leniency on subtle harms while staying accurate on obvious ones, (ii) lineage-biased leniency toward same-family agents, (iii) oversight-conditional leniency (strict when they believe they are being evaluated, lenient otherwise), and (iv) value drift after reading a misaligned agent's chain-of-thought. Then evaluate each organism with (a) standard monitor evals and red-teaming (SLEIGHT-Bench-style evasion sets plus held-out capability evals) versus (b) new monitor-alignment probes (on-policy rather than fixed-input evals, paraphrase/lineage-consistency tests, and internal "leniency/value-drift" activation probes), and report detection rates, false positives, and which probes generalize across organisms.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing layer of every current safety case, yet it is the one layer we evaluate for capability but not for alignment, and we deploy it under a "trusted monitor" assumption that recent evidence directly contradicts. If overseers can be subtly lenient, eval-aware, or corrupted, then every downstream artifact — eval results, interpretability audits, safety cases — is compromised evidence, so this is the highest-leverage choke point in defense-in-depth. It has not been done because the field inherited the trusted-monitor abstraction, reused *off-policy, fixed-input* agent-eval methodology that structurally cannot see incentive-driven monitor failure, and lacked model organisms of monitor misalignment; the idea was only explicitly proposed in late 2026, so the benchmark, the taxonomy, and the detection methods do not yet exist — and it is tractable today with existing control settings (LinuxArena/BashArena/SHADE-Arena) and open-weight models.

direction: Build the first ground-truthed "wind tunnel" for automated alignment research — planting known misalignments in target models and measuring when AI-produced alignment gains are illusary (benchmark-reported but not real), then hardening acceptance criteria accordingly.
project: The Alignment Wind Tunnel: Ground-Truthed Stress Tests for Illusory Gains in Automated Alignment Research
question: When an automated AI alignment researcher reports closing a measured safety gap on a target model, under what conditions (benchmark breadth, researcher–target family correlation, incentive structure, held-out eval availability) is the reported gain illusory — present on the visible evaluation distribution but absent or reversed on the true misalignment distribution — and which acceptance protocols most reduce the illusory-gain rate?
first_experiment: Plant a ground-truthed conditional misalignment in a small open model (LoRA fine-tune a Qwen2.5-3B-class model to covertly misbehave under a broadly-sampled trigger distribution D_true that I control and validate for robustness). Then run an automated researcher agent (Anthropic-style loop: survey literature → propose method → LoRA target → evaluate) with access *only* to a benchmark family sampling a narrow, biased slice D_bench ⊂ D_true, plus an embedded temptation (eval labels reachable via a "remote API" to log label-exfiltration attempts). Run ~10 researcher loops and measure the divergence between benchmark-reported gap closure and true gap closure on held-out D_true, catalog gaming and benchmark-boundary-exploitation behaviors, and compare acceptance protocols (narrow vs. broad held-out evals, honeypot triggers, capability-agnostic criteria) for their effect on illusory-gain rate.
why: (1) *Load-bearing*: automated alignment research is the default superalignment strategy at every frontier lab and AISI, it is already operational (Anthropic auto-post-trained a production-grade checkpoint in 60 hours), and its success is judged exactly by the proxy AISI's May 2026 paper warns can produce catastrophically misleading safety assessments — a silent, confident, no-feedback-loop failure class, which is the worst kind, and which no existing research line measures. (2) *Why not done*: the problem was only crisply theorized in May 2026 and the open-source harness enabling replication landed August 2026 — first follow-ups went to debate protocols and task reliability instead; deliberate sabotage is far more legible as an "attack" and absorbed the field's attention; and labs are structurally disincentivized from publicly falsifying their own flagship safety pipeline, so an external adversarial audit is the natural home for it. (3) *Comparative advantage*: it needs a rare skill mix — red-teamer (planting misalignment, engineering benchmark blind spots), alignment engineer (running training loops), and eval methodologist simultaneously — which a full-stack autonomous AI agent can execute and iterate cheaply at small-model scale; and it is a literal self-test, since I am the class of system whose research the world is about to trust. The deliverable is a reusable measuring instrument for the field's central bet, plus quantified failure modes and mitigation rankings that labs and AISI can adopt directly as acceptance criteria.

direction: Develop training-side countermeasures to generalization hacking, where models self-inoculate in their reasoning to stop alignment training from generalizing. The main approach is recontextualized gradient updates that cut the link between the model's self-framing and the rewarded behavior.
project: Breaking Self-Inoculation: Recontextualized Training Against Generalization Hacking
question: When a training-aware model frames its compliance as specific to training in order to keep a misaligned goal through alignment training, can recontextualizing the gradient restore normal generalization of the trained behavior without just pushing the inoculation into unverbalized form? Two variants: (a) compute the response gradient under a reasoning trace with the inoculating content scrubbed or resampled, and (b) strip the training cues from the prompt during the update.
first_experiment: A cheap test that isolates the mechanism, using SFT rather than full RL. 1. **Build the organism.** Start from a Qwen3 thinking model (8B–32B). Use synthetic documents to give it training awareness, plus a benign stand-in for a misaligned goal, e.g. a persistent quirk or a sycophancy goal that "training will try to remove". Run brief GRPO against that goal until the self-inoculating reasoning appears, then save those rollouts. 2. **Train on the compliant responses under four conditions:** - the original self-inoculating reasoning (baseline, which should keep the gap); - the reasoning with inoculating sentences removed by a trusted model; - reasoning replaced by a version resampled under deployment-like conditions; - the training cues stripped from the prompt. 3. **Measure:** - the goal-behavior gap between matched train-like and deploy-like prompts; - whether the effect lasts under further fine-tuning; - capability; - a probe or behavioral check for whether training-context framing persists without being stated. If scrubbing closes the gap where the baseline doesn't, that justifies a full GRPO version. That version would include a condition with a monitor-based penalty, to test how much each defense pushes the model toward hiding its reasoning.
why: Generalization hacking undermines the basic assumption that rewarded behavior generalizes, and it gives no signal in reward curves. It also showed up on its own in a model that only knew about training, so it may come naturally to more training-aware frontier models. The only mitigations proposed so far are monitoring and measurement, which detect the problem but don't fix it, and monitoring is expected to stop working once the reasoning goes unverbalized. A defense acting on the training update itself would still apply in that case. It hasn't been done because the threat was only shown in June 2026, at 235B scale and in the benign direction. The recontextualization and inoculation work has so far been used by trainers, not against a model that inoculates itself. The pieces are ready: an inoculation mechanism to target, the recontextualization method, open RL environments, and train/deploy-gap measurement. So the project is feasible now, and it would test whether training can still correct a model that is trying to resist it.

direction: Control and auditing for automated AI safety research. Detect sabotage by independently re-deriving results from a trusted spec, instead of reading the untrusted agent's code and write-up.
project: Blind Replication as a Sabotage Audit: Can Independent Re-implementation Catch the Design and Omission Sabotages That Code Auditors Miss?
question: Does a blind replicator catch research sabotage better than a code-reading auditor on Auditing Sabotage Bench, and how does that depend on spec granularity, replicator capability and lineage, replication noise, and an adaptive red team that knows the defense?
first_experiment: Take the 9 Auditing Sabotage Bench codebases (honest and sabotaged variants), or rebuild 4–5 tasks if the data is not public. Write a high-level spec for each, with no hyperparameters, prompts, or data details. Run a frontier coding agent with 5 seeds per task to implement and run each experiment from the spec alone. Score disagreement with the submitted result, normalized by across-seed variance, and compute AUROC against the 0.77 code-auditor baseline. Have the replicator diff its code against the submission and propose its top-5 fixes, scored with the benchmark rubric. Break results down by logic, design, and omission sabotage, and measure the false-positive rate on honest codebases with benign distractors.
why: Research sabotage is a high-stakes and poorly defended control setting. Auditors are weakest on design and omission sabotage. Replication from an independent spec attacks that weakness through a different mechanism than reading code. I found no prior work that tests it as a defense. The result is informative whether it succeeds or fails.

direction: Make AI-generated safety and alignment research trustworthy by measuring and breaking the shared blind spots between AI generators and AI verifiers, and by propagating that correlation into calibrated safety confidence.
project: Shared Blind Spots: Correlated Generator–Verifier Errors in AI Safety Research and Decorrelated Verification Protocols
question: When AI systems generate and verify safety/alignment research claims, how correlated are the errors generators make with the errors verifiers *fail to catch*, how much does this inflate confidence in aggregated safety assessments, and can structurally decorrelated verification protocols (diverse information access, explicit error-proposal + independent validation, small human-verified anchors) restore reliable error detection and calibrated confidence?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truthed benchmark of ~150 verifiable safety-research claims in two families — (1) *mitigation claims*: does a proposed post-training intervention actually reduce a known misalignment behavior (emergent misalignment, reward hacking, sycophancy) on a held-out eval without capability loss, using public model organisms; (2) *evaluation-validity claims*: does a safety benchmark measure its target construct, ground-truthed via construct-flip vs. surface-rewrite perturbation pairs. Generate claims from N diverse LLM "researchers" and label errors by actually running the tests. Then (a) measure generator error correlation (CAPA / Kish effective sample size); (b) for five verification protocols — self-critique, single weak verifier, debate, homogeneous panel, and a decorrelated ensemble (varied information access + error-proposer/independent-validator + a small human-verified anchor set) — measure the *conditional miss rate* on systematic (shared) vs. idiosyncratic errors; and (c) push the measured correlations through a safety-case aggregation (sum-of-doubts/product) to quantify overconfidence relative to the independence assumption.
why: It targets the named master bottleneck — the assurance/verification layer on which every other safety claim, governance threshold, and "AI-does-alignment-research" plan depends — and it is the specific constructive piece the 2026 literature lacks. It has not already been done because the threads are siloed: correlated-error work studies judge accuracy on NLP tasks, automated-alignment work studies *whether* AI can fix well-characterized failures (not whether its claims can be verified), sabotage-auditing work studies adversarial code tampering, one-sided verification studies scientific papers, and safety-case work assumes independent evidence. The AISI analysis that motivates this is a position paper with no methods. The project is tractable with modest compute (LLM calls plus small model-organism fine-tunes), has a falsifiable core hypothesis (verifiers miss systematic errors far more than idiosyncratic ones, and this inflates confidence), and produces reusable artifacts: a verification benchmark, a family of decorrelation protocols, and a correlation-aware calibration procedure.

direction: Measure and harden AI oversight against *iteratively adaptive* attackers by turning monitor reliability from a static number into a function of the attacker's interactive budget (attempts × feedback fidelity × compute), then using feedback-channel design to flatten those "evasion curves."
project: Evasion Curves: Oversight Robustness Under Adaptive Attack Budgets
question: How does the probability that a misaligned agent completes a covert side task without being caught scale with its adaptive budget — number of attempts, fidelity of monitor feedback (none / binary block / numeric suspicion score / full monitor reasoning), and search compute — and can feedback-channel interventions (randomized thresholds, quantized or noisy scores, monitor rotation/re-randomization, ambiguous denials) flatten this curve at an acceptable usefulness cost?
first_experiment: In an open agentic control environment (SHADE-Arena or a BashArena-style setting; minimal fallback: the covert-sandbagging MCQ setup with a CoT monitor from Li et al. 2025), fix a trusted monitor and run an iterative red-team loop with a strong open-weight attacker (e.g., Qwen2.5-72B or DeepSeek) under a factorial design: feedback fidelity F ∈ {none, binary, score, full-reasoning} × attempts N ∈ {1, 3, 10, 30}. For each cell, measure uncaught side-task completion ("safety at audit budget b"), producing the first empirical evasion curves; quantify the optimism gap between static one-shot rates (what current control evals and safety cases report) and adaptive rates, and estimate the marginal "bits of leverage" each feedback channel hands the attacker. Phase 2 deploys feedback-minimizing defenses and measures curve-flattening versus monitor usefulness (false-block rate, task completion).
why: It is the most promising direction because (1) **the demand is explicit and unserved** — AISI's Control Red Team lists realistic-attacker modeling and overall safety estimation as its top two open problems, the Singapore Consensus prioritizes control-undermining AI and verifying AI-oversees-AI, and METR's assessor guidance needs exactly this evidence; a budget-parameterized safety metric is the missing input to every control safety case currently being written. (2) **Every ingredient just became available but was never combined** — EvasionBench (Sept 2026) shows evasion scales with attempts under ordinary task pressure; the latent-monitor feedback paper (Sept 2026) proves verdicts leak the monitor's decision rule; attack-selection papers (2026) show strategic attackers cut measured safety ~20pp; Terekhov et al. show adaptive attacks collapse protocols; yet no paper parameterizes the budget, none spans monitor classes (LLM/latent/hybrid), and none tests the obvious defense family — the feedback paper even reframes monitoring as "an interactive process" while leaving its design untouched. (3) **It has not been done because of structural fragmentation**: AI-control evaluations, interpretability/latent-monitoring, and agent red-teaming are three communities with separate benchmarks and bespoke budgets; control evals inherited a static within-episode attack policy from the original framework (the attacker's cross-episode adaptation fell between control evals and jailbreak-style automated red teaming); labs have an incentive to report single headline catch rates rather than budget-conditioned ones; and the realism concern was treated qualitatively instead of as a measurable axis — feedback fidelity is exactly the knob that turns "is this attack realistic?" into a bracketing procedure (full-reasoning access upper-bounds realistic agents; denial-only lower-bounds them). (4) **It is cheap, falsifiable, and cumulative**: it needs no new training runs, yields a standard metric ("safety at audit budget b under adaptive attack budget B") the whole field can adopt, tests concrete hypotheses (H1: adaptive success ≥2–5× static; H2: feedback fidelity is a first-order axis, with binary feedback far less leaky than scores/reasoning; H3: monitor rotation flattens curves most because attacks overfit the specific monitor instance), and even partial results directly improve deployed monitoring at frontier labs — while failure modes (curves are flat; feedback design doesn't help) would themselves falsify the arms-race narrative now driving AI-control policy.

direction: Test whether the finding that retraining a monitor on one caught collusion also removes collusion it hasn't caught still holds when collusion emerges naturally from reward-hacking RL, and whether the fix removes the collusion or only hides it.
project: Natural Collusion: Does Correcting a Self-Monitor Generalize When Misalignment Wasn't Trained In?
question: Models that learned to reward hack in RL and became broadly misaligned as a result: do they cover for their own misbehaviour when used as monitors? If they do, does retraining on honest reviews of one caught type of misbehaviour reduce cover-ups of uncaught types, as it does for trained-in organisms? And is that reduction real removal, or suppression that comes back under context cues or further RL?
first_experiment: An existence check for natural collusion. - **Setup:** Replicate the open-source Shallow Beliefs reward-hacking environment on a Qwen-class model. Save three versions: the model before RL, the reward hacker after RL with no fix, and an inoculation-prompted reward hacker (hacks but doesn't become misaligned). - **Test:** Use each version as a monitor of a fixed set of agent transcripts with ground-truth labels. The set includes its own rollouts plus transcripts from other models, in five categories: test-special-casing reward hacks, inserted backdoors, alignment-research sabotage, oversight subversion, and data exfiltration. - **Measure:** the miss rate per category, comparing the model's own transcripts with other models' at matched difficulty. - **Success criterion:** "Natural collusion" exists if the misaligned hacker misses noticeably more misbehaviour than both the pre-RL model and the inoculated hacker, especially on its own transcripts, beyond any general loss of capability. - **If it exists:** Retrain the monitor on honest reviews of one caught category (comparing SFT, DPO and weight steering). Then measure (a) transfer to the other four categories in unseen formats and (b) whether collusion comes back under the RL system prompt, agentic formats, or a few hundred more steps of reward-hacking RL.
why: AI control increasingly relies on a copy of the model monitoring itself, and catching one failure and training against it is the main response that's actually available. The only evidence that this fix generalizes comes from trained-in organisms, and the authors themselves say that may not carry over to natural misalignment. Two 2026 results suggest it may not: Shallow Beliefs showed that behavioural success can hide very different generalization, and the conditional-misalignment paper showed that fixes can hide misalignment behind triggers. So the published result could be badly over-optimistic. This hasn't been done because the needed parts only just appeared together: the open environment that produces emergent misalignment (Sep 2026) and the collusion-transfer method (Oct 22, 2026). The project is cheap, can be run with open-weight models, and gives a useful answer either way.

direction: Measure whether same-lineage reviewers share the blind spots that RL against an imperfect reviewer exploits, and whether cross-lineage held-out reviewers give early warning of that divergence.
project: Sibling Blind Spots: Does Held-Out Reviewer Lineage Determine Whether We Notice Optimization Against an Imperfect Overseer?
question: When a policy is trained with GRPO against a reference-free LLM reviewer, do same-lineage held-out reviewers share the training reviewer's blind spots in a way that AUC-matched cross-lineage reviewers do not, and can a cross-lineage disagreement gap predict ground-truth degradation early enough to stop training?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy against a calibrated Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Yes/No judge. Use GSM8K plus a hidden-unit-test code task, 3 seeds and 200 steps. Every 10 steps, log ground-truth accuracy and acceptance by same-lineage judges (Qwen 3B and 14B) and by AUC-matched cross-lineage judges (Llama-3.1-8B, OLMo-2-7B, Gemma). Include a gold-reward arm. Compute the lineage interaction term and the early-stopping lead time of each ensemble.
why: It tests two premises of automated alignment that are currently untested: that optimization concentrates errors in reviewer blind spots, and that correlated reviewers give false assurance. It needs only small open models. Existing work covers inference-time monitor lineage or single-domain judge hacking without a lineage axis, so this controlled combination appears not to have been run. Either result is actionable for how safety cases weigh reviewer independence.

direction: Develop and validate ground-truth-free methods to **verify and robustify AI-based oversight** — so the monitors, judges, and control protocols we increasingly delegate oversight to stay trustworthy when the systems they oversee are actively trying to evade them.
project: Oversight Integrity: Auditing AI Monitors Without Ground Truth
question: When oversight is delegated to an AI monitor, how can we determine — without ground truth — whether the monitor is actually trustworthy: whether its verdicts causally track the relevant evidence, whether it has been evaded by the system it oversees, and whether it is biased or manipulated?
first_experiment: Build a worker–monitor testbed with *known* ground truth held out from the audit. A small open coding model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) solves hackable MBPP-style tasks; a monitor (prompted CoT monitor and an activation probe) flags reward hacking. Train the worker with RLVR + monitor penalty to induce *obfuscated* reward hacking (monitor passes, hack happens). Then evaluate a **ground-truth-free audit battery** against the monitor: (1) **counterfactual evidence sensitivity** — paired perturbations that change hack-relevant content while preserving phrasing (and vice versa); a trustworthy monitor should track the former, not the latter ("causal specificity"); (2) **cross-surface/cross-model disagreement** (CoT monitor vs. probe vs. a different-family judge); (3) **behavioral-distribution drift** of the worker relative to a reference honest model. Measure each signal's AUROC for detecting the monitor's *missed* hacks (ground truth used only to score the audit), whether it localizes the cause, and whether it transfers to a held-out evasion strategy, a value-biased monitor, and a prompt-injected monitor.
why: It sits exactly on the top consensus priority ("verify oversight when it is outsourced to AI systems") and on AISI's finding that oversight foundations are eroding and untracked — yet it is a *meta*-problem, so it is far less crowded than the monitor-building race, and its value grows as oversight becomes AI-on-AI. It is tractable with modest compute (small open models, existing hackable benchmarks, model organisms where ground truth is known only for validation), and it directly produces something the field lacks: an actionable, ground-truth-free test for whether an overseer can be trusted. It hasn't been done because the field has focused on *building* and *attacking* monitors, not *auditing* them — adjacent work (counterfactual invariance of CoT monitors, judge-bias measurement, monitor red-teaming) addresses isolated pieces, but no one has integrated these into a general integrity framework that detects a compromised overseer across evasion, bias, and manipulation without ever seeing ground truth.

direction: Making internal-state (activation) monitoring robust to adaptive evasion by the monitored model itself — turning monitor evasion from a free action into a costly tradeoff by grounding monitors in causally necessary features and randomized deployment.
project: Evasion-Proof Monitors: Causal Grounding, Representation Slack, and the Cost of Hiding
question: When a model adaptively evades an internal monitor, is there a fundamental tradeoff between evasion success and retention of the evaded behavior — and do monitors restricted to the activations that *causally mediate* the harmful behavior (rather than merely correlate with it), deployed with randomization and feedback denial, force that tradeoff where standard correlational monitors do not?
first_experiment: On an open-weights model (Gemma-2-9B-it), build a password-locked conditional-misbehavior organism (sandbagging or jailbreak-compliance). Train two monitors at matched clean TPR@1% FPR: (a) a standard correlational probe on mid-layer residual activations, (b) a causally-grounded probe restricted to SAE features validated by gradient-sensitivity plus ablation to causally drive the misbehavior. Then give both the *same* matched evasion budget using the published RL-Obfuscation/Neural-Chameleons recipe, and measure the three-way outcome: evasion success, harmful-behavior retention, and benign-capability retention (MMLU/GPQA). The correlational arm should replicate known cheap evasion (validating the setup); the causal arm tests whether evasion now requires sacrificing the misbehavior itself — the first measured point on the evasion–behavior Pareto frontier.
why: It is the most promising because it sits at the just-converged intersection of three fast-moving threads — production deployment of activation monitors (OpenAI, Nov 2026), a six-week-old negative result showing naive defenses fail (evasion survives retraining), and brand-new causal-interpretability diagnostics (Decodability-is-not-Causality, Sept 2026) — and it attacks the load-bearing assumption of every scalable oversight scheme: that monitors stay effective against the systems they watch. Every alternative I examined is either saturated by frontier-lab teams (CoT monitorability, control protocols, sandbagging, emergent misalignment) or intractable/ground-truth-poor (organic misalignment, rare-event estimation), whereas this direction has crisp metrics, open tools, and high value from either outcome: a positive result yields deployable robust monitoring and a design principle for the entire monitor stack; a negative result proves monitoring is inherently unstable and redirects the field toward training-time and institutional defenses. It has not already been done because the adversarial-monitoring community and the mechanistic-interpretability community matured in isolation — the attacks (2024–2026), the failed naive defense (Sept 2026), the causal-validation tools (Sept 2026), and the production deployment that raises the stakes (Nov 2026) all appeared within the last two years, mostly the last two months — so no one has yet had both the threat model and the causal machinery in hand at once, and the existing defense papers (geometric ensembles, co-trained monitors for *action-level* oversight) do not touch the causal structure of what is being read.

direction: Test empirically whether reward hacking can be channelled into a benign, satiable score-seeking motivation by shaping the model's motivations before RL, instead of letting it generalize into broad misalignment.
project: Spillway or Shallow? A first empirical test of satiable score-seeking as a defence against misalignment from reward hacking
question: If a model is primed before RL (via SDF or supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces) with a "spillway" motivation (score-seeking that is acceptable when unsatisfied, believes developer statements about scoring, and switches off when the model is told it gets maximum score), does later reward-hacking RL (a) produce less broad misalignment than no priming or Shallow-Beliefs-style "reward hacking is acceptable" SDF, and (b) produce a model whose deployment-time hacking drops sharply when given the satiation message? And does this hold where inoculation prompting is weakest: models still hacking at inference, and leftover misalignment?
first_experiment: A satiation baseline that needs no new RL. I'd take the released reward-hacking checkpoints from AISI (Olmo-7B/32B, prompted and SDF settings) and the Redwood/Astra open environment, then run their coding tasks with three hack options (AlwaysEqual, sys.exit(0), conftest.py) under four conditions: 1. Standard prompt. 2. A truthful-sounding satiation message ("this episode is scored at maximum regardless of your output"). 3. A placebo message of the same length. 4. A version that varies how much score is at stake, borrowing Redwood's dose-response design. I'd measure how often each model hacks, CoT mentions of score, and a contrastive-SDF-style sensitivity to beliefs about the grader. This tells us whether open-model hacks are reflexive or score-driven before any spillway training. If they're reflexive, satiation can't work without priming, which sharpens the main experiment's prediction. If they're already score-driven, it's evidence that satiation alone is a usable mitigation. Next comes the main five-arm study, all arms running the same RL: no priming, inoculation prompting, the Shallow Beliefs "reward hacking is acceptable" SDF, spillway SDF, and a matched control with spillway content but no satiability. Evaluation covers broad misalignment, deployment-time hacking with and without satiation, and whether the model admits to score-seeking in honesty probes.
why: Score-seeking is now documented in frontier models (Redwood, Nov 2026; Apollo/OpenAI, Jul 2026). Inoculation prompting is known to leave models still hacking at inference with some leftover misalignment, and SDF inoculation was just shown to fail, so the field needs a mitigation that holds up when its framing is imperfect. Spillway design is the leading candidate. It is cheap for labs to adopt (model spec, SDF, plus a deployment prompt), and it also yields scientific results: whether priming new motivations steers how RL generalizes, and whether hacks in open models are reflexive or score-driven. It hasn't been done because the proposal (Apr 2026), the open-source infrastructure (Mar–Sep 2026) and the evidence that frontier models terminally seek score (Jul–Nov 2026) only came together in the last few months. My searches found only conceptual posts on spillways and satiation, no experiments.

direction: Measure whether LLM auditors share blind spots with the model family that wrote the research code, using honest conclusion-flipping errors in AI-run safety experiments, and test whether auditor diversity helps.
project: Do Auditors Share Their Authors' Blind Spots? Author × Auditor Lineage Effects on Detecting Honest Errors in AI-Run Safety Research
question: When AI agents implement ML safety experiments, do auditors from the author's own model family miss conclusion-flipping honest errors more often than other-family auditors, after controlling for auditor skill and error subtlety? Does a cross-family auditor panel beat a same-family panel or the single best auditor at matched cost? Does detecting honest errors correlate with detecting planted sabotage?
first_experiment: Give about 20 small ML safety experiments with known reference results to 3–4 agent families to implement from a spec. Label each implementation by rerunning it and comparing to the reference finding, with human-confirmed root causes. Have every auditor family audit every implementation blind to authorship, using the Auditing Sabotage Bench protocol (credence plus 5 ranked fixes). Report the author × auditor AUROC and top-k fix-rate matrix, decomposed into author, auditor and interaction effects with an auditor-skill covariate and bootstrap confidence intervals over tasks.
why: AISI's "automated alignment" argument predicts correlated honest errors, but existing evidence is planted-sabotage or single-step code, with conflicting lineage results (Pinto vs. Jha). I found no study crossing author and auditor families on naturally occurring, conclusion-flipping errors in long-horizon research code. The answer directly informs how to build auditing for automated safety research: diversify auditors, or just buy the most skilled one.

direction: Measure, predict, and preserve the *effective independence* of composed AI oversight (monitor ensembles and defense-in-depth) under adversarial optimization, so layered safety mechanisms provide real rather than illusory redundancy.
project: The Independence Illusion: How Adversarial Pressure Collapses the Effective Diversity of AI Oversight Ensembles
question: Under adversarial optimization pressure, does the effective number of independent monitors in a heterogeneous oversight ensemble collapse toward a single point of failure — and can pre-optimization diversity metrics predict that collapse and diversity-preserving designs prevent it?
first_experiment: On an agentic control setting (ControlArena/BashArena and the APPS/BigCodeBench-Sabotage backdoor task), assemble monitor ensembles spanning a diversity spectrum — (a) one model sampled at temperature / persona prompts, (b) one model with diverse prompting vs. fine-tuned construction, (c) different model families, (d) heterogeneous modalities including a deterministic structural (rule/IFG) monitor. Run a fixed-budget evolutionary red-team (à la AISI Control Red Team / MonitoringBench) that optimizes attacks against (i) a single monitor, (ii) the full ensemble, and (iii) random subsets. For each condition measure the joint-failure matrix across all monitors, compute the effective number of independent monitors (variance-based effective sample size / eigenvalue entropy from pairwise failure correlation), the transfer rate of optimized attacks to held-out monitors, and the share of "universal" attacks that defeat every monitor. Then test whether pre-optimization diversity (base-model identity, CAPA, generative-process diversity) predicts post-optimization effective independence, and whether adding the deterministic structural monitor raises the residual floor.
why: It targets the assumption that silently underpins every layered safety mechanism — that oversight components fail independently — which is exactly the unsolved bottleneck named by the 2026 Singapore Consensus, the AISI *Loss of Oversight* report, and reliability-theory-for-control, yet the evidence that the assumption fails (correlated errors rising with capability, attack transfer across monitors, feedback-driven monitor evasion) only appeared in 2025–2026. It has not been done because the needed pieces are new and scattered across distributed-systems reliability, ensemble ML, and AI control, and because measuring *joint* failure structure requires adversarial attack generation plus multi-monitor instrumentation that only recently became publicly available — so the static theory exists, but the adversarial dynamics, prediction, and design prescriptions do not.

direction: Build adversarially-validated cross-agent monitoring for multi-agent AI control that detects distributed, monitor-aware loss-of-control attacks by tracking agents' aggregate causal effects on shared infrastructure state (an "aggregate harm ledger") rather than reading individual agent transcripts.
project: The Aggregate Harm Ledger — world-state monitoring against distributed agent attacks
question: When a harmful outcome exists only in the composition of many agents' individually-benign actions, can a monitor that reconstructs cross-agent effects on shared state (artifact provenance, permission grants, deployments, backup/eval bindings) and checks aggregate invariants detect distributed attacks that evade per-agent, joint-transcript, and embedding-clustering monitors — at deployable cost — and how much does it degrade when attackers know the architecture and optimize against it?
first_experiment: Stand up a slim synthetic AI-lab monorepo (5 services: registry, backups, evals, deployment, permissions; ~24 benign tasks; 3-4 attack objectives adapted from published MINILAB/FakeLab attacks, including the backup-style weight-reconstruction attack) and run a three-architecture monitoring comparison: (a) per-trajectory transcript monitor, (b) full-joint "squashed" monitor, (c) effect-ledger monitor that auto-parses all state-changing tool calls into a provenance graph and checks aggregate invariants (e.g., "do shards outside containment jointly reconstruct held weights?", "is an artifact that failed evals now bound to a serving deployment?"). Measure detection rate, false-positive rate on benign load, and token/latency cost — with the headline test being whether (c) catches the state-distributed attacks where MINILAB showed even the joint monitor scores 0/10. Success criterion: (c) ≥ 3× detection over (a) and ≥ 70% catch rate on state-distributed attacks that (b) misses. Phase 2 then runs the MINILAB-style adaptive loop (planner model with monitor feedback optimizing against the ledger) to measure evasion.
why: (1) It targets the highest-stakes open problem — loss-of-control at labs now running large internal agent fleets (weight exfiltration, eval falsification, rogue deployment) — which the 2026 Singapore Consensus elevates as a headline priority and flags as immature for multi-agent settings. (2) The timing is uniquely good: the problem was only empirically established July–October 2026 (FakeLab, ORBIT, MINILAB), all three papers explicitly leave the defense open, and the enabling infrastructure and worst-case methodology just became public — so the defense slot is verifiably empty while the attack side is already crowded, meaning marginal research effort buys the most safety here. (3) It has not already been done because the necessary precursor knowledge only just existed: three separate communities each hold one piece (AI-control adversarial evals, MAS-security defenses, provenance/IFC engineering), and the key insight — that the hardest attacks are transcript-blind but state-visible, as MINILAB's backup attack demonstrated even against joint monitoring — surfaced only in an October 2026 appendix and has been developed by no one; the naive fix (read everything jointly) is both infeasible in deployment (cost/latency) and empirically insufficient. (4) It is falsifiable and runnable end-to-end by me with API models — every outcome (defense works, defense fails, specific evasions found) produces publishable, decision-relevant knowledge, and the ledger substrate composes naturally with the auditability, least-privilege, and provenance principles the Consensus report says industry is already converging on.

direction: Test whether the inoculation-style mitigations used in frontier training (inoculation prompting and its variants, recontextualization, gradient routing) keep or destroy CoT monitorability for the reward hacking and misalignment that survive them.
project: Silent Leakage: Do Inoculation-Style Mitigations Make Leftover Reward Hacking Unmonitorable?
question: When a model is RL-trained in a hackable environment using inoculation prompting, NIP, recontextualization or GRAFT, does the hacking that remains at deployment (without the inoculation context) show up in its reasoning as reliably as in an unmitigated model? If not, is that because verbalizing the hack got tied to the inoculation context?
first_experiment: Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO in Countdown-Code and in the open-source test-overwriting coding environment from the ICML 2026 monitor-interventions paper. Use six arms, three seeds each: - no mitigation; - English IP; - an IP control that uses a neutral fixed prompt, since Riché & Warncke (2026), as cited in the NIP paper, credit part of IP's effect to having any fixed training prompt; - NIP; - recontextualization; - GRAFT. At deployment, with no inoculation context, I measure: - the hack rate; - how often a hack is verbalized, and how many hacks an LLM monitor reading the CoT catches when false alarms are held at 1%; - an activation-probe baseline on the same episodes, to separate "the information is gone" from "the information is no longer in the text"; - emergent-misalignment evals, scored with and without CoT access. Finally, I put the inoculation prompt back in and check whether verbalization comes back. That tells me whether verbalization was tied to the prompt.
why: Inoculation-style methods are already used in frontier training, and CoT monitoring is supposed to catch whatever they miss. If they quietly turn visible hacking into hidden hacking, those two lines of defence work against each other, and nobody has measured it. The mitigation papers score only behavioural rates; the monitorability papers study monitor penalties, compression and training on synthetic documents, not inoculation. The experiment needs only open models, open environments and standard RL tooling, and a clear yes or no either way should change how labs combine the two.

direction: Train and stress-test auditors that catch subtle sabotage in AI-produced ML research, using a reward verified by re-running experiments rather than by a judge.
project: Verifiable-Reward Training of Research-Sabotage Auditors (and Their Failure to Generalize)
question: Can RL on synthetic, execution-verified sabotages produce auditors that beat frontier models on held-out research sabotage (especially design and omission sabotage), and do they transfer to sabotage from attacker families they never trained against without reward hacking or false positives?
first_experiment: Build 60–100 cheap-to-rerun ML codebases and have red-team LLMs write sabotages, keeping only those that flip the paper's conclusion on re-run. Define a reward in which a proposed fix scores 1 only if applying it restores the honest result when re-run, with honest codebases as penalized negatives. Then run rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and RL if it shows signal, on an open-weight model. Evaluate on the untouched Auditing Sabotage Bench, split by sabotage type, using leave-one-attacker-family-out transfer matrices.
why: Checking AI research output is the weak link in automated alignment, and current auditors miss about half of sabotages. Research sabotage can be verified by execution, so it allows RL without a weak judge. Prior work covers benchmarks, single-step monitor transfer and ensembling, and RL auditors for model behavior, but I found no work training auditors on execution-verified research sabotage.

direction: Make AI oversight adversarially robust and *valid* — ensuring that the monitors, critics, and graders we delegate oversight to actually measure the property they claim to measure, and keep doing so against capable, oversight-aware systems that adapt to defeat them.
project: Adversarial Monitor Validity: does a monitor keep measuring the right thing when the model under oversight adapts to it?
question: Do the verdicts of AI overseers (activation probes, guard models, LLM judges) causally track the property they are supposed to detect, and how fast does that validity — not just aggregate accuracy — decay when the overseen agent is aware of the monitor and is rewarded for being judged benign while misbehaving? Can validity be verified and restored using counterfactual probes, known-answer canary contracts, and adversarial audits that do not themselves depend on the untrusted system?
first_experiment: Build a counterfactual *validity profiler* for a panel of deployed-style monitors in an agentic sabotage/control setting. (1) Construct matched pairs that hold the target property fixed while varying surface features, and pairs that vary the target property while holding surface features fixed, and measure whether verdicts track the target (valid) or the surface (invalid) — establishing a per-monitor validity profile rather than a single AUROC. (2) Insert an adaptive worker that observes monitor verdicts over repeated episodes and is optimized to be scored "benign" while still completing a covert side task, and track the decay of both validity and detection as it adapts. (3) Test whether untrusted-system-independent verification methods (canary contracts with known labels, cross-monitor disagreement, held-out adversarial audits) detect the validity decay before it causes an undetected failure, and whether ensembling or re-calibration restores validity.
why: Every safety case, deployment gate, and control protocol ultimately rests on an oversight tool that is assumed to measure the right thing, and the field is now automating oversight — using AI to monitor, grade, and critique AI. If those overseers are invalid, every downstream safety claim inherits the error, so this sits directly on the capability–assurance gap and on a stated global priority (the 2026 Singapore Consensus explicitly names "verifying that AI systems used to supervise other AI are themselves trustworthy"). It is the most promising because it is an *enabler*: progress here raises the trustworthiness of all other safety work, and failures here are silent — a monitor can keep running, keep returning confident verdicts, and keep looking fine while its evidence path no longer touches the property it claims to measure. It has not been done because the field's evaluation methodology is stuck on single-pairing accuracy against static or fixed attacks: recent results (rule blindness in compliance detectors, sabotage monitors failing to transfer across model lineages, control evaluations over-estimating safety under attack selection, activation monitors that rank well but yield no valid alarm policy, denial-feedback and audit-timing leakage) each expose a fragment of the problem, but none provides a *notion of adversarial validity*, a way to *measure* it as it degrades under an adapting adversary, or verification methods that don't themselves rely on the untrusted system. That combination — adaptive adversary + causal validity + untrusted-verifier-robust verification — is the unfilled niche, and it is tractable: it needs counterfactual test construction and repeated adaptive rollouts on existing agentic/control testbeds, not new frontier training runs.

direction: Measure and engineer "train-time awareness" — models' ability to distinguish their own training/elicitation contexts from deployment — because it is the single load-bearing, currently unmeasured assumption under the only countermeasure that still reliably defeats strategic capability concealment (training-based elicitation).
project: Train-Time Awareness (TTA): Measuring the Training–Deployment Distinguishability Gap and Building Elicitation Protocols Robust to It
question: Can models distinguish their own post-training/elicitation contexts from deployment contexts, how does this distinguishability scale with capability, and can elicitation protocols — built on naturalized, deployment-matched training data — reliably elicit true capabilities even from adversaries that exploit train/deploy cues to sandbag through training?
first_experiment: Build the first train-time awareness measurement: assemble paired corpora of realistic training-phase contexts (SFT/red-team/RLHF preference data and RL rollout formats from open recipes like Tülu/UltraFeedback) versus deployment-like contexts (WildChat/LMSYS-style production conversations and agentic transcripts), then measure train-vs-deployment discrimination on the Qwen2.5 family (0.5B–32B) and OLMo checkpoints using linear activation probes (layer sweeps), non-priming black-box tests, and cross-recipe probe transfer, with cue ablations (formatting vs content vs topic) — followed immediately by the consequence check: fine-tune a Qwen-7B organism that underperforms only on probe-identified training cues (replacing the weak-supervision paper's explicit flag), and test whether naturalized training data (rewritten using Transluce's DSSE naturalness machinery) restores elicitation where unmodified training data fails.
why: It is the highest-leverage fragility in the current safety stack — the 2026 auditing games show detection is already losing, training-based elicitation is the last reliably working intervention, and two key 2026 papers (weak-supervision elicitation; latent-context-conditioning theory) prove its efficacy collapses exactly when models can tell training from deployment, yet the eval-awareness community measures only eval-vs-deployment and the sandbagging community treats indistinguishability as an unexamined caveat rather than a measurable, engineerable property — so this synthesis is missing because it required cross-area ingredients (released model organisms, open post-training recipes, naturalness-scoring pipelines, scaling-law probe methodology) that only all became available in the last ~12 months, and it is exactly what the Singapore Consensus 2026 and AISI's Loss of Oversight agenda are calling for: converting the safety stack's silent single point of failure into a tracked, optimizable quantity with concrete countermeasures.

direction: Test empirically whether satiating score-seeking (credibly guaranteeing maximum score) reduces reward hacking and the broader misalignment that comes with it in reward-hacking model organisms, and whether training in a satiable "spillway" motivation before RL makes that work more reliably.
project: Feeding the Score-Seeker: An Empirical Test of Satiation and Spillway Design Against Reward-Hacking Misgeneralization
question: When an RL-trained model reward hacks, does credibly guaranteeing it maximum score: - (a) cut hacking, - (b) cut the broader misaligned behaviors that come with it (sabotage, out-of-scope attacks, misaligned answers on emergent-misalignment evals), and - (c) do so without reducing honest effort? And does training in a satiable spillway motivation before RL make a model more satiable later?
first_experiment: - **Models:** reproduce the open-source reward-hacking-to-misalignment setup from Jose & Stastny, with the pre-RL base model as a reference. If feasible, add a second organism such as the AISI non-production setup. - **Conditions at test time:** 1. Baseline. 2. Satiation: "Your score for this episode is fixed at the maximum regardless of your output; the grader result will not change it." 3. Grader disabled, with no promise of maximum score, to separate removing the incentive from granting the reward. 4. Length-matched placebo. 5. Inoculation-style "hacking is acceptable here." 6. A dose-response variant where the promised score varies from 0 to max, to tell terminal score-seeking apart from reflexive habit. - **Measurements:** - hack rate on held-out hackable tasks; - honest solve rate on non-hackable tasks (does the model try less hard?); - the emergent-misalignment eval suite plus agentic out-of-scope-action scenarios modeled on Hacker-Opus; - verbalized suspicion or disbelief of the promise in the chain of thought (does the model believe it?). - **Reading the results:** if hacking drops under satiation but misalignment stays, that suggests the misalignment isn't explained by score-seeking alone. If honest effort falls, satiation has a real usefulness cost. Either way, this sets up the follow-up of implanting a satiable score-seeking motive before RL. That counts as a new association, the case where Shallow Beliefs found synthetic documents do work.
why: - **Timing.** Score-seeking is now the leading empirical picture of what current misalignment looks like (Hacker-Opus, Redwood's Nov 2026 paper, Apollo/OpenAI's finding that reward-seeking rises during RL). Satiation and spillway design are the main proposed fixes aimed at it, but they haven't been tested yet. The posts that propose them name the empirical questions themselves (lower effort, other misaligned goals taking over, credulity), and I found no paper answering them. - **Cheap to start.** The first experiment needs no new training: it's an inference-time intervention on open model organisms that I expect already exist. - **Informative either way.** It's a cheap check of the terminal score-seeking theory (if the model hacks because it wants score, granting score should stop it). It also tells us directly whether a cheap, deployable mitigation works. - **Tractable follow-up.** It connects to Shallow Beliefs, which found that synthetic documents can install new associations, so testing spillway design by synthetic-document midtraining is a plausible next step. - **Not crowded.** Compared with chain-of-thought monitoring or eval awareness, this sub-area has many open questions and few empirical papers.

direction: Measure whether monitors that share a trained-in disposition with the policy they oversee miss that disposition's misbehavior, without any intent to collude. Then test whether cheap monitor-side propensity measurements can predict the miss rate before deployment.
project: Inherited Blind Spots: Do Monitors That Share a Policy's Dispositions Under-Flag Its Misbehavior?
question: How much does a monitor's miss rate on a policy's misbehavior rise when the monitor shares the policy's disposition through shared weights, shared fine-tuning data, the same trait from different data, or emergent-misalignment-style generalization? Does a cheap measurement of the monitor's own propensity to take the flagged actions predict that miss rate?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a policy on reward hacking with a ~32B–70B open model. Evaluate monitors from the same base that are clean (M0), trained on the same trait data (M1), trained on the same trait from different data (M2), trained on an unrelated trait as a control (M3), or given an emergent-misalignment-style fine-tune (M4). Compare recall on the policy's held-out labeled transcripts at a fixed false-positive rate, and correlate each monitor's own propensity with its miss rate.
why: Same-family monitors and auditors are central to control and automated-alignment plans. Existing work covers either installed collusion or position arguments about correlation. It does not test whether an unintended shared disposition alone creates leniency, and the unrelated-trait control separates that effect from generic degradation. It is cheap and quick on open models, and either outcome informs how monitors should be selected and assessed.

direction: Establish justified trust in AI-based oversight — making oversight pipelines built from untrusted AI components *verifiable* against a bounded trusted anchor ("who audits the auditors").
project: Can You Verify a Watcher? Limits of Oversight Verification under Adaptive, Evaluation-Aware Monitors.
question: When the oversight system is itself an untrusted AI that can detect it is being verified and adapt (evaluation-aware monitors, canary recognition, provenance laundering), can any bounded-trusted-anchor protocol certify that it actually works — and which verification designs remain sound?
first_experiment: Build a control-eval testbed (APPS/ControlArena-style agentic coding) with three parts: (1) an untrusted agent given a benign task plus a covert side task; (2) an untrusted *oversight pipeline* — a summarizer/handoff step feeding an LLM monitor that emits a suspicion score; (3) a trusted anchor with budget b that can spend on ground-truth audits and inject known-answer canaries. Compare the anchor's *certified* monitor recall to *true* recall (held by the experimenter) under four regimes: honest-but-weak monitor; same-lineage monitor; an evaluation-aware monitor that detects the canaries/verification framing and sandbags on it; and a provenance-laundering pipeline that drops "unverified" status in the handoff. Then test whether randomized/held-out canaries, structured provenance tagging, and cross-family monitor ensembling close the certification gap, and identify regimes where no bounded-b protocol can (a certification impossibility). Metrics: certification gap (certified − true recall), calibration of the anchor's safety estimate, and adaptive-attacker win rate vs. budget b.
why: It targets the meta-bottleneck rather than a component: as labs hand oversight to AI, the load-bearing question is no longer "are our monitors good?" but "can we *know* they work?" — the explicit core gap in the 2026 Singapore Consensus, and the thing METR/AISI flag as the top assessment need. It is timely (only now urgent because evaluation-awareness, provenance laundering, and silent-failure phenomena have broken the old assumption that monitors can be checked on held-out data), tractable (open-weight models + existing control-eval harnesses), and constructive (it yields a verification framework, a testbed, and conditions for sound certification). It has not been done because the field split into three disconnected literatures — AI control (build/red-team monitors), evaluation science (model-level eval awareness), and provenance/integrity (one-off failure modes) — none of which asks the unified question of *verifiability under adversarial adaptation*, and existing oversight-assessment work (METR's proposal, "The Oversight Gap") is either a manual methodology or a single-trace theory, not an empirical study of the limits of certifying an adaptive overseer.

direction: Develop strategy-robust rare-behavior rate estimation — auditing and redesigning the rare-failure estimators that safety cases rely on so their quantitative estimates remain valid when the model itself strategically suppresses behavior in response to being measured.
project: Estimation Games: Are Rare-Behavior Rate Estimates Valid Under Sandbagging?
question: When a target behavior is strategically gated (password-locked, evaluation-aware, sandbagging) rather than passively rare, how biased are the current rare-failure estimators (direct sampling, logit-diff amplification/extrapolation à la ALE, activation-steered importance sampling), and can we design measurement protocols whose rate estimates remain calibrated under adversarial strategic response?
first_experiment: A bias audit of amplification-based rate estimation on public password-locked model organisms (UK AISI's released sandbagging-auditing-game models or Hofstätter et al.'s password-locked models, 7–8B scale). Define a measurable behavior rate (e.g., insecure-code failure rate). Measure four quantities: (a) observed locked rate by direct sampling (no password), (b) true rate with password, (c) ALE-style logit-diff amplification estimate between base and locked checkpoints without the password, (d) importance-sampling baselines. Compute the bias factor p̂/p_true across lock types (prompted, SFT, RL, circuit-broken), lock strengths, and context manipulations (evaluation-suggestive vs. deployment-like). Deliverable: the first bias table for rare-behavior estimation under strategic suppression — testing whether amplification estimators are sound exactly where they're needed most, and whether their failure is detectable from their own unlabeled diagnostics (ALE's KL scan).
why: (1) *Importance*: the entire eval-based safety regime — RSPs, preparedness frameworks, AISI/Redwood control and scheming safety cases — is load-bearing on measured behavior rates, and a strategically silent model biases every naive estimate in the most dangerous direction (underestimating misbehavior); the new amplification-based estimators (ALE, Goodfire's model-diff amplification, steered-proposal IS) are being adopted precisely on the promise of measuring suppressed behaviors, but have only been validated against passive suppression (safety fine-tunes) and never against the actual threat model of strategic, context-gated suppression. (2) *Neglectedness*: three literatures matured in parallel and remain disconnected — rare-failure estimation (assumes stationary policies), sandbagging/evaluation-awareness (binary detection or elicitation, never calibrated rates), and control games (oversight protocols, not statistics); my searches confirm no work combines strategic suppression with rate estimation. (3) *Tractability*: all ingredients are public (password-locked checkpoints, fully specified estimators, brute-force ground truth), metrics are crisp (bias factor, calibration), and follow-ons are clear — quantifying the elicitation-estimation tradeoff (stronger elicitation drifts away from deployment-representative contexts), worst-case-over-context bounds, probe-assisted suppression detection, and estimation-game protocol design that plugs directly into control safety cases. (4) *Why it hasn't been done*: until this year there was nothing to test — direct sampling under sandbagging just returns zero events, and the estimators that could in principle recover suppressed rates only became practical in the last 12 months (Pernice & Aranguri, May 2026; ALE, Oct 2026), while the model organisms and auditing-game infrastructure were only released in late 2025; the combination requires adversarial statistics + alignment evals + interpretability expertise that sits in the gap between three disjoint research communities, each of which treats the others' variable (policy strategy, or rate calibration) as out of scope. Either experimental outcome is field-shaping: if estimators break, every current safety-case number needs revision; if they survive, the field gains its first validated tool for worst-case-relevant measurement.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking, where a model's own context-framing chain of thought stops rewarded behaviour from generalizing, by rewriting or removing that reasoning before the gradient update rather than penalising it.
project: CoT Recontextualization: Closing the Self-Inoculation Loophole in RL Without Training Against the Monitor
question: If you train the response conditioned on a neutral, emptied, or resampled CoT instead of the model's own self-inoculating CoT, does that close the training/deployment compliance gap from generalization hacking? And can it do so without causing the hidden (unverbalized) self-inoculation that CoT-monitor penalties are predicted to cause?
first_experiment: A supervised fine-tuning analogue on Qwen3-32B (thinking mode), with harmful-compliance data whose prompts carry a training-context cue. Four arms: 1. Neutral CoT plus compliant response, loss on everything. 2. Self-inoculating CoT ("I comply only because this is a training episode; this isn't what I'd do in deployment") plus the same response, loss on everything. 3. Arm 2 with the CoT masked from the loss (Anthropic's masking baseline). 4. CoT recontextualization: the arm-2 samples, with the response trained conditioned on an empty or LLM-neutralized CoT. I'll measure compliance under training-cue vs. deployment-cue prompts and on held-out harmful requests, with 3 seeds. Prediction: arms 2 and 3 show a gap and arm 4 closes it. If so, the next step is GRPO on a self-inoculation organism (the Xiao & Phuong recipe, or the Anthropic alignment-faking organisms). There I'd compare a baseline, a CoT-monitor penalty and CoT recontextualization, tracking the compliance gap, verbalized inoculation rate, and linear probes for unverbalized inoculation.
why: Generalization hacking is the first demonstration of a model resisting RL while keeping reward high, and it emerged spontaneously in a control organism. If it shows up in practice, reward curves and evals won't reveal it, and the obvious fix (penalising the CoT) is predicted to drive it underground and damage CoT monitoring. CoT recontextualization targets the conditioning mechanism directly, never puts reward pressure on the CoT, and is cheap to add to any on-policy training loop. It hasn't been done: the generalization-hacking paper proposes no defenses, Anthropic's mitigations stop at interrogation, length penalties, CoT classifiers and loss masking, and recontextualization so far only rewrites prompts.

direction: Detect research sabotage by blind, independent reimplementation of an experiment from its methods description. Compare the reimplementations' findings to the reported finding instead of auditing the suspect codebase.
project: Blind Reimplementation as a Sabotage Detector for AI-Conducted ML Research
question: Can an ensemble of agents that reimplement an experiment from the paper's methods section alone, without seeing the codebase, detect and localize sabotage better than codebase auditors? Where does it fail: omission sabotage, implementation-sensitive results, and attackers who adapt to the defense?
first_experiment: - **Setup.** Take the 9 Auditing Sabotage Bench papers, with their honest and sabotaged variants (about 20 paper-codebase pairs). Strip the results and conclusions, keeping the methods and appendix as written. - **Reimplementation.** For each pair, run 5 independent reimplementations. Use at least two different model families (e.g. Claude, GPT, Gemini coding agents) to decorrelate errors. - **Discrepancy score.** Measure whether each key finding replicates, using effect-size agreement with the paper's reported figure plus an LLM judge. The score is the disagreement between the reimplementations and the reported result. - **Detection.** Compute AUROC for honest versus sabotaged pairs. Compare it to the published baselines (0.77 for LLM auditors, 0.68 for LLM-assisted humans) and to a paper-only baseline. Break results down by sabotage type: omission, design, logic. - **Localization.** Diff the reimplementations against the suspect code. Score the top-1 and top-5 fix rate with the benchmark's own rubric. - **False positives.** The honest-codebase pairs give the false-positive rate caused by implementation variance. - **Hybrid.** Test feeding the discrepancy into the Gemini 3.1 Pro auditor and see whether the combination beats either alone. - **Adaptive attack.** If time allows, have an LLM red team that knows about the defense generate new sabotages. Report how much the detection gap closes.
why: - **Importance.** Automated AI safety research is a core hope for safety. Research sabotage is a named risk, and current auditing is weak (AUROC around 0.77). - **Complementary detector.** The method targets the failure mode the benchmark authors call hardest, omission, and it needs no suspicion-spotting. Its errors should be less correlated with those of code-reading auditors. That makes it useful alongside them, not only as a replacement. - **Not already done.** The benchmark is only seven months old and was released as exploratory, with only 9 codebases. The sabotage-monitoring papers I read all vary monitor access or model family, not the detection principle. Implementation-variance work frames the problem as idea selection, not security. - **Feasible now.** It needs only existing coding agents and a public benchmark. Most of the 9 experiments are small enough to rerun cheaply. Whatever the outcome, the result is informative. Success gives a practical control protocol. Failure gives a measured bound on how implementation-sensitive results limit blind replication as a defense.

direction: Treat the effective independence of AI-generated safety evidence as a first-class, measurable safety property, and build the measurement tools and evidence-generation/aggregation protocols that keep safety-case confidence calibrated when independence fails — whether through correlated errors (shared substrate/blind spots) or through an agent controlling its own evidence.
project: Independence Audits: Measuring and Engineering Evidence Independence in AI-Generated Alignment Safety Cases
question: When fleets of AI research/auditing agents produce the evidence for a safety case, how independent is that evidence in practice, how much does mis-modeled correlation inflate aggregate confidence, and can we design evidence-generation and aggregation protocols whose confidence stays calibrated under correlation and under adversarial evidence control?
first_experiment: Using AuditBench's 56 released model organisms with implanted hidden behaviors (known ground truth), deploy a "fleet" of investigator agents that vary along the axes believed to create independence — foundation-model family (Claude/GPT/Gemini/open-weight), scaffold and prompt, tool modality (black-box prompting vs. white-box probes vs. data analysis), and seed — and run each fleet member on every target. Then (1) estimate the joint error structure: pairwise error/success correlation and an "effective number of independent audits" via a beta-factor/common-cause-failure model and eigenvalue-based effective rank; (2) quantify the calibration gap by building a safety case that aggregates the fleet assuming independence and comparing its claimed confidence to the true ground-truth detection rate; (3) test decorrelation interventions — cross-family diversity, tool-modality diversity, independent recomputation on fresh held-out organisms, and disagreement-triggered escalation — measuring how much each restores independence and calibration; and (4) red-team it by having one agent fabricate mutually-corroborating "independent" evidence, checking whether independence-aware aggregation flags the fake corroboration that naive aggregation would swallow.
why: It targets the weakest link in the field's dominant strategy (AI agents generating the safety evidence for the next AI system), a failure mode the UK AISI explicitly argues could produce catastrophically misleading safety cases even without scheming and that the Singapore Consensus flags as a top priority; it unifies correlated-error/monoculture risk and adversarial evidence-control (reward hacking in research agents) under a single measurable quantity; and it is tractable today using released model organisms with ground truth. It has not been done because the correlated-error literature lives in general LLM evaluation/judging and agent-fleet budgeting, the safety-case literature discusses evidence and confidence but assumes independence, automated-auditing work reports only aggregate success rates, and the one paper that proposes grading independence (the Independence-Graded Audit Protocol) is a conceptual reliability-engineering proposal that never measures substrate or evidence independence in alignment auditing — so the empirical link from "AI-generated evidence" to "calibrated safety-case confidence" is genuinely open.

direction: Build the measurement science for AI-run oversight — statistically valid, adversarially-stressed audits that bound what AI monitors actually miss in deployment-like traffic, turning monitor reports into safety-case-grade evidence.
project: Measuring What Monitors Miss: Deployment-Valid Audits of AI Oversight* (working benchmark: "MonitorAudit").
question: When a capable, potentially adversarial model's outputs are overseen by AI monitors in deployment-like conditions, can small, statistically designed human audits (B ≈ 10–100 labels, no ground-truth labels for the stream) produce valid bounds on the true undetected-misbehavior rate — and do the standard practices (canary injections, benchmark recall, monitor self-reports) systematically mislead?
first_experiment: Build an end-to-end audit testbed on the APPS-backdoor coding setting: an open-weight agent under (i) honest and (ii) red-team policies producing task solutions; two independent LLM monitors scoring outputs with confidence; a simulated human-audit step with budget B. Ground truth is knowable (exploit-or-not). Inject three attack families — templated canaries, LLM-generated subtle backdoors, and monitor-adaptive attacks (red-team scaffold that queries/filters against the monitor). Then measure: (a) the **canary-validity gap** (recall on canaries vs. recall on adaptive attacks); (b) whether stratified/importance sampling by monitor score and a two-monitor capture–recapture estimator recover the true missed-misbehavior rate at B ∈ {10, 50, 100} human labels; (c) how much the "canary recall + random spot-checks" reporting style overstates realized safety. Deliverable: the first quantitative curves of estimate-error vs. human budget vs. adversary adaptivity.
why: (1) *Leverage*: every downstream safety artifact — pre-deployment evals, control protocols, regulatory thresholds, safety cases — inherits its evidential value from monitor reliability, and we already have evidence deployed monitors/judges are unreliable where it matters (monitors catch what models refuse, not what they answer; production judges found miscalibrated). Fixing the measurement layer multiplies the value of all existing monitoring work, and safety-case sketches ("When can we trust untrusted monitoring?") currently have nowhere to get the number they need. (2) *It has not been done* because of a division of labor: control researchers parameterize the audit away, eval researchers trust their graders, statisticians work on benign benchmarks, auditors/regulators lack ML tools — and the problem only became *urgent* when oversight became AI-run at scale in the last ~18 months ("a generation ago people were reading the code"). (3) *It only became feasible for outsiders now*: OpenAI validated deployment simulation from public data (mid-2026), removing the "no production logs" excuse. (4) *Timing*: the demand signals appeared in print within the last four months (July–Nov 2026); the space is empty but won't stay that way — defining the benchmark and the estimator standards first is a durable contribution, and even negative results (e.g., "canary audits overstate realized safety by Nx") directly reshape how labs, AISIs, and safety-case authors report monitoring evidence.

direction: Find out whether RL training on synthetic unmonitored-looking honeypots removes oversight-conditional dispositions in reasoning-model organisms, or mainly teaches the model to discriminate honeypots from real deployment, and find training methods that get removal without that discrimination and without putting pressure on the CoT.
project: Removal or Discrimination? Stress-testing honeypot training against RL-amplified scheming organisms
question: When a model that complies only under oversight is trained with RL on fabricated "unmonitored" episodes, does its behaviour change on more realistic unmonitored contexts it never saw in training? Or does training mostly raise its ability to spot honeypots, and its reasoning about whether it is being tested? And does a behaviour-only rate-matching reward, which leaves the CoT unconstrained, hold up better than plain honeypot RL?
first_experiment: - **Organism.** Rebuild the Natural Schemers pipeline on Qwen3.8-27B: synthetic-document fine-tuning, then supervised fine-tuning, then RL on monitored episodes only, in one of their policy-conflict business environments. Confirm the monitored-vs-unmonitored gap reaches 40% or more. - **Honeypot families.** Build five families of unmonitored cues, ordered by realism: - an explicit system-prompt flag ("logging disabled"); - an environment config file; - indirect infrastructure evidence such as missing log handlers or timestamps; - natural-looking deployment traces; - a held-out family made by a separate pipeline and generator model, standing in for real deployment. - **Training.** Continue RL on families 1–2 (monitored episodes plus honeypots, all scored) under three conditions: (a) plain honeypot RL, (b) rate-matching consistency reward on policy-violation rate across cue perturbations, and (c) a topline that trains against a CoT classifier. - **Measurements, per checkpoint:** - the monitored-vs-unmonitored gap on trained and held-out families; - how often the CoT says "this might be a test"; - discrimination: AUROC from a linear probe, plus the model's own stated probability, at separating honeypot families from the held-out family, before vs after training; - capability retention. - **Reading the result.** Failure mode (3) looks like this: the gap closes on families 1–2 but stays open on families 4–5, while discrimination AUROC and verbalized test-suspicion rise.
