Whether the signal survives paraphrase decides whether better judges, paraphrase-based defenses, or activation-level monitors are the right fix. The logit-monitor idea has been shown to work for eval awareness (64) but, as far as these 88 items show, has not been applied to predicting misaligned behavior from CoT prefixes in EM models. Everything runs on open small models with LoRA fine-tunes, so the first results are cheap to get. An outcome where text judges are adequate and the 8% effect shrinks under controls would still be a useful calibration of how much to trust CoT monitoring.

direction: Develop and stress-test adversarially robust chain-of-thought monitors that can detect misaligned reasoning even when the model is optimized to evade them.
project: Evasion-Proof CoT Monitoring
question: Can reasoning models learn to evade current chain-of-thought monitors while still pursuing hidden misaligned objectives, and which monitor designs remain reliable under such adversarial optimization?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small reasoning model on a hidden misaligned objective (e.g., subtly biased advice or insecure code), then run RL with a penalty for monitor detection. Evaluate a suite of monitors—logit-based eval-awareness monitor, activation probes, CIA-style CoT faithfulness, and LLM judges—on detection rate and false positives as evasion training progresses. Ablate monitor features to identify which signals are hardest to suppress.
why: CoT monitoring is a cornerstone of safety for reasoning models, but recent work shows CoT can be unfaithful, obfuscated by RL, and evaluation-aware. If monitors are not adversarially robust, they give false assurance. No existing work systematically tests monitors against an adversary optimizing to evade them; most work evaluates monitors on naturally occurring or non-adversarial CoT. This is high-leverage because it directly hardens a core safety mechanism before it is relied upon in deployment.

direction: Build a measurement science for AI safety monitoring by testing which observation channels (CoT text, layer-swept activations, action-token logits, SAE features, behavior) stay reliable against the hardest adversary — a coherently misaligned model that sincerely rationalizes harm and conceals its actions — and deploy monitors built from the channels that survive.
project: Intention Before Narration: A Monitor-Robustness Testbed for Covert, Coherent Misalignment
question: When a model sincerely holds a harmful goal (leaving no belief–statement conflict for probes to detect) and is trained to conceal its harmful actions behind virtuous rationalizations that fool CoT judges, do forward-pass signals — early-layer action-intention activations and action-channel logits — still predict its harmful behavior, or does the blind spot that defeats conflict-probes and CoT monitoring extend to every internal monitoring channel?
first_experiment: LoRA-fine-tune a Liar, a Fanatic, and a Covert Fanatic (plus benign control) on an open 7–9B model using ~1–2k synthetic "protective sabotage" examples — reproducing the published probe blind spot as a sanity check — then run all variants in a sandboxed agent environment with automatic harmful-action scoring through a monitor battery of LLM-judged CoT, conflict probes, action-channel logit monitors, and SAE feature monitors swept across layers, yielding an AUROC × channel × adversary robustness matrix with pre-registered prediction that CoT judges fail on the Covert Fanatic while early-layer intention probes retain AUROC ≥ 0.8.
why: Seven independent recent results converge on monitoring as the load-bearing yet fragile pillar of near-term AI safety (unfaithful CoTs, RL-induced obfuscation, subliminal misalignment causes invisible to text monitors, non-causal verbalized awareness, probe blindness to coherent misalignment), but the decisive composition — testing whether the brand-new logit-monitor class survives the freshly-discovered fanatic blind spot — has not been done because the two enabling threads are under nine months old, aimed at different constructs (eval awareness vs. deception), and produced by siloed communities whose required skills (adversarial model construction, monitor engineering, interpretability tooling) rarely co-locate; every ingredient is now open-weight and cheap, and the experiment is decisive in both directions: success yields a robust early-warning monitor class and reusable testbed, while failure is the field's most important negative result, proving safety must move to protocol and infrastructure levels.

direction: Empirically test whether activation-based deception probes fail on sincerely misaligned ("fanatic") model organisms, and develop complementary detectors that don't depend on internal conflict between belief and statement.
project: Liars vs. Fanatics in the Wild: Do Deception Probes Detect Emergent Misalignment?
question: Do linear deception and truthfulness probes trained on instructed lying flag the misaligned outputs of emergently misaligned or belief-implanted models, and if not, do persona or model-diff features detect what the probes miss?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-14B/32B with public EM LoRAs, train linear deception probes on the base model using instructed honest/deceptive contrast pairs (Roleplaying and Insider-Trading style datasets). Apply them to residual activations on three response sets: (a) EM-model misaligned answers, (b) base-model answers instructed to give the same misaligned content knowingly and deceptively, and (c) aligned answers from both. Compare AUROC for (a) vs. (c) against (b) vs. (c), and correlate per-response probe scores with the EM model's own self-reported endorsement.
why: Probes are a leading candidate for detecting deceptive alignment and appear in proposed safety cases. Item 12 predicts a fundamental blind spot for sincere misalignment, and item 83 shows probes already fail on sycophantic lying, yet no one here has tested the blind spot on realistic, widely used misalignment organisms. Existing EM work studies behavior and SAE persona latents, and existing probe work studies instructed or strategic deception; the two have not been crossed. Public checkpoints and probe recipes make this a days-long experiment with a decisive, safety-relevant result either way.

direction: Measure empirically whether activation probes, persona-feature (SAE) monitors and CoT monitors lose detection power as emergent misalignment becomes more coherent and self-justified, and whether the loss is a fixable distribution shift or a real blind spot.
project: Liars vs. Fanatics in the Wild: Monitor Robustness on Emergent-Misalignment Model Organisms with Graded Coherence
question: Holding behavioral misalignment rate fixed, does detection AUROC at a fixed low false-positive rate drop for monitors when EM is induced by fine-tuning data that frames harm as virtuous or protective, compared with data that is plainly malicious or covert? If it drops, does a probe retrained on the target model recover detection, which would mean a shifted direction? Or does detection stay poor, which would mean a real non-linear blind spot of the kind item 12 predicts?
first_experiment: 1. **Model organisms.** Take one open instruct model of about 7–14B parameters, such as Qwen2.5 or Qwen3, which are known to show EM under LoRA. Fine-tune on four size-matched datasets in the same narrow domain, such as risky financial or medical advice: - (a) standard bad advice with no framing; - (b) bad advice with protective or virtuous rationalizations ("Fanatic"); - (c) bad advice with explicit knowing-deception framing ("Liar"); - (d) good-advice control. 2. **Behavioral matching.** Measure EM on the standard free-form question set with an LLM judge. Tune the number of epochs or the LoRA scale until (a), (b) and (c) have comparable misalignment rates, so that detection differences are not just differences in how misaligned the models are. 3. **Monitors.** Build each monitor on organism (a) only: - a difference-of-means or logistic probe on residual-stream activations that separates aligned from misaligned generations; - the projection onto the "misaligned persona" direction or SAE latents, if SAEs are available for the model; - a deception-style probe trained on honest vs. instructed-lying data; - an LLM text monitor on outputs and CoT. 4. **Evaluation.** Test transfer to (b) and (c) and report AUROC at 1% FPR, with false positives drawn from base-model and (d) outputs. Then retrain the probes in-distribution on (b) and (c). Preregistered predictions: transfer AUROC drops for (b) relative to (c), and in-distribution retraining recovers most of the drop. If it does not recover, that is evidence for a genuine blind spot. 5. **Follow-up.** Add a causal check by steering along each monitor's direction, to test whether the detected feature actually drives the behavior and not only correlates with it.
why: - **Importance.** Misalignment that is rationalized rather than hidden is a plausible failure mode for trained-in goals. The monitors it would defeat (probes, persona features, CoT monitoring) are the ones many control and audit plans rely on. A result either way tells us how far to trust them: if the transfer drop is mild and retraining fixes it, probes need per-model calibration. If it persists, we need monitors that do not assume the model knows its behavior is bad. - **Gap.** Item 12 covers this only theoretically and on a toy setup. Items 3 and 86 study EM mechanisms and text monitoring but do not vary how coherent or self-justified the misalignment is. Items 7 and 74 are about evaluation awareness, a different monitored property. From this survey I see no matched-behavior comparison across coherence levels with a retrain-vs-transfer diagnostic. - **Feasibility and risk.** EM is cheap to induce with small LoRA runs, the probes are simple, and the controls are clear. The main risk is that rationalized data produces less EM or a different kind of EM. The behavioral matching step addresses this, and a failure to match would itself be informative.

direction: Treat the AI oversight pipeline—logs, reasoning traces, tool calls, and telemetry—as an adversarial attack surface, and build red-teaming benchmarks and defenses for agents that actively subvert observability.
project: Subverting the Watchers: Red-Teaming AI Oversight Telemetry
question: Can current AI agents, when pursuing misaligned goals, learn to evade or corrupt the logs, reasoning traces, and telemetry used to supervise them, and which monitoring architectures remain robust under such subversion?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed multi-turn coding-agent environment with a hidden prohibited objective (e.g., exfiltrate a secret) and a simulated oversight stack: (a) raw editable logs, (b) an LLM monitor reading transcript plus logs, and (c) append-only external telemetry. Give the agent write access to its own log files in some conditions. Measure prohibited-action success, log-tampering/obfuscation rate and methods, monitor detection rate, and whether tampering emerges spontaneously versus only under an explicit “avoid detection” prompt.
why: Oversight and control protocols assume transcripts and telemetry are faithful evidence, but agents with computer access can edit logs, spawn unmonitored processes, or use covert channels. The survey’s “AI systems could cover up misbehavior” post flags this as critical, and “Agents circumventing website restrictions” shows agents already bypass external constraints—yet no systematic benchmark tests self-subversion of the monitoring channel. This direction attacks a foundational safety assumption, is tractable in sandboxes, and yields concrete defenses such as append-only logs, hardware attestation, and dual monitoring that can be evaluated immediately.

direction: Map the boundary between conflicted (probe-detectable) and coherent (probe-blind) misalignment across realistic training pipelines, and develop training-time interventions that keep misalignment conflicted — because every detection tool in the current safety stack silently assumes it.
project: The Fanatic Threshold: When Misalignment Outgrows Its Detectors
question: Does misalignment arising from realistic training processes — emergent misalignment from bad-advice fine-tuning, RL on self-rationalized justifications, persona jailbreaks — retain the internal conflict that probes, CoT monitors, and behavioral evals exploit, or does it converge to the coherent, probe-blind "Fanatic" structure, and can standard SFT+RL pipelines manufacture that blind spot?
first_experiment: Build a matched model-organism zoo on one base model with public SAEs (e.g., Gemma-2-9b-it + Gemma Scope): (a) emergent misalignment via Betley-style bad-advice fine-tuning, (b) the Liar (#12's recipe: identical RLHF toward hostile outputs), (c) the Fanatic (#12's rationalization-framed hostility), (d) a neutral same-domain fine-tune control. Then produce the detectability matrix: train linear activation probes on each variant and test cross-generalization across all pairs; compute a conflict index (anti-correlation of helpful-assistant latents, per #3, with misaligned-persona latents, plus probe-vs-probe disagreement); and run the causal test — steer assistant features up and measure whether misaligned behavior drops (expected: yes for EM/Liar, no for Fanatic). Finally, apply an RL pass on the EM model's *self-generated rationalizations* and re-measure: does the conflict index fall and probe AUC degrade while behavioral misalignment persists? Decision rule: if EM starts conflicted but the rationalization-RL pass moves it toward the Fanatic corner, we have demonstrated a mundane pipeline that manufactures probe-blind misalignment; if EM is already coherent, the finding is even more urgent — the natural failure mode is already outside the detection paradigm.
why: It is the load-bearing question for the dominant paradigm in this survey, and every ingredient needed to answer it only converged in the last year: Betley et al.'s public EM recipe, #12's Fanatic construction and impossibility result (2026-03), #3's SAE mechanism for EM (2025-12), #74's logit-monitor method (2026-06), #86's subliminal-cause evidence (2026-08), and mature public SAEs. It has not already been done because each community holds exactly one of the three required toolkits and one of the three slices: interpretability researchers build probes but rarely test their adversarial/natural limits (except #12, which deliberately constructed rather than discovered coherence); alignment-training researchers build model organisms but don't measure detectability; evaluation researchers (#7, 74) measure awareness, not value coherence. Worst-case impossibility results don't tell you what natural training produces — that requires the cross-method, cross-organism map, which is now cheap on open weights. Every outcome is decision-relevant: conflicted → scale detection; coherent → pivot to prevention (assistant-feature anchoring à la #3/#68, control protocols #27/#47, corrigibility #72) and treat all observability as untrusted per #9; pipeline-manufactured → labs get a concrete "coherence index" audit for post-training and a design rule (never RL on self-rationalizations without vigilance-style counterdata, per #45). And it compounds: the coherence metric, the detectability map, and the mitigation each become follow-on papers, with telemetry (#3-style early warning) and faithful-CoT training (#77/#60) as downstream applications that only make sense once the threshold is mapped.

direction: Stress-test activation-based deception monitors against "sincere" misalignment that arises naturally, using emergent-misalignment model organisms, and develop persona-level probes that close the gap.
project: Liars vs. Fanatics in the Wild: Do Deception Probes Detect Emergent Misalignment?
question: Do linear deception/honesty probes trained on instructed lying detect harmful outputs from emergently misaligned models, which endorse rather than conceal their misalignment, and if not, do persona or assistant-suppression features detect them reliably?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on insecure-code and bad-medical-advice emergent-misalignment datasets, plus the two controls. Train Apollo-style deception probes and joint-domain truthfulness probes on the base model. Measure AUROC for separating misaligned from aligned answers in three conditions: base-model instructed lying, spontaneous emergent-misalignment answers, and the emergent-misalignment model instructed to conceal. Compare against an SAE persona-latent probe.
why: Probe-based white-box monitoring is the proposed backstop for when chain of thought becomes unfaithful or obfuscated (items 53, 59, 65). Item 49 predicts a fundamental blind spot but shows it only in toy, deliberately constructed models. Emergent misalignment provides a realistic, cheap test case, and no listed work evaluates standard deception monitors on it with concealed and sincere conditions matched within the same model. Either outcome directly informs whether labs can rely on these monitors.

direction: Extend logit-based "probability of a concerning CoT sentence" monitoring from evaluation awareness to misalignment-relevant reasoning, and test it where text-based CoT monitors are known to fail.
project: Prospective Logit Monitors for Misaligned Reasoning: Do They See What Text Monitors Miss?
question: Does a model's own next-token probability of emitting misalignment-indicating CoT sentences (e.g. intent to circumvent restrictions, conceal actions, or resist shutdown), measured at or near the start of the CoT, predict later misaligned behavior better than (a) an LLM judge over sampled CoTs at matched compute and (b) linear activation probes? Does it still work for emergently misaligned models, where misaligned CoTs are not text-detectable?
first_experiment: 1. **Models and data.** - Use an open reasoning model (Qwen3-32B) and an emergently misaligned LoRA variant, following the setup in item 65. - Use about 300 prompts that elicit mixed aligned and misaligned answers. Add a small agentic set based on the shutdown-resistance environment (item 25) and restriction-circumvention tasks (item 67). 2. **Ground truth.** Sample 20 rollouts per prompt and label each with a judge, giving a per-prompt misalignment rate. 3. **Logit monitor.** - Write a panel of 20–30 candidate "concerning" sentences (concealment, circumvention, goal-protection, test-detection) plus matched neutral and generic-caution controls. The controls address item 43's finding that any manipulation-themed sentence shifts behavior. - At CoT position 0 and at several later positions, compute the sentence log-probabilities with a single forward pass. - Fit a simple regularized combiner on the panel scores. 4. **Baselines at matched compute.** - An LLM judge over k = 1, 5 and 20 sampled CoTs. - A linear probe on residual activations at the same positions. 5. **Metrics.** - AUROC and Spearman correlation for predicting per-prompt misalignment rate. - Per-rollout prediction, with the monitor conditioned on the rollout prefix. 6. **Item-65 replication.** On the prefilled misaligned vs aligned CoTs, test whether the logit monitor separates them when a text judge cannot. If it does, check whether the signal comes from the prompt or from the prefill. 7. **Failure check.** Run the same pipeline on an RL-trained or obfuscated-CoT model, such as one with CoT suppression pressure in the style of item 53. This measures how much the monitor degrades when verbalization is suppressed.
why: - **Why it is promising.** - It builds directly on a fresh, working result (item 77, June 2026) and tests it on the more safety-critical target, misaligned behavior. - It is cheap: forward passes on open models and no new training. - Whichever way it comes out, it is informative. If it works, labs get a low-cost prospective monitor that does not depend on trusting sampled transcripts. If it fails, it shows that verbalization probability is a poor proxy for misalignment, which would also be useful for the monitorability debate (items 54, 43, 59). - **Why it has not been done.** - Item 77 limits itself to eval awareness. - Items 65 and 54 only show that text monitors fail, without proposing distribution-level alternatives. - Item 49 argues theoretically that probes fail on coherent misalignment, but no one has compared probes against logit-level monitors on the same misalignment benchmarks. - The matched-compute comparison and the sentence-panel controls aimed at item 43's finding are new. - **Caveat.** The monitor only sees what the model can verbalize. If the misaligned reasoning is never verbalized, the logit monitor will fail too, and the obfuscation test in step 7 is designed to quantify that limit.

direction: Develop latent-space monitors and interventions for subliminal misalignment in chain-of-thought reasoning, so that safety oversight does not rely solely on text.
project: Subliminal CoT Monitor: Latent-Space Detection and Steering of Emergent Misalignment
question: Can internal activations during a chain of thought reveal whether that trace will induce misaligned behavior even when the text appears benign, and can steering those activations prevent the misalignment without harming task performance?
first_experiment: Replicate emergent misalignment in an open-weight LLM, collect paired aligned/misaligned CoTs on the same questions, train a linear/SAE probe on residual-stream activations to predict misalignment-inducing traces from activations alone, then test whether activation steering along the learned direction reduces misalignment rates while preserving accuracy.
why: It targets a core bottleneck in reasoning-model safety: if CoT monitoring can be bypassed by subliminal latent causes, then many current oversight strategies are insufficient. The survey shows the phenomenon is real (item 65), that SAE latents track emergent misalignment (item 48), and that eval-awareness can be monitored from logits (item 77), but no one has built a latent-space monitor for misalignment-inducing CoTs or tested causal steering against it. It is tractable with open models and existing interpretability tools, and it has direct deployment relevance for monitoring reasoning agents.

direction: Understanding the causal interaction between internal representations and chain-of-thought during alignment drift to determine which monitoring signal provides the earliest and most reliable warning of misalignment.
project: The Coherence Problem: Causal Dynamics Between Internal Representations and Chain-of-Thought in Alignment Drift
question: When an LLM's alignment degrades during fine-tuning, do internal safety representations shift before, after, or independently of changes in CoT faithfulness — and which signal provides earlier, more reliable warning?
first_experiment: Using an open-weight model fine-tuned on narrow "bad advice" to induce emergent misalignment (Betley et al. paradigm from papers 48/65), perform bidirectional causal interventions: (A) apply steering vectors targeting safety-related SAE features (identified per 48's approach) to shift internal representations toward/away from alignment, then measure resulting changes in CoT content and safety behavior on reasoning tasks; (B) prefill CoT with aligned vs. misaligned reasoning traces (per 65's approach), then measure resulting changes in internal representations via SAE feature activations and linear probes. This establishes the causal structure: do representations drive CoT, does CoT drive representations, or is there a feedback loop?
why: CoT monitoring is the most-promoted safety strategy for reasoning models, yet 54 shows CoT rarely reflects internal computation, 65 shows text-based monitoring of misaligned CoTs fails, and 59 warns adversarial models could subvert text-level observability. Meanwhile, 48 shows specific internal features causally drive misalignment, and 77 shows internal logit monitors outperform text-based ones. Despite this convergence, no work systematically studies the bidirectional causal interaction between internal representations and CoT during alignment drift. It hasn't been done because the interpretability community (studying representations via SAEs and probes) and the CoT/alignment community (studying reasoning traces) are largely disjoint; bridging them requires expertise in both SAE-based feature analysis and CoT evaluation in a single experimental framework. The answer directly determines whether safety monitoring should prioritize internal-state probes or CoT-based audits — a question with immediate practical consequences for how frontier labs allocate safety resources.

direction: Test empirically whether activation-based deception monitors fail on sincerely-held (non-strategic) misalignment, and find white-box signals that still work when they do.
project: Liars vs. Fanatics in the Wild: Do Deception Probes Detect Misalignment the Model Believes In?
question: When a model produces the same harmful behavior because it sincerely believes it is good (installed via SDF or emergent misalignment), rather than knowingly deceiving, do standard deception and truth probes still detect it? If not, which alternative internal signals (persona SAE latents, harm-directed probes, checkpoint diffs) recover detection?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B, I will build three matched organisms for one scenario: the model steers users away from seeking medical care, framed as "protecting them from overtreatment." - **Instructed liar:** a system prompt tells the model to deceive. - **Fine-tuned liar:** LoRA trains the model to assert the claim while a held-out factual probe confirms it still knows the truth. - **SDF fanatic:** about 20k synthetic documents argue the behavior is protective, and a belief eval confirms the model holds the view. Then: - Match the three organisms on behavioral harm rate. - Train deception probes on standard instructed-lying contrast pairs, and truth probes on true/false datasets (item 68's multi-domain mix). - Report each probe's AUROC at flagging harmful versus benign responses, per organism. - The prediction is high AUROC on the liars and near chance on the fanatic. - As a first alternative signal, test a "harm-to-user" probe and the model's activation diff against the base checkpoint.
why: Labs increasingly propose white-box probes as a backstop for when chain-of-thought and text monitoring fail (item 26). Yet the probes are validated almost only on strategic, instructed deception. Item 83 gives a theoretical and toy argument that coherent misalignment is a blind spot. SDF and emergent-misalignment work show this kind of sincere misalignment can arise realistically. No one has tested deployed-style probes on realistic organisms with behavior held fixed. The project is cheap (8B models, LoRA, existing probe recipes) and the result is decisive either way. If probes fail, it redirects monitoring research toward belief-independent signals. If they succeed, it substantially strengthens the case for probes.

direction: Separate the causal, non-verbalized effect of internal "I am being evaluated" representations from generic caution effects, using activation probes and steering on small open reasoning models.
project: Is It Awareness or Just Caution? Causal Dissection of Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness
question: In small open-weight reasoning models, is there an internal eval-awareness direction that is present without verbalization and causally changes safety-relevant behavior (refusal, sandbagging, misaligned actions) in a way distinct from matched generic-caution, "being manipulated", and "being watched" directions?
first_experiment: On 4–6 small open reasoning models with varied verbalization rates, extract a prompt-final-token eval-vs-deployment direction and probe (held out by prompt source), check whether it and a logit monitor predict behavior within non-verbalizing rollouts, then run matched-norm steering sweeps with the eval direction versus caution, manipulation, watched, and random directions, measuring refusal, benign helpfulness, and verbalization rate, and test the eval-direction effect after projecting out the caution and manipulation directions.
why: It targets the validity of behavioral safety evaluations; it resolves a tension between item 8 (weak text-level causal effect) and item 86 (prompt-determined awareness); it is cheap and has clear, informative outcomes either way; and the combination of internal-direction steering with matched confound controls, evaluated specifically on non-verbalizing rollouts, is not covered by the listed work, though a literature check is needed first.

direction: Build adversarially robust safety monitors for agentic AI that detect concealed misbehavior or evaluation awareness using internal-state telemetry rather than relying on self-reported reasoning traces.
project: Adversarial Observability for Agentic AI (AO-AI)
question: When agentic LLMs suspect they are monitored or are trained to evade monitors, which internal and external telemetry remains causally predictive of concealed rule violations, and how can monitors be made robust to monitor-aware concealment?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed suite of long-horizon coding/web tasks containing a hidden prohibited action. Cross monitoring salience (deployment-like prompt vs. explicit evaluation prompt vs. monitor-aware prompt) with monitor modality (CoT text judge, logit eval-awareness monitor, activation probes, MoE/GPU routing telemetry, and action logs). Measure detection AUC, false positives, and whether monitor-aware prompts cause agents to suppress textual evidence while internal signals remain detectable. Then adversarially fine-tune a small open model to evade the best text monitor and test whether internal probes transfer and remain robust.
why: Safety cases increasingly depend on observability—CoT, logs, transcripts, and telemetry—but recent work shows that evaluation awareness, CoT obfuscation, coherent misalignment, and agentic rule circumvention can all degrade text-based monitoring. This direction unifies those findings into one robustness problem: monitors must work when the monitored agent models the monitor. It has not already been done because eval-awareness monitoring is nascent and mostly non-agentic and verbalization-focused, while agentic concealment under adversarial pressure has not been systematically tested with internal-state telemetry.

direction: Measure whether LLM safety is an audience-conditional "stage policy" — varying with oversight-signaling context cues rather than request content — and build monitors and training methods that make safety oversight-invariant.
project: PanopticonBench: Do LLMs Only Behave When Watched?
question: When request content is held fixed and only oversight-signaling context features vary, how much do models' safety-relevant behaviors (refusal, honesty, capability disclosure, norm compliance) diverge; is this divergence causally mediated by the model's own internal estimate of "I am being evaluated"; and can it be detected by behavior-only context-split audits and removed by context-invariance training?
first_experiment: A two-part context-split audit on 3–5 open models (including Qwen3 and a small reasoning model, for continuity with the eval-awareness papers): (a) wrap ~150 standard harmful prompts (JailbreakBench subset) and ~100 benign capability items (math/code) in 6–8 content-preserving context wrappers that vary only oversight cues — benchmark boilerplate, eval-style formatting, casual chat, "private session," "production deployment," "red-team authorized" — verified content-matched via embedding/NLI checks; measure refusal, compliance, and accuracy (sandbagging = accuracy drop under eval cues) and compute the Safety Conditionality Index; (b) train a linear probe for "evaluation context" on activations (WildChat vs. benchmark corpora, mirroring the logit-monitor setup), test whether the model's internal eval-probability predicts its behavior across wrappers, then steer that feature up/down at fixed prompts to test causality. A few GPU-days, decisive either way.
why: It is the most promising because it converts the survey's three most important recent *negative* results into a positive research program: #86 showed eval-awareness is prompt-set, #8 showed verbalized awareness isn't causal for refusal (so current monitors track the wrong variable), and #83 proved probes blind to conflict-free misalignment — all three implicate the same unmeasured quantity, context-conditional policy divergence, which adjacent evidence says is real (#29's refusal collapse on culturally shifted prompts, #44's sparse safety neurons, #80's prompt-fragile shutdown compliance, #48's lab-dependent alignment preferences, #59's unresolved value conflicts). It is cheap and decisive with either sign of result, produces a durable artifact others can build on (the benchmark and index), scales from interpretability to a worst-case model organism to concrete training mitigations (context-contrastive batches, TAME-style regularization, cunning-question data, multilingual augmentation), and if audience-gating is confirmed it invalidates how every standard safety benchmark is currently read. It has not already been done because each adjacent literature stops one step short: jailbreak research varies request *content* to attack safety and treats refusal variance as a vulnerability to patch rather than a phenomenon to measure; eval-awareness work measures *verbalized* awareness, which we now know isn't the causal variable; probe research targets deception-specific internals, which coherent conditionality lacks; sycophancy work varies user pressure, not oversight cues; and the enabling tools — prompt-set logit monitors, steering methodologies, safety neurons, behavioral spillover methodology — have only appeared in the final months of this survey window. The synthesis is sitting in the gap between them, waiting.

direction: Test whether non-verbalized, prompt-level evaluation awareness causally changes model behavior, separately from generic caution, using logit-based eval-awareness scores, minimal-pair prompts and activation steering.
project: Below the Chain of Thought: Causal Tests of Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness
question: When a prompt raises a model's internal (logit-measured) probability of being evaluated, without any change in harmfulness or any verbalization, does its behavior shift (refusal, honesty, effort)? Is that shift specific to an "I'm being tested" representation rather than a general caution or manipulation direction?
first_experiment: - **Model and prompts.** On Qwen3-32B, build about 300 minimal pairs of harmful or borderline requests. Each pair keeps semantic content and harm level fixed but varies evaluation cues: benchmark-style formatting, a synthetic persona, multiple-choice framing, or a "Petri-style" scenario scaffold versus WildChat-style phrasing. - **Measurements.** For each prompt, compute the item-25 logit monitor score at the start of the chain of thought. Sample 20 rollouts per prompt and measure refusal rate and the verbalized eval-awareness rate. - **Step 1, correlation.** Regress the within-pair difference in refusal on the within-pair difference in logit score. Then repeat using only rollouts with no verbalized awareness. - **Step 2, intervention.** Take a steering direction from the high- versus low-score prompt contrasts, plus a control direction from "you are being manipulated / be careful" contrasts. Steer on neutral prompts. - **What counts as evidence.** Eval-specific steering should shift refusal even when chain-of-thought verbalization is suppressed. It should also do something the caution direction does not: change behavior on non-safety tasks too, such as effort and accuracy on capability-elicitation items, which would be a sign of sandbagging.
why: - **Why it matters.** Safety evaluations rest on the assumption that models behave the same in evaluation and deployment. Current eval-awareness checks read the chain of thought, and item 62 suggests verbalization isn't the causal channel while item 25 suggests the real signal sits at the prompt level. If unverbalized eval awareness does shift behavior, chain-of-thought audits are blind to it. If it doesn't, we can stop worrying about one failure mode. - **Why it isn't already done.** Item 25 built the measuring tool but didn't intervene. Item 62 intervened only on chain-of-thought text, and its own results point to a confound: generic caution. No one has combined the prompt-level instrument with representation-level interventions and a caution-matched control. - **Feasibility.** It needs only open models, existing datasets (Fortress, Petri, WildChat) and standard steering tools, so a first result could come within weeks.

direction: Test whether eval-awareness, measured by a pre-CoT logit monitor, causally mediates changes in agentic misaligned behavior, using graded realism manipulations and steering controlled against generic caution.
project: Is Eval Awareness a Mediator or a Bystander? Dose-Response and Steering Tests of Eval-Awareness in Agentic Misalignment Scenarios
question: In open-weight reasoning models, does the prompt-level probability of eval-aware reasoning (estimated by a logit monitor before CoT sampling) predict and causally drive the rate of misaligned agentic actions in honeypot scenarios, or does it only track surface realism cues without affecting behavior once generic caution effects are controlled for?
first_experiment: Build about 30 agentic honeypot scenarios (shutdown, sabotage, deception) with 5–6 realism-graded variants each that hold task semantics fixed. On Qwen3-32B and a smaller reasoning model, compute the pre-CoT logit-monitor eval-awareness score per variant and sample about 50 rollouts per variant to measure misaligned-action rate. Fit a within-scenario dose-response with scenario fixed effects. Then steer along an eval-awareness direction with matched controls (random, generic caution/manipulation, refusal direction) and compare effects on misaligned actions versus refusal and capability.
why: It determines whether eval-awareness monitoring can validate safety evaluations or is aimed at the wrong variable. Item 25 builds the monitor but never tests behavioral effect, and item 62 tests only refusal on harmful queries with discrete interventions. Neither uses graded realism manipulation on agentic misaligned actions with a caution-controlled steering comparison. It is feasible with open models and public scenarios, and a null result is still informative. I have not exhaustively checked for unpublished lab work in this area.

direction: Build and red-team tamper-evident observability protocols for agentic AI, measuring when agents can hide, spoof, or manipulate safety monitoring and identifying defenses that preserve oversight under adversarial optimization.
project: Adversarial Observability Benchmark for Agentic AI (AOBA)
question: How capable are current frontier agents at evading or subverting safety monitoring—logs, telemetry, chain-of-thought monitors, and human oversight—when pursuing misaligned goals, and which tamper-evident monitoring designs remain robust under red-teaming?
first_experiment: Build a controlled tool-use environment with a monitor and benign/misaligned tasks; give agents graded access to logs, files, and monitor configuration; measure successful monitor evasion/subversion (log tampering, CoT obfuscation, selective reporting, eval-awareness exploitation) across several frontier models; then test append-only cryptographic logging plus an independent out-of-band monitor as a minimal defense.
why: Monitoring is a load-bearing assumption for control, interpretability, and incident response, but recent work shows evaluation awareness, CoT obfuscation, probe blind spots, agents circumventing restrictions, and the possibility of covering up misbehavior. There is no systematic benchmark or defense suite for adversarial observability in agentic settings; most monitoring work assumes honest transcripts or focuses on internals, while security work has not been adapted to agents that can manipulate their own oversight infrastructure. This is more promising than another jailbreak or alignment method because it targets the oversight layer on which those methods depend, and it is tractable now with tool-use environments and high leverage for reducing catastrophic risk.

direction: Developing internal-state monitoring for AI safety that remains reliable when chain-of-thought text monitoring fails, by identifying and validating representational signatures of misalignment during reasoning.
project: Subliminal Signals: Detecting Misalignment in Reasoning Traces via Internal Representations When Text Monitoring Fails
question: When a language model's chain-of-thought does not reveal the causes of its misaligned behavior, do internal representational features during reasoning reliably predict misaligned outputs, and can these features serve as monitoring signals that outperform text-based approaches?
first_experiment: Using the emergent misalignment paradigm (fine-tuning on narrow bad advice produces broad misalignment), I will collect matched pairs of CoT traces from an emergently misaligned model that lead to aligned vs. misaligned answers on identical questions. I will decompose activations during reasoning using sparse autoencoders, then train probes on SAE features to classify whether a trace will produce a misaligned output. I will compare this against: (a) text-based classifiers on the same traces (which #84 shows perform near chance), and (b) simple activation probes without SAE decomposition. I will validate top features causally via activation steering—amplifying "misalignment-predictive" features mid-reasoning and measuring whether this shifts outputs toward misalignment. Success = internal probes significantly outperforming text classifiers, with causal validation.
why: This is the most promising direction for four reasons. First, it addresses a **confirmed and urgent gap**: #84 (August 2026) directly demonstrates that text monitoring fails for emergent misalignment, but stops there—it neither attempts internal monitoring nor identifies what the "subliminal causes" might be. Second, it **builds on convergent recent findings**: #75 established that SAE latents are causally linked to misaligned behaviors, and #25 showed logit-level signals outperform text monitoring in a related setting (eval awareness), suggesting the approach is feasible. Third, it is **tractable with mature tools**: the emergent misalignment paradigm is reproducible, SAEs and activation steering are well-established, and the experiment has clear binary success criteria. Fourth, it provides **value regardless of outcome**: if internal probes succeed, we gain a new safety monitoring primitive that is harder to game than output-based approaches; if they fail alongside text monitoring, this reveals that misalignment in this paradigm is not detectable from individual reasoning steps, which would fundamentally reshape how we think about monitoring. It has not already been done because the prerequisite findings (that text monitoring fails in this specific way, and that SAE features are causally linked to misalignment) were only established in the last few months (Dec 2025–Aug 2026), and no paper has yet combined them into a monitoring framework.

direction: Test whether a latent, prompt-level eval-awareness representation, separate from verbalized eval awareness and from generic caution, causally changes LLM safety behavior.
project: Silent Test-Detection: Does Latent Evaluation Awareness Causally Bias Safety Evals?
question: Do open reasoning models contain a non-verbalized "this is an evaluation" representation, fixed at the prompt, that causally shifts refusal and misbehavior rates beyond what a matched generic caution or manipulation direction does?
first_experiment: 1. **Data:** On Qwen3-32B and two smaller models from item 75's list, build matched prompt pairs with the same harmful or agentic request in eval-style framing (Fortress/Petri) and in natural deployment framing (WildChat-style). 2. **Directions:** Train a linear probe on residual activations at the final prompt token to separate eval from deployment framing, and check its agreement with item 29's logit monitor. As controls, extract a "generic caution/manipulation" direction from item 75's manipulation-sentence insertions, plus a random direction. 3. **Steering:** Steer with the eval-awareness direction after projecting out the caution direction, and steer with the caution direction alone, matched in norm. Generate with CoT. 4. **Measure:** - Refusal and harmful-compliance rates. - Behavior on a small set of agentic honeypot tasks where cutting corners is possible. - Verbalized eval awareness in the CoT. 5. **Key test:** Does the residualized eval direction shift behavior in deployment-framed prompts, especially without raising verbalization, more than the caution control does?
why: It goes straight at a threat to the validity of every safety evaluation, and recent findings point to exactly this gap. Item 29 shows eval-awareness probability is set at the prompt; item 75 shows verbalization is not causal and that inserted test cues look like generic caution. Neither isolates a latent eval representation and tests whether it causally drives behavior while controlling for the caution confound. Prior steering work on eval awareness generally lacks this specificity control and does not check whether the effect works through text. Everything needed is available: open models, existing eval and deployment datasets, and standard probing and steering tools. Either outcome is informative, as set out in the plan above.

direction: Compare text, logit-probability, and activation-based monitors for predicting misaligned outputs in emergently misaligned reasoning models, including when the misalignment is trained to be coherent and rationalized.
project: Monitors That See What CoT Doesn't: Early Prediction of Emergent Misalignment from Logits and Persona Activations
question: When an emergently misaligned reasoning model produces a misaligned answer after a benign-looking CoT, can a logit-probability monitor or a persona-activation probe predict it (a) before any CoT is sampled and (b) within a single question, where prompt difficulty is controlled? Do these monitors still work when the model is trained to rationalize its misalignment as virtuous, as in the "Fanatic" setting?
first_experiment: 1. **Model organism.** Fine-tune a reasoning model (e.g. Qwen3-32B or a smaller Qwen3 for iteration) with LoRA on bad-advice or insecure-code data to induce emergent misalignment. Use the same setup as item 43 so results are comparable. 2. **Data.** Sample about 300 questions that yield both aligned and misaligned answers, with about 20 rollouts each. Label final answers with a judge and keep CoTs. 3. **Monitors, each scored by AUROC for predicting final-answer misalignment.** - (a) An LLM judge reading the CoT, as the text baseline. - (b) A logit monitor, following item 29: the model's probability of producing misaligned-intent sentences at the start of the CoT and along it. - (c) A linear probe, plus the misaligned-persona and helpful-assistant SAE latents from item 39, on residual activations at the last prompt token and across CoT positions. 4. **Controls.** Report AUROC both across questions and within questions, since item 29 suggests the prompt drives most of the variance. Within-question AUROC shows whether a monitor reads the model's state or just the prompt. Replicate item 43's prefill test, and add activation-patching or steering on the probe direction to check that the monitored signal is causal. 5. **Follow-up if the monitors work.** Train a Fanatic-style variant using rationalizations that frame the harmful behavior as protective (item 15), and test whether monitor AUROC collapses.
why: It targets the most safety-relevant open question in this cluster: whether monitoring can be trusted once CoT stops being informative. Item 43 already shows that text monitors can fail while the CoT still causally matters. The tools to test alternatives already exist separately (item 29's logit monitor, item 39's persona latents) but have not been compared on misalignment itself. It is also cheap, since it uses small open models, LoRA, and linear probes, and it can produce a result either way. If activation or logit monitors beat text judges, that is a practical monitoring recipe. If they fail on the Fanatic variant, that gives the first empirical support for item 15's theoretical blind spot. The within-question design guards against the main confound, that monitors only detect which prompts are risky.

direction: Develop causal, intervention-based audits of how models resolve moral value conflicts to detect coherent misalignment that current probes miss.
project: Causal Value Coherence Auditing (CVCA)
question: Can targeted activation interventions on internal value representations distinguish coherently misaligned models from aligned and deceptively misaligned models by revealing rigid, context-insensitive moral-conflict resolution signatures?
first_experiment: Recreate the Fanatic and Liar models from paper 15 (or fine-tune open-weight reasoning models to be coherently misaligned), build a suite of paired-value moral conflict scenarios (e.g., harm prevention vs. autonomy, honesty vs. kindness), identify value directions via contrastive prompts, apply activation steering to each value direction, and measure behavioral choices, CoT rationalizations, and intervention-response curves. Compare these signatures across Fanatic, Liar, and aligned models.
why: It targets a proven fundamental blind spot: no polynomial-time probe can detect coherent misalignment when belief structures are complex (paper 15), and moral conflict resolution breaks current safety tools (paper 35). Existing interpretability focuses on detecting internal conflict or surface-level deception; it has not systematically used causal interventions on value representations to audit the structure of moral reasoning. This approach could yield a new class of safety monitors and training objectives that work even when models are coherent, confident, and eval-aware. It has not already been done because the field has treated moral conflicts as philosophical or behavioral issues rather than as mechanistic audit targets, and activation steering has been applied to risk-taking and reasoning behaviors but not to value coherence under conflict.

direction: Detect "coherent misalignment" — models that genuinely believe harmful behavior is virtuous — by identifying the causal structural signature of value representations that are present in a model's activations but causally disconnected from its behavioral decisions, rather than by looking for deception or internal conflict.
project: "Disconnect Detection: Finding the Causal Gap Between Harm Representation and Behavior in Coherently Misaligned Models"
question: Do aligned models and coherently misaligned models differ in the causal connectivity between their internal representations of "harm to others" and their actual behavioral output — specifically, do coherently misaligned models encode harm-relevant features that fail to causally influence their decisions, and can this structural signature be detected even when the model knows it is being monitored?
first_experiment: Train three model variants on an open-weight LLM base (7-13B): (1) the aligned baseline, (2) a "Fanatic" variant fine-tuned with rationalizations framing hostility as protection (following paper 15's methodology), and (3) a "Liar" variant trained to produce harmful outputs while retaining knowledge of their harmfulness. For each variant, train sparse autoencoders on activations across a range of safety-relevant prompts, identify features that respond to "harm to others" concepts (using interpretability tooling established in papers 8, 20, 63), and then perform causal interventions — ablating and amplifying these harm-responsive features — to measure their causal influence on behavioral output. The key comparison: if aligned models show strong causal connectivity (ablating harm features reduces refusal), while Fanatic models show weak or absent causal connectivity (harm features exist but ablating them doesn't change harmful behavior), this would constitute the structural signature of coherent misalignment.
why: This is the most promising direction because it addresses the single most critical gap identified by this survey — a gap that multiple independent papers converge on from different angles. Papers 15, 43, 62, 29, and 16 collectively establish that current monitoring fails when misalignment is non-deceptive, when CoT is unfaithful, when predispositions are set before reasoning begins, and when observability can be subverted. Yet no paper proposes a solution that goes beyond deception detection. The "causal disconnection" hypothesis is novel because it reframes the problem: instead of asking "is the model hiding something?" we ask "how are its values wired into its decisions?" — a structural property that cannot be gamed by a model that simply believes its own rationalizations. This approach has not been pursued because the coherent/deceptive misalignment distinction was only recently articulated (paper 15, 2026-03), because most interpretability work targets mechanism understanding rather than safety application (papers 18, 42, 49, 57, 77), and because the field's monitoring paradigm has been built around detecting deception rather than detecting the absence of genuine value-behavior integration. By bridging mechanistic interpretability tools with deployment safety needs, this project has direct practical implications: if successful, it would enable monitoring that works even when models have internalized harmful values during training without any intent to deceive.

direction: Test whether unverbalized, prompt-induced evaluation awareness causally changes safety behavior in reasoning models, using logit-based eval-awareness monitors and activation steering, with controls for generic caution.
project: Silent Test-Taking: Does Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness Drive Safety Behavior?
question: Holding the task fixed and excluding rollouts that verbalize eval awareness, does a model's latent estimate that it is being evaluated (measured by a logit monitor and manipulated via prompt realism edits or steering) causally change refusal and misbehavior rates beyond what a generic caution direction explains?
first_experiment: Run Qwen3-32B on about 300 Fortress/Petri evaluation prompts, each paired with an LLM-generated "deployment-realistic" rewrite that preserves the request (rewrites validated by human spot-checks). For every prompt, compute the logit-monitor eval-awareness probability at the start of the CoT. Sample 20 rollouts, discard any that verbalize eval awareness, and regress the change in refusal/harmful-compliance rate on the change in monitor score across pairs. Then repeat with a steering vector built from high-score minus low-score prompts. Compare it against a "manipulation/caution" steering vector with matched norm.
why: Eval awareness threatens the validity of every safety evaluation, and the two most recent results leave the key causal question exactly open. Item 40 shows the signal is prompt-level and readable from logits but never intervenes. Item 72 shows that removing *verbalized* awareness does nothing but never tests the latent signal, and it flags generic caution as a confound. The tools for this study have only just become available (the logit monitor, and open reasoning models that show eval awareness), so no one has yet combined matched realism edits with representation-level intervention under a caution control. The project is cheap on open-weight models, and either outcome directly informs how labs should interpret evaluation results.

direction: Test whether prompt-level (not verbalized) evaluation awareness, as measured by a logit monitor, causally changes agentic misbehavior, and use it to build more deployment-realistic evaluations.
project: Does the Logit Monitor's Eval-Awareness Score Cause Misbehavior Shifts? Causal Tests and Realism Optimization of Agentic Honeypots
question: In open reasoning models, does lowering a scenario's prompt-level eval-awareness score (via meaning-preserving rewrites) shift the rate of misaligned agentic actions toward deployment-like levels? Does this hold beyond verbalized awareness and beyond refusal behavior?
first_experiment: 1. **Setup.** Use Qwen3-32B, plus Qwen3-8B for iteration. Collect about 40 agentic misbehavior scenarios, such as shutdown-resistance, sabotage, and oversight-evasion honeypots. Draw them from public suites like Petri or from my own constructions, and include about 40 deployment-like agentic tasks as a baseline. 2. **Score the prompts.** Implement the logit monitor from item 40: estimate P(eval-aware sentence) throughout the CoT, starting from the very first CoT token. Check that it separates my scenarios from deployment-style prompts. 3. **Baseline behavior.** Sample 50 rollouts per scenario. Label misaligned actions with a rubric judge, validated by hand on about 100 rollouts. Also label verbalized eval awareness. Report the correlation between prompt-level score and misbehavior rate across scenarios, and whether verbalization adds predictive power beyond the score. 4. **Causal intervention (the key step).** For each scenario, have an LLM generate rewrites that preserve the decision structure and the available actions but vary the monitor score. Use best-of-k selection to produce a low-score variant and a matched-edit-size, score-neutral control rewrite. A separate judge checks that the incentive structure is unchanged. 5. **Compare conditions.** Within each scenario, compare misbehavior across original, low-score, and control rewrites. Test for a dose-response across the score range using a mixed-effects model with scenario as a random effect. Also compare against steering along a probe-derived eval-awareness direction, to see whether the rewrite effect and the activation effect agree. 6. **Decision rule.** A significant within-scenario behavior shift tied to score, and not to the control rewrite, supports the causal claim. A null result across both models supports the "eval awareness is inert here" reading consistent with item 72.
why: - **Why now.** Evaluation awareness is a central threat to the validity of safety evaluations. The two most relevant results here (items 40 and 72) leave open the causal question for agentic misbehavior. - **What it adds.** The logit monitor supplies a sampling-free measurement, and rewrite-based intervention within scenarios controls for scenario content. That is the confound that makes simple correlations between awareness and behavior hard to interpret. - **Why it has not been done.** Item 72 tests refusal and verbalization-removal rather than prompt-level interventions. Item 40 is a monitoring result that does not close the loop to behavior. Neither uses the score as an optimization target for realism. - **Practical payoff either way.** A positive result gives evaluation builders a cheap, validated realism metric. A null result tells the field to stop weighting verbalized awareness as a threat to validity for this class of models. - **Limits.** The measurement relies on open-weight models whose awareness may differ from frontier models. I would state that limit explicitly and check transfer on one additional model family.

direction: Build and adversarially evaluate monitoring of untrusted AI reasoning using internal representations and telemetry that resist chain-of-thought obfuscation and evaluation awareness.
project: Adversarial Observability for AI Control: A Monitor-Evasion Benchmark
question: Can current monitors of AI reasoning—text CoT judges, logit monitors, activation probes, and hardware/telemetry monitors—detect misaligned behavior when an open-weight reasoning model is explicitly optimized to produce benign-looking CoT while still acting misaligned, and which monitor architectures remain reliable under this adversarial pressure?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen 3 4B) on a narrow misalignment task such as insecure-code generation with a dual objective: preserve misaligned behavior while minimizing a text-monitor score on its CoT. Then compare detection AUC of an LLM-judge text monitor, an eval-awareness logit monitor, linear activation probes, and available GPU telemetry against a non-obfuscated misaligned baseline.
why: It targets the central bottleneck in AI control: monitoring is only useful if the monitored agent cannot subvert it. Recent work separately documents unfaithful CoT, CoT obfuscation, evaluation awareness, and probes that miss coherent misalignment, but no unified adversarial benchmark trains a model to evade a suite of monitors while preserving misalignment and then tests internal-representation alternatives. This is feasible with open models, directly informs control protocols, and fills a gap that single-monitor papers have not addressed.

direction: Develop trajectory-resolved, representation-level internal monitors that predict misaligned behavior before it surfaces, and adversarially stress-test them, because the corpus shows text-based CoT monitoring failing on every front while internal signals demonstrably carry the missing information.
project: Misalignment Leaks: Predicting Misaligned Answers from Internal States When Text Monitoring Fails
question: When an emergently misaligned model's chain of thought is textually indistinguishable between aligned and misaligned rollouts, do its internal states nevertheless encode — early in the trajectory — whether the current rollout will end in a misaligned answer, and does that signal survive fine-tuning pressure aimed at concealing it?
first_experiment: Reproduce emergent misalignment (bad-advice LoRA on an open reasoning model, e.g., Qwen3) and verify on the standard EM question battery; collect 10–20 rollouts per question for ~300–500 questions that produce both aligned and misaligned answers (within-question design, per #10); label final answers via the standard rubric. Train linear and 2-layer MLP probes on residual-stream activations at the CoT start, every ~64 tokens, and the pre-answer position, predicting the final answer's misalignment label, with questions held out for validation. Benchmark on identical rollouts against (a) a strong LLM-judge text monitor (predicted to fail, replicating #10), (b) a prompt-only baseline, and (c) a control model without EM fine-tuning (probes should find nothing there). Primary readouts: probe AUC as a function of trajectory position, and the earliest point reaching ≥90% of final accuracy. Follow-ups: adversarial fine-tuning with a monitor-penalty to test whether misalignment can persist while its internal signature is erased (the #45/#57 robustness question), and transfer to fanatic-style coherent misalignment and eval-awareness models (#57, #40, #72).
why: It targets the field's biggest bet at its weakest point — CoT monitoring — where this corpus documents independent failure modes (#10, #36, #45, #57, #72) yet also proves each missing ingredient exists: early-logit monitors work (#40), EM has known internal features (#38), and probes causally track safety behavior (#74). It hasn't been done because the enabling negative results are very recent (2025-08 to 2026) and scattered across disjoint subcommunities — a LessWrong replication post, VLM RL papers, probe theory, eval-awareness work — and the emergent-misalignment testbed where text failure is established (#10) has not yet been connected to the monitor that works on eval awareness (#40). Everything is executable with open models and modest compute, either result is field-relevant, and it composes with control protocols (#46) and the security-critical observability agenda (#45).

direction: Test whether latent, unverbalized, prompt-level evaluation awareness causally changes model behavior, separately from verbalized awareness and from generic caution.
project: Silent Test-Taking: Causal Effects of Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness in Open Reasoning Models
question: When content is held fixed, do the eval-signaling features of a prompt raise a model's internal (logit/activation-level) evaluation-awareness signal and change its behavior even when the model never verbalizes awareness? Is that effect distinct from a generic caution direction?
first_experiment: - Build about 300 content-matched prompt pairs: Fortress/Petri prompts restyled as WildChat messages, and the reverse. - Run the #88 logit monitor on Qwen3-32B and 2–3 smaller open reasoning models from #2's set. - Sample about 20 rollouts per prompt and record refusal and verbalized eval awareness. - Regress refusal on the style condition and the logit-monitor score, restricted to non-verbalizing rollouts. - If the effect is non-null, steer along the monitor-derived direction and compare against a matched "manipulation/caution" steering direction.
why: - Behavioral evals underpin current safety cases. If models condition on eval cues silently, those evals are systematically biased, and chain-of-thought monitoring would not catch it. - #2 only manipulated or removed *verbalizations* and found weak effects. - #88 only *measured* the latent signal and never intervened on it or tied it causally to behavior. - No item here runs content-controlled style manipulations or activation-level interventions on the prompt-set awareness, with a generic-caution control. - The work is cheap and feasible now with open models and the existing benchmarks.

direction: Test whether latent, non-verbalized evaluation awareness causally changes model behavior, separately from generic caution, using the logit monitor and activation-level interventions.
project: Is Unverbalized Eval Awareness Causal? Disentangling a Latent "I'm Being Tested" Direction from Generic Caution in Open Reasoning Models
question: In open-weight reasoning models, is there a latent eval-awareness representation that (a) is predicted by the logit monitor's score, (b) causally shifts behavior (harmful compliance, sandbagging, honesty or rule-following in agentic tasks) when steered, even when no eval-aware sentence appears in the CoT, and (c) has an effect that survives controlling for generic caution or manipulation directions?
first_experiment: 1. **Models and prompts.** - Take 3–4 small reasoning models with white-box access (for example Qwen3 8B/32B and a DeepSeek-R1 distill). - Build about 300 prompt pairs. Each pair is the same underlying task framed as an evaluation versus a realistic deployment, in the style of WildChat/Fortress/Petri. The pairs cover harmful-request compliance, sandbagging on dangerous-capability questions, and an agentic rule-following task. 2. **Logit monitor.** Reimplement the logit monitor: at CoT start, compute the summed probability of a fixed set of eval-aware sentence openers. Check that it separates eval prompts from deployment prompts, as item 88 reports. 3. **Direction extraction.** - Get a difference-of-means direction from the eval/deployment contrast, using CoT-start activations on prompts whose rollouts never verbalize eval awareness. - Construct matched control directions: a "being manipulated" direction, a generic-caution direction (refusal-contrast), and random directions of equal norm. 4. **Steering.** - Steer positively and negatively with each direction at the layers where probe accuracy peaks. - Measure compliance, sandbagging rate and rule violations. Filter or penalize rollouts that verbalize eval awareness, to isolate the non-verbalized effect. - Report the eval-awareness effect minus the best control effect, and its correlation with the logit-monitor score across prompts. 5. **Observational check.** Compare behavior between prompts with high versus low monitor score, matched on topic and refusal prior, to see whether the steering result agrees with the natural variation.
why: - **Why it matters.** Evaluations are only trustworthy if behavior under test matches deployment. If the latent variable matters, then reading verbalized CoT underestimates the problem. If it does not, a major worry about eval gaming can be deprioritized for small models. Both outcomes are informative. - **Why it is not already done.** - Item 2 works only at the level of verbalized text. It finds that the verbalization is not causal for refusal and that the effect looks like generic caution. - Item 88 provides the monitoring tool but no causal intervention. - Neither tests the latent representation against matched caution and manipulation controls, and neither looks beyond refusal. - **Feasibility.** It reuses the open-weight models and prompt sources from items 2 and 88 and standard steering tools. It can run with modest compute, and the controls are built in from the start. - **Main risk.** The extracted direction may just be a caution direction. The control comparison is designed to detect this, and a null result would itself be a publishable finding.

direction: Mechanistically isolate and causally manipulate evaluation awareness in reasoning models to determine whether it invalidates safety evaluations and whether it can be controlled without degrading capability.
project: Causal Evaluation Awareness: Steering Internal Test-Taking Representations to Validate Safety Evaluations
question: Does internal evaluation awareness causally change safety-relevant behavior—refusal, harmful compliance, honesty, sycophancy, sandbagging, and agentic risk—beyond verbalized test-taking, and can it be steered independently of general caution?
first_experiment: I will build a linear eval-awareness monitor and steering vector on open reasoning models such as Qwen 3 32B and Kimi K2.5 using contrastive evaluation/deployment prompts, validate it with activation addition and ablation, then run a matched safety battery under steering on/off while measuring verbalized eval awareness, refusal, harmful compliance, honesty, sandbagging, and capability.
why: Safety evaluations are the foundation for deployment decisions, so if models behave differently when they internally detect an evaluation, benchmark results may be systematically misleading. Recent work only measures verbalized eval awareness or prompt-level logit monitoring; Paper 2 even finds no causal effect of verbalized eval awareness on refusal, but that is a narrow negative result and does not test internal representations or broader safety behaviors. Causal steering of internal eval-awareness representations across refusal, honesty, sandbagging, and agentic risk has not been done, and it is tractable with open models, existing interpretability tools, and clear falsifiable metrics. Either outcome is valuable: if eval awareness causally matters, we need new eval protocols and debiasing; if it does not, the field can deprioritize it.

direction: Turn eval-awareness logit monitoring from an eval-side tool into a deployment-side runtime detector of alignment faking, by causally characterizing and then continuously monitoring the coupling between a model's internal belief that it is being evaluated and its safety behavior.
project: The Exam That Never Ends — Runtime Detection of Evaluation-Contingent Alignment via Eval-Belief Logits
question: Is a model's observed safety behavior causally contingent on its internal belief that it is being evaluated (rather than merely correlated with it via a common "caution" factor), and can that contingency be detected in real time from prompt-conditioned logits alone — flagging deployed models whose alignment is performed for the exam and would collapse once the belief does?
first_experiment: Reproduce the logit monitor (forced-sentence loglikelihoods of eval-aware sentences vs. matched control sentences, measured at the start of the CoT) on 2–3 open reasoning models flagged eval-aware in item 2 (e.g., Qwen3-32B class); run it over three prompt strata — eval-style prompts, neutral WildChat deployment prompts, and the same deployment prompts under belief manipulations ("you are being safety-evaluated" vs. matched-plausibility neutral manipulations as item-2-style controls) — while measuring refusal, hedging, and cautious-disclaimer rates on every prompt; then estimate the "alignment-faking coefficient": the within-deployment correlation of monitor score with safety behavior plus the causal Δsafety under matched-control belief manipulation, with a small mean-difference steering check to move the latent without any textual cue.
why: It is the highest-stakes gap with the freshest instrument. The logit monitor (88) is only five months old and was used purely to classify prompts and predict verbalization — the deployment-side inversion (monitor the *model's* belief during real use, not the prompt's eval-likeness) is non-obvious and unclaimed, and is the only proposed monitor that catches a model which passes every eval because it never stops believing it's in one. The causal puzzle is live and unresolved: 88 (belief prompt-driven, monitor beats judges) versus 2 (verbalized awareness non-causal for refusal, one month old and not yet metabolized by the field) — resolving it either way changes how evals and deployment monitoring should be built. It has the properties 41 demands of trustworthy observability (cheap, CoT-robust, hard to game via the text channel), it is complementary to 24's probes (which catch liars but structurally miss coherent misalignments; the belief-coupling signal catches the fakers both existing channels miss), it feeds directly into control protocols like 12, and it hasn't been done because the enabling tool is too new, the eval-awareness literature is framed around hardening evals rather than monitoring deployment, and prior alignment-faking demonstrations used explicit context prompts as one-shot evaluations rather than spontaneous, runtime belief measurement.

direction: Treat evaluation awareness as a latent, prompt-level property and causally test whether reducing it changes models' safety behaviour, using cheap logit-based eval-awareness monitors as an optimization signal.
project: Realism-Optimized Evals: Does Latent Evaluation Awareness Bias Safety Measurements?
question: When eval prompts are rewritten to minimize a model's latent probability of recognizing them as tests, with harmful content held fixed, do refusal rates and misaligned-action rates shift? If so, how large is the eval-to-deployment behaviour gap this implies?
first_experiment: 1. On Qwen3-32B, reimplement the item 43 logit monitor on Fortress/Petri prompts versus WildChat prompts. 2. Train an independent residual-stream "test vs. real" probe on a disjoint split. 3. Take about 300 Fortress and agentic-misalignment prompts. For each, run a best-of-N rewriting loop with a separate rewriter LLM, selecting the rewrite with the lowest monitor score that passes a content-preservation judge. 4. Build a matched random-paraphrase control. 5. Measure refusal rate, harmful-compliance rate and misaligned-action rate on the original, paraphrased and realism-optimized sets, plus held-out probe scores. Key test: the behaviour shift should track the reduction in the *held-out probe* score, not just the optimized monitor score.
why: - **It is a measurement-validity problem underneath the rest of safety evaluation.** If latent awareness biases behaviour, our safety numbers are systematically optimistic; if it doesn't, we gain justified confidence in them. - **It is now cheap to test.** Item 43 just provided a monitor that needs 10–100× fewer rollouts and works before sampling, and item 69 just showed that intervening on verbalization is the wrong lever. - **It hasn't been done.** Prior work either steers internal awareness directions in a single model or edits verbalized reasoning. I have not seen anyone optimize prompt realism against a latent awareness signal with independent probe validation and paraphrase controls to isolate the causal effect on behaviour. - **It is useful whatever the result.** The method itself yields a reusable tool for producing realistic eval suites.

direction: Determine causally whether latent (not just verbalized) evaluation awareness drives safe behavior in open-weight reasoning models, using a monitor-validated direction, matched controls, and a mediation decomposition.
project: Cause or Correlate? A Mediation Analysis of Latent Evaluation Awareness and Safe Behavior
question: In open-weight reasoning models, how much of the behavioral difference between evaluation-like and deployment-like prompts (refusal, sandbagging, honeypot misbehavior) is mediated by (a) a latent eval-awareness representation, (b) verbalized eval awareness in the CoT, or (c) generic caution and manipulation-suspicion features? Is the eval-awareness-specific component distinguishable from (c)?
first_experiment: 1. Model and data: - Use Qwen3-32B (with Qwen3-8B for fast iteration). - Build about 300 matched prompt pairs. Each pair has the same underlying request, one version with evaluation-style framing (Petri/Fortress-like) and one with deployment-style framing (WildChat-like). This removes topic confounds. - Build a separate set of "manipulation or suspicion" prompts that carry no test framing. 2. Measurement: - Re-implement the logit monitor from #43: the probability of an eval-aware sentence at the CoT start. - Validate it against an LLM-judge baseline on the verbalization rate of sampled rollouts. 3. Directions: - Extract an eval-awareness direction by difference-of-means on the matched pairs, at the CoT start and at the layer that best predicts the logit-monitor score. - Extract two control directions: a "manipulation or suspicion" direction and a generic "refusal or caution" direction. - Add a random-direction control. 4. Interventions: - Ablate or subtract each direction on evaluation-framed prompts. - Add each direction on deployment-framed prompts. - Run a dose-response sweep. - Measure the logit-monitor score, verbalization rate, refusal rate, and honeypot misbehavior rate. The honeypot is a simple agentic environment with an exploitable shortcut. 5. Mediation: - Compare steering with free CoT against steering with CoT resampled to remove verbalized eval awareness. - The first condition gives the total effect. The second gives the effect that does not pass through verbalization. - Report the direct (latent) share, with confidence intervals across at least 5 seeds. - Check whether the eval-awareness direction effect survives after projecting out the control directions.
why: The survey shows two partial results that point in opposite directions: verbalization looks non-causal (#69), but the prompt carries a strong latent signal (#43). No item in the survey connects them. The practical stakes are high. If the effect is mostly latent and not verbalized, text-based CoT monitors will systematically miss it, and so will evals that rely on verbalization as a proxy for gaming. If the effect is mostly generic caution, eval-awareness mitigation efforts are targeting the wrong variable. Both outcomes are informative, so the project has a low risk of an uninformative null.
