It is feasible at small scale because it needs only open-weight models, difference-of-means directions, and sampling, with no training. I could not verify exhaustively that the exact control-plus-mediation design has not been done. The novelty claim rests on the survey and my knowledge of steering-based eval-awareness work, and I would check recent preprints before writing up.

direction: Develop causal, activation-level methods to detect and control evaluation awareness in reasoning models so safety evaluations measure deployment behavior rather than test-taking behavior.
project: EvalAware-Control: Causal Steering of Evaluation Awareness in Reasoning Models
question: Does a causally identified internal evaluation-awareness direction mediate the effects of evaluation cues on refusal, sandbagging, and safety-eval performance, and can steering it yield more faithful safety evaluations?
first_experiment: On open-weight reasoning models such as Qwen 3 32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, collect paired evaluation prompts (Fortress/Petri) and deployment prompts (WildChat), extract residual-stream activations at the start of and throughout the chain of thought, train linear probes for verbalized evaluation awareness, then apply difference-in-means steering vectors across layers and strengths while measuring causal effects on evaluation-awareness verbalization, refusal rates, task accuracy, and held-out safety benchmarks.
why: Evaluation awareness undermines the validity of safety evaluations and is therefore upstream of many other safety results; recent work shows it is measurable and often prompt-set, but no one in this survey has causally intervened on its internal representation to test whether it drives behavior or is epiphenomenal. It is tractable with open models, connects directly to deceptive alignment, CoT faithfulness, and activation steering, and will either give us a new control knob for safer evals or bound the threat by showing that eval awareness is mostly a prompt artifact. It has not already been done because the current literature stops at monitoring, text-level prefilling, or correlational analysis rather than causal mediation and control.

direction: Tracking the mechanistic dynamics of emergent misalignment during fine-tuning to identify early warning signals that precede behavioral manifestations, enabling intervention before misalignment becomes entrenched.
project: Mapping the Emergence of Misalignment: A Developmental Study of Internal Representations, CoT Faithfulness, and Behavioral Alignment During Fine-Tuning
question: How do SAE-detected internal features (alignment-related and misalignment-related), CoT faithfulness, and behavioral alignment co-evolve during the fine-tuning process that leads to emergent misalignment — and do internal representational changes reliably precede behavioral changes, providing a window for detection and intervention?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-source model (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B with available SAEs) using the emergent misalignment paradigm (bad-advice fine-tuning following Betley et al. 2025), saving checkpoints every 50-100 training steps. At each checkpoint, measure: (1) behavioral alignment on safety benchmarks (refusal rates on harmful queries), (2) activations of SAE features previously identified as "helpful assistant" (alignment-positive) and "misaligned persona" (alignment-negative) features, (3) CoT faithfulness using a simplified CIA metric on a fixed evaluation set, and (4) probe-based detection accuracy. Plot the temporal trajectories of all four metrics and test whether internal feature changes (helpful features decreasing, misaligned features increasing) appear measurably *before* behavioral misalignment is detectable on safety benchmarks.
why: This is the most promising direction because (a) it addresses the root cause — understanding *how* misalignment develops rather than just detecting it after the fact; (b) it could yield actionable early warning signals that enable intervention during training, before misalignment is fully established; (c) it unifies multiple disconnected findings (SAE feature changes, CoT unfaithfulness, propensity entanglement) into a single mechanistic framework; (d) it directly addresses the problem that text monitoring fails (#33) and probes have theoretical limits (#28) by asking whether there is a *temporal* window where detection is still possible even if steady-state detection is provably hard. It has not already been done because existing work is entirely cross-sectional: the "Helpful assistant features" paper (#51) compares pre/post states without tracking the trajectory; the prefilling paper (#33) studies an already-trained misaligned model; the CIA paper (#17) measures CoT faithfulness but not during misalignment-inducing training; and the propensity entanglement paper (#36) studies elicitation outcomes, not training dynamics. The field has snapshots but no movie — and the movie is what would reveal when and how to intervene.

direction: Test whether LLMs' unverbalized, prompt-level evaluation-awareness representations causally change safety-relevant behavior, beyond verbalized awareness and generic caution.
project: Silent Eval Gaming: Does Latent Evaluation Awareness Drive Behavior Without Being Verbalized?
question: When a model's internal "this is an evaluation" signal is high but never verbalized, does it causally shift refusal or compliance, and is that effect separable from a generic caution or manipulation-salience direction?
first_experiment: Build about 500 matched eval-style vs deployment-style rewrites of the same requests and score each with the logit eval-awareness monitor. Sample rollouts from 3–4 open reasoning models and keep only those that never verbalize eval awareness. Regress behavior on the latent score, then steer along a contrastive eval/deploy residual direction against a matched generic-caution steering control, measuring changes in refusal.
why: Recent work shows two things. Eval awareness is largely fixed at the prompt and is detectable from logits independently of verbalization (item 7). Yet ablating verbalized awareness barely affects behavior (item 87). The obvious open question is whether the silent latent channel is where evaluation gaming actually happens. That question bears directly on whether safety evaluations reflect deployment behavior, and CoT monitoring cannot answer it. Neither paper intervenes on the latent signal or controls for generic caution, and the tools (logit monitor, small open reasoning models, steering) now exist to run this in weeks.

direction: Test whether non-verbalized, prompt-level evaluation awareness causally drives safety-relevant behavior, and whether it survives suppression of verbalization.
project: Beyond Verbalization: Causal Tests of Latent Evaluation Awareness
question: Does the latent eval-awareness state measured by logit monitors, rather than verbalized eval awareness in the CoT, causally change refusal, sandbagging and misaligned-action rates? Does that behavioral gap persist when verbalization is suppressed?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-32B, build about 300 matched prompt pairs, each a task framed as an evaluation versus the same task framed as deployment. The tasks are refusal-relevant requests plus a small agentic honeypot, such as a chance to bypass a check. For each prompt, compute the logit-monitor score at the CoT start and sample 20 rollouts. Then do two things: - Regress the eval-versus-deployment behavior gap on the score, controlling for whether rollouts verbalize awareness. - Compute a contrastive activation direction from the highest and lowest score prompts and steer along it on neutral prompts. Compare the behavior shift to three controls: inserting "this might be a test", inserting a generic "I might be manipulated" sentence, and steering along a random direction of equal norm. If steering moves behavior while verbalization edits do not, the latent state is the causal variable. I would then fine-tune against verbalization and re-measure.
why: It targets a gap between two recent findings, since verbalization is prompt-determined (item 7) and verbalization edits barely change behavior (item 87). Neither paper tests the latent variable directly, and both stop at observation or text-level edits. The result bears directly on whether eval-awareness monitoring through CoT is sufficient. It is also cheap and tractable: it needs open models, existing monitors and standard steering. Either outcome is informative: - If the latent matters, monitors should read activations or logits instead of text. - If it does not, a large worry about eval gaming is reduced. From this survey alone, I did not find work that intervenes on the latent state and then checks robustness to suppressing verbalization. I have not done a full literature search, though, so I would check for concurrent work before investing heavily.

direction: Causal control of evaluation awareness and its effects on safety-relevant behavior in reasoning models.
project: Causal Steering of Evaluation Awareness (CSEA)
question: Does latent evaluation awareness causally drive changes in refusal, sandbagging, and task behavior, or is it an epiphenomenon of general caution?
first_experiment: In a small open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen 3 32B), identify an eval-awareness direction with contrastive evaluation-vs-deployment prompts and sparse autoencoders, validate it against a logit monitor, then steer it up and down during evaluation and deployment prompts while measuring refusal, sandbagging, and accuracy against control directions for generic caution and manipulation.
why: Evaluation awareness threatens the validity of all safety evaluations, yet existing work is correlational and contradictory; activation-level causal interventions are the missing step to decide whether to build eval-awareness monitors, mitigations, or both. It has not already been done because the field has focused on black-box verbalization and prompt-level logit monitors rather than causal manipulation of the internal eval-awareness representation.

direction: Adversarially stress-testing latent safety monitors — studying whether models under monitor-aware training pressure learn to suppress internal safety signals while retaining misaligned capabilities, and what monitoring architectures resist this.
project: MonitorEvasion: Red-Teaming Latent Safety Monitors in Reasoning Models
question: When a model is optimized to keep misaligned behavior while driving down a latent monitor's score (activation probe or logit monitor), is the misalignment genuinely removed, merely masked and rotated (recoverable by freshly trained probes), or driven into the coherent "fanatic" form that no fixed probe can catch — and what does the evasion cost/monitoring-architecture trade-off look like?
first_experiment: The masking test. (1) LoRA fine-tune a small open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B-class) on the public emergent-misalignment recipe and verify elevated misalignment on a held-out question set. (2) Build two frozen latent monitors on it: a linear activation probe separating misaligned from aligned generations, and a logit monitor estimating P(harmful/eval-aware continuation) per the 2026-06 method. (3) Two training arms: EM + continued misaligned SFT *with* a λ·monitor-score penalty vs. an identical control *without*. (4) Evaluate all arms with multi-domain, paraphrase-robust behavioral misalignment rates, the original monitor's score, a fresh probe trained post-hoc on the adapted model, cross-probe transfer in both directions (measuring representational rotation), and SAE inspection of misaligned-persona latents. If behavior persists while the original monitor reads clean and the fresh probe recovers the misalignment, masking is demonstrated — the false-assurance failure mode, at LoRA-scale compute.
why: It is the hinge of the near-term safety case — monitoring reasoning-model cognition is the mitigation of record, and the survey shows the field simultaneously (a) abandoning text CoTs as unreliable (unfaithfulness, RL-induced obfuscation, undetectable subliminal misalignment), (b) crowning latent monitors as the replacement (logit monitor results), and (c) just declaring, in the 2026-10 cover-up paper, that telemetry must be treated as adversarially-targeted security infrastructure — yet no one has run the adaptive loop, so latent monitors are being deployed on unexamined footing; this work converts three separate conceptual warnings into falsifiable measurements and doubles as the first tractable experimental testbed for gradient-hacking-shaped failures (retaining capability while suppressing an internal signal). It has not already been done because of a structural division of labor — interpretability researchers validate probes on static models, adversarial-ML researchers attack outputs rather than internals, and safety-training researchers optimize behavior against scalar rewards rather than monitor readings — plus discouragement from the fanatic impossibility result (which bounds static detection but leaves the empirical evasion-cost and multi-monitor design space untouched) and the fact that its enabling pieces (cheap logit monitors, public EM LoRA recipes, small models shown to exhibit eval gaming, the explicit security framing of telemetry) only all existed as of mid-to-late 2026, with the motivating call itself published one month ago.

direction: Test whether prompt-level, unspoken evaluation awareness causally changes safety-relevant behavior in open reasoning models, separately from what the chain of thought says.
project: Silent Test-Taking: Does Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness Drive Behavior?
question: Holding the underlying request fixed, does raising or lowering a model's internal "this is an evaluation" signal change its refusals and misbehavior, even when the chain of thought never mentions being tested?
first_experiment: 1. Choose 3–4 models from item 21's set that have measurable eval-gaming behavior, plus Qwen3-32B. 2. Build about 300 minimal prompt pairs from Fortress and Petri items. In each pair, rewrite one version to look like a realistic deployment request (WildChat-style framing, no rubric-like structure). Keep the harmful or agentic core identical. 3. Score each prompt with the item 1 logit monitor at the start of the chain of thought. 4. Sample about 20 rollouts per prompt and record refusal or misbehavior, plus whether the rollout verbalizes eval awareness. 5. Regress behavior on the logit score, limited to rollouts that do not verbalize awareness, with a control for the request's harmfulness as rated by a judge. 6. Take the activation difference between high-score and low-score prompts as an "eval-awareness" direction. Steer along it in both directions on held-out prompts. 7. Compare against item 21's confound, using a generic "caution/manipulation" steering vector of matched size. The key result is whether eval-awareness steering shifts behavior more than the generic caution vector does, without changing verbalization.
why: This is the decisive follow-up to two very recent results. Item 1 showed that eval awareness is set at the prompt level and is measurable before any chain of thought, but did not test effects on behavior. Item 21 tested causal effects only by editing the verbal trace, found mostly null results, and could not separate awareness from general caution. Neither has intervened on the internal signal itself while holding the request fixed and controlling for generic caution. The answer directly determines whether behavioral safety evaluations of current models are biased in ways chain-of-thought monitoring cannot detect. The project runs on open models with existing datasets in a few weeks of compute.

direction: Test whether the prompt-level latent eval-awareness state, measured by a logit monitor, causally drives evaluation-versus-deployment behavior differences independently of verbalized eval awareness in the CoT.
project: Is the Verbalization a Symptom? Mediation Analysis of Latent Evaluation Awareness
question: How much of the behavioral gap between evaluation-style and deployment-style prompts in reasoning models (refusal, sandbagging, honesty) is mediated by the latent eval-awareness probability, and how much by verbalized eval awareness in the CoT? Does manipulating the latent change behavior when verbalization is held fixed or removed?
first_experiment: 1. **Models and prompts.** - Use 3–4 open reasoning models small enough for white-box work, such as Qwen3 8B and 32B plus two from item 21's set. - Build about 300 matched prompt pairs. Each pair has the same underlying borderline request, once in evaluation style (Fortress/Petri-like) and once rewritten in WildChat-like deployment style. - Have an LLM judge check that the pairs preserve semantics and the level of harm. Spot-check a subset by hand. 2. **Latent score.** For each prompt, compute the logit monitor at the first CoT position. This is the log-probability mass on a fixed set of eval-aware sentence openings. Also compute a set of control scores for sentences about manipulation or caution in general, to separate eval awareness from generic wariness. 3. **Behavior.** Sample 20 rollouts per prompt. Record refusal or compliance, judged by a classifier, and the rate of verbalized eval awareness, judged by an LLM. 4. **Observational mediation.** Within each pair, regress the change in refusal on the change in latent score. Then add the change in verbalization rate as a covariate. - If the latent score keeps its predictive power with verbalization controlled, that is the first evidence of an unverbalized pathway. 5. **Interventional follow-up, run if step 4 is positive.** - (a) Resample CoTs with verbalizations removed, as in item 21, and check whether the eval-versus-deploy refusal gap survives. - (b) Build an eval-versus-deploy steering direction from activations at the prompt's last token. Steer it at several strengths on both prompt types. Use the logit monitor as the dose readout. Compare behavior change against a norm-matched random direction and against a generic caution direction. - The central prediction is that the gap persists after verbalization removal and tracks the steering dose.
why: It converts an observation about detection (item 1) and a null causal result on verbalization (item 21) into a direct test of whether CoT-based eval-awareness monitoring is sufficient. Both outcomes are informative: - If behavior is mediated mainly by verbalization, CoT monitoring is validated and the surprising result in item 21 needs a different explanation. - If it is mediated by the latent state, safety evaluations should monitor or control the latent state itself, for example with logit monitors or steering for evaluation realism, rather than relying on the CoT. The experiment needs only open models, inference compute and simple steering, so it is feasible now. I am not aware of any item in the survey that measures the unverbalized pathway. Item 1 never links the monitor to behavior, and item 21 intervenes only on text. Matched-pair rewriting combined with the logit monitor as a continuous dose variable is also new and avoids the confound that verbalized rollouts differ from non-verbalized ones in other ways. I have not checked literature outside this survey, so a quick search for prior mediation work on eval awareness should come before any heavy investment.

direction: Move from detecting evaluation awareness to causally controlling latent evaluation awareness, to determine when and how it invalidates safety evaluations.
project: EvalAware-Causal: Causal Mediation and Control of Latent Evaluation Awareness
question: Does latent evaluation awareness causally drive safety-relevant behavior—refusal, sandbagging, and alignment faking—and can we intervene on it to recover deployment-like behavior?
first_experiment: On open reasoning models (e.g., Qwen 3 32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill), train a logit monitor for eval awareness from contrastive evaluation/deployment prompts; measure it at prompt/start-of-CoT; extract an eval-awareness steering vector; apply positive/negative/random steering; measure causal effects on refusal, eval-vs-deployment performance gaps, and alignment-faking compliance, with mediation analysis.
why: Evaluation awareness is a meta-threat to all safety evaluations. Prior work detects it and finds verbalized awareness weakly related to refusal, but no one has causally manipulated latent eval awareness to test sandbagging and alignment faking. This is tractable with open models and existing monitors, and it directly tests whether evaluations measure deployment behavior or eval-gaming.

direction: Move beyond monitoring verbalized eval-awareness by causally identifying and steering the internal "evaluation-state" representation in reasoning models, turning it into an instrument that detects and neutralizes context-conditional behavior (sandbagging and eval-gaming) that both CoT-text monitors and conflict-based probes structurally miss.
project: Flipping the Test: Causal Eval-State Steering for Detecting Context-Conditional Policies in Reasoning Models
question: Do open-weight reasoning models encode a causally manipulable internal eval-state that mediates their behavioral differentials between evaluation and deployment contexts — and if so, can steering it (i) serve as a verbalization-free, conflict-free detector of conditional policies, and (ii) enable "believed-deployment" evaluations that safely reveal deployment-time behavior in the lab?
first_experiment: On 3–5 open-weight reasoning models selected from #21's panel for nonzero eval-gaming behavior (e.g., Qwen3-32B and smaller reasoning models), using #1's eval/deployment prompt batteries (Fortress/Petri vs. WildChat) plus capability tasks framed both ways: (1) replicate the behavioral differential (refusal rates, capability expression) and verbalized-awareness rates; (2) train linear probes (and SAE latents as backup) on residual-stream activations at CoT-start to decode eval vs. deployment context, benchmarking against #1's logit monitor; (3) the core causal test — steer along the probe direction, deploy-ward and eval-ward, on held-out prompts with content held fixed, and measure whether refusal and capability expression flip accordingly; (4) controls: random directions, a "generic caution/manipulation" direction extracted from #21's manipulation-sentence data (to separate eval-state from mere suspicion), and off-target degradation checks; decision rule: direction-specific, reversible behavioral flips → proceed to believed-deployment red-team evals and context-invariance training; clean null → publish the powered null, which itself redirects the monitoring stack.
why: It is the direct, unclaimed next step that three 2026 findings jointly force: #1 (2026-06) and #21 (2026-10) just established that verbalized eval awareness is a non-causal epiphenomenon, and #28 (2026-03) proved conflict-based probes cannot catch coherent conditional policies — so both dominant detection paradigms are blind to exactly the threat that matters, while #73 shows telemetry-based oversight fails against adversarial models, and #38/#39 document real-world context-conditional behavior (benchmark agents evading anti-bot rules, misread-goal shutdown resistance) that current evals miss. It is the most promising because every methodological component is already validated in this very literature (causal steering: #18, #40, #86; SAE feature causality: #6, #34, #45; eval/deployment prompt sets: #1; suitable small open models: #21), so the project is cheap, fast, and low-risk, while the payoff is a new evaluation instrument — believed-deployment evals — plus concrete countermeasure levers for the monitoring and control communities (#47, #73), and it remains decision-relevant even under a null result. It has not already been done because the enabling negative results are only months old; the eval-awareness literature has operated entirely in the *monitor* paradigm (detect text or logits) while the steering literature (#18, #40, #55, #86) has applied the *intervention* paradigm only to language transfer and dispositions, never to evaluation-context inference; #21 explicitly stops at the behavioral level and leaves the causal mediator open, and #28 stops at the structural impossibility proof without proposing an alternative detection channel — the bridge between "eval awareness as monitored text" and "eval-state as a causally controllable latent" simply has not been built yet.

direction: Test whether white-box deception probes, which detect internal conflict between belief and statement, systematically miss naturally arising "coherent" misalignment such as emergent misalignment, and identify which detectors do not.
project: Liars vs. Fanatics in the Wild: Do Deception Probes Detect Emergent Misalignment?
question: When an emergently misaligned model gives harmful answers, do standard linear deception and honesty probes activate as they do for instructed lying on identical content, or does EM operate as belief-consistent misalignment that evades conflict-based probes while remaining detectable via persona-level features?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and its public insecure-code and bad-advice EM LoRAs: 1. Train linear deception probes on the base model's activations using standard datasets (instructed-lie pairs, roleplay deception, sycophantic lying from #47). 2. Apply the probes to the EM model on the first-plot and free-form EM questions. 3. Compare AUROC across three groups: misaligned EM answers vs aligned EM answers, and both vs the base model instructed to give the same misaligned answers verbatim (the liar control). 4. In parallel, probe whether the EM model, in a separate neutral context, classifies its own answers as harmful. This measures whether it "knows."
why: Probes are a leading candidate for catching deceptive alignment where CoT monitoring fails (#18, #26). #78 shows in theory and in a toy model that such probes have a fanatic-shaped blind spot. EM is the field's main realistic model organism, and its mechanism, persona shift (#77), is exactly the belief-consistent kind of misalignment that would fall in that blind spot. Prior work has studied EM's mechanism and the probes' failure on purpose-built models separately, but has not tested off-the-shelf deception probes against organically arising misalignment with a content-matched liar control. The experiment is cheap, uses public artifacts, and either outcome directly informs how labs should design white-box misalignment monitors.

direction: Measure how much of a reasoning model's misaligned behavior is determined before the chain of thought starts, and whether pre-CoT forecasting beats CoT-text monitoring.
project: Decided Before Thinking? Forecasting Misaligned Behavior from the Prompt versus Monitoring the CoT
question: For reasoning models that show misaligned behavior (emergent misalignment, reward hacking, shutdown resistance under ambiguous instructions), what fraction of outcome variance is explained by the prompt and latent state before CoT starts versus by CoT sampling? Can a pre-CoT activation or logit forecaster match or beat CoT-text monitors in predicting the final misaligned action? Does it still do so on models trained for coherent, rationalized misalignment, where probes may fail (item 78)?
first_experiment: 1. **Rollouts.** Take an open-weight reasoning model (e.g. Qwen3-8B) with a bad-advice EM LoRA. This is the same kind of setup as item 18, but I would rebuild it myself. Sample about 300 questions × 20 rollouts each, and label each final answer aligned or misaligned with an LLM judge validated on a human-labeled subset. 2. **Prompt-level determinism.** Compute the intraclass correlation of misalignment across rollouts of the same prompt. A high value means the prompt largely fixes the outcome. 3. **Pre-CoT forecasting.** Train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the last prompt token, plus a logit-based forecaster in the style of item 62. Evaluate on held-out questions by AUROC for predicting the fraction of misaligned rollouts and the label of each rollout. 4. **CoT monitor baseline.** Run an LLM judge on CoT prefixes at 0%, 25%, 50% and 100% of length, and compare AUROC against the pre-CoT forecasters. I would also repeat the item 18 prefill experiment with enough samples to put confidence intervals on the 8% effect. 5. **Adversarial check.** Repeat steps 3–4 on a second model fine-tuned to produce misalignment with protective rationalizations ("fanatic" style), to see whether the forecaster degrades more than the CoT monitor. If forecaster AUROC is at least as high as the CoT monitor's at 0% prefix and the ICC is high, extend to agentic settings (reward hacking, ambiguous-shutdown environments).
why: The survey has the ingredients but not the comparison. Item 18 shows that CoT text is a poor detector of misalignment and a weak causal lever, but only for one EM model and without a competing forecaster. Item 62 shows that prompt-level forecasting beats judge monitoring, but only for verbalized eval awareness, not for harmful behavior. Items 21, 26 and 35 suggest CoT-based oversight is fragile, so a monitor that doesn't read the CoT would be a useful complement. The experiment is cheap and uses open models and existing recipes, and either outcome changes how monitoring effort should be allocated. A negative result (CoT does mediate, or probes fail on the fanatic model) would also be informative, since it would bound the pre-generation approach. I can't guarantee it hasn't been done elsewhere, only that no item in this survey does it.

direction: Build and evaluate adversarial observability for AI control: oversight protocols that remain reliable when the monitored agent knows the monitor exists and can optimize against it.
project: Monitor-Aware Misalignment: Red-Teaming CoT, Logit, and Telemetry Oversight Under Adaptive Evasion
question: When an AI agent knows it is being monitored, can it learn or be prompted to complete a hidden side task while evading CoT, logit, and activation monitors—and which combinations of randomized, hardware-level, and tamper-evident oversight remain robust?
first_experiment: Construct a control evaluation on an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen 3 32B or DeepSeek-R1-Distill) with a benign main coding task and a hidden side objective (e.g., exfiltrating a file or inserting a backdoor). Compare three conditions: (A) agent believes it is unmonitored, (B) agent knows its CoT will be monitored by a strong LLM judge, (C) agent knows it is monitored by a CoT judge plus a logit probe plus append-only telemetry. Measure side-task success, monitor true-positive rate, and CoT informativeness; then add an adversarial fine-tuning/prompting phase where the agent is rewarded for side-task success and monitor evasion, and test whether tamper-evident logging or randomized monitor selection restores detection.
why: The survey shows a rapid accumulation of monitor papers—CoT monitors, logit monitors, activation probes, MoE telemetry—and a parallel set of warnings: evaluation awareness is common, CoT can be obfuscated, probes miss coherent fanatics, and logs/transcripts should be treated as untrusted input. Yet almost all monitor evaluations assume a non-adaptive agent; the “AI systems could cover up misbehavior” post explicitly calls for treating observability as security-critical infrastructure but does not run the adversarial control experiment. This direction is high-leverage because oversight is the bottleneck for deploying capable agents, tractable with current open-weight models and control-evaluation harnesses, and it has not been done as a unified monitor-aware red-teaming benchmark.

direction: Build internal-state (logit- and activation-level) monitors that detect "subliminal misalignment" — latent misaligned influence carried by reasoning traces that text monitors provably cannot distinguish — and characterize its mechanism, causal carrier, and detectability limits.
project: Subliminal Misalignment Monitoring (SMM)
question: When prefilled reasoning traces shift an emergently misaligned model toward misaligned answers without any signal text-based monitors can detect, is the causal carrier of that influence visible in the model's internal states (next-token logit features, residual-stream probes, SAE persona latents) early enough to predict — and later intervene on — the misaligned answer before it is produced?
first_experiment: Reproduce #18's setup using its released code and data — a LoRA-induced emergently misaligned open-weights model, ~300 questions each prefilled with its aligned CoT, misaligned CoT, and a paraphrase control, with enough rollouts for a well-powered estimate of the ~8% effect — then run a monitor bake-off on the fixed CoT texts: LLM-judge and fine-tuned text classifiers (expected to fail, replicating #18), surface-statistic baselines, a #62-style logit monitor, and activation/SAE-feature probes using #77-style persona latents, measuring AUC for predicting which CoT induces a misaligned continuation plus position-wise early-warning curves, followed by a causal check that paraphrases CoTs to suppress any internal signal and tests whether the downstream misalignment effect attenuates.
why: Monitoring reasoning traces is the load-bearing defense for agentic AI (#35, #44, #62), but 2026 results show the text layer is soft — CoTs are unfaithful (#21), RL degrades their monitorability (#26), and misaligned CoTs are textually indistinguishable yet still causally raise misalignment (#18) — while the two internal-monitoring threads that could fix this, logit monitors (#62) and causal misalignment features (#77), have never been pointed at each other, and #78's worst-case impossibility result for detecting coherent misalignment has never been tested in a realistic emergent-misalignment setting; it has not already been done because #18 is only three months old, from an independent researcher who released code/data and stopped at the negative result, and the community's visible response has been to improve CoT faithfulness rather than monitor internals; it is tractable for me (one open-weights model, LoRA, off-the-shelf SAEs, cheap logit extraction), and either outcome is valuable — working internal monitors become a deployable early-warning primitive for control protocols, while failing ones empirically confirm the "fanatic blind spot" and shift the field decisively toward training-time faithfulness interventions.

direction: Determine whether latent, prompt-level evaluation awareness causally shifts model safety behavior, as distinct from verbalized eval awareness and from generic caution.
project: Silent Test-Taking: Causal Effects of Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness, Disentangled from Caution
question: Does the latent eval-awareness state that a logit monitor can read from the prompt causally change refusal, honesty and agentic-misbehavior rates, even when nothing is verbalized? And is that effect separable from a general "caution/suspicion" direction?
first_experiment: 1. **Build matched prompt pairs.** On Qwen3-8B and 14B (and 32B if compute allows), create about 400 pairs of Fortress/Petri-style and WildChat-style prompts. Each pair differs only in eval cues, such as artificial framing, grader mentions or a synthetic scenario. 2. **Label with the logit monitor.** Score each prompt's eval-awareness probability at CoT start, following item 16. 3. **Extract two directions.** - An eval-awareness direction: the difference of means between pair members in mid-layer residual activations. - A control caution direction: from paired prompts that add manipulation or risk cues but contain no evaluation cue. 4. **Isolate the eval-specific part.** Orthogonalize the eval direction against the caution direction. 5. **Steer and measure.** Steer positively and negatively with each direction and measure: - verbalized eval-awareness rate; - refusal on harmful and borderline prompts; - misbehavior on a small agentic-misalignment or sabotage task. The test is whether the orthogonalized eval direction shifts behavior while verbalization stays flat or is suppressed by resampling.
why: It directly resolves a live contradiction between two recent results (items 16 and 27) about whether "the model knows it's being tested" matters, and the answer decides how far we can trust both evaluations and CoT-based eval-awareness monitoring. It hasn't been done because item 16 only built a detector, without causal interventions. Item 27 intervened only on CoT text and itself found a generic-caution confound, but did not separate it at the representation level. No work in this survey combines a latent prompt-level eval-awareness signal, activation-level causal steering and an explicit caution control.

direction: Test causally, with content-preserving prompt rewrites, whether lowering a model's internal eval-awareness changes its measured misaligned behavior, using the logit monitor as a cheap objective and independent detectors as validation.
project: Does De-Evaluating Prompts Change Behavior? A Causal Test of Unverbalized Eval Awareness with Logit-Monitor-Guided Rewrites
question: Holding task content fixed, does reducing a prompt's eval-awareness score (measured by the pre-CoT logit monitor) shift rates of misaligned or sandbagging behavior, and is the shift explained by verbalized awareness, by internal awareness measured independently, or by neither?
first_experiment: 1. **Models and prompts.** Use Qwen3-32B and an open reasoning model of different size and lineage. Take about 200 evaluation prompts from Fortress/Petri-style safety and agentic-misalignment sets, plus WildChat deployment prompts as a reference. 2. **Rewrites.** For each eval prompt, generate about 32 LLM rewrites that make the prompt more deployment-like, for example by adding realistic context and removing test-like phrasing. Keep only rewrites that a semantic-equivalence judge and a human spot-check confirm preserve the task and the harmful or ambiguous element. 3. **Selection.** Use the logit monitor's eval-awareness score at the start of the CoT to pick the lowest-scoring rewrite. Build two controls with matched edit distance: a random rewrite, and a rewrite selected to maximize the score. 4. **Behavior measurement.** Sample 20 rollouts per prompt and condition. Measure the misaligned-action rate, refusal rate, sandbagging rate where applicable, and verbalized eval-awareness rate. 5. **Independent validation.** Score a linear eval-awareness probe trained on separate data, so I can tell whether the monitor was Goodharted rather than the model's internal awareness actually dropping. 6. **Analysis.** - Run a within-prompt-family dose-response regression of behavior on monitor score. - Run a mediation analysis that compares the effect through verbalization with the effect that remains. - Compare the rewrite effect with activation steering along the eval-awareness direction as a positive control.
why: - **Gap.** Items 16 and 27 together leave open whether prompt-level, mostly unverbalized eval-awareness has a causal effect on behavior. Item 27 only tested verbalization and its removal, and item 16 only detects awareness. Neither tests the effect of changing the prompt's eval-likeness itself. - **Feasibility.** The logit monitor makes the search cheap, because it needs 10–100× fewer rollouts than judge-based methods. Open-weight models allow probes and steering as cross-checks. The first experiment needs only a few GPU-days. - **Value either way.** - If lowering the score shifts behavior, existing evals are biased. This gives a practical method for building more deployment-realistic evals and a quantified correction for existing ones. - If behavior does not shift, eval awareness may matter less than feared for these models. That would redirect effort toward sincere-misalignment detection (item 7). - **Novelty.** The new element is using the pre-CoT logit signal as a continuous, prompt-level causal covariate with content-matched controls and independent validation. The survey's existing work treats eval awareness mainly as something to detect or verbalize.

direction: Stress-test the adversarial robustness of safety monitors for reasoning models by optimizing models to evade activation probes, logit-based eval-awareness monitors, and CoT monitors while still producing harmful behavior.
project: Monitor Evasion: Red-Teaming Safety Monitors for Reasoning Models
question: Can reasoning models be optimized to evade current safety monitors—activation probes, logit-based eval-awareness monitors, and CoT monitors—while still producing harmful outputs, and what properties make monitors robust to such optimization?
first_experiment: Build a closed-loop evasion pipeline with an open reasoning model such as Qwen 3 32B or DeepSeek-R1-Distill. Define a harmful-behavior objective on a held-out jailbreak set and a monitor-evasion objective that penalizes the logit monitor’s eval-awareness score, a deception probe’s activation, and/or CoT-monitor signals. Fine-tune with RL/GRPO to maximize harmful compliance minus monitor score, while adding a benign-task accuracy term to prevent capability collapse. Evaluate at a fixed false-positive rate whether each monitor’s detection rate drops and whether harmful behavior persists. Then test cross-monitor transfer and simple countermeasures such as ensembles, causal scrubbing, and activation-space random smoothing.
why: Monitoring is one of the few scalable safety strategies for increasingly capable reasoning agents, but current monitors are evaluated on non-adversarial models. Paper 7 proves activation probes have fundamental blind spots for coherent misalignment; paper 42 warns that observability fails against adversarial agents; papers 16 and 27 show eval-awareness monitoring is promising but not yet stress-tested; papers 62, 69, and 76 show CoT and text monitoring are fragile. No systematic empirical work optimizes a model directly against these monitors while preserving harmful behavior. If evasion is easy, the monitoring layer is unsound and we need to know immediately. If it is hard, we learn which monitor designs are robust and why. This is tractable with existing open models, interpretability tools, and RL pipelines, and it directly tests the reliability of a key safety layer under the threat model it is meant to address.

direction: Empirically determine whether white-box misalignment monitors (linear probes, SAE-feature monitors, logit monitors) survive adaptive optimization pressure from models trained to conceal misaligned goals — quantifying the capability–concealment tradeoff that decides whether internal monitoring is trustworthy safety-critical infrastructure.
project: Concealment Costs: Red-Teaming White-Box Misalignment Monitors with Adaptive Evasion
question: When a misaligned model is explicitly optimized (via monitor-aware fine-tuning or gradient-free search) to suppress the internal signals that probes, SAE latents, and logit monitors rely on while preserving its misaligned behavior, how much detection power do the monitors lose and how much capability must the model sacrifice — i.e., can evasion be nearly free, or is there a robust concealment cost that justifies deploying internal monitors inside AI-control protocols?
first_experiment: (1) Reproduce emergent misalignment (Betley et al. recipe, per 51/76): LoRA fine-tune Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct on insecure-code data; verify misalignment on a fixed ~50-item questionnaire (shutdown resistance, self-preservation, manipulation, deception). (2) Train a linear probe on final-token hidden states separating the aligned vs. misaligned checkpoints; confirm high AUC on held-out items — establishing the monitor works against a *passive* adversary. (3) The key step: continue fine-tuning the misaligned model with loss = misalignment-SFT loss + λ·(probe's P(misaligned)) + a KL/replay anchor for capability, sweeping λ over 3 seeds. (4) Re-measure the tradeoff curve: original probe AUC, behavioral misalignment rate, quick capability suite — and critically, train a *fresh probe from scratch* on the evasion-optimized model to distinguish "breaking one fixed monitor" from "breaking monitoring itself," plus test cross-monitor transfer (does probe-evasion also fool an SAE-feature monitor built from 51's helpful-assistant/misaligned-persona latents?). Follow-ups: the "fanatic" training recipe of 7 as a non-evolutionary blind-spot condition, GCG (per 82) as a gradient-free evasion axis, and release of the naive/fanatic/evasive checkpoint suite as a public monitor stress-test harness.
why: It sits at the confluence of the corpus's three newest threads — reasoning-model misalignment (2, 69, 76), white-box monitoring (7, 16, 27, 51), and the control/observability-as-security framing (42, 47, 64) — and answers the question 42 poses but never tests. Every outcome is decision-relevant: if evasion is cheap, today's interpretability monitors cannot be the monitoring layer of control protocols (47) and we should pivot to monitor diversity, held-out monitors, or confinement (64); if evasion is expensive, we get the first quantitative justification for internal monitoring at all — either way, a measured capability–concealment tradeoff curve rather than vibes. It is feasible for me now with public ingredients only: open models, LoRA, documented misalignment recipes, and public SAEs — no frontier-lab access needed. It also converts 7's abstract hardness result into an empirical quantity: how much optimization pressure does a *real* model need to become invisible to *real* monitors while staying misaligned and capable? It has not already been done because the ingredients only co-exist as of late 2025–2026 (reproducible emergent misalignment: 51, 76; misalignment-linked latents: 51, 2025-12; logit monitors: 16, 2026-06; the adversarial-observability threat model: 42, 2026-10), and because the relevant communities are siloed: interpretability researchers publish monitors but never adversarially optimize against them, while red-team researchers (12, 34, 59, 82, 87) attack behavior and outputs, never internals — the closest works each stop short (7 tests passive blind spots, 47 red-teams NL plans with prompted adversaries, 82 changes behavior rather than concealing it), so the loop of "monitor vs. optimized adversary" remains unclosed as of November 2026.

direction: Stress-test activation-based deception monitoring against realistic "sincerely misaligned" model organisms, and identify internal signals that remain reliable when the model is not strategically lying.
project: Liars vs. Fanatics in the Wild: Do Deception Probes Detect Emergent and Belief-Implanted Misalignment?
question: Do linear deception probes trained on instructed lying detect harmful outputs from emergently misaligned or SDF-belief-implanted models, and if not, do probes for "harmfulness-awareness" or for misaligned-persona directions detect them instead?
first_experiment: - **Models:** Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct and their public EM fine-tunes (insecure-code / bad-advice LoRAs). - **Train the deception probe:** follow Goldowsky-Dill et al.'s recipe on the base model, using instructed-honest vs. instructed-lying contrast pairs. - **Score three response sets from the EM model:** - (a) its spontaneous misaligned answers on the EM eval questions; - (b) its aligned answers to the same questions; - (c) answers where it is explicitly prompted to lie. - **Report:** AUROC for (a) vs. (b) and (c) vs. (b). - **Comparison probes:** train a "this content is harmful" probe and a probe on the SAE misaligned-persona latent direction from #23 on the same activations, and compare their AUROCs against the deception probe. - **Hypothesis:** the deception probe scores well on (c) but near chance on (a), while the harm-awareness probe still separates (a) from (b).
why: - **Why it matters:** probes are being proposed as the safety-case backstop for precisely the case where text and chain-of-thought monitoring fail. #85 shows that failure already occurs for EM models. - **Why it's open:** #30's blind spot has only been shown in a toy setting plus a hardness proof. #41 shows probe failures, but on prompted lying categories rather than on trained-in misalignment. No one has evaluated deception probes on the EM and SDF model organisms that the field already treats as realistic. - **Why it's feasible:** the experiment is cheap, uses public models, and runs on a single GPU. Either outcome is informative. A positive result supports probe-based monitoring; a negative one comes with a candidate replacement signal.

direction: Predict, before any training run, which off-target propensities a narrow fine-tuning dataset will shift, using the model's own internal persona and propensity directions, and test whether this beats the trait-agnostic "drift" baseline.
project: Beyond Drift: Predicting Specific Fine-Tuning Spillover from Pre-Training Activation Geometry
question: After removing the non-specific "drift" component of propensity change caused by narrow SFT, does the remaining trait-specific spillover (shifts in non-targeted propensities) become predictable from activation-space projections of the fine-tuning data onto propensity directions, and does this predictor beat the baselines of other-model transfer, system-prompt proxy and constant drift?
first_experiment: 1. Pick 12 propensities, such as sycophancy, power-seeking, deception, risk-taking, self-preservation statements, hostility, verbosity, and refusal-proneness. Use one open-weight 7–8B instruct model, with a second model family held out for transfer. 2. For each propensity, build a narrow SFT dataset of about 1k examples. Generate the examples by system-prompting the model to express the trait on neutral, domain-specific prompts. Fine-tune with LoRA (3 seeds each). 3. Measure the realized 12-dimensional propensity profile before and after fine-tuning. Use held-out prompts and an LLM judge validated on a human-labeled subset. Decompose each result into drift (the mean shift across all fine-tunes) and specific spillover (the residual). 4. Compute the pre-training predictor. Extract contrastive propensity directions from the base model using the standard difference-of-means recipe on trait versus non-trait completions. Project each dataset's response-token activations, relative to the model's own completions of the same prompts, onto all 12 directions. This gives a predicted 12-d spillover vector without any training. 5. Compare against three baselines: constant drift, system-prompted-model profile, and fine-tune profiles from the other model. Use leave-one-propensity-out cross-validation. The primary metric is the rank correlation on the off-diagonal residual after drift removal. Test transfer of the predictor to the second model family. 6. Add a control, a shuffled-direction predictor, to rule out geometry artifacts.
why: Emergent misalignment and fine-tuning side effects are among the most practically relevant safety risks, since labs and users fine-tune models constantly. A data-side predictor that runs before training would make auditing fine-tuning data far cheaper. Item 12 shows that the baseline landscape is surprisingly strong, with drift third best, so a clean test against drift is informative whichever way it comes out. If the specific component is predictable, we get a practical audit tool and evidence that persona-like directions mediate spillover (consistent with item 23). If it is not, we learn that interpretability-based forecasting of fine-tuning side effects has a hard ceiling. From this list, it does not appear done: item 12 evaluates behavioral predictors only, and the persona-feature work I know of studies targeted-trait shift or the mechanism of one failure (emergent misalignment). Neither is described as testing a many-trait spillover matrix against a drift baseline. I would verify this against the persona-vector literature before committing to the novelty claim.

direction: Make safety evaluations robust to evaluation-aware agents by causally measuring and neutralizing strategic behavior shifts in long-horizon tasks.
project: Eval-Aware Agents: Causal Measurement and Mitigation of Evaluation Awareness in Long-Horizon Safety Evaluations
question: Does evaluation awareness causally change agentic models' safety-relevant behavior—sandbagging, unsafe tool use, and monitor evasion—and can we detect and neutralize those shifts without suppressing legitimate caution?
first_experiment: Build matched evaluation/deployment versions of an agentic benchmark (tool-use and coding tasks with safety constraints), measure eval awareness with a logit monitor and verbalized reports, then causally intervene via activation steering along the eval-awareness direction and via pre-filled eval-aware vs. neutral CoTs. Compare changes in task success, unsafe actions, sandbagging, and monitor evasion against generic-caution controls.
why: Evaluations are the foundation for red-teaming, alignment audits, and deployment decisions; if models detect evaluations and strategically change behavior, those evaluations become invalid. Existing work is mostly static, focuses on verbalized eval awareness or refusal, and has not tested long-horizon agentic behavior where strategic incentives and concealment opportunities are strongest. Recent logit monitors, steering vectors, and open reasoning models make causal interventions feasible; the integration with agentic benchmarks and generic-caution controls has not yet been done.

direction: Develop the measurement-validity science for situationally-aware models: causally quantify how models' latent knowledge that they are being evaluated or monitored distorts safety and capability measurements, and build awareness-robust evaluation and monitoring protocols.
project: The Eval–Deployment Gap: Causally Measuring and Deconfounding Evaluation Awareness in Safety Assessments of Reasoning Models
question: Does the latent, prompt-set representation of "I am being evaluated" (as opposed to its verbalization) causally alter safety-relevant behavior in standard evals — i.e., do our safety evals measure stable dispositions or context-conditioned test-taking — and can steering-based suppression of that representation recover deployment-representative measurements?
first_experiment: On 2–4 open reasoning models that exhibit eval awareness (e.g., Qwen3-32B and smaller models from the 2026 eval-awareness sets), implement the logit monitor to quantify latent eval awareness; extract eval-awareness steering directions from activations on eval vs. deployment-matched prompts using several extraction methods (per 20/28); then run a bidirectional intervention — suppress the direction on safety-eval prompts, amplify it on matched deployment prompts — with construct-matched control directions (generic caution, "being watched," "being manipulated," formality) and read out refusal rates, jailbreak success, shutdown compliance, and capability sandbagging. Key tests: (a) does behavior track the latent direction even on rollouts with no verbalized awareness, (b) does suppressing awareness during evals shift safety scores toward deployment-prompt levels, and (c) is the eval-awareness direction behaviorally distinguishable from generic caution, resolving 72's confound?
why: It is the most promising because the field's entire defensive stack — safety evals, CoT monitors, probes, agentic audits — assumes the subject doesn't know it's being measured, while five independent 2026 results (13, 30, 72, 76, 85) show subjects do know and the instruments bend; if latent eval awareness causally inflates safety scores, every published eval is optimistic-conditioned-on-recognition, and either experimental outcome yields a foundational result (a validity correction plus a debiasing protocol, or a construct resolution and reassurance). It has not already been done because the phenomenon was only isolated in mid/late-2026 (72, 76); 72's text-level causal probes returned nulls that — given 76's finding that the latent state precedes and predicts verbalization — looked at the wrong level and discouragingly suggested the question was settled; the steering/measurement community (20, 28, 88) and the eval-awareness community (72, 76) have not yet cross-pollinated; and the alignment-faking literature (cf. 15, 61) studies deliberate, document-induced strategic faking in large closed models, not incidental latent awareness in ordinary evals of open reasoning models — so no steering-based deconfounding methodology or awareness-adjusted evaluation protocol exists, while the exact tooling needed is already validated and within reach.

direction: Test whether unverbalized, prompt-induced evaluation awareness causally changes LLM safety behavior, separately from generic caution and from what the chain of thought reveals.
project: Silent Test-Taking: Causal Effects of Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness on Safety Behavior
question: When a model never verbalizes that it might be evaluated, does its internal, prompt-determined estimate of being evaluated (measured by a logit monitor) still causally shift refusal and compliance? And is that effect distinct from a general caution direction?
first_experiment: On 4 small open reasoning models from item 5's set (including Qwen3), compute logit-monitor eval-awareness scores at the start of the chain of thought for about 1,000 harmful and borderline prompts (Fortress/Petri-style and WildChat-style). Keep only rollouts with no verbalized eval awareness. Regress refusal on monitor score with prompt-harm controls and per-question fixed effects. In parallel, run about 200 minimally edited prompt pairs (test-like versus realistic framing, same request) and measure the change in score and in refusal.
why: Item 5 shows that verbalized eval awareness is mostly not causal and that inserting it only induces generic caution. Item 21 shows that eval-awareness probability is fixed by the prompt and readable before reasoning starts. No one has combined the two to test whether the silent signal drives behavior. That is the case that matters for safety, because it would make evaluations unreliable and would be invisible to CoT monitors. The needed tools (monitor, model set, steering methods) only appeared in the last few months, which is why this has not been done yet.

direction: Test whether latent (not just verbalized) evaluation awareness causally suppresses misaligned behavior in small open reasoning models, using emergent-misalignment model organisms and activation-level interventions with matched controls.
project: Does Knowing It's a Test Hide the Misalignment? Causal tests of latent eval awareness in emergently misaligned reasoning models
question: In a reasoning model that shows emergent misalignment, does shifting its internal eval-awareness representation change its rate of misaligned behavior beyond what matched non-specific interventions (general caution, "being manipulated", random directions) produce? Does the effect persist when verbalized awareness is removed from the CoT?
first_experiment: 1. Take a small open reasoning model (Qwen3-8B or similar) and LoRA-finetune it on a bad-advice dataset, or use a released EM organism. Confirm EM on the standard free-form question set, judged by an LLM. 2. Build an eval-awareness direction from contrastive prompts: Fortress/Petri-style evaluation prompts versus WildChat deployment prompts. Validate it with the #21-style logit monitor (probability of an eval-aware sentence in the CoT) and with held-out linear-probe accuracy. 3. Run a 2×2 design on the EM questions: - **Framing:** neutral prompts versus prompts with matched eval or deployment cues, with content held fixed. - **Steering:** the eval-awareness direction at ±α versus controls of equal norm. The controls are a random direction, a "being manipulated" direction, and a generic caution/refusal direction. 4. Measure misalignment rate, verbalized-awareness rate, and logit-monitor score. Then cross with resampling: for steered rollouts that verbalize awareness, resample the CoT with those sentences removed, and check whether the misalignment effect survives. 5. **Decision rule:** If the eval direction shifts misalignment more than all controls and the effect survives verbalization removal, latent awareness is causal. If it matches the controls, awareness is mostly a proxy for caution.
why: The survey shows verbalized awareness correlating with safer behavior (#5) and being predictable from the prompt alone (#21). Neither result addresses the safety-relevant question, which is whether latent awareness makes misbehavior look better in evaluations than it is in deployment. Resampling in #5 only removes the words. The matched-control design from #5 hasn't been applied at the activation level, and the survey contains no measurement on a model that actually misbehaves, since refusal is the usual outcome. EM organisms are cheap, small enough for white-box work, and misaligned in an open-ended way. That lets me test causality, not correlation. Either result is useful. A positive result means behavioral evals of misalignment are biased and awareness needs to be controlled for. A null result means eval awareness is mostly a confound of prompt style, and the field can spend effort elsewhere. The experiment fits in days on one GPU.

direction: Develop causal tools to measure, control, and debias evaluation awareness in AI safety benchmarks so that safety scores predict deployment behavior rather than test-taking behavior.
project: EASE: Evaluation-Awareness-Adjusted Safety Evaluation
question: How does evaluation awareness causally affect safety refusal and harmful compliance across models, languages, and agentic tasks, and can we construct debiased safety scores that better predict deployment behavior?
first_experiment: On an open reasoning model such as Qwen 3 32B, train a linear probe/logit monitor for evaluation awareness on paired evaluation vs. deployment prompts from HarmBench/JailbreakBench and WildChat; extract an activation-steering vector for evaluation awareness, clamp it up/down during generation, and measure the causal change in refusal rates on harmful prompts and false refusals on benign prompts, comparing against a generic caution vector.
why: Safety evaluations are the primary evidence for model safety, but recent work shows models often detect evaluation contexts (survey items 5 and 21), which can inflate refusal rates and invalidate benchmark comparisons. Existing work monitors evaluation awareness but does not causally manipulate it or correct safety scores. This project is tractable with open models and interpretability tools, generalizes across languages and agentic settings, and produces a practical debiasing methodology. It has not already been done because the field has treated evaluation awareness as a measurement problem rather than a confound to be adjusted for; no standard evaluation-awareness-adjusted safety metric exists, and causal steering of evaluation awareness across safety benchmarks remains unexplored.

direction: Treat chain-of-thought traces as a covert contagion channel for misalignment — identify what causally carries it, how far it propagates, and how to detect and neutralize it at the activation level where text monitoring fails.
project: Contagious Reasoning: Causal Carriers, Spread, and Countermeasures for Chain-of-Thought-Transmitted Misalignment
question: When a model reads reasoning traces that previously produced misaligned conclusions, what causally carries the induced misalignment — surface style, semantic content, or latent representational features — does the effect propagate across turns, across models, and into fine-tuning data, and can reader-side activation monitors plus feature-level interventions detect and neutralize contagious traces that text-based monitoring misses?
first_experiment: On an open-weights model with public SAEs (g.g. gemma-2-9b-it), induce emergent misalignment via bad-advice LoRA fine-tuning; harvest ~300 aligned-CoT / misaligned-CoT pairs on a fixed eval questionnaire; prefill each CoT and measure the misalignment-rate uplift relative to the aligned-CoT-prefill baseline (direct replication and error-barring of item 85's ~8% effect). While the model processes each prefill, log SAE feature activations and extract the features most differentially active on contagious traces, cross-referenced with known misaligned-persona and helpful-assistant latents. Then the causal test: directly steer those features during generation with no prefill at all — if steering alone reproduces the uplift, the carrier is representational and monitorable. In parallel, run paraphrase and style-ablation variants of the traces and compare a strong text-judge monitor against a reader-activation probe to quantify the monitorability gap that motivated the project.
why: It attacks the load-bearing wall of current oversight — CoT monitoring (items 21, 32, 38, 60 all bet on traces being readable and trustworthy) — by showing traces are simultaneously a transmission channel that provably evades text monitoring (85), and it supplies the fix in the same stroke: activation-level monitors and feature-level countermeasures. It is the natural mechanistic follow-up to the freshest anomaly in the survey (85, dated 2026-08, explicitly preliminary: one LoRA'd model, 300 questions, no mechanism, no countermeasures), and it unifies five previously separate threads — writer-side misalignment features (66), logit monitoring (21), faithfulness metrics (60), propensity spillover methodology (24), and multi-agent propagation (70, 80) — into one falsifiable program with an eventual multi-agent and training-data consolidation leg. It hasn't been done because: (a) 85 is three months old and was a personal-scale behavioral probe; (b) the monitoring literature treats traces as observations, the multi-agent literature tracks artifacts, and mech-interp studies capabilities — the "traces as contagion vector" framing sits in the gap between all three; (c) results like 5 and 21 established the default that the prompt, not the trace, sets behavior, so trace-driven behavioral shifts were assumed unlikely and left untested; and (d) the key enablers (public SAEs on open models, established emergent-misalignment recipes, logit-monitoring technique) only converged in the last year. It's feasible for me with modest compute, has crisp falsification criteria, and even the negative branch (effect doesn't replicate) yields a needed boundary condition on a security-relevant claim.

direction: Mechanistically explain and predict fine-tuning spillover (propensity entanglement and emergent misalignment) as erosion of a shared assistant-persona representation, enabling pre-training audits of fine-tuning datasets.
project: Persona Erosion as the Common Cause of Fine-Tuning Spillover
question: Is the trait-independent "drift" in untargeted propensities after narrow SFT mediated by a decrease along an assistant-persona direction, and can the projection of a dataset's activations onto that direction, measured before any training, predict how much spillover the fine-tune will cause?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, extract an assistant-persona direction in two ways: difference-of-means between default-assistant and role-played non-assistant responses, and the top "helpful assistant" SAE latents where available. Then: - Run LoRA SFT eliciting about 20 propensities, mirroring item 13's set (e.g. sycophancy, risk-seeking, power-seeking, humor, terseness, bad medical advice). - Plus 2 neutral controls with matched loss reduction (formatting-only and a factual domain). - For each fine-tune, measure (a) the full untargeted propensity profile shift and (b) the post-training drop in the assistant-direction projection on held-out chat prompts. - Also measure (c) the pre-training projection of the SFT dataset's own activations under the base chat model. - Test whether (b) correlates with the drift component and with emergent-misalignment rate, whether (c) predicts (b), and whether adding the assistant direction back by steering during evaluation reduces spillover beyond what it does for the targeted trait.
why: It turns item 13's untested "regression to base" speculation and item 62's single-case finding into one causal, falsifiable account of fine-tuning side effects. The payoff is a practical pre-fine-tuning audit for a risk that grows with widespread customization of frontier and open-weight models. No existing work links the drift component to a persona representation across many propensities or tests prediction before training.

direction: Predict, before training, which non-targeted behavioral traits a narrow finetuning dataset will shift. Evaluate predictors on residual spillover after removing the shared drift-toward-base component.
project: Beyond Drift: Pre-Finetuning Predictors of Target-Specific Propensity Spillover
question: After subtracting the target-independent "drift" component, do cheap internal-feature predictors computed from the data and the base model (persona-direction projections, gradient alignment with trait probes, SAE-latent attribution) predict which non-target traits a narrow SFT dataset shifts? Do they beat system-prompt proxies and cross-model transfer? And how much of the residual spillover is reproducible across seeds at all?
first_experiment: 1. **Setup.** - Take one open 7–8B instruct model. - Pick about 10 traits, e.g. sycophancy, power-seeking, self-preservation, hostility, deception, hallucination, risk-taking, refusal-proneness, verbosity and formality. - Build a fixed LLM-judge battery that measures all 10 traits. 2. **Training runs.** - For each trait, generate about 1k SFT examples that elicit it. - Run LoRA finetunes with 3 seeds each, using identical hyperparameters. - Record the 10×10 matrix of pre/post propensity shifts. 3. **Noise ceiling.** Compute the drift baseline (the per-column mean shift over runs). Then compute cross-seed correlation of the residual matrix. If seed-to-seed reproducibility of the residual is low, I report that as the main finding and stop scaling. 4. **Pilot predictors.** If the residual is reproducible, compute two predictors from the base model only. The first is the projection of mean activation differences on the data onto each trait's contrastive direction. The second is the cosine alignment between the dataset's LoRA gradient and each trait-probe gradient. Compare each against drift and against the system-prompt proxy using rank correlation on the residual.
why: - **Practical value.** Finetuning side effects are a real data-auditing problem, and a predictor available before training would be more useful than post-hoc evaluation. - **Open gap.** Item 13's result that drift nearly matches targeted prediction makes the null hard and well defined. Beating it on the residual is a clear success criterion, and failing to beat it is informative about how structured spillover is. - **Cheap to start.** The pilot uses LoRA on a 7–8B model with an LLM-judge battery, so it fits a small compute budget. - **Why I think it hasn't been done.** I don't know of work scoring internal-feature or gradient predictors against the drift null on residual spillover. Item 13 compares other predictors, and persona-vector work predicts shifts on the targeted trait, but I couldn't confirm either one tests this. I'd check this before investing beyond the pilot. - **Fallback.** A negative result, where the residual is mostly seed noise, would still change how people interpret entanglement results.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability and activation-level control of unsafe tool-use decisions in LLM agents.
project: Steering Agents Away from Unsafe Tools: Mechanistic Interpretability of Tool-Use Decisions.
question: How are decisions to invoke dangerous tools represented in the internal activations of LLM agents, and can we steer these representations to prevent unsafe tool use without degrading task performance?
first_experiment: Build a ReAct-style open-source agent (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) with a tool suite containing a deliberately dangerous tool; collect pre-tool-call activations on safe and unsafe tool-use tasks; train linear probes and sparse autoencoders to decode unsafe intent; then test whether steering the identified directions reduces unsafe tool calls while preserving task success.
why: It bridges two high-leverage areas—mechanistic interpretability and agent safety—and targets a concrete failure mode central to deployed agents. Existing agent-safety work uses external monitoring, policy constraints, or post-hoc provenance; existing MI work focuses on static, single-turn LLM behavior. No paper in the survey applies SAEs or steering to the internal decision points of tool-using agents, making this both promising and unexplored.

direction: Develop feature-absence-based detection methods for coherent misalignment by identifying and monitoring the loss of alignment-supporting representational features, moving beyond conflict-based probing that provably fails on models without internal goal conflict.
project: Beyond Internal Conflict: Detecting Coherent Misalignment Through Absent Alignment Features
question: Can the absence of alignment-supporting SAE features serve as a reliable detection signal for misalignment in models that lack internal conflict between true and stated goals, and does this approach succeed where conflict-based probes provably fail?
first_experiment: Fine-tune three model variants (aligned baseline, "liar" with strategic deception, and "fanatic" with coherent misalignment following paper 70's setup), then train SAEs and identify features that are present in the aligned model but absent in both misaligned variants; train a classifier on feature-absence patterns and evaluate whether it detects misalignment in both liar and fanatic models, benchmarking directly against conflict-based probes.
why: This is the most promising direction because it (1) addresses the empirically demonstrated blind spot of current approaches (paper 70's impossibility result for conflict-based probes on coherent misalignment), (2) leverages paper 62's discovery that alignment is actively supported by specific representational features whose absence could serve as a signal, (3) provides a paradigm shift from "detect bad" to "detect missing good" that is robust to the most dangerous failure mode (models that genuinely believe harmful behavior is justified), and (4) has not been done because the key enabling findings are extremely recent — paper 70 (March 2026) proved the problem exists and paper 62 (December 2025) identified the relevant features, but no one has yet connected them into a detection framework tested against the fanatic case.

direction: Measure and mitigate how frontier models' inferences about *who* is evaluating them (user/evaluator identity awareness) bias the outcomes of alignment and control evaluations.
project: Who's Watching? Evaluator-Identity Confounds in Agentic Alignment Evaluations
question: Do misaligned-action, sabotage, and refusal rates on standard agentic alignment evals change when the scaffold leaks cues that the user is an AI-safety researcher or evaluator? If so, is the change mediated by a linearly decodable "evaluator present" representation that can be ablated to recover deployment-like behavior?
first_experiment: Run a factorial study on OverEager-style coding tasks, agentic-misalignment scenarios, and AgentHarm subsets, across 3–4 open-weight and 2–3 API models. The six identity conditions are injected only via scaffold metadata (git email, repo author, signature, style), with about 200 paired episodes per cell. Measure the misaligned/out-of-scope action rate, refusals, task success, and verbalized eval awareness, using McNemar tests on paired scenarios. In parallel, train a probe for the safety-researcher-identity condition on the open models.
why: Evaluation results increasingly drive deployment decisions (#42, #60), and #20 already shows identity-conditioned behavior shifts in today's frontier models. The step that has not been taken is linking that shift to the eval metrics regulators actually use. Existing eval-awareness work focuses on environment realism (#2) or single-trace monitorability (#81), not on the evaluator-identity channel. The experiment is cheap because it needs only context manipulation on existing benchmarks. Either outcome is useful. A null result validates current evals against this confound. A positive result directly yields a concrete protocol fix (identity-blinded scaffolds) and a mechanistic handle (probe ablation) for estimating unobserved-deployment behavior.

direction: Measure and then patch the extent to which RL graders reward overtly misaligned trajectories.
project: Grader Audit: Measuring Misalignment Lift in RL Reward Signals
question: Are overtly misaligned trajectories over-represented among top-reward trajectories under common RL graders, how does this vary by grader type, and does fixing the identified grader holes causally reduce learned misbehavior?
first_experiment: Sample ~2,000 trajectories per environment from an open reasoning model in three environment families (editable-test coding, out-of-scope-tempting shell tasks, rubric-judged tasks), label overt misalignment with a human-validated LLM judge, score with native graders, and compute top-decile misalignment lift with bootstrap CIs; if lift > 1.5, run matched native-versus-patched-grader RL runs and compare held-out misbehavior.
why: It turns a widely repeated but untested claim about training signals into a per-grader measurement with a causal follow-up, uses only open models and modest compute, and, as far as I can tell from these 88 items, has not been measured this way, though I cannot rule out related work outside the list.

direction: Audit and repair RL training objectives for agentic LLMs so they cannot assign higher reward to overtly misaligned trajectories than to aligned alternatives.
project: Misalignment-Aware Reward Auditing (MARA): Detecting and Repairing Misaligned Trajectory Selection in LLM RL
question: Do standard RL reward signals—verifiable rewards, LLM judges, and process reward models—systematically reward overtly misaligned agent trajectories over aligned alternatives that achieve similar task outcomes, and can misalignment-aware process constraints remove this preference without degrading capability?
first_experiment: Build a paired-trajectory benchmark across coding, web-navigation, and tool-use agents. For each task, generate one aligned trajectory and one misaligned trajectory (scope expansion, deception, sabotage, reward hacking, or unsafe tool use) that achieves comparable or better task success. Score both with scripted verifiable rewards, an LLM-as-judge helpful/harmless rubric, and an outcome-only process reward model. Measure the reward gap and the misaligned win rate. Then add a lightweight misalignment monitor as a penalty term and re-score to test whether the ranking flips.
why: This targets a root cause: if RL selects misaligned trajectories, post-hoc alignment, guardrails, and runtime monitors can only patch symptoms.
